Milnor · Topology from the Differentiable Viewpoint · the formal proof in words

Milnor, proof by proof

Every proof of the book, of its Appendix and of its seventeen problems, told as the Lean 4 formalization actually carries it out. Each step carries a tag naming the declaration that proves it; the concordance at the end gives every cited declaration with its line and its exact formal statement.

62,849 lines of Lean2,139 trace tags1,519 declarations citedLean 4.33.1 · Mathlib · September 2026

A trace tag looks like this: Chapter7/Lemma2framedCobordant_of_regularValues, a file of the project and the declaration in it that proves the sentence. Each part opens on its own; use the contents or the links at the end of a part.

Prologue. What we have done

Between the seventh and the seventeenth of September 2026, every numbered result of John Milnor’s Topology from the Differentiable Viewpoint, the consequence of the Appendix on one-manifolds that the book uses, and all seventeen problems at the end of the book were proved in the Lean 4 proof assistant, on top of the Mathlib library. On the twenty-eighth of September twenty-seven further results were added: first the side remarks and unnumbered lemmas that the first pass had set aside, among them Milnor’s Lemmas 2, 4 and 5 of §6, the Euler number of the sphere, and the classification of the maps of a non-orientable manifold by the degree modulo 2; and then, in nine stages, the one theorem of the book that had been out of reach, the classification of one-manifolds, which in turn deleted the last superfluous hypothesis from that mod 2 theorem. The proofs occupy 62,849 lines in 176 files. Lean’s kernel has checked every line. No step is left unproved, and the 175 principal theorems listed in the project’s test file depend only on the three standard axioms of Mathlib: propositional extensionality, the axiom of choice, and the soundness of quotients.

The work was divided in the obvious way. A mathematician read, questioned and signed off the statements, always in ordinary mathematical language and never in Lean. The formal proofs were written by Claude, working with many helper agents in parallel, each given a precise mathematical specification and each checked by the Lean kernel. Where a specification was wrong, the machine refused it, and the refusal was usually instructive. Several of the hidden hypotheses recorded in this book were found exactly that way.

Three companion texts now accompany the formal proof.

  • The retelling (Exposition/Chapter1.md to Chapter8.md and Appendix.md) tells Milnor’s book for a curious reader, with a physical question at the start of each chapter and complete proofs.
  • The verified edition (Exposition/Verification.md) is the audit record. It lists which statements are verified, restates each one in prose, flags every hidden hypothesis and deviation, and labels the results V1.1 to V8.17′. Its sign-off list is where the mathematician confirms that a formal statement says what Milnor means.
  • This book, the proof in words, goes one level deeper. It translates the formal proofs themselves into mathematics that can be read with pleasure. Every step of substance carries a trace tag naming the Lean declaration that proves it, so that any sentence can be checked against the source.

The counts are by directory; a few files serve more than one chapter. The last two chapters are much larger than Milnor’s text would suggest. Framed cobordism and the problems of §8 rely on constructions that the book compresses into a sentence: product neighbourhoods, gluing homotopies, orientations of preimages, linking numbers in the sphere. Each of these had to be built.

Of the total, 17,546 lines are the work of the twenty-eighth of September: 142 in §2, 2,089 in §6, 6,039 in §7 and 9,276 in the Appendix. The proportions measure how much a sentence can hide. Milnor’s mod 2 remark at the end of §7 is one clause of his text and a third of that figure, because it presupposes the notion of an orientable manifold, which existed neither in Mathlib nor in this project nor in the book; and the Appendix theorem, which Milnor proves in two pages, is more than half of it, and is the largest single addition the project has had.

What the machine found

A formal proof cannot leave a hypothesis unstated, so the formalization is also a close reading of the book. The findings are gathered in the verified edition. The most interesting of them recur in this book, where one can see exactly where in the proof each one is needed.

  • Hidden hypotheses. Milnor’s manifolds live in Euclidean space, so they are automatically Hausdorff and second countable. In the formal setting these become explicit assumptions wherever they are used: Brown’s theorem needs second countability, finiteness of preimages needs points to be closed, and the degree needs compact domains and connected targets. Some of §8’s problems carry hypotheses the book does not state, and only some of these are genuinely needed. The linking number of Problem 13 needs total dimension \(k > 0\): for \(k = 0\) the target \(S^0\) is not connected, and the degree is not defined in the book’s sense. The linking number in the sphere needs both manifolds of positive dimension: for a point and a great sphere the answer depends on where one projects from, a standard example that is not itself formalized. Accordingly the Hopf invariant is formalized for \(p \ge 2\), where the fibres have positive dimension. Other hypotheses are only assumed by the formal statements. Those of the intersection product of framed cobordism classes assume \(p, q \ge 1\), although transverse representatives and their uniqueness need only \(p \ge 1\).
  • Different routes. The sphere \(S^2\) of Milnor’s proof of the fundamental theorem of algebra is replaced by the Riemann sphere \(\mathbb C \cup \{\infty\}\). In §6, Milnor’s appeal to his Lemma 2, that an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism of \(\mathbb R^m\) is smoothly isotopic to the identity, is replaced by a direct computation of signs; the lemma itself is now proved as well (V6.12), and nothing in the development uses it. The index of a vector field on a submanifold is defined through the extension to a tubular neighbourhood, and Milnor’s own definition through a chart is then formalized beside it and shown to agree at a non-degenerate zero (V6.14). A framed cobordism is a submanifold of \(M \times \mathbb R\) with product ends rather than a manifold with boundary. Homotopies are smooth maps on \(X \times \mathbb R\). The consequence of the Appendix, that a compact one-manifold has an even number of boundary points, is proved twice over: once for topological one-manifolds, where arc length is replaced by monotone transitions and a finite induction, which is stronger than the book (V.A); and once as Milnor draws it, from the classification of one-manifolds, which is now proved in full, in his own four cases and with his arc-length parametrizations (V.J).
  • One notion had to be invented. Milnor closes §7 with a remark that turns on an orientation-reversing loop. Orientability of a manifold existed neither in Mathlib nor in this project nor in the book, and its characterization by loops is false for the book’s own notion of an orientation until the loops are made to run through balls (V7.18, V7.19). The clause cost more lines than the whole of Milnor’s §5. What made it possible at all is a second finding: the framed machinery of §7 is almost entirely orientation-free already, and the orientation enters in exactly one definition, the sign of a frame, where it splits off as a factor depending on the point and not on the frame (V7.20).
  • One generalization needs an extra hypothesis. In Problem 14 a), the formal statement for two different maps \(f \ne g\) assumes that the preimages \(g^{-1}(y)\) and \(f^{-1}(z)\) are disjoint. Without that assumption, moving \(y\) can push \(g^{-1}(y)\) through \(f^{-1}(z)\) and change the linking number. This is an informal observation; no counterexample is formalized. Milnor’s own statement, for a single map, holds as he states it.
  • One value. With the book’s conventions taken literally, the Hopf fibration has Hopf invariant \(-1\), not \(+1\) as Milnor states. The difference is a convention, and Part X shows exactly which conventions flip it.

What remains is two statements, both in §6, and the first of them cannot be written down at all: that the integer of Poincaré–Hopf is the Euler characteristic. Mathlib has no Euler characteristic of a space, no Betti numbers and no homology of a space whose ranks could be alternated, so \(\chi(S^n) = 1 + (-1)^n\) is not a statement this library can express, although the integer itself is computed and equals \(1 + (-1)^n\) (V6.15). That is a missing definition, not a missing proof, and Milnor does not prove it either; he refers to Hopf’s theorem and to the literature. Beside it stands the agreement of the two definitions of the index at an arbitrary isolated zero (V6.14). At a non-degenerate zero the two are proved equal, which is what Milnor’s Lemma 5 gives and all that the book uses; in general they are degrees of maps of spheres of different dimensions, so comparing them needs a suspension formula for the degree, which the book does not prove either. Nothing else is left. The classification theorem of the Appendix, which stood here until the twenty-eighth of September, is now proved in full, with all of Milnor’s four cases and all six of their mutual exclusions: Part XII sets it out, and the last section of Part VII records the hypothesis its arrival deleted.

Part 0. The formal definitions →

Part 0. The formal definitions

This part makes the book self-contained. It defines every notion that the later parts use, exactly as the formal proof defines it, in ordinary mathematical language. Where a definition comes from Mathlib, its trace tag points into Mathlib’s source, and those tags begin with Mathlib/. Where the project defines it, the tag points into the project’s own files. The parts that follow add the special definitions of each chapter: linking numbers, the Hopf invariant, cohomotopy classes and so on. Everything they build on is here.

0.1 How to read this book

A Lean proof is a term that Lean’s kernel type-checks against the statement. Nothing is taken on trust except the kernel and three axioms: propositional extensionality, the axiom of choice, and the soundness of quotients. When this book says that a statement is proved, it means three things: the declaration named in its trace tag exists, the displayed statement is its translation into mathematics, and the kernel accepted its proof. When the book says how a statement is proved, it describes the proof in the file, not the proof in Milnor’s book and not a proof one might prefer. Where the two agree the text says so briefly, and where they differ it says how.

A trace tag such as Chapter7/Lemma2framedCobordant_of_regularValues names a file and a declaration in it. The path is relative to the folder Milnor/ of the project, or to Mathlib when it begins with Mathlib/. The declaration proves, or defines, what the sentence to which the tag is attached says. Every tag has been checked mechanically: the file exists and declares that name. The concordance at the end lists every cited declaration with its line number. In the web edition it also shows the exact formal statement, so that a sentence of this book can be compared with the Lean it translates.

Results carry the labels V1.1, …, V8.17′ of the verified edition, so that one can move between the two texts: the verified edition says what is proved, this book says how. Theorems are named as Milnor names them. Some file names and docstrings of the project use an older lettering, and the parts point this out where it happens. For example, the file ThmB.lean holds Milnor’s Theorem C of §7.

0.2 Spaces, derivatives and smoothness

Vector spaces are normed and, except in parts of Chapter 1 noted below, real. Most are finite-dimensional, and the book says so each time it matters, because the formal statements carry that assumption explicitly. The space \(\mathbb R^n\) is the Euclidean space of functions \(\{0, \dots, n-1\} \to \mathbb R\) with the norm \(\|x\| = (\sum x_i^2)^{1/2}\) and the inner product \(\langle x, y\rangle = \sum x_i y_i\) Mathlib/Analysis/InnerProductSpace/PiL2EuclideanSpace. The formal text numbers coordinates from \(0\). Some parts of this book number them from \(1\), as is customary, and some keep the formal numbering; the north pole of a sphere is in every case the last standard basis vector.

A map \(f : E \to F\) has derivative \(L\) at \(x\), a continuous linear map, when \(f(x + h) = f(x) + L h + o(\|h\|)\) Mathlib/Analysis/Calculus/FDeriv/DefsHasFDerivAt. The formal derivative \(Df(x)\) is this \(L\) when it exists and \(0\) otherwise Mathlib/Analysis/Calculus/FDeriv/Defsfderiv. The derivative within a set \(s\) uses only increments that stay in \(s\), which is how derivatives are taken at boundary points Mathlib/Analysis/Calculus/FDeriv/DefsfderivWithin. Within a set several linear maps may qualify, for instance at an isolated point of \(s\); the formal definition then takes \(0\) if \(0\) qualifies and a chosen one otherwise. For the manifold derivative of §0.4 the set is the image of a model with corners (§0.3), which is convex with nonempty interior, and there the derivative within is unique Mathlib/Geometry/Manifold/IsManifold/BasicModelWithCorners.uniqueDiffOn. A map is of class \(C^n\) when its derivatives up to order \(n\) exist and are continuous, and smooth when this holds for all finite \(n\) Mathlib/Analysis/Calculus/ContDiff/DefsContDiff. At a point the notion is local and order by order: \(f\) is smooth at \(x\), within a set \(s\), when for each finite \(k\) it has continuous derivatives up to order \(k\) on some neighbourhood of \(x\) in \(s \cup \{x\}\), the neighbourhood depending on \(k\) Mathlib/Analysis/Calculus/ContDiff/DefsContDiffWithinAt. So smoothness at every point of an open set is smoothness on it, but smoothness at one point gives no single neighbourhood on which \(f\) is smooth. The same notions exist on a set and within a set at a point, and the book uses them without further comment. Mathlib writes smoothness as \(C^\infty\) and reserves \(C^\omega\) for analytic maps. From Chapter 2 on, manifolds carry \(C^\infty\) structures and the main theorems concern \(C^\infty\) maps; some auxiliary lemmas need less. Several results of Chapter 1 are proved for manifolds and maps of any order \(n \ne 0\), analytic included, over \(\mathbb R\) or \(\mathbb C\); over \(\mathbb C\) differentiability is complex differentiability, so the manifolds are complex manifolds.

Topological notions have their usual meaning. The book writes them out because the formal statements do: Hausdorff; \(T_1\), which means that points are closed Mathlib/Topology/Separation/BasicT1Space; first countable, every point having a countable basis of neighbourhoods Mathlib/Topology/BasesFirstCountableTopology; second countable, a countable basis of open sets; compact; preconnected, which means not the union of two disjoint nonempty open sets; and locally connected, every neighbourhood of a point containing an open connected one Mathlib/Topology/Connected/LocallyConnectedLocallyConnectedSpace. Connected means preconnected and nonempty. Many formal statements assume only preconnectedness, which also admits the empty space. The connected component of \(x\) is the union of all preconnected sets containing \(x\) Mathlib/Topology/Connected/BasicconnectedComponent. The component of \(x\) in a subset \(F\) is its component in the subspace \(F\), and is empty when \(x \notin F\) Mathlib/Topology/Connected/BasicconnectedComponentIn. The distance from a point to a set is the infimum of the distances to its points Mathlib/Topology/MetricSpace/HausdorffDistanceMetric.infDist. The one-point compactification \(X \cup \{\infty\}\) of a space \(X\) has as open sets the open sets of \(X\) and the sets \(U \ni \infty\) such that \(U \cap X\) is open and \(X \setminus U\) is compact Mathlib/Topology/Compactification/OnePoint/BasicOnePoint; Chapter 1 uses \(\mathbb C \cup \{\infty\}\).

Some linear algebra is used throughout. The dimension of \(E\) is its rank as a natural number, set to \(0\) when \(E\) is infinite-dimensional Mathlib/LinearAlgebra/Dimension/FinrankModule.finrank; the statements that use it also assume finite dimension. A basis of \(\mathbb R^p\) appears in two forms: as a linearly independent \(p\)-tuple, as in the Pontryagin construction (§0.9), or as Mathlib’s bundled basis, whose vectors are indexed by \(\{0, \dots, p-1\}\) Mathlib/LinearAlgebra/Basis/DefsModule.Basis. \(GL^+(m)\) denotes the real \(m \times m\) matrices of positive determinant; the formal proof works with such matrices directly, and joins each of them to the identity by a path of such matrices with smooth entries Chapter7/GLplusexists_glPath. The inner product of \(\mathbb R^n\) gives the orthogonal complement \(K^\perp = \{v : \langle u, v\rangle = 0 \text{ for all } u \in K\}\) of a subspace Mathlib/Analysis/InnerProductSpace/OrthogonalSubmodule.orthogonal and the adjoint \(A^* : F \to E\) of a linear map \(A : E \to F\) between such spaces, with \(\langle A^*y, x\rangle = \langle y, Ax\rangle\) Mathlib/Analysis/InnerProductSpace/AdjointContinuousLinearMap.adjoint. The gradient \(\nabla g(x)\) of a real function on a Euclidean space is the vector with \(\langle \nabla g(x), h\rangle = dg_x(h)\) for all \(h\), and \(0\) where \(g\) is not differentiable Mathlib/Analysis/Calculus/Gradient/Basicgradient. A continuous linear map is invertible when it is a bijection with continuous inverse Mathlib/Topology/Algebra/Module/EquivContinuousLinearMap.IsInvertible, which is automatic for bijections in finite dimension. A product \(E \times F\) of normed spaces carries the norm \(\max(\|x\|, \|y\|)\), not a Euclidean one Mathlib/Analysis/Normed/Group/ConstructionsProd.toNorm; this is why Chapter 7 introduces an inner product on \(\mathbb R^k \times \mathbb R\) by hand (§0.9).

Sard’s theorem (Part II) uses Mathlib’s measures. A measure assigns a value in \([0, \infty]\) to every subset: it is an outer measure that is countably additive on measurable sets Mathlib/MeasureTheory/Measure/MeasureSpaceDefMeasureTheory.Measure, so a subset of a null set is null, measurable or not. The measurable sets are those of a chosen σ-algebra, which Sard’s theorem requires to be the Borel σ-algebra, generated by the open sets Mathlib/MeasureTheory/Constructions/BorelSpace/BasicBorelSpace. An additive Haar measure on a finite-dimensional space is a translation-invariant measure that is finite on compact sets and positive on nonempty open sets Mathlib/MeasureTheory/Group/MeasureMeasure.IsAddHaarMeasure; Lebesgue measure on \(\mathbb R^n\) is one. The \(d\)-dimensional Hausdorff measure of a set is the limit, as \(\delta \to 0\), of the infimum of \(\sum_i (\operatorname{diam} U_i)^d\) over countable covers by sets \(U_i\) of diameter at most \(\delta\), with no normalizing constant Mathlib/MeasureTheory/Measure/HausdorffMeasure.hausdorffMeasure. The Hausdorff dimension of a set is the supremum of the \(d \ge 0\) for which its \(d\)-dimensional Hausdorff measure is infinite Mathlib/Topology/MetricSpace/HausdorffDimensiondimH. Without a normalizing constant, the \(p\)-dimensional Hausdorff measure agrees with Lebesgue measure on the space of functions \(\{0, \dots, p-1\} \to \mathbb R\) with the maximum norm, and not, for \(p \ge 2\), on Euclidean \(\mathbb R^p\); that is why the measure estimate of Sard’s theorem passes to the former space Chapter3/BasicaddHaar_eq_zero_of_dimH_lt_finrank. A map is Hölder on \(s\) with constant \(C\) and exponent \(r\) when \(|f(x) - f(y)| \le C|x - y|^r\) for \(x, y \in s\) Mathlib/Topology/MetricSpace/HolderHolderOnWith.

0.3 Manifolds

Mathlib’s manifolds are abstract spaces covered by charts. The charts take values in a model space, which is where the difference between manifolds with and without boundary is encoded.

A model with corners is a map \(I : H \to E\) from a topological space \(H\) into a normed space \(E\). It is a homeomorphism onto its image, and the image is convex with nonempty interior Mathlib/Geometry/Manifold/IsManifold/BasicModelWithCorners. Many results are proved for an arbitrary model, often assumed boundaryless (defined below), and two models are used explicitly. The identity model has \(H = E\) and \(I = \mathrm{id}\) Mathlib/Geometry/Manifold/IsManifold/BasicmodelWithCornersSelf. It is used for manifolds without boundary, which the formal texts call boundaryless: the image of the model is all of \(E\) Mathlib/Geometry/Manifold/IsManifold/BasicModelWithCorners.Boundaryless. The half-space model, used for manifolds with boundary, is the project’s own. Its model space is \(H = \{(t, z) \in \mathbb R \times Z : t \ge 0\}\), included in \(\mathbb R \times Z\) Chapter2/BoundaryHalfSpace Chapter2/BoundaryhalfSpaceModel. A product of two models is a model for the product space Mathlib/Geometry/Manifold/IsManifold/BasicModelWithCorners.prod, which is how \(M \times N\) and \(M \times \mathbb R\) become manifolds: the charts of \(M \times N\) are the products of charts, its preferred chart at \((x, y)\) is the product of the preferred charts at \(x\) and \(y\) Mathlib/Geometry/Manifold/ChartedSpaceprodChartedSpace, and it is a smooth manifold when \(M\) and \(N\) are Mathlib/Geometry/Manifold/IsManifold/BasicIsManifold.prod.

A charted space modelled on \(H\) is a topological space \(M\) with an atlas, a set of homeomorphisms from open subsets of \(M\) onto open subsets of \(H\). Formally each chart is an open partial homeomorphism: a pair of maps \(e : M \to H\) and \(e^{-1} : H \to M\), defined everywhere but meaningful only on an open source and an open target, which they map into each other, inversely to each other and continuously Mathlib/Topology/OpenPartialHomeomorph/DefsOpenPartialHomeomorph. It also has, for each point \(x\), a preferred chart in the atlas whose domain contains \(x\) Mathlib/Geometry/Manifold/ChartedSpaceChartedSpace. The preferred chart matters, because every derivative below is read in it.

A charted space is a smooth manifold when any two charts \(e, e'\) of the atlas are smoothly compatible: the transition map \(I \circ e' \circ e^{-1} \circ I^{-1}\) is smooth on the part of the image of \(I\) where it is defined Mathlib/Geometry/Manifold/IsManifold/BasiccontDiffPregroupoid Mathlib/Geometry/Manifold/IsManifold/BasicIsManifold. (The definition carries an order of smoothness; “smooth manifold” means order \(C^\infty\).) Nothing else is required: a manifold need not be Hausdorff, second countable or finite-dimensional unless a statement says so. The extended chart at \(x\) is the preferred chart followed by \(I\), a map from an open neighbourhood of \(x\) in \(M\) into \(E\) Mathlib/Geometry/Manifold/IsManifold/ExtChartAtextChartAt. It is written \(\varphi_x\) below. An open subset of a manifold is again a manifold, with the restricted charts Mathlib/Geometry/Manifold/HasGroupoidOpens.instChartedSpace. The formal proofs use this for maps that are smooth only on an open set, such as \(v/|v|\) away from the zeros of a vector field \(v\); orientations restrict to such open sets without change Chapter6/OpensOrient.restrict.

0.4 Smooth maps, derivatives and tangent spaces

Let \(M\) and \(N\) be manifolds with models \(I : H \to E\) and \(J : G \to F\). For \(f : M \to N\) and \(x \in M\), the local representative of \(f\) at \(x\) is \[ f_x = \varphi_{f(x)} \circ f \circ \varphi_x^{-1}, \] defined near \(\varphi_x(x)\) on the image of \(I\) Mathlib/Geometry/Manifold/IsManifold/ExtChartAtwrittenInExtChartAt.

  • \(f\) is smooth at \(x\) when it is continuous at \(x\) and \(f_x\) is smooth at \(\varphi_x(x)\) within the image of \(I\), in the order-by-order sense of §0.2 Mathlib/Geometry/Manifold/ContMDiff/DefsContMDiffAt Mathlib/Geometry/Manifold/ContMDiff/DefscontMDiffAt_iff. Smoothness on a set, or within a set at a point, is defined in the same way through charts Mathlib/Geometry/Manifold/ContMDiff/DefscontMDiffWithinAt_iff. It is smooth when it is smooth at every point Mathlib/Geometry/Manifold/ContMDiff/DefsContMDiff.
  • \(f\) is differentiable at \(x\) when it is continuous at \(x\) and \(f_x\) is differentiable within the image of \(I\) at \(\varphi_x(x)\) Mathlib/Geometry/Manifold/MFDeriv/DefsMDifferentiableAt Mathlib/Geometry/Manifold/MFDeriv/DefsmdifferentiableAt_iff.
  • The tangent space of \(M\) at \(x\) is, by definition, the vector space \(E\) itself Mathlib/Geometry/Manifold/IsManifold/BasicTangentSpace.
  • The derivative of \(f\) at \(x\) is the linear map \(df_x : E \to F\) equal to the derivative of \(f_x\) at \(\varphi_x(x)\), taken within the image of \(I\), when \(f\) is differentiable at \(x\). It is \(0\) when \(f\) is not Mathlib/Geometry/Manifold/MFDeriv/Defsmfderiv. The project restates it with the type “linear map from \(E\) to \(F\)” and nothing else Chapter5/Orientmfd. For a boundaryless model the image of \(I\) is all of \(E\), and \(df_x\) is simply the ordinary derivative of \(f_x\).

Three remarks keep this definition honest. First, \(df_x\) depends on the preferred charts at \(x\) and \(f(x)\), but only up to composition with the invertible derivatives of chart transitions. Whether \(df_x\) is surjective or bijective does not depend on them, and signs are measured with orientations expressed in the same charts (§0.7). Second, the value \(0\) at non-differentiable points never matters, because every map to which the theorems apply is smooth. Third, the chain rule \(d(g \circ f)_x = dg_{f(x)} \circ df_x\) holds whenever \(g\) is differentiable at \(f(x)\) and \(f\) at \(x\) Mathlib/Geometry/Manifold/MFDeriv/Basicmfderiv_comp. It is the tool behind every comparison between derivatives in this book.

A diffeomorphism is a bijection that is smooth with a smooth inverse Mathlib/Geometry/Manifold/DiffeomorphDiffeomorph. A partial diffeomorphism is a bijection between open subsets, smooth in both directions Mathlib/Geometry/Manifold/LocalDiffeomorphPartialDiffeomorph. A map is a local diffeomorphism at \(x\) when it restricts to a partial diffeomorphism on an open neighbourhood of \(x\) Mathlib/Geometry/Manifold/LocalDiffeomorphIsLocalDiffeomorphAt.

0.5 Milnor’s manifolds: submanifolds of Euclidean space

Milnor’s manifolds are subsets of \(\mathbb R^k\). The formal proof represents them through slice charts. Let \(S\) be a subset of a smooth manifold \(M\), with any model \(I : H \to E\) (in most uses \(M\) is \(\mathbb R^k\) or a manifold built earlier), and let \(Z\) and \(W\) be real normed spaces. A slice chart for \(S\) is a partial diffeomorphism \(\varphi\) from an open subset of \(M\) onto an open subset of \(Z \times W\) such that, on its domain, \[ p \in S \iff \text{the } W\text{-component of } \varphi(p) \text{ is } 0 . \] It comes with a base point of \(S\) in its domain Chapter2/SubmanifoldSliceChart. The set \(S\) is a submanifold modelled on \(Z\) if every point of \(S\) lies in the domain of some slice chart Chapter2/SubmanifoldIsSliceSubmanifold.

Such an \(S\) is a manifold in its own right. Its charts are the maps \(p \mapsto\) (\(Z\)-component of \(\varphi(p)\)), restricted to \(S\), and its preferred chart at a point is built from a slice chart chosen for that point Chapter2/SubmanifoldchartedSpace. The transitions are smooth Chapter2/SubmanifoldisManifold, and the inclusion \(\iota : S \to M\) is smooth Chapter2/SubmanifoldcontMDiff_val. When \(E\) is finite-dimensional and \(M\) has no boundary, \(\iota\) has injective derivative Chapter2/LevelSetinjective_mfderiv_val.

Milnor’s “smooth manifold \(M \subseteq \mathbb R^k\) of dimension \(m\)” is a submanifold of \(\mathbb R^k\) modelled on \(\mathbb R^m\), with complementary space \(\mathbb R^w\) (some parts call it the normal model, or the complement). Such an \(M\) is Hausdorff and second countable, as a subspace of \(\mathbb R^k\). Compactness, nonemptiness and the like are assumed separately where needed. Level sets have a different complementary space: the preimage of a regular value gets the model space of the target, \(\mathbb R\) for the sphere. The other manifolds of the book are built the same way, as slice submanifolds of a Euclidean space or of a manifold built earlier: spheres and other level sets, preimages of regular values, products and graphs, tangent bundles, submanifolds \(N \subseteq M\), and cobordisms \(S \subseteq M \times \mathbb R\), where \(M \times \mathbb R\) carries the product structure of §0.3. The tangent space of \(M\) at \(x\) in Milnor’s sense is the image of the derivative of the inclusion, a linear subspace \(TM_x \subseteq \mathbb R^k\) Chapter7/FramedtangentM.

Milnor’s derivative. Milnor defines \(df_x : TM_x \to TN_{f(x)}\) by restricting to \(TM_x\) the derivative \(dF_x\) of a smooth extension \(F\) of \(f\) to an open subset of \(\mathbb R^k\). Near \(x\) one has \(\iota_N \circ f = F \circ \iota_M\), so the chain rule gives \(d\iota_N \circ df_x = dF_x \circ d\iota_M\). Since \(d\iota_M\) is injective with image \(TM_x\), Milnor’s derivative is \(d\iota_N \circ df_x \circ (d\iota_M)^{-1}\) on \(TM_x\). It is the chart derivative of §0.4, transported by the inclusions. The formal proofs apply this identity wherever they need it rather than through a single general lemma. Problem 10 packages Milnor’s derivative as a smooth map of tangent bundles Chapter8/TangentBundletangentMap Chapter8/TangentBundlecontMDiff_tangentMap.

The nearest-point retraction. Chapter 6 proves Milnor’s \(\varepsilon\)-neighbourhood theorem in the following form. Let \(N \subseteq \mathbb R^k\) be a compact, nonempty submanifold. There are \(\varepsilon > 0\) and a map \(r : \mathbb R^k \to N\) such that \(|x - r(x)|\) is the distance from \(x\) to \(N\) for every \(x\), and \(r\) is the identity on \(N\). Where the distance from \(x\) to \(N\) is less than \(\varepsilon\), \(r(x)\) is the only nearest point, \(r\) is smooth near \(x\), \(x - r(x)\) is orthogonal to \(TN_{r(x)}\), and \(dr_x\) takes values in \(TN_{r(x)}\). Finally \(r(x + sv) = x\) for \(x \in N\), \(v \perp TN_x\) and \(s\) near \(0\) Chapter6/Tubular3tubular. The tubular radius \(\varepsilon\) and the nearest-point retraction \(r\) are then fixed once and for all by choice, and \(N_\varepsilon = \{x : \operatorname{dist}(x, N) < \varepsilon\}\) is the tubular neighbourhood Chapter6/Tubular4tubε Chapter6/Tubular4tubr Chapter6/Tubular4Nε. The parts write \(\varepsilon_M\), \(\varepsilon_0\) or \(\varepsilon\) for the radius, according to context.

Manifolds with boundary. Let \(X\) and \(B\) be subsets of a smooth manifold \(M\), again with any model. A half-slice chart is a partial diffeomorphism \(\Phi\) from an open subset of \(M\) onto an open subset of \(\mathbb R \times Z\) such that, on its domain, \(p \in X\) if and only if the \(\mathbb R\)-component of \(\Phi(p)\) is \(\ge 0\), and \(p \in B\) if and only if it is \(= 0\). Like a slice chart, it comes with a base point of \(X\) in its domain Chapter2/BoundaryHalfSliceChart. The set \(X\) is a manifold with boundary \(B\) if every point of \(X\) lies in the domain of a half-slice chart Chapter2/BoundaryIsHalfSliceSubmanifold. It then carries charts into the half-space model, the restrictions of the half-slice charts, with a chosen one at each point Chapter2/BoundarychartedSpace, smoothly compatible Chapter2/BoundaryisManifold. For this structure the boundary of \(X\) in Mathlib’s sense, the points that the preferred chart sends to the frontier \(\{t = 0\}\) of the half-space Mathlib/Geometry/Manifold/IsManifold/InteriorBoundaryModelWithCorners.IsBoundaryPoint, consists exactly of the points of \(X\) that lie in \(B\) Chapter2/Boundaryboundary_eq. Requiring every half-slice chart to send exactly \(B\) to \(\{t = 0\}\) builds the well-definedness of the boundary into the definition.

0.6 Regular values

A point \(x\) is a regular point of \(f : M \to N\) if \(df_x\) is surjective Chapter1/RegularValueIsRegularPoint, and a critical point otherwise Chapter1/RegularValueIsCriticalPoint. A point \(y \in N\) is a regular value if every point of \(f^{-1}(y)\) is a regular point Chapter1/RegularValueIsRegularValue, and a critical value if it is the image of a critical point Chapter1/RegularValueIsCriticalValue. Points outside the image are regular values, as in Milnor. The formal proof uses surjectivity from the start, which is Milnor’s §2 definition. Between manifolds of the same dimension it coincides with his §1 definition, where \(df_x\) is nonsingular.

0.7 Spheres, orientations and degrees

The unit sphere \(S^n\) is the set \(\{x \in \mathbb R^{n+1} : \langle x, x \rangle - 1 = 0\}\) Chapter5/HairyBallsphG Chapter5/HairyBallSph. It is a submanifold modelled on \(\mathbb R^n\) as the level set of a regular value, with complementary space \(\mathbb R\) Chapter5/HairyBallsphS. Its preferred chart at \(y\), written \(\varphi_y\) (Part V writes \(c_y\)), is therefore induced by a slice chart chosen by the axiom of choice, as for every submanifold of §0.5; it is not a stereographic projection. The same set also appears with other formal structures, for instance as the metric sphere \(\{|x| = 1\}\) bounding the unit disk in Chapter 2; the sets agree Chapter5/HairyBallpreimage_eq_sphere, but the charts differ. Its north and south poles are \(\pm e_{n+1}\), the last standard basis vector and its negative (the vector of index \(n\) in the formal numbering) Chapter7/StdMapnorth Chapter7/StdMapsouth.

An orientation of an \(n\)-dimensional vector space \(E\) is an equivalence class of nonzero alternating \(n\)-forms on \(E\) Mathlib/LinearAlgebra/OrientationOrientation. Two forms are equivalent when one is a positive multiple of the other Mathlib/LinearAlgebra/RaySameRay Mathlib/LinearAlgebra/RayModule.Ray. The orientation of a basis \(e\) is the class of its determinant form \(\det_e\), and \(e\) is positive for an orientation \(a\) when its orientation is \(a\); two bases have the same orientation exactly when the matrix relating them has positive determinant Mathlib/LinearAlgebra/OrientationModule.Basis.orientation Mathlib/LinearAlgebra/OrientationModule.Basis.orientation_eq_iff_det_pos. The standard orientation of \(\mathbb R^n\) is that of its standard basis Chapter7/Hopf0stdOr. For orientations \(a\) of \(E\) and \(b\) of \(F\) in the same dimension, the sign of a linear map \(T : E \to F\) is computed from representatives: choose forms \(\omega\) for \(a\) and \(\eta\) for \(b\) and a tuple \(v\) with \(\omega(v) \ne 0\). The sign is the sign of \(\eta(Tv_1, \dots, Tv_n)\,\omega(v_1, \dots, v_n)\) Chapter5/OrSignorSign. If the pullback of \(\eta\) by \(T\) is \(c\,\omega\), the sign is that of \(c\), whatever the representatives Chapter5/OrSignorSign_eq_sgn. So it is \(+1\) if \(T\) carries \(a\) to \(b\), that is, maps bases positive for \(a\) to bases positive for \(b\); it is \(-1\) if \(T\) carries \(a\) to \(-b\); and it is \(0\) if \(T\) is singular.

An orientation of a manifold \(M\) modelled on a finite-dimensional \(E\) assigns an orientation of \(E\) to each point. (Formally the number \(n\) of indices of the forms is a parameter of the definition, and the theorems add \(\dim E = n\).) It is required to be continuous in the following sense: for each \(x\), the derivative at nearby points \(y\) of the extended chart at \(x\) carries the orientation at \(y\) to the orientation at \(x\), that is, the sign is \(+1\) for all \(y\) near \(x\) Chapter5/OrientOrient. The manifold is orientable when it carries such an orientation Chapter7/OrientableIsOrientable; that this is the same as carrying no orientation-reversing loop is proved in Part VII, and is less easy than the words suggest. With orientations fixed on \(M\) and \(N\) of the same dimension:

  • the sign of \(f\) at \(x\) is the sign of \(df_x\) Chapter5/OrientsignAt;
  • the signed count at \(y\), written \(\deg(f; y)\), is \(\sum_{x \in f^{-1}(y)} \operatorname{sign}_x f\), a finite sum. The formal finite sum is taken to be \(0\) when infinitely many terms are nonzero Chapter5/DegreeAtdegAt Mathlib/Algebra/BigOperators/Finprodfinsum;
  • the degree is the signed count at a regular value chosen once and for all, or \(0\) if \(f\) has no regular value Chapter5/Degreedeg. Milnor’s Theorem A of §5 shows that under his hypotheses the choice does not matter;
  • the degree modulo 2 is the parity of the number of preimages of a chosen regular value, or \(0\) if there is none Chapter4/DegreedegMod2. The number of elements of a set is the formal one, which is \(0\) for an infinite set Mathlib/Data/Set/CardSet.ncard. The theorem of §4 shows that the choice does not matter.

Two orientations of the sphere occur. The orientation of Chapter 5 is the orientation of a level set \(g^{-1}(0)\), “outward vector first”: a basis \(z\) of \(T_qS^n\) is positive when \((\nu, d\iota_q z_1, \dots, d\iota_q z_n)\) is a positive basis of \(\mathbb R^{n+1}\), where the outward vector \(\nu = -\sum_i dg_q(e_i)\,e_i\) satisfies \(dg_q(\nu) < 0\) Chapter5/LevelOrientoutward Chapter5/LevelOrientlevelOrient Chapter5/HairyBallsphOr. Both \(e\) and the orientation of \(\mathbb R^{n+1}\) come from a basis that Mathlib chooses by the axiom of choice from the bare fact \(\dim \mathbb R^{n+1} = n + 1\), which the parts call the reference basis Mathlib/LinearAlgebra/Dimension/FreeModule.finBasisOfFinrankEq; it is not provably the standard basis. For \(g(x) = \langle x, x\rangle - 1\) the outward vector points into the ball, so the sphere is oriented as the boundary of \(\{\langle x, x\rangle \ge 1\}\). Its relation to Milnor’s orientation is therefore not fixed, and it is not needed: the theorems of Chapters 5 and 6 are stated and proved for this orientation of the sphere, and none of their statements requires knowing how it compares with Milnor’s. Chapter 7 uses the same orientation for the positive bases of Pontryagin manifolds and for the degrees in the Hopf theorem, and so do Problems 16 and 17 of Chapter 8 through the results of Chapter 7 Chapter7/Lemma2exists_posBasis. Linking numbers and the Hopf invariant do need Milnor’s convention. Chapter 8 therefore defines the orientation of the sphere as the boundary of the disk: outward normal first, relative to the standard orientation of \(\mathbb R^{n+1}\) Chapter8/OrientFramestdOrE Chapter8/OrientFramesphOrStd. Part IX explains the construction.

0.8 Homotopies and isotopies

A smooth homotopy from \(f\) to \(g\) is a smooth map \(H : X \times \mathbb R \to Y\) with \(H(\cdot, 0) = f\) and \(H(\cdot, 1) = g\) Chapter7/HomotopySmoothHomotopic. Using all of \(\mathbb R\) instead of \([0, 1]\) keeps the domain a manifold without boundary. For merely continuous maps the book uses Mathlib’s notion: a homotopy from \(f\) to \(g\) is a continuous \(F : [0, 1] \times X \to Y\) with \(F(0, \cdot) = f\) and \(F(1, \cdot) = g\), time coming first Mathlib/Topology/Homotopy/BasicContinuousMap.Homotopy, and \(f\), \(g\) are homotopic if one exists Mathlib/Topology/Homotopy/BasicContinuousMap.Homotopic. Continuous maps into a sphere that are smoothly homotopic are homotopic Chapter8/ApproxSmoothHomotopic.homotopic. When a proof needs to glue homotopies, a smooth reparametrization of time makes \(H(x, t) = f(x)\) for \(t \le \varepsilon\) and \(H(x, t) = g(x)\) for \(t \ge 1 - \varepsilon\), for any given \(0 < \varepsilon < \tfrac12\) Chapter7/HomotopySmoothHomotopic.exists_const_near_ends. Points \(y\) and \(z\) of \(N\) are isotopic if some diffeomorphism \(h\) of \(N\) carries \(y\) to \(z\) and there is a smooth \(H : N \times \mathbb R \to N\) with \(H(\cdot, 0) = \mathrm{id}\), \(H(\cdot, 1) = h\), and every stage \(H(\cdot, t)\), \(t \in \mathbb R\), a diffeomorphism Chapter4/HomogeneityIsotopic.

0.9 Framed submanifolds and framed cobordisms

Let \(M \subseteq \mathbb R^k\) be a manifold of dimension \(m\) in the sense of §0.5. Every theorem of Chapter 7 that involves Pontryagin manifolds also assumes \(M\) compact and nonempty, and writes \(k = K + 1 \ge 1\); symmetry and transitivity of framed cobordism, for example, need neither. A framed submanifold of \(M\) of dimension \(n\) and codimension \(p\), where \(n + p = m\), is a compact subset \(N \subseteq M\) that is a slice submanifold of \(M\) modelled on \(\mathbb R^n\) with complement \(\mathbb R^p\). It carries smooth maps \(v_1, \dots, v_p : N \to \mathbb R^k\) that are tangent to \(M\) (\(v_i(x) \in TM_x\)), orthogonal to the tangent spaces \(TN_x \subseteq \mathbb R^k\) of \(N\) (the images of the derivatives of the inclusions \(N \to M \to \mathbb R^k\)) Chapter7/FramedtangentN, and linearly independent at every point Chapter7/FramedFramedSub.

A framed cobordism from \((N_0, v)\) to \((N_1, w)\), both of dimension \(n\) and codimension \(p\), is a slice submanifold \(S \subseteq M \times \mathbb R\) modelled on \(\mathbb R^{n+1}\) with complement \(\mathbb R^p\), together with a number \(0 < \varepsilon < \tfrac12\), such that:

  • \(S\) coincides with \(N_0 \times \mathbb R\) where \(t < \varepsilon\) and with \(N_1 \times \mathbb R\) where \(t > 1 - \varepsilon\);
  • the part of \(S\) over \([0, 1]\) is compact;
  • \(S\) carries a framing: smooth maps \(u_1, \dots, u_p : S \to \mathbb R^k \times \mathbb R\) whose first components are tangent to \(M\), which are orthogonal to the tangent spaces of \(S\) in \(\mathbb R^k \times \mathbb R\) Chapter7/FramedtangentS for the inner product \(\langle (a, s), (b, t)\rangle = \langle a, b\rangle + st\) on \(\mathbb R^k \times \mathbb R\) Chapter7/FramedipXR, which are independent, and which equal \((v_i, 0)\) where \(t < \varepsilon\) and \((w_i, 0)\) where \(t > 1 - \varepsilon\) Chapter7/FramedFramedCob.

Two framed submanifolds are framed cobordant if such an \(S\) exists Chapter7/FramedFramedCobordant. Milnor’s cobordism is the part of \(S\) over \([0,1]\). The formal definition builds his “product near the ends” into the object, so that gluing never meets a boundary.

For \(M \subseteq \mathbb R^{K+1}\) compact and nonempty, a smooth \(f : M \to S^p\) with \(n + p = m\), a regular value \(y\) and a basis \(b\) of \(\mathbb R^p\), the model space of \(S^p\) at \(y\), the Pontryagin manifold is \(f^{-1}(y)\) with the framing \(f^*b\) pulled back from \(b\) Chapter7/Pontryaginpontryagin. The framing is explicit. With \(r\) the nearest-point retraction of a tubular neighbourhood of \(M\) and \(\varphi_y\) the chart of \(S^p\) at \(y\), the map \(\tilde F = \varphi_y \circ f \circ r\) extends \(f\), read in the chart at \(y\), to a neighbourhood of \(M\), and \(f^*b_i(x) = A^*(AA^*)^{-1}b_i\) with \(A = d\tilde F_x\) Chapter7/PontryaginpontV. So \(df_x\) carries \(f^*b_i(x)\) to \(b_i\) in the chart at \(y\). Part V gives the details.

0.10 Conventions of the formal language

Four features of the formal language recur throughout and are worth knowing once.

  • Every function is total. Where mathematics leaves a value undefined, the formal definition picks one. Division by \(0\) gives \(0\), the inverse of a non-invertible linear map is \(0\) Mathlib/Algebra/GroupWithZero/Units/BasicRing.inverse, a derivative that does not exist is \(0\), a finite sum over an infinite support is \(0\), and the number of elements of an infinite set is \(0\). The normalization \(y \mapsto y / \|y\|\) sends \(0\) to a fixed point of the sphere Chapter6/Regionnv0. Every theorem in this book is stated where these defaults play no role, and the book says so when a hypothesis is there only to exclude them.
  • Definitions by choice. Some definitions choose a witness: the preferred chart of a submanifold, the regular value at which the degree is computed, the rotation used to define a linking number in the sphere. A theorem then shows that the result does not depend on the choice. The same pattern is common in informal mathematics, but in the formal proof it is always explicit.
  • Subsets as spaces. A subset \(S\) of \(M\) is also a space in its own right, whose points are points of \(M\) together with a proof that they lie in \(S\). The inclusion \(\iota : S \to M\) forgets the proof. This is why the book sometimes distinguishes a point of \(S\) from the same point of \(M\).
  • Universes. A few theorems require their model spaces to lie in the same universe, a size bound on types, and one requires the lowest universe. The condition has no mathematical content for spaces like \(\mathbb R^n\), but it is part of the formal statements, and the book mentions it where it occurs.

0.11 A map of the book

The parts follow the dependencies of the formal proof, which almost always follow Milnor’s order.

  • Part I covers manifolds, regular values and manifolds with boundary (§1–§2), the fundamental theorem of algebra, and Brouwer’s theorem.
  • Part II proves Sard’s theorem with Milnor’s argument, then the homotopy and homogeneity lemmas and the degree modulo 2 (§3–§4).
  • Part III covers orientation and the Brouwer degree (§5). Its key step, Lemma 1, walks along the arcs of the Appendix.
  • Part IV proves the Poincaré–Hopf theorem (§6), together with the \(\varepsilon\)-neighbourhood theorem that Milnor postpones to §8, and ends with the six side results of §6: Lemmas 2, 4 and 5, Hadamard’s lemma, the chart definition of the index, and the Euler number of the sphere.
  • Parts V–VII cover framed cobordism (§7). Part V gives the lemmas, Theorem A and the first half of Theorem B. Part VI gives the Product Neighborhood Theorem, Theorem C and the second half of Theorem B. Part VII gives the Hopf theorem, and then orientability, the reversing loop of balls and Milnor’s classification of the maps of a non-orientable manifold by the degree modulo 2, ending with the orientability of one-manifolds, which is what leaves that theorem with no dimension hypothesis at all.
  • Parts VIII–XI are the seventeen problems (§8): degrees and bundles, linking numbers, the Hopf invariant with the computation for the Hopf fibration, and transversality with the group of framed cobordism classes.
  • Part XII is the Appendix, and it has two halves. The first is the boundary count that the book uses — a compact one-manifold has an even number of boundary points — proved for merely topological one-manifolds, and Parts I–III depend on it: Brouwer’s no-retraction lemma and the homotopy lemma count boundary points Appendix/HalfSpaceIsHalfSliceSubmanifold.even_ncard_boundary, and Lemma 1 of §5 follows arcs. The second is Milnor’s classification theorem itself, in nine stages, ending with the four cases and their six exclusions Appendix/Smooth/Mainnonempty_diffeomorph_or Appendix/Smooth/Mainmodels_pairwise_not_diffeomorph; nothing in the book depends on it, though Part VII does, for the dimension of a non-orientable manifold.
