Part I. Manifolds, regular values and the first theorems (Milnor §1–§2)

Milnor’s first two sections build the machinery the book runs on (derivatives, regular values, the inverse function theorem, the finiteness and local constancy of the number of preimages of a regular value) and draw two dividends from it: the fundamental theorem of algebra and Brouwer’s fixed point theorem. The formal proofs follow Milnor’s closely, but Mathlib’s manifolds are abstract spaces with atlases, not subsets of \(\mathbb R^k\), and this creates work the book never needed. Hausdorffness becomes a hypothesis. Every subset that Milnor calls a manifold (a level set, a sphere, a disk, a region \(\{g \ge 0\}\)) must be given an atlas; this Part does it once and for all with slice charts, shaped after the diffeomorphisms of Milnor’s own proofs. Steps the book cites or calls easy are proved in full. The largest departure from the book is that the fundamental theorem of algebra is proved on \(\mathbb C \cup \{\infty\}\) rather than on \(S^2\); smaller ones are flagged where they occur.

Map.

  • Chapter1/InverseFunction: the inverse function theorem between manifolds, from the Euclidean one.
  • Chapter1/RegularValue: regular values; finiteness and local constancy of the fibre count, with two strengthenings.
  • Chapter1/Counting: a connected set of regular values that meets the image lies in the image.
  • Chapter1/RiemannSphere: \(\mathbb C \cup \{\infty\}\) as a smooth surface with the charts \(z\) and \(1/z\).
  • Chapter1/FTA: the fundamental theorem of algebra.
  • Chapter2/Submanifold: slice charts and the manifold structure they induce on a subset.
  • Chapter2/LevelSet: Lemmas 1 and 2, level sets of regular values and their tangent spaces.
  • Chapter2/Normal: the second clause of Lemma 2, the normal isomorphism.
  • Chapter2/Boundary: the half-space model and half-slice charts (manifolds with boundary inside a manifold).
  • Chapter2/WithBoundary: Lemmas 3 and 4.
  • Chapter2/Disk: the closed ball, with boundary the sphere.
  • Chapter2/Corestrict: maps with values in a slice submanifold.
  • Chapter2/Retraction: the retraction formula of Lemma 6, verified.
  • Chapter2/Brouwer: the smooth fixed point theorem (Lemmas 5 and 6 for the disk) and Brouwer’s theorem.

Conventions: abstract manifolds and derivatives read in charts

A Mathlib manifold is a space \(M\) with an atlas of charts onto open subsets of a model space \(H\), together with a model with corners \(I : H \to E\) embedding \(H\) in a normed space \(E\). The image of \(I\) is all of \(E\) for a boundaryless model and a half-space for a manifold with boundary; \(M\) is \(C^n\) when the transition maps, read in \(E\), are \(C^n\). At each \(x\) the atlas designates a preferred chart, which composed with \(I\) is the extended chart \(\varphi_x\), a partially defined map \(M \to E\).

Derivatives are read in these charts. For \(f : M \to N\), with \(\psi\) the extended chart of \(N\) at \(f(x)\), the derivative \(df_x : E \to F\) is the derivative of \(\psi \circ f \circ \varphi_x^{-1}\) at \(\varphi_x(x)\), taken within the image of \(I\). Thus \(T_xM\) is the model space \(E\), and \(df_x\) is a linear map between model spaces. To compare \(df_x\) with \(f\) written in other charts, the proofs use a small lemma: on a manifold without boundary, the derivative of an extended chart at any point of its domain is invertible, by the chain rule applied to \(\varphi^{-1} \circ \varphi = \mathrm{id}\) and \(\varphi \circ \varphi^{-1} = \mathrm{id}\) Chapter2/LevelSetisInvertible_mfderiv_extChartAt.

A partial diffeomorphism is a \(C^n\) diffeomorphism between open subsets of \(M\) and \(N\), and \(f\) is a local diffeomorphism at \(x\) if it agrees with one on a domain containing \(x\). Both notions are Mathlib’s; the project adds restriction to an open subset of the domain Chapter2/SubmanifoldPartialDiffeomorph.restrOpen.

Two more conventions matter. Mathlib’s “\(C^\infty\) at \(x\)” means \(C^k\) on some neighbourhood for each \(k\), the neighbourhood depending on \(k\); it does not provide a neighbourhood on which the map is \(C^\infty\), so theorems that need one assume smoothness at every point of a neighbourhood Chapter1/InverseFunctionisLocalDiffeomorphAt_of_isInvertible_mfderiv. And abstract manifolds need not be Hausdorff or second countable; the statements below list these hypotheses where Milnor uses them silently.

V1.1 The inverse function theorem on manifolds

Milnor cites the Euclidean inverse function theorem and applies it between manifolds without comment. Mathlib listed the manifold version as an open item; the project proves it, more generally than the book needs.

Theorem (V1.1). Let \(\mathbb K\) be \(\mathbb R\) or \(\mathbb C\) and \(1 \le n \le \omega\) (\(n\) finite, \(\infty\), or \(\omega\) for analytic). Let \(M\), \(N\) be \(C^n\) manifolds without boundary modelled on normed \(\mathbb K\)-spaces \(E\), \(F\), with \(E\) complete. If \(f : M \to N\) is \(C^n\) at every point of a neighbourhood of \(x\) and \(df_x : E \to F\) is invertible as a continuous linear map, then \(f\) is a \(C^n\) local diffeomorphism at \(x\). Chapter1/InverseFunctionisLocalDiffeomorphAt_of_isInvertible_mfderiv

For \(f\) globally \(C^n\) the neighbourhood hypothesis is automatic, and for finite \(n\) or \(n = \omega\) being \(C^n\) at \(x\) suffices Chapter1/InverseFunctionContMDiff.isLocalDiffeomorphAt_of_isInvertible_mfderiv Chapter1/InverseFunctionContMDiffAt.isLocalDiffeomorphAt_of_isInvertible_mfderiv.

The idea. Read \(f\) in charts and apply the Euclidean theorem. Its local inverse is known to be \(C^n\) only at the base point, so one first shrinks to a neighbourhood on which the derivative stays invertible, then carries everything back through the charts.

The proof as formalized.

  1. Let \(\varphi\), \(\psi\) be the extended charts at \(x\) and \(f(x)\), and \(g = \psi \circ f \circ \varphi^{-1}\). As the model of \(M\) is boundaryless, \(\varphi\) carries neighbourhoods of \(x\) to neighbourhoods of \(\varphi(x)\); so \(g\) is \(C^n\) at every point near \(\varphi(x)\) Chapter1/InverseFunctioneventually_contDiffAt_writtenInExtChartAt, and \(Dg(\varphi(x)) = df_x\) Chapter1/InverseFunctionhasFDerivAt_writtenInExtChartAt.
  2. \(Dg\) is continuous at \(\varphi(x)\) and the isomorphisms form an open set, so \(Dg(u)\) is invertible for all \(u\) near \(\varphi(x)\) Chapter1/InverseFunctioneventually_isInvertible_fderiv.
  3. The Euclidean theorem gives a partial homeomorphism \(\Phi\) of \(E\) into \(F\), defined near \(\varphi(x)\), whose forward map is \(g\).
  4. Let \(T\) be the interior of the set of points of the domain of \(\varphi\) at which \(f\) is \(C^n\) and lands in the domain of \(\psi\); \(x \in T\). Choose an open \(V \ni \varphi(x)\) on which \(g\) is \(C^n\) with invertible derivative, contained in the domain of \(\Phi\) and in the image of \(\varphi\), with \(\varphi^{-1}(V) \subseteq T\).
  5. The partial diffeomorphism is \(f\) from \(U = \varphi^{-1}(V)\) onto \(U' = \psi^{-1}(\Phi(V))\) (open, since \(\Phi\) is a partial homeomorphism), with inverse \(\varphi^{-1} \circ \Phi^{-1} \circ \psi\); the inverse identities follow from \(\psi \circ f = \Phi \circ \varphi\) on \(U\). The map \(f\) is \(C^n\) on \(U \subseteq T\). The inverse is \(C^n\) as a composite, because \(\Phi^{-1}\) is \(C^n\) at each \(\Phi(u)\), \(u \in V\): the inverse of a partial homeomorphism is \(C^n\) at the image of any point where the map is \(C^n\) with invertible derivative. Step 2 makes this available at every point of \(V\), not only at \(\varphi(x)\). Chapter1/InverseFunctionisLocalDiffeomorphAt_of_isInvertible_mfderiv

A subtlety of the formal definitions, not of the book. For \(n = \infty\) the neighbourhood hypothesis cannot be weakened to smoothness at \(x\): a map that is \(C^\infty\) at \(x\) in Mathlib’s sense need not be \(C^\infty\) on any neighbourhood of \(x\), and then it agrees near \(x\) with no \(C^\infty\) diffeomorphism. Milnor’s maps are smooth everywhere, so for the book nothing is lost.

V1.2 Regular points and regular values

Milnor defines regular points by invertibility of \(df_x\) in §1 (equal dimensions) and by surjectivity in §2. The formal text uses the §2 definition throughout.

Definition (V1.2). A point \(x\) is a regular point of \(f\) if \(df_x\) is surjective, a critical point otherwise; \(y\) is a regular value if every point of \(f^{-1}(y)\) is regular, a critical value if it is the image of a critical point. Chapter1/RegularValueIsRegularPoint Chapter1/RegularValueIsRegularValue Chapter1/RegularValueIsCriticalValue

Each \(y\) is exactly one of the two Chapter1/RegularValueisRegularValue_iff_not_isCriticalValue, and points outside \(f(M)\) are regular values Chapter1/RegularValueIsRegularValue.of_notMem_range. For \(E\), \(F\) finite-dimensional of equal dimension, rank–nullity makes surjectivity equivalent to invertibility Chapter1/RegularValueIsRegularPoint.isInvertible_mfderiv Chapter1/RegularValueIsRegularPoint.of_isInvertible_mfderiv. This recovers the §1 notion and brings V1.1 to bear: a \(C^n\) map (\(n \ge 1\)) between manifolds without boundary of equal finite dimension is a local diffeomorphism at each regular point Chapter1/RegularValueIsRegularPoint.isLocalDiffeomorphAt.

V1.3 A regular fibre is finite

Theorem (V1.3). Let \(\mathbb K \in \{\mathbb R, \mathbb C\}\), \(1 \le n \le \omega\), and let \(M\), \(N\) be \(C^n\) manifolds without boundary modelled on finite-dimensional \(\mathbb K\)-spaces of equal dimension, with \(M\) compact and the points of \(N\) closed. If \(f : M \to N\) is \(C^n\) and \(y\) is a regular value, then \(f^{-1}(y)\) is finite. Chapter1/RegularValueIsRegularValue.finite_preimage

The idea. The fibre is compact, and by the inverse function theorem each of its points has a neighbourhood containing no other point of it.

The proof as formalized. The fibre is closed, since points of \(N\) are, and hence compact. Each of its points \(x\) has an open neighbourhood \(U_x\), the domain of the local diffeomorphism of V1.2, on which \(f\) is injective Chapter1/RegularValueIsRegularPoint.isLocalDiffeomorphAt. Finitely many \(U_{x_1}, \dots, U_{x_k}\) cover the fibre, and a point \(z\) of the fibre lying in \(U_{x_i}\) has \(f(z) = f(x_i)\), hence \(z = x_i\). So the fibre lies in \(\{x_1, \dots, x_k\}\). Milnor’s appeal to compactness and discreteness becomes a direct subcover argument. Hidden hypothesis: points of \(N\) are closed.

V1.4 The count is locally constant

Theorem (V1.4). In the setting of V1.3, assume also that \(M\) and \(N\) are Hausdorff. Then \(\#f^{-1}(y') = \#f^{-1}(y)\) for all \(y'\) in a neighbourhood of \(y\). Chapter1/RegularValueIsRegularValue.eventually_ncard_preimage_eq

The idea. Near each of the finitely many preimages of \(y\), \(f\) has a local inverse. For \(y'\) close to \(y\), the preimages of \(y'\) are exactly the images of \(y'\) under these local inverses.

The proof as formalized is Milnor’s, with every set named.

  1. Let \(x_1, \dots, x_k\) be the points of \(f^{-1}(y)\), and \(L_i\) the local inverse of \(f\) at \(x_i\): a diffeomorphism from an open neighbourhood of \(y\) onto one of \(x_i\), with \(L_i(y) = x_i\) and \(f \circ L_i = \mathrm{id}\).
  2. \(M\) being Hausdorff, take pairwise disjoint open sets \(W_i \ni x_i\). Put \(U_i = W_i \cap (\text{image of } L_i)\) and \(V_i = L_i^{-1}(U_i)\), an open set (it is \(f(U_i)\)).
  3. \(C = f(M \setminus \bigcup_i U_i)\) is compact, hence closed as \(N\) is Hausdorff, and \(y \notin C\). Put \(V = \bigcap_i V_i \setminus C\).
  4. For \(y' \in V\), the map \(x_i \mapsto L_i(y')\) is a bijection \(f^{-1}(y) \to f^{-1}(y')\): it lands in the fibre as \(f \circ L_i = \mathrm{id}\); it is injective as the \(W_i\) are disjoint; it is onto because a preimage \(b\) of \(y'\) lies in some \(U_i\) (else \(y' \in C\)), so \(b = L_i(f(b)) = L_i(y')\). Chapter1/RegularValueIsRegularValue.eventually_ncard_preimage_eq

Deviation (stronger). Milnor lets \(y'\) range over regular values only; the formal statement covers all \(y'\) near \(y\). The same construction gives the two forms that later chapters use. All \(y'\) near \(y\) are regular values, since their preimages lie where \(f\) is a local diffeomorphism Chapter1/RegularValueIsRegularValue.eventually_isRegularValue_and_ncard (Chapter 4). And for \(w : M \to \mathbb Z\) locally constant near each \(x_i\), the weighted count \(\sum_{x \in f^{-1}(y')} w(x)\) is constant near \(y\): shrink each \(U_i\) to where \(w\) is constant Chapter1/RegularValueIsRegularValue.eventually_finsum_preimage_eq (the signed counts of Chapter 5).

V1.5 The counting principle

Theorem (V1.5). Let \(\mathbb K\), \(n\), \(M\), \(N\), \(f\) be as in V1.3, with \(M\) compact and \(M\), \(N\) Hausdorff. (a) If \(R \subseteq N\) is a connected set of regular values containing a point of \(f(M)\), then \(R \subseteq f(M)\). (b) If the set of all regular values is connected and meets \(f(M)\), then \(f\) is onto. Chapter1/Countingsubset_range_of_isPreconnected Chapter1/Countingsurjective_of_isPreconnected_regularValues

The formal hypothesis is preconnectedness, which for a nonempty set is connectedness. The theorem isolates the end of Milnor’s proof of the fundamental theorem of algebra, which uses nothing about polynomials.

The idea. A locally constant function on a connected set is constant, and here it is positive at one point.

The proof as formalized. By V1.4, \(y \mapsto \#f^{-1}(y)\) is locally constant on \(R\), hence continuous into the discrete space \(\mathbb N\), hence constant on \(R\) Chapter1/Countingncard_preimage_eq_of_isPreconnected. At the given \(y_0 \in R \cap f(M)\) the fibre is finite Chapter1/RegularValueIsRegularValue.finite_preimage and nonempty, so every count on \(R\) is positive. For (b), critical values lie in \(f(M)\) by definition. That \(R\) meets the image is Milnor’s remark that the count cannot vanish identically; in the fundamental theorem it has to be earned.

V1.6 The fundamental theorem of algebra

Theorem (V1.6). Every complex polynomial \(P\) of positive degree has a root: \(P(z) = 0\) for some \(z \in \mathbb C\). Chapter1/FTAfundamental_theorem_of_algebra

The idea is Milnor’s. Extend \(P\) to a smooth self-map \(f\) of a compact surface. It has finitely many critical values, so a connected set of regular values remains, on which the count is constant and somewhere nonzero. So \(f\) is onto, and \(0\) has a preimage.

The Riemann sphere in place of \(S^2\)

Where the formal proof departs from Milnor. Instead of \(S^2 \subset \mathbb R^3\) with stereographic projection, the formal proof uses the one-point compactification \(\hat{\mathbb C} = \mathbb C \cup \{\infty\}\), compact and Hausdorff by general topology, with two charts: \(z \mapsto z\) on \(\hat{\mathbb C} \setminus \{\infty\}\) and \(p \mapsto 1/p\) on \(\hat{\mathbb C} \setminus \{0\}\) Chapter1/RiemannSpherechart₀ Chapter1/RiemannSpherechartInf. The second is the first composed with the inversion exchanging \(0\) and \(\infty\) Chapter1/RiemannSphereinvert, a homeomorphism because \(1/z \to 0\) as \(z \to \infty\) and \(1/z \to \infty\) as \(z \to 0\) Chapter1/RiemannSpherecontinuous_invert. The preferred chart is \(1/p\) at \(\infty\) and \(z\) elsewhere Chapter1/RiemannSphereinstChartedSpace. The transition maps are the identity and \(z \mapsto 1/z\) on \(\mathbb C \setminus \{0\}\), so \(\hat{\mathbb C}\), modelled on \(\mathbb C\) as a real vector space, is a smooth real surface without boundary Chapter1/RiemannSphereinstIsManifold. Stereographic projection extends to a diffeomorphism \(S^2 \cong \hat{\mathbb C}\), so the two surfaces are the same manifold; this identification is not formalized and not needed, since the theorem concerns \(P\) alone. The gain is that the chart \(1/p\) reads \(f\) with the original coefficients, without the complex conjugates of Milnor’s formula.

The polynomial as a smooth self-map

Write \(P(z) = \sum_{k=0}^n c_k z^k\) with \(n = \deg P \ge 1\) and \(c_n \ne 0\), and let \[\tilde P(w) = w^n P(1/w) = \sum_{k=0}^n c_{n-k} w^k\] be the reversed polynomial, so \(\tilde P(0) = c_n \ne 0\). Put \(f(z) = P(z)\) on \(\mathbb C\) and \(f(\infty) = \infty\) Chapter1/FTApolyMap; \(f\) is continuous at \(\infty\) because \(|P(z)| \to \infty\) as \(|z| \to \infty\) Chapter1/FTAcontinuousAt_polyMap_infty. In the chart \(z\) at both ends, \(f\) is \(P\), which is \(C^\infty\) over \(\mathbb R\) Chapter1/FTAcontDiff_eval Chapter1/FTAcontMDiffAt_polyMap_coe. Near \(\infty\), in the chart \(1/p\) at both ends, everything rests on the identity \[P(1/w) = \tilde P(w)\, w^{-n} \qquad (w \ne 0)\] Chapter1/FTAeval_inv_eq. On the open set \(\{\tilde P \ne 0\}\), which contains \(0\), the chart expression of \(f\) therefore equals \(Q(w) = w^n / \tilde P(w)\): at \(w = 0\) both vanish since \(n \ge 1\), and for \(w \ne 0\) the identity gives \(P(1/w) \ne 0\) and \(1/P(1/w) = Q(w)\). \(Q\) is complex-smooth at \(0\), hence real-smooth, and \(f\) is smooth everywhere Chapter1/FTAcontMDiffAt_polyMap_infty Chapter1/FTAcontMDiff_polyMap.

Finitely many bad values, a connected complement

At \(z \in \mathbb C\) the derivative \(df_z\) is multiplication by \(P'(z)\), as a real-linear map of \(\mathbb C\) Chapter1/FTAhasMFDerivAt_polyMap_coe, and it is onto when \(P'(z) \ne 0\) Chapter1/FTAisRegularPoint_polyMap_coe. Let \[K = \{\infty\} \cup P(\{z : P'(z) = 0\}).\] \(K\) is finite, \(P'\) being a nonzero polynomial Chapter1/FTAfinite_zeros_derivative Chapter1/FTAcritVals_finite. It lies in the image of \(f\) Chapter1/FTAcritVals_subset_range, and every \(y \notin K\) is a regular value, its preimages being points \(z \in \mathbb C\) with \(P'(z) \ne 0\) Chapter1/FTAisRegularValue_of_notMem_critVals.

A choice the formal proof makes. Milnor observes that \(P\) fails to be a local diffeomorphism only at the zeros of \(P'\), and concludes that \(f\) has finitely many critical points without discussing the north pole, which is in fact critical when \(n \ge 2\) (the chart expression \(Q\) above has vanishing derivative at \(0\)). The formal proof never decides whether \(\infty\) is critical. It puts \(\infty\) into \(K\) Chapter1/FTAcritVals and applies the counting principle to the connected set \(\hat{\mathbb C} \setminus K\) of regular values rather than to the set of all regular values, which is why V1.5(a) allows an arbitrary connected \(R\).

The set \(\hat{\mathbb C} \setminus K\) is the image of \(\mathbb C \setminus P(\{P' = 0\})\) under the inclusion Chapter1/FTAcompl_critVals_eq. The complement of a countable set in a real vector space of dimension at least two is path-connected (a Mathlib theorem), so its image \(\hat{\mathbb C} \setminus K\) is connected; the formal statement records preconnectedness, the form V1.5 uses Chapter1/FTAisPreconnected_compl_critVals.

What the book leaves implicit. The count must be nonzero somewhere on \(\hat{\mathbb C} \setminus K\). Each fibre \(\{P = c\}\) is finite, as the zero set of the nonzero polynomial \(P - c\) Chapter1/FTAfinite_fiber, so \(P(\mathbb C)\) is infinite Chapter1/FTAinfinite_range_eval and contains a value outside the finite set \(P(\{P' = 0\})\). That value is a regular value in the image Chapter1/FTAexists_regularValue_mem_range.

Conclusion

By V1.5(a) with \(M = N = \hat{\mathbb C}\) and \(R = \hat{\mathbb C} \setminus K\) Chapter1/Countingsubset_range_of_isPreconnected, and since \(K\) lies in the image, \(f\) is onto. A preimage of \(0\) is not \(\infty\), as \(f(\infty) = \infty\); so it is some \(z \in \mathbb C\) with \(P(z) = 0\) Chapter1/FTAexists_root.

V2.1 Slice submanifolds: how a subset becomes a manifold

Milnor’s proof of Lemma 1 produces a diffeomorphism from a neighbourhood of a point of \(f^{-1}(y)\) onto an open set, carrying \(f^{-1}(y)\) to a coordinate hyperplane, and concludes that \(f^{-1}(y)\) is a manifold; for subsets of \(\mathbb R^k\) this is immediate from the definition. Mathlib has no notion of an embedded submanifold of an abstract manifold, so the project defines one, and it takes exactly what Milnor’s proof produces: a subset covered by straightening diffeomorphisms Chapter2/SubmanifoldIsSliceSubmanifold. One construction turns such a family into an atlas, so every later “is a manifold” (level sets, spheres, the level set in Brouwer’s theorem) reduces to exhibiting straightening diffeomorphisms. Nothing is lost mathematically, since a manifold in Milnor’s sense admits such charts in \(\mathbb R^k\) by the inverse function theorem; but that general fact is not formalized, and in this Part the charts are always constructed explicitly.

Definition (V2.1). Let \(M\) be a smooth manifold modelled on a real normed space (boundary allowed), let \(Z\), \(W\) be real normed spaces, and \(S \subseteq M\). A slice chart for \(S\) is a smooth diffeomorphism \(\varphi\) from an open set \(U \subseteq M\) onto an open subset of \(Z \times W\), with a base point \(x_0 \in S \cap U\), such that for all \(p \in U\) \[p \in S \iff \varphi(p) \in Z \times \{0\}.\] \(S\) is a slice submanifold (modelled on \(Z\), with normal model \(W\)) if every point of \(S\) lies in the domain of a slice chart. Chapter2/SubmanifoldSliceChart Chapter2/SubmanifoldIsSliceSubmanifold

The base point is a formal device: the inverse chart must be a map defined everywhere, and \(x_0\) is its value off the chart’s image Chapter2/SubmanifoldinvChart.

Theorem (V2.1). A slice submanifold \(S\), with the subspace topology and the atlas of charts induced by all its slice charts, is a smooth manifold without boundary modelled on \(Z\), and the inclusion \(S \to M\) is smooth. Chapter2/SubmanifoldchartedSpace Chapter2/SubmanifoldisManifold Chapter2/SubmanifoldcontMDiff_val

The idea. Forget the normal coordinate: a slice chart restricted to \(S\) and followed by the projection to \(Z\) is a chart of \(S\), and two such charts differ by a smooth map.

The proof as formalized. A slice chart \(\varphi\) induces the chart \(p \mapsto \mathrm{pr}_Z\,\varphi(p)\) on \(S \cap U\), with open image \(\{z : (z, 0) \in \varphi(U)\}\) and inverse \(z \mapsto \varphi^{-1}(z, 0)\), which lies in \(S\) by the slice condition Chapter2/Submanifoldsymm_mem. For \(p \in S \cap U\) one has \(\varphi(p) = (\mathrm{pr}_Z\,\varphi(p), 0)\); this shows that the chart lands in its image and that \(\varphi^{-1}(\mathrm{pr}_Z\,\varphi(p), 0) = p\), while the other inverse identity is \(\varphi(\varphi^{-1}(z, 0)) = (z, 0)\) Chapter2/Submanifoldmk_zero_mem_target Chapter2/SubmanifoldtoChart. The preferred chart at \(p\) comes from a slice chart chosen around \(p\). Transition maps are \(z \mapsto \mathrm{pr}_Z\,\varphi_2(\varphi_1^{-1}(z, 0))\), composites of smooth maps Chapter2/SubmanifoldcontDiffOn_trans, and in charts the inclusion is \(z \mapsto \varphi_M(\varphi^{-1}(z, 0))\) for a chart \(\varphi_M\) of \(M\).

Two features matter later. The atlas consists of the charts induced by all slice charts of \(S\), not only the chosen ones Chapter2/Submanifoldmem_atlas_iff, so any slice chart may be used to compute in \(S\); within this Part, Lemma 2 (V2.3) and corestriction (V2.8) need only the chart chosen at the point in question Chapter2/LevelSetinjective_mfderiv_val Chapter2/CorestrictextChartAt_eq. And the dimension of \(S\) is that of \(Z\): Milnor’s dimension count \(m - n\) becomes a hypothesis on \(Z\), such as \(\dim Z + \dim F = \dim E\).

V2.2 Lemma 1: the level set of a regular value

Theorem (V2.2, Lemma 1). Let \(M\), \(N\) be smooth manifolds without boundary modelled on finite-dimensional real spaces \(E\), \(F\); let \(Z\) be a finite-dimensional real space with \(\dim Z + \dim F = \dim E\); let \(f : M \to N\) be smooth and \(y\) a regular value. Then \(f^{-1}(y)\) is a slice submanifold of \(M\) modelled on \(Z\) with normal model \(F\), hence a manifold of dimension \(\dim M - \dim N\). More precisely, each \(x \in f^{-1}(y)\) lies in the domain of a slice chart whose second component is \(p \mapsto \psi(f(p)) - \psi(y)\), where \(\psi\) is the extended chart of \(N\) at \(y\). Chapter2/LevelSetisSliceSubmanifold_preimage Chapter2/LevelSetexists_sliceChart_preimage

Lemma 3 uses the refined form.

The idea is Milnor’s: complete \(f\) by a linear map \(L\) that is nonsingular on the kernel of the derivative, invert \((L, f)\) locally, and see the level set as a coordinate slice. Reading \(N\) through \(\psi\) turns Milnor’s map \(\xi \mapsto (f(\xi), L(\xi)) \in N \times \mathbb R^{m-n}\) into a map to the vector space \(Z \times F\).

The proof as formalized.

  1. With \(\varphi\) the extended chart at \(x\), let \(\tilde f = \psi \circ f \circ \varphi^{-1}\), smooth where defined, and \(D = D\tilde f(\varphi(x))\).
  2. \(D = d\psi \circ df_x \circ d(\varphi^{-1})\) is onto: \(d\psi\) is invertible and \(d(\varphi^{-1})\) is onto Chapter2/LevelSetisInvertible_mfderiv_extChartAt Chapter2/LevelSetsurjective_mfderiv_extChartAt_symm, and \(df_x\) is onto because \(y\) is regular.
  3. By rank–nullity \(\mathcal N = \ker D\) has dimension \(\dim E - \dim F = \dim Z\). Choose an isomorphism \(j : \mathcal N \to Z\) and a complement of \(\mathcal N\), and let \(L = j \circ \mathrm{pr}\), with \(\mathrm{pr}\) the projection onto \(\mathcal N\) along the complement: Milnor’s map nonsingular on the null space.
  4. \((L, D) : E \to Z \times F\) is injective (if \(Dv = 0\) then \(v \in \mathcal N\) and \(Lv = j(v)\)), hence an isomorphism by dimension count.
  5. \(\Phi(p) = \big(L(\varphi(p)),\ \psi(f(p)) - \psi(y)\big)\) is smooth on the open set \(U_1\) of points in the domain of \(\varphi\) that \(f\) sends into the domain of \(\psi\), and \(d\Phi_x = (L, D) \circ d\varphi_x\) is invertible.
  6. By V1.1, \(\Phi\) agrees with a partial diffeomorphism on a domain containing \(x\) Chapter1/InverseFunctionisLocalDiffeomorphAt_of_isInvertible_mfderiv; restrict it to \(U_1\) Chapter2/SubmanifoldPartialDiffeomorph.restrOpen.
  7. On that domain, \(p \in f^{-1}(y)\) iff \(\psi(f(p)) = \psi(y)\) iff the second component of \(\Phi(p)\) vanishes. The first equivalence uses that \(\psi\) is injective on its domain, which contains \(f(p)\) and \(y\); this is why the domain was cut down to \(U_1\). Chapter2/LevelSetexists_sliceChart_preimage

V2.3 Lemma 2: the tangent space of a level set

Theorem (V2.3, Lemma 2). In the setting of V2.2, give \(f^{-1}(y)\) the structure of V2.1 and let \(\iota : f^{-1}(y) \to M\) be the inclusion. For \(p \in f^{-1}(y)\) and \(v \in E = T_pM\), \[v \in \operatorname{im}(d\iota_p) \iff df_p(v) = 0.\] Chapter2/LevelSetmem_range_mfderiv_val_iff

The statement is elementwise because the two tangent spaces are different model spaces, \(Z\) and \(E\).

The idea. The tangent space of the level set lies in \(\ker df_p\) because \(f\) is constant on the level set, and both have dimension \(\dim Z\).

The proof as formalized is Milnor’s. Since \(f \circ \iota\) is constant, \(df_p \circ d\iota_p = 0\) Chapter2/LevelSetmfderiv_comp_val_eq_zero. For any slice submanifold, \(d\iota_p\) is injective: if \(\varphi\) is the slice chart chosen at \(p\), then \(\mathrm{pr}_Z \circ \varphi \circ \iota\) is the preferred chart at \(p\), whose derivative there is the identity Chapter2/LevelSetinjective_mfderiv_val. So \(\operatorname{im} d\iota_p \subseteq \ker df_p\), and both have dimension \(\dim Z\), the second because \(df_p\) is onto; they are equal.

V2.12 The second clause of Lemma 2: the normal isomorphism

Milnor’s Lemma 2 has a second sentence, which follows “therefore” from the first: the derivative carries the orthogonal complement of the tangent space of the level set isomorphically onto the tangent space of the target. Write \(T = \operatorname{im}(d\iota_p)\) for the tangent space of the level set as a subspace of the model space \(E\), which is what the equivalence above describes Chapter2/NormaltangentSubspace Chapter2/Normalmem_tangentSubspace_iff.

Theorem (V2.12). In the setting of V2.2, \(df_p\) is injective on \(T^\perp\) and carries it onto \(F = T_yN\), so it restricts to a linear isomorphism \(T^\perp \to F\), whose underlying map is \(df_p\) itself. Chapter2/Normalmfderiv_injOn_tangent_orthogonal Chapter2/Normalmfderiv_surjOn_tangent_orthogonal Chapter2/NormalnormalEquiv

The proof as formalized is the dimension count Milnor leaves to the reader. By V2.3, \(T\) is the kernel of \(df_p\), of dimension \(\dim E - \dim F\) because \(y\) is regular, so \(T^\perp\) has dimension \(\dim F\) Chapter2/Normalfinrank_tangentSubspace_orthogonal. Injectivity on \(T^\perp\) is V2.3 together with \(T \cap T^\perp = 0\), and an injective map between spaces of the same finite dimension is onto.

One hypothesis is added that Milnor would not state. The orthogonal complement needs an inner product on the model space \(E\) of the source, where V2.2 and V2.3 ask for a norm only; Milnor has it for nothing, his manifolds being subsets of \(\mathbb R^k\). The target needs none, and \(M\), \(N\) and the boundaryless model are otherwise as general as in V2.3.

V2.4 Manifolds with boundary: the half-space model and half-slice charts

Mathlib represents manifolds with boundary through a model with corners whose image is not the whole vector space. The formal text builds one and repeats the slice construction with half-spaces.

Definitions (V2.4). For a real normed space \(Z\) the half-space is \(H(Z) = \{(t, z) \in \mathbb R \times Z : t \ge 0\}\), Milnor’s \(H^m\) with the distinguished coordinate first Chapter2/BoundaryHalfSpace. The model is the inclusion into \(\mathbb R \times Z\), with formal inverse \((t, z) \mapsto (\max(t, 0), z)\) Chapter2/BoundaryhalfSpaceModel; its image has interior \(\{t > 0\}\) and frontier \(\{t = 0\}\) Chapter2/Boundaryinterior_range_halfSpaceModel Chapter2/Boundaryfrontier_range_halfSpaceModel. Let \(M\) be a smooth manifold modelled on a real normed space and \(X, B \subseteq M\). A half-slice chart for \(X\) with boundary \(B\) is a smooth diffeomorphism \(\Phi\) from an open \(U \subseteq M\) onto an open subset of \(\mathbb R \times Z\), with a base point in \(X \cap U\), such that for all \(p \in U\), with \(\Phi_1\) the \(\mathbb R\)-component, \[p \in X \iff \Phi_1(p) \ge 0, \qquad p \in B \iff \Phi_1(p) = 0.\] \(X\) is a half-slice submanifold over \(Z\) with boundary \(B\) if every point of \(X\) lies in the domain of such a chart. Chapter2/BoundaryHalfSliceChart Chapter2/BoundaryIsHalfSliceSubmanifold

Theorem (V2.4). Such an \(X\), with the subspace topology and the charts induced by all its half-slice charts, is a smooth manifold with boundary modelled on \(H(Z)\); its boundary in Mathlib’s sense is \(X \cap B\); and the inclusion \(X \to M\) is smooth. Chapter2/BoundaryisManifold Chapter2/Boundaryboundary_eq Chapter2/BoundarycontMDiff_val

The idea is that of V2.1, with half-spaces in place of slices; the boundary comes out right because the charts are required to respect it.

The proof as formalized. The induced chart is \(p \mapsto \Phi(p) \in H(Z)\) with inverse \(h \mapsto \Phi^{-1}(h)\) Chapter2/BoundarytoChart, and transition maps are restrictions to the half-space of maps smooth on open subsets of \(\mathbb R \times Z\) Chapter2/BoundarycontDiffOn_trans. Mathlib calls a point a boundary point when its preferred extended chart sends it into the frontier \(\{t = 0\}\) of the model’s image; by the second condition this happens exactly on \(B\) Chapter2/Boundaryboundary_eq.

Where the formal proof departs from Milnor. Milnor remarks that \(\partial X\) is well defined, which needs an argument that diffeomorphisms between open subsets of \(H^m\) preserve boundary points. The formal definition sidesteps it: \(B\) is prescribed, and every chart must send exactly \(B\) to \(\{t = 0\}\) Chapter2/BoundaryHalfSliceChart. The manifolds with boundary built in the book (Lemmas 3 and 4) come with such charts.

V2.5 Lemma 3: the region \(\{g \ge 0\}\)

Theorem (V2.5, Lemma 3). Let \(M\) be a smooth manifold without boundary modelled on a finite-dimensional real space \(E\), let \(Z\) be a finite-dimensional real space with \(\dim Z + 1 = \dim E\), and let \(g : M \to \mathbb R\) be smooth with \(0\) a regular value. Then \(\{g \ge 0\}\) is a half-slice submanifold over \(Z\) with boundary \(\{g = 0\}\). Chapter2/WithBoundaryisHalfSliceSubmanifold_of_regularValue

The idea. Milnor says the proof is like that of Lemma 1, and the formal proof makes this literal: at a boundary point, the slice chart of Lemma 1 for \(g\), with its factors swapped, has \(g\) as first coordinate. At an interior point any chart will do, once translated so that its first coordinate is positive.

The proof as formalized. Let \(g(p) \ge 0\).

Boundary points, \(g(p) = 0\). The refined Lemma 1 for \(g\) Chapter2/LevelSetexists_sliceChart_preimage gives a slice chart \(\varphi : U \to Z \times \mathbb R\) at \(p\) whose second component is \(\psi(g(q)) - \psi(0)\) for the chart \(\psi\) of \(\mathbb R\) at \(0\), which is the identity; so the second component is \(g\). Composing with the swap \(Z \times \mathbb R \to \mathbb R \times Z\) Chapter2/WithBoundaryPartialDiffeomorph.ofHomeomorph gives a chart whose first coordinate is \(g\), and both half-slice conditions hold by definition.

Interior points, \(g(p) > 0\). Take the extended chart of \(M\) at \(p\), a partial diffeomorphism onto an open subset of \(E\) because \(M\) has no boundary Chapter2/WithBoundaryPartialDiffeomorph.ofExtChartAt. Follow it by a linear isomorphism \(E \to \mathbb R \times Z\) and a translation by \((c, 0)\) that puts \(p\) at first coordinate \(1\), and restrict to the open set where \(g\) and the first coordinate are both positive. There both membership conditions are true and both boundary conditions false, so this is a half-slice chart without boundary points. Regularity of \(0\) is used only at boundary points.

V2.6 Lemma 4: level sets in a manifold with boundary

In Milnor’s Lemma 4, \(X\) is an \(m\)-manifold with boundary, \(f : X \to N\) is smooth with \(m > n\), and \(y\) is regular both for \(f\) and for \(f|\partial X\); the conclusion is that \(f^{-1}(y)\) is an \((m-n)\)-manifold with boundary \(f^{-1}(y) \cap \partial X\).

Theorem (V2.6, Lemma 4). Let \(M\), \(N\) be smooth manifolds without boundary modelled on finite-dimensional real spaces \(E\), \(F\); let \(Z\), \(Z'\) be finite-dimensional real spaces with \(\dim Z + \dim F = \dim E\) and \(\dim Z' + 1 = \dim Z\); let \(f : M \to N\) be smooth with \(y\) a regular value, and \(g : M \to \mathbb R\) smooth. Assume that for every \(x\) with \(f(x) = y\) and \(g(x) = 0\) some \(v \in T_xM\) satisfies \[df_x(v) = 0, \qquad dg_x(v) \ne 0.\] Then, inside the manifold \(f^{-1}(y)\) of V2.2 (modelled on \(Z\)), the set \(\{g \ge 0\}\) is a half-slice submanifold over \(Z'\) with boundary \(\{g = 0\}\). So \(f^{-1}(y) \cap \{g \ge 0\}\) is a manifold of dimension \(\dim M - \dim N\) with boundary \(f^{-1}(y) \cap \{g = 0\}\). Chapter2/WithBoundaryisHalfSliceSubmanifold_levelSet

Where the formal statement departs from Milnor. The manifold with boundary is \(X = \{g \ge 0\}\) inside a manifold without boundary on which \(f\) is defined; this suffices for every application in the formal text, beginning with the disk (V2.10) and the cylinder of §4. Regularity of \(y\) for \(f|\partial X\) becomes the displayed transversality condition, which is what Milnor’s proof extracts from it: the null space of \(df_x\) is not contained in the tangent space of the boundary. Further, \(y\) must be regular for \(f\) on all of \(M\), not only on \(X\), while \(0\) need not be a regular value of \(g\), since transversality already forces \(dg_x \ne 0\) where it matters. Milnor’s \(m > n\) is the existence of \(Z'\). Chapter2/WithBoundaryisHalfSliceSubmanifold_levelSet

The idea is Milnor’s: \(f^{-1}(y)\) is a manifold without boundary (Lemma 1), transversality says that \(g\) restricted to it has \(0\) as a regular value (Lemma 2), and Lemma 3 finishes.

The proof as formalized. By V2.2 and V2.1, \(f^{-1}(y)\) is a manifold modelled on \(Z\) with smooth inclusion \(\iota\), so \(\pi = g \circ \iota\) is smooth. At \(q\) with \(g(q) = 0\), take \(v\) as in the hypothesis: Lemma 2 writes \(v = d\iota_q(w)\) Chapter2/LevelSetmem_range_mfderiv_val_iff, and \(d\pi_q(w) = dg_q(v) \ne 0\), so \(d\pi_q\) is onto \(\mathbb R\) and \(0\) is a regular value of \(\pi\). Lemma 3, applied to \(f^{-1}(y)\), \(\pi\) and \(Z'\), concludes Chapter2/WithBoundaryisHalfSliceSubmanifold_of_regularValue Chapter2/WithBoundaryisHalfSliceSubmanifold_levelSet.

V2.7 The disk

Theorem (V2.7). Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and \(Z\) a finite-dimensional real space with \(\dim Z + 1 = \dim E\). Then the closed unit ball of \(E\) is a half-slice submanifold over \(Z\) with boundary the unit sphere. In particular, for every \(m \ge 0\) the closed unit ball of \(\mathbb R^{m+1}\) is a manifold with boundary \(S^m\), modelled on the half-space over \(\mathbb R^m\). Chapter2/DiskisHalfSliceSubmanifold_closedBall Chapter2/DiskisHalfSliceSubmanifold_unitDisk

This is Lemma 3 for the smooth function \(g(x) = 1 - \|x\|^2\) Chapter2/DiskdiskFun Chapter2/DiskcontMDiff_diskFun, whose derivative at \(x\) is \(v \mapsto -2\langle x, v\rangle\). On the sphere, \(v = -\tfrac t2 x\) is sent to \(t\), so \(0\) is a regular value Chapter2/DiskisRegularValue_diskFun.

V2.8 Corestriction

Theorem (V2.8). Let \(S\) be a slice submanifold of \(M\), let \(M'\) be a smooth manifold modelled on a real normed space, and let \(F : M' \to M\) be smooth with \(F(M') \subseteq S\). Then \(F\) is smooth as a map \(M' \to S\). Chapter2/CorestrictcontMDiff_codRestrict

In the chart of \(S\) at \(F(x)\), which is induced by a slice chart \(\varphi\) Chapter2/CorestrictextChartAt_eq, the map reads \(\mathrm{pr}_Z \circ \varphi \circ F\). Milnor uses this silently whenever a map into \(\partial X \subseteq X\) is regarded as a map into the manifold \(\partial X\).

V2.9 Lemma 6: the retraction formula, verified

Milnor writes down the retraction determined by a fixed-point-free \(P\) and leaves its properties to the reader. The formal text checks them, by calculus in a real inner product space \(E\). For \(P : E \to E\) put \[u = \frac{x - P(x)}{\|x - P(x)\|}, \qquad \Delta = 1 - \|x\|^2 + \langle x, u\rangle^2, \qquad t = -\langle x, u\rangle + \sqrt{\Delta}\] Chapter2/RetractionuVec Chapter2/Retractionrad Chapter2/RetractiontVal. The retraction is \(r(x) = x + t\,u\), considered on \(\Omega_P = \{x : x \ne P(x),\ \Delta(x) > 0\}\) Chapter2/Retractionretr Chapter2/Retractiongood.

Theorem (V2.9). Let \(E\) be a real inner product space with closed unit ball \(D\), and \(P : E \to E\).

    1. On \(\Omega_P\), \(\|r(x)\| = 1\). Chapter2/Retractionnorm_retr
    1. If \(x \in \Omega_P\), \(\|x\| = 1\) and \(\|P(x)\| \le 1\), then \(r(x) = x\). Chapter2/Retractionretr_eq_self
    1. If \(P(D) \subseteq D\) and \(P\) has no fixed point in \(D\), then \(D \subseteq \Omega_P\). Chapter2/RetractionclosedBall_subset_good
    1. If \(P\) is continuous, \(\Omega_P\) is open; if \(P\) is smooth, \(r\) is smooth on \(\Omega_P\). Chapter2/RetractionisOpen_good Chapter2/RetractioncontDiffOn_retr

The idea. The parameter \(t\) solves \(\|x + tu\| = 1\) by the quadratic formula, and each claim is an identity or inequality about that root.

The proof as formalized. For (a), let \(a = \langle x, u\rangle\) and \(s = \sqrt\Delta\), so \(t = s - a\) and \(\|u\| = 1\); then \(\|x + tu\|^2 = \|x\|^2 + 2ta + t^2 = \|x\|^2 + s^2 - a^2 = 1\). For (b), \(a = (1 - \langle x, Px\rangle)/\|x - Px\| \ge 0\) by Cauchy–Schwarz, which is where \(\|Px\| \le 1\) enters Chapter2/Retractioninner_uVec; so \(\sqrt\Delta = a\) and \(t = 0\). For (c), \(x \ne Px\) by hypothesis; if moreover \(\Delta(x) \le 0\) with \(\|x\| \le 1\), both \(1 - \|x\|^2\) and \(a^2\) vanish, so \(\|x\| = 1\) and \(\langle x, Px\rangle = 1\); then \(\|x - Px\|^2 = \|Px\|^2 - 1 \le 0\) and \(Px = x\). For (d), the norm is smooth away from \(0\) and the square root on \((0, \infty)\).

V2.10 Lemma 5 for the disk and the smooth Brouwer theorem

Theorem (V2.10). Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional real inner product space with closed unit ball \(D\), and let \(P : E \to E\) be smooth with \(P(D) \subseteq D\). Then \(P(x) = x\) for some \(x \in D\). Chapter2/Brouwerexists_fixedPoint_of_contDiff

Smoothness on all of \(E\) is how a smooth self-map of the disk is represented; V2.11 removes the assumption. Milnor’s Lemma 5, that a compact manifold with boundary has no smooth retraction onto its boundary, is proved inside this proof and for the disk only.

The idea is Milnor’s. A fixed-point-free \(P\) yields a smooth retraction \(f\) of \(D\) onto the sphere. For a regular value \(y\), the set \(f^{-1}(y) \cap D\) is a compact 1-manifold with boundary \(\{y\}\), whereas compact 1-manifolds have an even number of boundary points. Two adjustments make this formal: the retraction is extended by a cutoff to all of \(E\), so that no manifold with boundary is ever a domain, and it is corestricted to the sphere (V2.8).

The proof as formalized. Suppose \(P\) has no fixed point in \(D\).

  1. If \(\dim E = 0\), then \(0\) is fixed. Otherwise let \(n = \dim E\) and fix \(e \ne 0\). The model spaces of dimensions \(n - 1\), \(1\) and \(0\) are taken inside \(E\): the hyperplane \(e^\perp\), the line \(\mathbb R e\) and the zero subspace.
  2. With \(g(x) = 1 - \|x\|^2\), the sphere \(S = g^{-1}(0)\) is a slice submanifold modelled on \(e^\perp\), by Lemma 1 and the regular value of V2.7 Chapter2/LevelSetisSliceSubmanifold_preimage Chapter2/DiskisRegularValue_diskFun.
  3. By V2.9, \(\Omega_P\) is open and contains the compact set \(D\), so it contains the closed ball of radius \(1 + \delta\) for some \(\delta > 0\) Chapter2/BrouwerclosedBall_subset_cthickening_closedBall. With \(h\) Mathlib’s smooth transition function (\(0\) on \((-\infty, 0]\), \(1\) on \([1, \infty)\), values in \([0, 1]\)), the cutoff \[\chi_\delta(x) = \Big(1 - h\Big(\frac{\|x\|^2 - 1}{(1 + \delta)^2 - 1}\Big)\Big)\, x\] is smooth, is the identity on \(D\), and takes values in that ball Chapter2/Brouwercutoff_contDiff Chapter2/Brouwercutoff_eq_self Chapter2/Brouwernorm_cutoff_le. So \(F = r \circ \chi_\delta : E \to E\) is smooth, \(\|F(x)\| = 1\) everywhere, and \(F(x) = x\) on \(S\) by V2.9(b), since \(\chi_\delta\) fixes \(D\) and \(P(D) \subseteq D\).
  4. By V2.8, \(F\) is a smooth map \(f : E \to S\) with \(f \circ \iota = \mathrm{id}_S\), where \(\iota : S \to E\) is the inclusion Chapter2/CorestrictcontMDiff_codRestrict.
  5. \(E\) is second countable, so by Brown’s theorem (Part II) the regular values of \(f\) are dense in \(S\), which is nonempty as it contains \(f(0)\); pick one, \(y\) Chapter2/Browndense_regularValues.
  6. Transversality. For \(x \in S\) with \(f(x) = y\), the map \(df_x : E \to e^\perp\) is onto and \(\dim E > \dim e^\perp\), so it kills some \(v \ne 0\). If \(dg_x(v) = 0\), Lemma 2 for \(S\) gives \(v = d\iota_x(w)\) Chapter2/LevelSetmem_range_mfderiv_val_iff, and differentiating \(f \circ \iota = \mathrm{id}\) gives \(w = df_x(v) = 0\), so \(v = 0\). Hence \(df_x(v) = 0 \ne dg_x(v)\). This is Milnor’s observation that \(y\) is regular for \(f\) on the boundary, where \(f\) is the identity, in the form Lemma 4 needs.
  7. By V2.6 with \(Z = \mathbb R e\) and \(Z' = 0\), inside the 1-manifold \(f^{-1}(y)\) the set \(X = \{g \ge 0\}\) is a half-slice submanifold over the zero space with boundary \(B = \{g = 0\}\) Chapter2/WithBoundaryisHalfSliceSubmanifold_levelSet.
  8. \(X\) is compact: the inclusion \(f^{-1}(y) \to E\) is an embedding carrying \(X\) onto \(f^{-1}(y) \cap D\), a closed subset of \(D\). The half-space over the zero space is a half-line, and the Appendix, in the form proved for this situation, says that a compact half-slice submanifold over a zero-dimensional space, in a Hausdorff manifold and with \(B \subseteq X\), has finitely many boundary points, an even number Appendix/HalfSpaceIsHalfSliceSubmanifold.even_ncard_boundary. But \(B = \{y\}\): a point \(q \in B\) lies on \(S\), where \(f(q) = q\), while \(f(q) = y\); and \(f(y) = y\). One boundary point is not an even number, which is the contradiction. Chapter2/Brouwerexists_fixedPoint_of_contDiff

Where the formal proof departs from Milnor. Besides the cutoff Chapter2/Brouwercutoff and the restriction of Lemma 5 to the disk, every fact Milnor takes for granted is proved: the retraction is smooth, lands in the sphere and fixes it; the level set is compact; \(y\) is regular for the restriction to the boundary.

V2.11 Brouwer’s fixed point theorem

Theorem (V2.11). Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional real inner product space with closed unit ball \(D\), and let \(G : E \to E\) be continuous on \(D\) with \(G(D) \subseteq D\). Then \(G(x) = x\) for some \(x \in D\). Chapter2/Brouwerexists_fixedPoint

The idea is Milnor’s reduction to the smooth case by approximation, with one substitution: the approximating map is smooth rather than polynomial, and comes from the Stone–Weierstrass theorem.

The proof as formalized.

  1. Suppose not. The continuous function \(x \mapsto \|G(x) - x\|\) attains its minimum \(\mu\) on the compact set \(D\), and \(\mu > 0\).
  2. The functions on \(D\) that extend to smooth functions on \(E\) form a subalgebra of \(C(D, \mathbb R)\) Chapter2/BrouwersmoothSubalgebra, and it separates points: for \(x \ne y\), the linear function \(z \mapsto \langle z, y - x\rangle\) takes different values at \(x\) and \(y\) Chapter2/BrouwersmoothSubalgebra_separatesPoints. Let \(b_1, \dots, b_N\) be an orthonormal basis, \(N = \dim E\). By Stone–Weierstrass on the compact set \(D\), each coordinate \(\langle b_i, G\rangle\) is within \(\varepsilon/(N + 1)\) of some smooth \(F_i\) on \(D\), so \(P_1 = \sum_i F_i\, b_i\) is smooth and on \(D\) \[\|P_1 - G\| \le \sum_i |F_i - \langle b_i, G\rangle| \le \frac{N\varepsilon}{N + 1} < \varepsilon\] Chapter2/Brouwerexists_contDiff_approx. Take \(\varepsilon = \mu/2\).
  3. With \(c = 1 + \mu/2\) put \(P = P_1/c\). On \(D\), \(\|P_1\| \le \|G\| + \mu/2 \le c\), so \(P(D) \subseteq D\), and \(P\) is smooth.
  4. By V2.10, \(P(x) = x\) for some \(x \in D\) Chapter2/Brouwerexists_fixedPoint_of_contDiff. Now \(\|P(x) - P_1(x)\| = (1 - c^{-1})\|P_1(x)\| \le c - 1 = \mu/2\), so \[\|G(x) - x\| = \|P(x) - G(x)\| \le \|P(x) - P_1(x)\| + \|P_1(x) - G(x)\| < \mu,\] contradicting the minimality of \(\mu\). Chapter2/Brouwerexists_fixedPoint

Milnor approximates by a polynomial map with error \(\varepsilon\) and divides by \(1 + \varepsilon\); the formal proof does the same with \(\varepsilon = \mu/2\) and a smooth map.

What the formalization taught us

  • Separation axioms become hypotheses. Finiteness of a regular fibre needs points of the target closed; local constancy needs both manifolds Hausdorff Chapter1/RegularValueIsRegularValue.finite_preimage Chapter1/RegularValueIsRegularValue.eventually_ncard_preimage_eq.
  • The inverse function theorem between manifolds had to be proved, with smoothness on a neighbourhood rather than at a point, and with invertibility of the derivative propagated to a neighbourhood so that the Euclidean inverse is smooth on an open set Chapter1/InverseFunctioneventually_isInvertible_fderiv.
  • Local constancy is stronger than stated: the count is constant for all values near a regular value, and those values are automatically regular Chapter1/RegularValueIsRegularValue.eventually_isRegularValue_and_ncard.
  • The fundamental theorem of algebra is proved on \(\mathbb C \cup \{\infty\}\), which removes Milnor’s conjugates Chapter1/FTAcontMDiffAt_polyMap_infty; \(\infty\) is put among the bad values instead of being classified; and the existence of a regular value in the image, which Milnor takes for granted, is proved from the infinitude of \(P(\mathbb C)\) Chapter1/FTAexists_regularValue_mem_range.
  • Submanifolds must be built. The slice charts are exactly the diffeomorphisms of Milnor’s proof of Lemma 1, with a base point added for formal reasons Chapter2/SubmanifoldSliceChart, and dimensions are carried by the choice of model spaces Chapter2/LevelSetisSliceSubmanifold_preimage.
  • Well-definedness of the boundary is replaced by construction: charts must send exactly the prescribed boundary to \(\{t = 0\}\) Chapter2/Boundaryboundary_eq.
  • Lemma 4’s hypothesis is transversality, the region is \(\{g \ge 0\}\) in a manifold without boundary, \(y\) must be regular on the whole ambient manifold, and \(0\) need not be regular for \(g\) Chapter2/WithBoundaryisHalfSliceSubmanifold_levelSet.
  • Silent identifications are lemmas: maps into a slice submanifold are smooth into it Chapter2/CorestrictcontMDiff_codRestrict, and the regularity of \(y\) on the boundary in the Brouwer argument is derived from Lemma 2 and the chain rule Chapter2/Brouwerexists_fixedPoint_of_contDiff.
  • What Milnor leaves to the reader in Lemma 6 is a page of inequalities: positivity of the radicand rests on the fact that \(\|x\| = 1\), \(\|Px\| \le 1\) and \(\langle x, Px\rangle = 1\) force \(Px = x\) Chapter2/RetractionclosedBall_subset_good, and a cutoff extends the retraction to all of \(E\) Chapter2/Brouwercutoff.
  • Stone–Weierstrass replaces Weierstrass, applied to the functions on the ball that extend smoothly to \(E\) Chapter2/Brouwerexists_contDiff_approx.
