Part II. Sard’s theorem and the degree modulo 2 (Milnor §3–§4)

Milnor’s §3 proves that critical values are rare, and §4 turns this into the first global invariant of the book, the degree modulo 2. The formal proof of Sard’s theorem keeps Milnor’s induction on the dimension of the domain, and his Steps 1 and 2 almost line by line, made coordinate-free; Step 3, the cube count, becomes a Hölder estimate for Hausdorff dimension taken from Mathlib. Brown’s theorem carries the result to manifolds, with second countability made explicit. In §4 the Homotopy Lemma is Lemma 4 on a cylinder plus the Appendix; the Homogeneity Lemma is proved with explicit bump-function diffeomorphisms of a chart instead of flows; the theorem of §4, which Milnor states as a single unlettered Theorem with two assertions, follows as in the book, with the degree defined through a chosen regular value. The docstrings of the formal source call its two assertions “Theorem B” and “Theorem A”; here they are the first and second assertions of the Theorem of §4. Throughout, manifolds are modelled on finite-dimensional real normed spaces, “without boundary” means that the model has no boundary, smooth means \(C^\infty\), and Hausdorff or second countable is said whenever it is assumed.

Map. - Chapter3/Basic: Milnor’s sets \(C\) and \(C_1 \supseteq C_2 \supseteq \cdots\), the statement proved by induction, closedness of \(C\) in \(U\), and “Hausdorff dimension below \(\dim F\) implies Haar-null”. - Chapter3/Straighten: the coordinate change \(h(x) = (w(x), x_2, \dots, x_n)\), without coordinates. - Chapter3/Step1: Step 1, \(f(C \setminus C_1)\) is null, by Fubini. - Chapter3/Step2: Step 2, \(f(C_k \setminus C_{k+1})\) is null; the countable-cover lemma. - Chapter3/Step3: Step 3, a Taylor bound and the Hölder estimate for \(f(C_k)\). - Chapter3/Sard: the induction, Sard’s theorem, density of regular values. - Chapter2/Brown: Brown’s theorem on manifolds. - Chapter4/Cylinder: Lemma 4 with two boundary functions. - Chapter4/Homotopy: transversality at the ends of the cylinder; the Homotopy Lemma. - Chapter4/BumpDiffeo: for a bump function \(\varphi\) and small \(c\), \(u \mapsto u + \varphi(u)c\) is a diffeomorphism of the model space. - Chapter4/Homogeneity: transport through a chart, isotopy, the Homogeneity Lemma. - Chapter4/Degree: the Theorem of §4 (independence of the regular value and homotopy invariance), the degree modulo 2, maps of nonzero degree are onto.

V3.1 Sard’s theorem

Theorem. Let \(E\) and \(F\) be finite-dimensional real normed spaces and \(\mu\) an additive Haar measure on the Borel sets of \(F\). Let \(U \subseteq E\) be open, \(f : E \to F\) of class \(C^\infty\) on \(U\), and \(C = \{x \in U : df_x \text{ is not surjective}\}\). Then \(\mu(f(C)) = 0\). Chapter3/Sardsard

The map is defined on all of \(E\) for convenience; its values off \(U\) play no role. (Formally \(E\) and \(F\) must also lie in one type universe, here and in most statements below; this is bookkeeping without mathematical content.)

The idea. Induct on \(n = \dim E\). Let \(C_k\) be the set where all derivatives of orders \(1\) to \(k\) vanish; \(C\) is covered by \(C \setminus C_1\), the layers \(C_i \setminus C_{i+1}\), and \(C_k\). On the first two kinds of piece a straightening coordinate reduces the problem to dimension \(n - 1\), through Fubini’s theorem for \(C \setminus C_1\) and directly for the layers. On \(C_k\), for \(k\) large, a Taylor estimate makes \(f\) so flat that the image is too thin to carry measure. Every piece is treated near one point and globalized by a countable cover.

The objects, and the statement proved by induction

The formal \(C\) and \(C_k\) are Milnor’s: \(C\) is the set of \(x \in U\) at which the Fréchet derivative \(df_x\) is not onto, and \[C_k = \{x \in U : D^j f(x) = 0 \text{ for } 1 \le j \le k\},\] with \(D^j f(x)\) the \(j\)-th derivative as a \(j\)-linear map, so that \(C_0 = U\) and the \(C_k\) decrease Chapter3/BasiccritSet Chapter3/BasicvanishSet Chapter3/BasicvanishSet_antitone. Of Milnor’s decomposition only the inclusion \(C \subseteq (C \setminus C_1) \cup \bigcup_{1 \le i < k} (C_i \setminus C_{i+1}) \cup C_k\) is proved, by taking the last \(i\) with \(x \in C_i\) Chapter3/BasiccritSet_subset_union.

The induction runs over the statement \(S(n)\): for every finite-dimensional real normed space \(E\) of dimension \(n\), every finite-dimensional \(F\) with any Haar measure \(\mu\), every open \(U \subseteq E\) and every \(f\) of class \(C^\infty\) on \(U\), \(\mu(f(C)) = 0\) Chapter3/BasicSardStatement. The quantification over all targets and all Haar measures is forced by the proof. Step 1 applies the hypothesis to a map from a hyperplane \(K \subseteq E\) to a hyperplane \(F_1 \subseteq F\), with a freshly chosen Haar measure on \(F_1\); Step 2 applies it to a map from \(K\) into \(F\) with the original \(\mu\). Neither hyperplane is \(\mathbb R^{n-1}\) or \(\mathbb R^{p-1}\) on the nose, and admitting every Haar measure makes the choice of measure on them irrelevant.

Null sets, measurability, countable covers, smoothness

Three devices carry the measure theory.

Countable covers. For any measure \(\mu\) on \(F\), any map \(f\) and any sets \(S, T \subseteq E\): if every \(x \in S\) has a neighbourhood \(V\) with \(\mu(f(T \cap V)) = 0\), then \(\mu(f(T \cap S)) = 0\), because \(E\) is second countable and countably many of the \(V\) cover \(S\) Chapter3/Step2measure_image_eq_zero_of_locally. This is Milnor’s “covered by countably many such sets \(V\)”, invoked once for each step.

Measurability, only where Fubini needs it. Mathlib’s measures are defined on all subsets and a subset of a null set is null, so Steps 2 and 3 never ask whether a set is measurable. Step 1 does. Where Milnor writes his set of critical values as a countable union of compact sets, the formal proof takes its neighbourhood to be a closed ball \(B\) and uses that \(C \cap B\) is compact. This holds for every compact \(B \subseteq U\) once \(f\) is \(C^1\), because surjectivity is an open condition on linear maps: if \(LR = 1\), then \(L'R\) is invertible for \(L'\) near \(L\) Chapter3/BasicisOpen_setOf_surjective Chapter3/BasicisCompact_critSet_inter.

Dimension and Haar measure. A set \(s \subseteq F\) of Hausdorff dimension less than \(p = \dim F\) is null for every Haar measure: a linear isomorphism from \(F\) onto the space of functions \(\{0, \dots, p-1\} \to \mathbb R\) with the maximum norm does not raise dimension; for that norm the \(p\)-dimensional Hausdorff measure equals Lebesgue measure (for the Euclidean norm the two would differ by a constant factor), so the image is Lebesgue-null; and Haar measures are mutually absolutely continuous Chapter3/BasicaddHaar_eq_zero_of_dimH_lt_finrank.

Smoothness. The hypothesis is \(C^\infty\) on \(U\) (not analyticity), and the proof never counts derivatives. It needs \(C^\infty\) to keep the induction closed: the maps to which \(S(n-1)\) is applied are composites of \(f\) with the inverse of a straightening, and in Step 2 the function straightened is built from \(D^k f\), which is \(C^\infty\) because \(f\) is Chapter3/Step2contDiffOn_iteratedFDeriv. Individual lemmas ask for less (closedness of \(C\) is proved for \(C^1\) maps), but no finite-smoothness version of the theorem is attempted.

The induction

  1. Zero target. If \(F = 0\), every linear map to \(F\) is onto and \(C = \emptyset\) Chapter3/SardcritSet_eq_empty_of_subsingleton. In each case of the induction it is dispatched first. On the zero space a Haar measure is a positive multiple of the point mass, and the arguments below use \(F \ne 0\) in three places: points must be null, a vanishing derivative must be critical Chapter3/Step2mem_critSet_of_fderiv_eq_zero, and Step 3 needs \(p \ge 1\). The theorem survives only because \(C\) is empty.
  2. \(n = 0\), \(F \ne 0\). \(E\) is a point, so \(f(C)\) has at most one point, which is null.
  3. \(n = m + 1\), \(p = \dim F \ge 1\). Take \(k = n\); then \((k+1)p > n\). Milnor asks only for \(k > n/p - 1\); the uniform choice costs extra layers in Step 2 and nothing else.
  4. Assembly. \(f(C \setminus C_1)\) is null by the cover lemma and Step 1; each \(f(C_i \setminus C_{i+1})\), \(1 \le i < k\), by the cover lemma and Step 2; \(f(C_k)\) by the cover lemma and Step 3 on a closed ball inside \(U\) around each point of \(C_k\) Chapter3/SardsardStatement. Theorem V3.1 is \(S(\dim E)\) Chapter3/Sardsard.

When \(p = 1\), Step 1 lands in the zero target \(F_1 = 0\), where the induction hypothesis is case 1; no separate treatment is needed.

The straightening

Milnor’s coordinate change \(h(x) = (w(x), x_2, \dots, x_n)\) becomes: given \(w\) of class \(C^\infty\) on an open set \(U\) and \(x_0 \in U\) with \(\ell = dw_{x_0} \ne 0\), choose \(v\) with \(\ell(v) = 1\), let \(K = \ker \ell\) (so \(\dim K + 1 = \dim E\)) and \(P(x) = x - \ell(x)v\), and set \[H(x) = (w(x), P(x)) \in \mathbb R \times K .\] Its derivative at \(x_0\) is \((\ell, P)\), with inverse \((t, z) \mapsto z + tv\). The inverse function theorem of Chapter 1 (V1.1) yields open sets \(V \ni x_0\) in \(U\) and \(V' \subseteq \mathbb R \times K\) and a \(C^\infty\) map \(G : V' \to V\) inverse to \(H|_V\); the first coordinate of \(H(x)\) is \(w(x)\) for every \(x\) Chapter3/StraightenStraightening Chapter3/Straightenexists_straightening.

Step 1: \(f(C \setminus C_1)\) is null

Step 1. Assume \(S(n-1)\), \(n = \dim E\). Let \(F \neq 0\) carry a Haar measure \(\mu\), let \(f\) be \(C^\infty\) on the open set \(U\), and \(x_0 \in C \setminus C_1\). Then \(x_0\) has a neighbourhood \(V\) with \(\mu(f(C \cap V)) = 0\). Chapter3/Step1step1_local

  1. The coordinate. As \(x_0 \notin C_1\), \(df_{x_0}u \ne 0\) for some \(u\), and Hahn–Banach gives a functional \(\ell_0\) on \(F\) with \(\ell_0(df_{x_0}u) = \|df_{x_0}u\|\). The function \(w = \ell_0 \circ f\), which plays the role of Milnor’s \(f_1\), has \(dw_{x_0} \ne 0\) and is straightened.
  2. The target. Put \(y_0 = df_{x_0}u / \ell_0(df_{x_0}u)\), \(F_1 = \ker \ell_0\) and \(Q(y) = y - \ell_0(y)y_0\); then \(e(y) = (\ell_0(y), Q(y))\) is a linear isomorphism \(F \to \mathbb R \times F_1\). The level sets of \(\ell_0\) replace Milnor’s hyperplanes \(t \times \mathbb R^{p-1}\), and \(Q\) identifies them with \(F_1\).
  3. The slices. \(g = f \circ G\) is \(C^\infty\) on \(V'\) with \(\ell_0(g(t,z)) = t\): \(g\) carries hyperplanes into hyperplanes. With \(V_t = \{z \in K : (t,z) \in V'\}\) and \(g^t(z) = Q(g(t,z))\), the hypothesis \(S(n-1)\), for a Haar measure \(\mu_1\) on \(F_1\), makes the critical values of each \(g^t\) a \(\mu_1\)-null set.
  4. Half of the block-matrix remark. If \((t, z)\) is critical for \(g\), then \(z\) is critical for \(g^t\). With \(D = dg_{(t,z)}\), differentiating \(\ell_0 \circ g = \mathrm{pr}_1\) gives \(\ell_0 \circ D = \mathrm{pr}_1\), and \(d(g^t)_z u = Q\,D(0,u)\). If \(d(g^t)_z\) is onto and \(y \in F\), choose \(u'\) with \(Q\,D(0,u') = Q(y - D(\ell_0(y), 0))\); both vectors lie in \(\ker \ell_0\), where \(Q\) is the identity, so \(D(\ell_0(y), u') = y\). Milnor states an equivalence; the converse is neither needed nor proved.
  5. A compact neighbourhood. Take a closed ball \(B \subseteq V\) around \(x_0\); then \(T = f(C \cap B)\) is compact.
  6. Slices of \(e(T)\). For every \(t\), the slice \(\{y_1 : (t, y_1) \in e(T)\}\) lies in the critical values of \(g^t\). If \(y_1\) comes from \(x \in C \cap B\), then \(H(x) = (t, z)\) with \(g(H(x)) = f(x)\); \(H(x)\) is critical for \(g\), since \(dg_{H(x)} = df_x \circ dG_{H(x)}\) and \(df_x\) is not onto; so \(z\) is critical for \(g^t\) by step 4, and \(g^t(z) = Q(f(x)) = y_1\).
  7. Fubini. \(e(T)\) is compact, hence measurable, and all its slices are \(\mu_1\)-null, so \((\lambda \otimes \mu_1)(e(T)) = 0\), \(\lambda\) Lebesgue measure. The image of \(\mu\) under \(e\) is a Haar measure on \(\mathbb R \times F_1\), hence absolutely continuous with respect to \(\lambda \otimes \mu_1\), and \(\mu(T) = 0\): the ball \(B\) is the neighbourhood sought.

The hypothesis \(F \ne 0\) is automatic here, since \(df_{x_0} \ne 0\).

Step 2: \(f(C_k \setminus C_{k+1})\) is null

Step 2. Assume \(S(n-1)\). Let \(F \ne 0\) carry a Haar measure \(\mu\), let \(f\) be \(C^\infty\) on the open set \(U\), \(k \ge 1\), and \(x_0 \in C_k \setminus C_{k+1}\). Then \(x_0\) has a neighbourhood \(V\) with \(\mu(f(C_k \cap V)) = 0\). Chapter3/Step2step2_local

  1. The function to straighten. Since \(D^{k+1}f(x_0) \ne 0\) (as \(x_0 \notin C_{k+1}\)), choose \(m_0, \dots, m_k \in E\) and a functional \(\ell_0\) with \(\ell_0(D^{k+1}f(x_0)(m_0, \dots, m_k)) \ne 0\), and put \(w(x) = \ell_0(D^k f(x)(m_1, \dots, m_k))\), Milnor’s \(\partial^k f_r / \partial x_{s_2} \cdots \partial x_{s_{k+1}}\) without coordinates. Then \(w\) is \(C^\infty\), vanishes on \(C_k\), and \(dw_{x_0}(m_0) \ne 0\) by the identity \(D^{k+1}f(x)(m_0, \dots, m_k) = (D(D^kf)(x)\,m_0)(m_1, \dots, m_k)\).
  2. Restriction to the hyperplane. Straighten \(w\). As \(w = 0\) on \(C_k\), \(H\) maps \(C_k \cap V\) into \(\{0\} \times K\). Let \(V_0 = \{z : (0,z) \in V'\}\) and \(\bar g(z) = f(G(0,z))\); the hypothesis \(S(n-1)\) is applied to \(\bar g : V_0 \to F\) with the original \(\mu\).
  3. Critical points. For \(x \in C_k \cap V\) write \(H(x) = (0, z)\); then \(\bar g(z) = f(x)\) and \(d\bar g_z = df_x \circ d(G \circ \iota)_z = 0\), with \(\iota(z) = (0,z)\), because \(df_x = 0\); a zero map to \(F \ne 0\) is not onto Chapter3/Step2fderiv_eq_zero_of_mem_vanishSet Chapter3/Step2mem_critSet_of_fderiv_eq_zero. Hence \(f(C_k \cap V)\) lies in the null set of critical values of \(\bar g\).

The neighbourhood is the open set \(V\) itself; no measurability is involved. Milnor’s reason, “since all derivatives of order \(\le k\) vanish”, is more than is used: only \(df_x = 0\) matters.

Step 3: the cube estimate as a Hölder estimate

Milnor cuts a cube of edge \(\delta\) into \(r^n\) subcubes, notes that each subcube meeting \(C_k\) is mapped into a cube of edge \(a/r^{k+1}\), and bounds the total volume by \(a^p r^{n-(k+1)p} \to 0\). The formal proof separates two ingredients: a Taylor bound, saying that \(f\) is Hölder of exponent \(k+1\) on \(C_k\), and the library theorem that a map Hölder of exponent \(\alpha\) multiplies Hausdorff dimension by at most \(1/\alpha\), whose proof is the same covering argument.

Taylor bound. Let \(G\) be a real normed space, \(f : E \to G\) of class \(C^\infty\) on the open set \(U\), \(A \subseteq U\) convex, \(\|D^{k+1}f\| \le c\) on \(A\), and \(x \in A\) with \(D^j f(x) = 0\) for \(1 \le j \le k\). Then \(\|f(y) - f(x)\| \le c\,\|y - x\|^{k+1}\) for all \(y \in A\). Chapter3/Step3norm_sub_le_of_iteratedFDeriv_eq_zero

The proof is an induction on \(k\) in which the target changes, which is why the statement quantifies over all \(G\). For \(k = 0\) it is the mean value inequality on the segment \([x, y] \subseteq A\). For \(k + 1\), apply the case \(k\) to \(df : E \to L(E, G)\), using \(\|D^j(df)\| = \|D^{j+1}f\|\) and \(df_x = 0\), to get \(\|df_z\| \le c\,\|z - x\|^{k+1}\) on \(A\); on the segment \(\|z - x\| \le \|y - x\|\) Chapter3/Step3norm_sub_le_of_mem_segment, and the mean value inequality gives \(c\,\|y-x\|^{k+2}\). The constant is \(c\), not Taylor’s \(c/(k+1)!\): bounding by the supremum on the segment gives the factorial away, harmlessly.

Step 3. Let \(\mu\) be a Haar measure on \(F\), \(f\) of class \(C^\infty\) on the open set \(U\), \(n < (k+1)p\), and \(A \subseteq U\) compact and convex. Then \(\mu(f(C_k \cap A)) = 0\). Chapter3/Step3measure_image_vanishSet_inter_eq_zero

For nonempty \(A\) let \(c\) bound \(\|D^{k+1}f\|\) on \(A\). The Taylor bound gives \(\|f(y) - f(x)\| \le c\,\|y - x\|^{k+1}\) for \(x, y \in C_k \cap A\), so \(\dim_H f(C_k \cap A) \le \dim_H (C_k \cap A)/(k+1) \le n/(k+1) < p\), and the set is null.

Where the formal proof departs from Milnor. The counting is done once, for Hausdorff dimension, in the library, and Milnor’s cubes become closed balls, the natural compact convex neighbourhoods in a space without coordinates.

V3.2 Density of regular values

Theorem. Let \(E\), \(F\) be finite-dimensional real normed spaces, \(F\) with its Borel σ-algebra, \(U \subseteq E\) open, \(f\) of class \(C^\infty\) on \(U\), and \(C\) as in V3.1. Then \(F \setminus f(C)\) is dense in \(F\). Chapter3/Sarddense_compl_image_critSet

Choose any Haar measure: \(f(C)\) is null by V3.1, and a Haar measure charges every nonempty open set, so \(f(C)\) has empty interior.

V3.3 Brown’s theorem

Theorem. Let \(M\) and \(N\) be smooth manifolds without boundary, modelled on finite-dimensional real normed spaces \(E\) and \(F\) of arbitrary dimensions, with \(M\) second countable, and let \(f : M \to N\) be smooth. Then the regular values of \(f\) are dense in \(N\). Chapter2/Browndense_regularValues

A point \(x\) is critical if \(df_x\), read in charts, is not onto; \(y\) is a regular value if every point of \(f^{-1}(y)\) is regular. So a point outside \(f(M)\) is a regular value, and the regular values are the complement of the image of the critical set Chapter2/BrowncritPoints Chapter1/RegularValueIsRegularValue Chapter2/BrownregularValues_eq_compl_image_critPoints.

The idea. Milnor’s proof is the clause that \(M\) is covered by countably many neighbourhoods diffeomorphic to open subsets of \(\mathbb R^m\). The formal proof argues by contradiction inside a single chart of \(N\), so only the source needs countability.

  1. Suppose a nonempty open \(W \subseteq N\), containing \(y_1\), consists of critical values. Let \(\psi\) be the chart of \(N\) at \(y_1\), with values in \(F\), and \(\mu\) a Haar measure on \(F\).
  2. By second countability, countably many chart domains \(\operatorname{dom}\varphi_{x_0}\), \(x_0 \in S\), cover \(M\).
  3. For each \(x_0\) the set \(U_{x_0}\) of points \(u\) in the (open) image of \(\varphi_{x_0}\) with \(f(\varphi_{x_0}^{-1}(u)) \in \operatorname{dom}\psi\) is open, and \(\psi \circ f \circ \varphi_{x_0}^{-1}\) is \(C^\infty\) on it; by V3.1 its critical values are \(\mu\)-null.
  4. If \(x\) is critical, \(x \in \operatorname{dom}\varphi_{x_0}\) and \(f(x) \in \operatorname{dom}\psi\), then \(\varphi_{x_0}(x)\) is critical for \(\psi \circ f \circ \varphi_{x_0}^{-1}\): in the chain rule \(d\psi \circ df_x \circ d(\varphi_{x_0}^{-1})\) the factor \(d\psi\) is injective, with left inverse \(d(\psi^{-1})\), so surjectivity of the composite would force that of \(df_x\) Chapter2/Brownmfderiv_extChartAt_injective Chapter2/Brownmem_critSet_of_mem_critPoints. Only this direction is proved.
  5. Hence \(\psi(W \cap \operatorname{dom}\psi)\) lies in a countable union of null sets. But it is a neighbourhood of \(\psi(y_1)\), as \(N\) has no boundary, and so has positive measure: contradiction.

What the book leaves implicit. Second countability of \(M\), automatic for subsets of \(\mathbb R^k\). Nothing else: no Hausdorff property, no relation between \(\dim M\) and \(\dim N\), no countability of \(N\), which only supplies one chart and a measure on its model space.

V4.1 Lemma 4 for the cylinder

Two conventions. A smooth homotopy is a smooth \(F : M \times \mathbb R \to N\) on the product manifold, with ends \(F(\cdot, 0)\) and \(F(\cdot, 1)\). Its domain is thus a manifold without boundary, to which Lemma 4 in the form V2.6 and Brown’s theorem apply directly, and level sets are cut down to \(M \times [0,1]\) by hand Chapter4/Homotopyhomotopy_lemma_of_isRegularValue Chapter4/Homotopyhomotopy_lemma. A manifold with boundary is a half-slice submanifold (V2.4): a set \(X\) with boundary \(B\) inside an ambient manifold (here always one without boundary), each point of \(X\) lying in the domain of a diffeomorphism onto an open subset of \(\mathbb R \times Z'\) under which, on that domain, \(X\) corresponds to \(\{t \ge 0\}\) and \(B\) to \(\{t = 0\}\) Chapter2/BoundaryHalfSliceChart Chapter2/BoundaryIsHalfSliceSubmanifold.

Lemma. Let \(M\), \(N\) be smooth manifolds without boundary, \(f : M \to N\) smooth, \(y\) a regular value, and \(Z\), \(Z'\) finite-dimensional with \(\dim Z + \dim N = \dim M\) and \(\dim Z' + 1 = \dim Z\). Let \(g_0, g_1 : M \to \mathbb R\) be smooth, such that (i) for \(i = 0, 1\) and each \(x \in f^{-1}(y)\) with \(g_i(x) = 0\) some \(v\) has \(df_x v = 0\) and \((dg_i)_x v \ne 0\), and (ii) \(g_0\) and \(g_1\) never vanish together on \(f^{-1}(y)\). Then, inside the manifold \(f^{-1}(y)\) modelled on \(Z\) (Lemma 1), the set \(\{g_0 \ge 0,\ g_1 \ge 0\}\) is a half-slice submanifold over \(Z'\) with boundary \(\{g_0 = 0\} \cup \{g_1 = 0\}\). Chapter4/CylinderisHalfSliceSubmanifold_levelSet_two

The idea. Being a manifold with boundary is local, and near each point at most one of the two functions matters.

Proof as formalized. Lemma 4 (V2.6) for \(g_0\) and for \(g_1\) gives half-slice structures for \(\{g_0 \ge 0\}\) and \(\{g_1 \ge 0\}\) in \(f^{-1}(y)\) Chapter2/WithBoundaryisHalfSliceSubmanifold_levelSet. A locality lemma restricts a half-slice chart to an open set on which two pairs \((X, B)\) agree Chapter4/CylinderIsHalfSliceSubmanifold.of_local. At a point with \(g_1 > 0\), use a chart for \(g_0\) restricted to \(\{g_1 > 0\}\), where the set is \(\{g_0 \ge 0\}\) and the boundary \(\{g_0 = 0\}\); at a point with \(g_1 = 0\), (ii) gives \(g_0 > 0\) and the roles are exchanged. The dimension hypotheses encode Milnor’s \(m > n\).

V4.2 Transversality at the ends

Lemma. Let \(M\), \(N\) be smooth manifolds without boundary of the same dimension, \(M\) modelled on \(E\). Let \(F : M \times \mathbb R \to N\) be smooth, \(y\) a regular value of \(F\) and of \(F(\cdot, c)\), and \(F(x, c) = y\). Then some \(v = (v_1, v_2) \in E \times \mathbb R\) has \(dF_{(x,c)}v = 0\) and \(v_2 \ne 0\). Chapter4/Homotopycylinder_transversality

This makes precise the hypothesis of Milnor’s Lemma 4 that \(y\) be regular for the restriction of \(F\) to \(\partial(M \times [0,1])\): it is hypothesis (i) of V4.1 for \(g_0 = t\) at \(c = 0\) and \(g_1 = 1 - t\) at \(c = 1\). Proof. \(dF_{(x,c)}\) maps a space of dimension \(n + 1\) to one of dimension \(n\), so it kills some \(v \ne 0\); this step does not need \(y\) to be regular for \(F\), and the formal proof in fact never uses that hypothesis. If \(v_2 = 0\) then, since \(x \mapsto (x, c)\) has derivative \((\mathrm{id}, 0)\) Chapter4/HomotopyhasMFDerivAt_inl, \(d(F(\cdot,c))_x v_1 = 0\); that derivative is a surjection between spaces of equal dimension, hence injective, so \(v = 0\).

V4.3 The Homotopy Lemma

Theorem. Let \(M\) be a compact, Hausdorff, second countable smooth manifold without boundary, \(N\) a Hausdorff smooth manifold without boundary of the same dimension, \(F : M \times \mathbb R \to N\) smooth, \(f = F(\cdot, 0)\), \(g = F(\cdot, 1)\). If \(y\) is a regular value of \(f\) and of \(g\), then \(\#f^{-1}(y) + \#g^{-1}(y)\) is even. Chapter4/Homotopyhomotopy_lemma

The formal cardinality is \(0\) on infinite sets, but every fibre counted in this part is finite, by compactness and regularity Chapter1/RegularValueIsRegularValue.finite_preimage.

The idea. Milnor’s: if \(y\) is also regular for \(F\), then \(F^{-1}(y) \cap (M \times [0,1])\) is a compact 1-manifold whose boundary is the two fibres, and a compact 1-manifold has an even number of boundary points. Otherwise, move \(y\) a little.

Case 1: \(y\) regular for \(F\) as well (compactness and Hausdorff, no countability) Chapter4/Homotopyhomotopy_lemma_of_isRegularValue. 1. \(F^{-1}(y)\) is a 1-manifold modelled on \(Z = \mathbb R\), as \(\dim (M \times \mathbb R) - \dim N = 1\). Take \(Z' = 0\), \(g_0(x,t) = t\), \(g_1(x,t) = 1 - t\). 2. V4.2 at \(c = 0\) and \(c = 1\) gives hypothesis (i) of V4.1, since \(dg_0 v = v_2\) and \(dg_1 v = -v_2\); (ii) holds because \(t\) and \(1 - t\) never vanish together. So \(X = F^{-1}(y) \cap (M \times [0,1])\) is a half-slice submanifold of \(F^{-1}(y)\) over the zero space, with boundary \(B = F^{-1}(y) \cap (M \times \{0, 1\})\). 3. \(X\) is compact: it is closed in \(M \times [0,1]\), since points of \(N\) are closed. 4. The Appendix (V.A′), for the Hausdorff 1-manifold \(F^{-1}(y)\), shows \(B\) finite with an even number of points Appendix/HalfSpaceIsHalfSliceSubmanifold.even_ncard_boundary. 5. \(B\) is the disjoint union of \(f^{-1}(y) \times \{0\}\) and \(g^{-1}(y) \times \{1\}\), both finite, so \(\#B = \#f^{-1}(y) + \#g^{-1}(y)\).

Case 2: general \(y\). Local constancy in its strengthened form (V1.4) gives an open \(W \ni y\) of regular values of \(f\) and of \(g\) with the counts of \(y\) Chapter1/RegularValueIsRegularValue.eventually_isRegularValue_and_ncard. Brown’s theorem for the homotopy itself, on the second countable but noncompact \(M \times \mathbb R\), gives a regular value \(y' \in W\) of \(F\), and Case 1 at \(y'\) finishes.

What the book leaves implicit. The Hausdorff hypotheses, for finiteness, for local constancy and for the Appendix (applied to a level set in \(M \times \mathbb R\)); second countability, whose only use here is Brown’s theorem for \(F\); and the meaning of “regular on the boundary”, which is V4.2.

V4.4 The Homogeneity Lemma

Theorem. Let \(N\) be a Hausdorff, preconnected smooth manifold without boundary. For all \(y, z \in N\) there are a diffeomorphism \(h : N \to N\) with \(h(y) = z\) and a smooth \(H : N \times \mathbb R \to N\) with \(H(\cdot, 0) = \mathrm{id}\), \(H(\cdot, 1) = h\), and every \(H(\cdot, t)\) a diffeomorphism. Chapter4/HomogeneityIsotopic Chapter4/Homogeneityisotopic_of_preconnected

Preconnected means connected or empty, so for nonempty \(N\) this is Milnor’s hypothesis. The formal definition of “isotopic” records Milnor’s full conclusion, an isotopy through diffeomorphisms.

The idea. “Isotopic” is an equivalence relation with open classes, and connectedness leaves one class. Openness is local: every point of a small chart neighbourhood of \(y\) is reached from \(y\) by a compactly supported diffeomorphism isotopic to the identity. Milnor obtains it from the flow of the vector field \(u \mapsto \varphi(u)\,c\), \(\varphi\) a bump function; the formal proof uses instead the explicit map \[\mathrm{sh}_c(u) = u + \varphi(u)\,c\] of the model space \(V\) of \(N\) Chapter4/BumpDiffeoshift.

Why not the flow. The flow needs the time-\(t\) map of a compactly supported vector field to be smooth in the initial point and jointly in time; as the verified edition records, Mathlib lacks smooth dependence of flows on initial conditions. The shift needs only the contraction principle and the inverse function theorem, and \(u + \sigma(t)\varphi(u)c\) is visibly smooth in \((u, t)\): it is one explicit Euler step for Milnor’s vector field. The price is that \(\mathrm{sh}_c\) is a diffeomorphism only for small \(c\), so it moves \(y\) only to nearby points, which is all the argument uses.

  1. The shift. Let \(\varphi\) be smooth and \(L\)-Lipschitz with \(\|d\varphi\| \le L\) (a compactly supported smooth \(\varphi\) has such an \(L\) Chapter4/BumpDiffeoexists_lipschitz_of_hasCompactSupport), and \(L\|c\| < 1\). Then \(\mathrm{sh}_c\) is injective, because \(u - v = \varphi(v)c - \varphi(u)c\) has norm at most \(L\|c\|\,\|u - v\|\); surjective, because \(u \mapsto w - \varphi(u)c\) is a contraction whose fixed point solves \(\mathrm{sh}_c(u) = w\); and its inverse is smooth by the inverse function theorem, as \(d\,\mathrm{sh}_c = 1 + d\varphi \otimes c\) is invertible by the Neumann series, \(\|d\varphi \otimes c\| \le L\|c\| < 1\) Chapter4/BumpDiffeoshift_injective Chapter4/BumpDiffeoshift_surjective Chapter4/BumpDiffeoshift_symm_contDiff.
  2. Transport through a chart. For the chart \(\kappa\) at \(y\), with open image in \(V\), and \(g : V \to V\), let \(\tau(g)(p) = \kappa^{-1}(g(\kappa(p)))\) on the chart domain and \(\tau(g)(p) = p\) elsewhere Chapter4/Homogeneitytransport. If \(g\) is smooth, maps the image of \(\kappa\) into itself, and is the identity outside a compact subset \(A\) of that image, then \(\tau(g)\) is smooth: on the chart domain it is a composite of smooth maps, and near a point off the chart domain it is the identity, because \(\kappa^{-1}(A)\) is compact and hence closed. This is the single use of the Hausdorff hypothesis Chapter4/HomogeneityisClosed_image_symm_of_isCompact Chapter4/HomogeneitycontMDiff_transport. Transports of mutually inverse maps are mutually inverse Chapter4/Homogeneitytransport_transport.
  3. The local construction. Choose \(\varepsilon > 0\) with the \(\varepsilon\)-ball about \(\kappa(y)\) inside the image of \(\kappa\), let \(\varphi\) be the smooth bump equal to \(1\) on the \(\varepsilon/4\)-ball and \(0\) outside the \(\varepsilon/2\)-ball, and take \(L\) as in step 1. For \(z\) in the chart domain with \(\|\kappa(z) - \kappa(y)\| < 1/(L+1)\) put \(c = \kappa(z) - \kappa(y)\), so \(L\|c\| < 1\). With \(\sigma\) Mathlib’s smooth transition function (\(0\) on \((-\infty,0]\), \(1\) on \([1,\infty)\), values in \([0,1]\)), every \(\sigma(t)c\) is admissible. Each \(\mathrm{sh}_{\sigma(t)c}\) and its inverse are the identity outside the \(\varepsilon/2\)-ball and injective, hence map the image of \(\kappa\) into itself Chapter4/BumpDiffeomapsTo_of_eq_id_outside. So \(h = \tau(\mathrm{sh}_c)\) and each \(H(\cdot,t) = \tau(\mathrm{sh}_{\sigma(t)c})\) are diffeomorphisms; \(H\) is jointly smooth Chapter4/HomogeneitycontMDiff_transport_shift; \(H(\cdot,0) = \mathrm{id}\), \(H(\cdot,1) = h\), and \(h(y) = \kappa^{-1}(\kappa(y) + c) = z\) because \(\varphi(\kappa(y)) = 1\) Chapter4/Homogeneityeventually_isotopic.
  4. Globalization. The relation is reflexive (the identity), transitive (\(H_2(H_1(x,t),t)\)) and symmetric (\(h^{-1}(H(x,1-t))\)), each construction keeping every slice a diffeomorphism Chapter4/HomogeneityIsotopic.refl Chapter4/HomogeneityIsotopic.trans Chapter4/HomogeneityIsotopic.symm. By step 3 the class of \(y\) and its complement are open, and preconnectedness makes the class all of \(N\) Chapter4/Homogeneityisotopic_of_preconnected.

V4.5 Diffeomorphisms preserve regular values

Lemma. Let \(M\), \(N\) be smooth manifolds without boundary, \(f : M \to N\) smooth, \(h\) a diffeomorphism of \(N\) and \(y\) a regular value of \(f\). Then \(h(y)\) is a regular value of \(h \circ f\), and \((h \circ f)^{-1}(h(y)) = f^{-1}(y)\). Chapter4/DegreeIsRegularValue.diffeomorph_comp Chapter4/Degreepreimage_diffeomorph_comp

The chain rule on \(h^{-1} \circ h = \mathrm{id}\) makes \(dh\) injective, hence onto, being an endomorphism of the model space Chapter4/Degreesurjective_mfderiv_diffeomorph; then \(d(h \circ f)_x = dh_{f(x)} \circ df_x\) is a composite of surjections.

V4.6 The Theorem of §4, first assertion: the parity does not depend on the regular value

Theorem (§4, first assertion). Let \(M\) be a compact, Hausdorff, second countable smooth manifold without boundary, \(N\) a Hausdorff, preconnected smooth manifold without boundary of the same dimension, and \(f : M \to N\) smooth. If \(y\) and \(z\) are regular values of \(f\), then \(\#f^{-1}(y) + \#f^{-1}(z)\) is even. Chapter4/Degreeeven_ncard_add_ncard_of_isRegularValue

Proof, as in the book. V4.4 gives \(h\) and \(H\) with \(h(y) = z\), and \(F(x,t) = H(f(x),t)\) is a smooth homotopy from \(f\) to \(h \circ f\). The value \(z\) is regular for \(f\) by hypothesis and for \(h \circ f\) by V4.5, with \((h \circ f)^{-1}(z) = f^{-1}(y)\); the Homotopy Lemma at \(z\) gives the parity. The slice-wise diffeomorphism clause of V4.4 is not needed here; Chapter 5 uses it (V5.5).

V4.7 The degree modulo 2

For any map \(f : M \to N\), \[\deg_2 f = \#f^{-1}(y_0) \bmod 2, \qquad y_0 \text{ a regular value of } f \text{ chosen by the axiom of choice},\] and \(\deg_2 f = 0\) if \(f\) has no regular value Chapter4/DegreedegMod2. For smooth \(f\) on a second countable \(M\), Brown’s theorem supplies a regular value whenever \(N\) is nonempty, so there the junk value serves only \(N = \emptyset\).

Theorem. For \(M\), \(N\), \(f\) as in V4.6 and every regular value \(y\) of \(f\), \(\deg_2 f = \#f^{-1}(y) \bmod 2\). Chapter4/DegreedegMod2_eq

The first assertion compares \(y\) with the chosen \(y_0\), and an even sum means equal residues Chapter4/DegreenatCast_zmod_two_eq_of_even_add.

V4.8 The Theorem of §4, second assertion: homotopy invariance

Theorem (§4, second assertion). For \(M\), \(N\) as in V4.6 and \(F : M \times \mathbb R \to N\) smooth, \(\deg_2 F(\cdot,0) = \deg_2 F(\cdot,1)\). Chapter4/DegreedegMod2_eq_of_homotopy

Proof. If \(N\) is nonempty, the two ends have a common regular value: those of \(F(\cdot,0)\) form an open set by local constancy Chapter4/DegreeisOpen_isRegularValue, nonempty because dense by Brown’s theorem, and those of \(F(\cdot,1)\) are dense, hence meet it Chapter4/Degreeexists_common_isRegularValue. V4.7 and the Homotopy Lemma at that value conclude. If \(N\) is empty, neither end has a regular value and both degrees are \(0\) by definition.

V4.9 Maps of nonzero degree are onto

Corollary. For \(M\), \(N\), \(f\) as in V4.6, if \(\deg_2 f \ne 0\) then \(f\) is surjective. Chapter4/Degreesurjective_of_degMod2_ne_zero

A point outside the image is a regular value with empty fibre and would give \(\deg_2 f = 0\) Chapter4/DegreedegMod2_eq_zero_of_notMem_range.

What the formalization taught us

  • The induction statement must be general. Sard is proved for all finite-dimensional targets and all Haar measures, because the induction passes to hyperplanes of both domain and target Chapter3/BasicSardStatement.
  • The zero target is a genuine special case. There a Haar measure is a multiple of the point mass; the theorem holds only because \(C = \emptyset\), and this is settled before the main argument Chapter3/SardcritSet_eq_empty_of_subsingleton Chapter3/SardsardStatement.
  • Measurability is needed once, for Fubini in Step 1, and comes from a closed-ball neighbourhood and the closedness of \(C\) Chapter3/BasicisCompact_critSet_inter Chapter3/Step1step1_local.
  • Milnor proves more than he uses. Step 1 needs half of the block-matrix remark, Step 2 only \(df = 0\) on \(C_k\) Chapter3/Step1step1_local Chapter3/Step2fderiv_eq_zero_of_mem_vanishSet.
  • The cube count is a dimension estimate, with Taylor’s constant lacking its factorial, balls for cubes, and \(k = n\) Chapter3/Step3measure_image_vanishSet_inter_eq_zero Chapter3/Step3norm_sub_le_of_iteratedFDeriv_eq_zero.
  • Brown’s theorem has one hidden hypothesis, second countability of the source; no Hausdorff property, no dimension relation, one chart of the target Chapter2/Browndense_regularValues.
  • Regularity on the boundary is transversality: a kernel vector with nonzero time component, which needs \(\dim M = \dim N\) Chapter4/Homotopycylinder_transversality.
  • Second countability enters the Homotopy Lemma only through Brown’s theorem for the homotopy, on the noncompact \(M \times \mathbb R\) Chapter4/Homotopyhomotopy_lemma.
  • A flow is replaced by one Euler step, \(u \mapsto u + \sigma(t)\varphi(u)c\), still an isotopy through diffeomorphisms; Hausdorff is used once, to make the image of a compact ball under the inverse chart closed Chapter4/Homogeneityeventually_isotopic Chapter4/HomogeneityisClosed_image_symm_of_isCompact.
  • The degree is a chosen parity with a junk value, so homotopy invariance (V4.8) treats \(N = \emptyset\) separately; “connected” is formalized as preconnected Chapter4/DegreedegMod2 Chapter4/DegreedegMod2_eq_of_homotopy.

Part III. Orientation and the Brouwer degree (Milnor §5)

Mathlib has orientations of vector spaces but no oriented manifolds, no sign of a derivative and no degree. This part builds all three and follows Milnor’s §5 to the hairy ball theorem. Most proofs are short once the definitions are in place; the exception is Lemma 1, which Milnor proves by walking along an arc of a one-manifold and watching an oriented tangent vector turn from inward to outward. The arcs supplied by the formal Appendix are only homeomorphisms onto intervals, with no derivative, so the walk is redone with local coordinates and monotone functions. That argument fills a third of the chapter and is the centre of this part.

Map. - Chapter5/OrSign: the sign of a linear map, the orientation of \(E \times \mathbb R\), two determinant formulas. - Chapter5/OrSignAlg: algebraic consequences of the definition of the sign. - Chapter5/Orient: oriented manifolds, the sign of a derivative and its local constancy, the orientation of \(M \times \mathbb R\). - Chapter5/DegreeAt: the signed count at a point and its local constancy. - Chapter5/ChartFun: chart functions along a one-dimensional level set; the sign of the pair map \((f, c)\). - Chapter5/MonoAt: the monotonicity sign of a real function. - Chapter5/LevelArc: transitions between chart functions; the boundary function as a chart function. - Chapter5/ArcSign: the invariant along an arc; opposite signs at the two ends. - Chapter5/LemmaOne: Lemma 1 in ambient form. - Chapter5/HomotopyInv: homotopy invariance at a common regular value (Milnor’s Lemma 2), the core of Theorem B. - Chapter5/Degree: isotopies preserve orientation, Theorem A (independence of the regular value), the degree and Theorem B. - Chapter5/LevelOrient: the orientation of a level set in a vector space. - Chapter5/HairyBall: the sphere, the antipodal map, the hairy ball theorem and its converse.

Standing conventions. \(M\) and \(N\) are smooth manifolds without boundary, modelled on finite-dimensional real normed spaces \(E\) and \(F\). Mathlib identifies \(T_xM\) with \(E\) through the chart \(\varphi_x\) at \(x\), and \(df_x : E \to F\) is the derivative read in the charts at \(x\) and \(f(x)\) Chapter5/Orientmfd. Further hypotheses are stated with each result. From Lemma 1 on (V5.3, V5.4, V5.6, V5.7) the formal statements also require \(E\) and \(F\) to lie in a common universe, the size condition of Part 0 (§0.10), harmless for Euclidean spaces; the displayed statements record it.

V5.0 Orientations: signs of linear maps and oriented manifolds

The verified edition asks its reader to confirm one definition of this chapter, that of an oriented manifold. It rests on the sign of a linear map.

The sign of a linear map

For Mathlib, an orientation of \(E\) with respect to \(n\) indices is a class of nonzero alternating \(n\)-forms on \(E\) up to positive multiples, and each class carries a representative \(\omega_a\) picked by choice. When \(\dim E = n\) every \(n\)-form is a multiple of any nonzero one, and a nonzero one vanishes on no basis Chapter5/OrSignexists_eq_smul_of_finrank Chapter5/OrSignne_zero_of_basis.

Let \(a\) orient \(E\) and \(b\) orient \(F\), and fix by choice a tuple \(v = (v_1, \dots, v_n)\) with \(\omega_a(v) \neq 0\) Chapter5/OrSignorTuple. The sign of a linear map \(T : E \to F\) is \[\operatorname{sign}_{a,b}(T) = \operatorname{sgn}\bigl(\omega_b(Tv_1, \dots, Tv_n)\,\omega_a(v_1, \dots, v_n)\bigr) \in \{1, -1, 0\}\] Chapter5/OrSignorSign, the sign of a ratio written as a product. The choices disappear at once. If \(\omega\), \(\eta\) are any representatives of \(a\), \(b\) and the pullback of \(\eta\) by \(T\) is \(c\,\omega\), then \(\operatorname{sign}_{a,b}(T) = \operatorname{sgn} c\), with no hypothesis on dimensions Chapter5/OrSignorSign_eq_sgn. When \(\dim E = n\) the sign can be computed with any representatives on any tuple where \(\omega\) does not vanish Chapter5/OrSignorSign_eq_sgn_mul. Every sign in the chapter is computed through these two lemmas.

Assume \(\dim E = \dim F = n\). For \(S : F \to G\) and an orientation \(d\) of \(G\) the sign is multiplicative, \(\operatorname{sign}_{a,d}(ST) = \operatorname{sign}_{b,d}(S)\operatorname{sign}_{a,b}(T)\); it equals \(1\) for the identity, and changes when either orientation is reversed Chapter5/OrSignorSign_comp Chapter5/OrSignorSign_id Chapter5/OrSignorSign_neg_right. It is nonzero exactly when \(T\) is bijective, since in bases \(e\) of \(E\) and \(e'\) of \(F\) the constant \(c\) is a nonzero multiple of \(\det_{e'}(Te_1, \dots, Te_n)\) Chapter5/OrSignorSign_ne_zero_iff. A companion file adds the expected algebra: values \(\pm 1\) on bijections, \(\operatorname{sign}_{a,b} = \operatorname{sign}_{b,a}\) for bijective endomorphisms, and \(\operatorname{sign}_{a,a}(T) = \operatorname{sgn}\det T\) for \(n > 0\) Chapter5/OrSignAlgorSign_eq_one_or_neg_one Chapter5/OrSignAlgorSign_symm Chapter5/OrSignAlgorSign_self_eq_sgn_det'.

Explicit representatives come from bases: with \(\epsilon_e(a) = 1\) if the basis \(e\) is positive for \(a\) and \(-1\) otherwise, \(\epsilon_e(a)\det_e\) represents \(a\) Chapter5/OrSignorEpsB Chapter5/OrSignrayOfNeZero_orEpsB_det. The basis used is usually the reference basis, which Mathlib extracts by choice from the bare fact \(\dim E = n\). It need not be any standard basis. Among the orientations defined in this part, only that of the sphere depends on which basis was chosen (V5.9).

The orientation \(\hat a\) of \(E \times \mathbb R\) is represented by \(\epsilon_e(a)\) times the determinant of the basis \((e_1, 0), \dots, (e_n, 0), (0, 1)\), \(e\) the reference basis. So a positive basis of \(E\) followed by \((0, 1)\) is positive Chapter5/OrSignorProd. Two determinant formulas are proved for it.

  • Block formula. If \(\dim E = \dim F = n\) and \(T(v, t) = (Av + tw,\ ct)\), then \(\operatorname{sign}_{\hat a, \hat b}(T) = \operatorname{sign}_{a,b}(A)\,\operatorname{sgn}(c)\), because the matrix of \(T\) is block triangular Chapter5/OrSignorSign_orProd.
  • Kernel formula. Let \(\dim E = n + 1\), \(\dim F = n\), and let \(T, T' : E \to F \times \mathbb R\) have the same surjective first component \(P\). For every \(v \neq 0\) with \(Pv = 0\), \[\operatorname{sign}_{a, \hat b}(T)\,\operatorname{sign}_{a, \hat b}(T') = \operatorname{sgn}\bigl((Tv)_2\,(T'v)_2\bigr).\] The proof uses a right inverse \(R\) of \(P\) and the basis \((v, Re'_1, \dots, Re'_n)\) of \(E\), \(e'\) the reference basis of \(F\). Against it and the product basis of \(F \times \mathbb R\), either map \(S\) has first column \((0, \dots, 0, (Sv)_2)\), and deleting that column and the last row leaves the identity. So its determinant is \((-1)^n (Sv)_2\), and all other factors appear in both signs and cancel Chapter5/OrSignorSign_prodReal_mul.

The kernel formula carries Lemma 1; the block formula carries products, Lemma 2 (V5.4) and the isotopy argument of V5.5.

Oriented manifolds

Definition. An orientation of \(M\) assigns to each \(x\) an orientation \(o_x\) of \(E\) such that every \(x\) has a neighbourhood whose points \(y\) satisfy \[\operatorname{sign}_{o_y,\, o_x}\bigl(d(\varphi_x)_y\bigr) = 1\] Chapter5/OrientOrient. Since \(T_yM\) is \(E\) read through \(\varphi_y\), the map \(d(\varphi_x)_y\) is the derivative of the transition \(\varphi_x \circ \varphi_y^{-1}\) at \(\varphi_y(y)\). So the condition says that near each point, the transitions into the chart at that point carry the orientation at \(y\) to that at \(x\). (Mathlib’s chart at \(x\) is a chart of the atlas whose domain contains \(x\); it need not send \(x\) to \(0\).) Equivalently, \(\varphi_x\) is orientation preserving near \(x\) when its target \(E\) is given the constant orientation \(o_x\). This is Milnor’s definition (p. 26), up to composing each chart with a linear isomorphism from \((E, o_x)\) to \(\mathbb R^m\) with its standard orientation. There is no oriented atlas, and the dimension \(n\) is a parameter; theorems add \(\dim E = n\).

The sign of \(f\) at \(x\) is \(\operatorname{sign} df_x = \operatorname{sign}_{o_x,\, o'_{f(x)}}(df_x)\) Chapter5/OrientsignAt. When \(\dim E = \dim F = n\) it is nonzero exactly when \(df_x\) is bijective, hence \(\pm 1\) at regular points Chapter5/OrientsignAt_ne_zero_iff Chapter5/OrientIsRegularPoint.signAt_ne_zero.

The product \(M \times \mathbb R\) is oriented by \((x, t) \mapsto \hat o_x\) Chapter5/OrientOrient.prodReal. The formal proof has to check the condition: the chart at \((x, t)\) is \(\varphi_x \times \mathrm{id}\), and the block formula reduces the condition to that of \(M\). The same formula computes the sign of any map \(M \times \mathbb R \to N \times \mathbb R\) whose derivative has the form \((v, t) \mapsto (Av + tw,\ ct)\) Chapter5/OrientsignAt_prodReal.

V5.1 Local constancy of the sign

Theorem. Let \(\dim E = \dim F = n\), let \(M\) and \(N\) be oriented, \(f : M \to N\) smooth, and \(x_0\) a regular point of \(f\). Then \(\operatorname{sign} df_x = \operatorname{sign} df_{x_0}\) for all \(x\) near \(x_0\) Chapter5/Orienteventually_signAt_eq.

The proof is written for \(f\) smooth only on an open \(W \ni x_0\), a variant that Lemma 1 needs Chapter5/Orienteventually_signAt_eq_of_contMDiffOn.

The idea. In the fixed charts at \(x_0\) and \(f(x_0)\), the sign of \(df_x\) is the sign of the derivative of the local representative, measured against the fixed orientations \(o_{x_0}\) and \(o'_{f(x_0)}\). That is the sign of a determinant, continuous in \(x\) and nonzero at \(x_0\).

The proof as formalized. 1. A family \(L(u)\) of linear maps, continuous at \(u_0\) with \(\operatorname{sign}_{a,b} L(u_0) \neq 0\), has constant sign near \(u_0\): in the reference bases \(e\), \(e'\) of \(E\), \(F\) the sign is \(\operatorname{sgn}\bigl(\epsilon_{e'}(b)\det_{e'}(L(u)e)\,\epsilon_e(a)\bigr)\) Chapter5/Orienteventually_orSign_eq_of_continuousAt. 2. Let \(g = \varphi_{f(x_0)} \circ f \circ \varphi_{x_0}^{-1}\), smooth on an open \(U \subseteq E\). For \(x\) near \(x_0\) the chain rule gives \(d(\varphi_{f(x_0)})_{f(x)} \circ df_x = dg_{\varphi_{x_0}(x)} \circ d(\varphi_{x_0})_x\). 3. Take signs. By the orientation condition of \(N\) at \(f(x_0)\), applied at \(f(x)\), which is near \(f(x_0)\), the left side has sign \(\operatorname{sign} df_x\). By the condition of \(M\) at \(x_0\), the right side has sign \(\operatorname{sign}_{o_{x_0}, o'_{f(x_0)}}(dg_{\varphi_{x_0}(x)})\). Step 1 applies to \(u \mapsto dg_u\), continuous because \(g\) is \(C^\infty\) on \(U\).

What the book leaves implicit. This continuity is used without comment on p. 27. The orientation conditions are used only at \(x_0\) and \(f(x_0)\), which is why the local form of the definition suffices.

V5.2 The signed count and its local constancy

For \(y \in N\) put \(\deg(f; y) = \sum_{x \in f^{-1}(y)} \operatorname{sign} df_x\) Chapter5/DegreeAtdegAt. This is Mathlib’s finite sum, which is \(0\) by convention when infinitely many terms are nonzero. For a smooth map on a compact manifold, with \(\dim E = \dim F\) and \(N\) a \(T_1\) space, the preimage of a regular value is finite (V1.3) Chapter1/RegularValueIsRegularValue.finite_preimage, and outside the image the count is \(0\) Chapter5/DegreeAtdegAt_of_notMem_range.

Theorem. Let \(M\) be compact and Hausdorff, \(N\) Hausdorff, \(\dim E = \dim F = n\), both oriented, \(f\) smooth and \(y\) a regular value. Then \(\deg(f; y') = \deg(f; y)\) for all \(y'\) near \(y\) Chapter5/DegreeAtIsRegularValue.eventually_degAt_eq.

The points \(y'\) need not be regular. Chapter 1 proves a weighted form of the local constancy of \(\#f^{-1}(y)\) (V1.4), valid for any integer weight that is locally constant near each point of \(f^{-1}(y)\) Chapter1/RegularValueIsRegularValue.eventually_finsum_preimage_eq, and V5.1 says that the sign is such a weight.

V5.3 Lemma 1 in ambient form

Theorem. Let \(\dim E = n + 1\) and \(\dim F = n\), with \(E\) and \(F\) in a common universe, let \(M\) and \(N\) be Hausdorff and oriented, \(f : M \to N\) smooth with a regular value \(y\), and \(g : M \to \mathbb R\) smooth. Suppose that at every \(x\) with \(f(x) = y\) and \(g(x) = 0\) some \(v\) has \(df_x v = 0\) and \(dg_x v \neq 0\), and that \(f^{-1}(y) \cap \{g \ge 0\}\) is compact. Then \(f^{-1}(y) \cap \{g = 0\}\) is finite and \[\sum_{x \in f^{-1}(y) \cap \{g = 0\}} \operatorname{sign} d(f, g)_x = 0,\] the signs of the pair map \((f, g) : M \to N \times \mathbb R\) being taken for the orientation of \(M\) and the product orientation of \(N \times \mathbb R\) Chapter5/LemmaOnelemmaOne_ambient' Chapter5/LemmaOnelemmaOne_ambient.

Finiteness is stated because for an infinite set the finite-sum convention would make the identity trivially true. The number \(0\) need not be a regular value of \(g\). The transversality condition stands in for Milnor’s hypothesis that \(y\) is a regular value of \(f|\partial X\), in the form that Lemma 4 of §2 (V2.6) uses. Only the Hausdorff property of \(M\) is used, through the level set, which the Appendix needs to be Hausdorff; that of \(N\) is a hypothesis of the statement which the proof never uses.

Relation to Milnor. His Lemma 1 concerns an abstract compact \(X\) with boundary and asserts \(\deg(f|\partial X; y) = 0\) for the boundary orientation. Here \(X = \{g \ge 0\}\) sits inside the boundaryless \(M\), and the boundary signs are those of the ambient pair map. For \(X\) in an oriented vector space, with \(0\) a regular value of \(g\), Chapter 6 proves \(\operatorname{sign} d(f|\partial X)_x = (-1)^{n+1}\operatorname{sign} d(f, g)_x\) for the orientation of V5.8, at every \(x \in \partial X\) where \(f\) is differentiable Chapter6/LevelSignsignAt_levelOrient_eq'. Under the hypotheses of the theorem above it deduces Milnor’s form, \(\deg(f|\partial X; y) = 0\) Chapter6/LevelSigndegAt_levelOrient_eq_zero.

The idea. \(A = f^{-1}(y) \cap \{g \ge 0\}\) is a compact one-manifold with boundary \(B = f^{-1}(y) \cap \{g = 0\}\). The Appendix pairs the points of \(B\) by arcs, and the two ends of an arc have opposite signs. Milnor proves the last claim by orienting the arc and following its positive unit tangent vector, which points inward at one end and outward at the other. The formal arcs have no tangent vector. Local coordinates of the level set replace it, and “points inward” becomes “the coordinate increases”.

Chart functions

Let \(\dim E = n + 1\), \(\dim F = n\), \(f\) smooth and \(y\) a regular value. At \(m \in f^{-1}(y)\) the kernel \(K_m\) of \(df_m\) is a line Chapter5/ChartFunexists_ne_zero_of_surjective Chapter5/ChartFunexists_smul_eq_of_ker. A chart function at \(m\) is a function \(c : M \to \mathbb R\), smooth on an open \(W \ni m\), with \(dc_m \neq 0\) on \(K_m \setminus 0\) Chapter5/ChartFunChartFun. The pair map \((f, c) : M \to N \times \mathbb R\) then has surjective derivative at \(m\) Chapter5/ChartFunisRegularPoint, so \(\varepsilon_c(m) = \operatorname{sign} d(f, c)_m\) is \(\pm 1\) Chapter5/ChartFunsign Chapter5/ChartFunsign_ne_zero. Four facts are proved.

  1. Two chart functions. For \(v \in K_m \setminus 0\), \(\ \varepsilon_c(m)\,\varepsilon_{c'}(m) = \operatorname{sgn}\bigl(dc_m(v)\,dc'_m(v)\bigr)\): the kernel formula with \(P = df_m\) Chapter5/ChartFunsign_mul_sign.
  2. Local constancy. Near \(m\), \(\operatorname{sign} d(f, c) = \varepsilon_c(m)\) by V5.1 for the pair map on \(W\) Chapter5/ChartFuneventually_signAt_eq, and \(c\) remains a chart function at nearby points Chapter5/ChartFunmove Chapter5/ChartFuneventually_move.
  3. Existence. A coordinate \(\lambda \circ \varphi_m\) of the chart at \(m\) is a chart function, for a coordinate functional \(\lambda\) of the reference basis that does not vanish on \(d(\varphi_m)_m(K_m)\) Chapter5/ChartFunexists_chartFun.
  4. The boundary function. At a point of \(f^{-1}(y) \cap \{g = 0\}\) the function \(g\) is a chart function with \(W = M\); this is exactly the transversality hypothesis Chapter5/LevelArcgChartFun.

The monotonicity sign

Let \(s\) be a nontrivial interval containing \(t_0\) and \(h : \mathbb R \to \mathbb R\). Put \(\mu_s(h, t_0) = 1\) if \(h\) is strictly increasing on \(s \cap (t_0 - \delta, t_0 + \delta)\) for some \(\delta > 0\), and \(-1\) otherwise Chapter5/MonoAtmonoAt. A continuous injective function on an interval is strictly monotone, by a lemma of the Appendix Appendix/OneManifoldstrictMonoOn_or_strictAntiOn_of_ordConnected, so for such \(h\) the value \(-1\) means strictly decreasing Chapter5/MonoAtexists_strictAntiOn_of_monoAt_eq_neg_one. The sign is locally constant where \(h\) is strictly monotone, and it depends only on \(h\) near \(t_0\) Chapter5/MonoAtmonoAt_eq_of_near Chapter5/MonoAtmonoAt_congr. Composition with a strictly increasing function preserves it, and composition with a strictly decreasing one reverses it Chapter5/MonoAtmonoAt_comp_of_strictMonoOn Chapter5/MonoAtmonoAt_comp_of_strictAntiOn. Finally, let \(h\) be continuous and injective near \(t_0\), with its minimum over \(s\) at \(t_0\). Then \(\mu_s(h, t_0) = 1\) if \(t_0\) is the left end of \(s\), and \(-1\) if it is the right end Chapter5/MonoAtmonoAt_eq_one_of_left_min Chapter5/MonoAtmonoAt_eq_neg_one_of_right_min.

Transitions between chart functions

Let \(S\) be a one-manifold and \(\iota : S \to M\) smooth with \(f \circ \iota = y\), the image of each \(d\iota_a\) being \(K_{\iota(a)}\); for \(S = f^{-1}(y)\) this is Lemma 2 of §2 (V2.3). Then \(v = d\iota_a(1)\) is a nonzero vector of the kernel line Chapter5/LevelArcmfd_ι_one_ne_zero Chapter5/LevelArcmfd_f_mfd_ι.

Lemma. Let \(c\), \(c'\) be chart functions at \(\iota(a)\). There are an open \(V \ni a\) on which \(c \circ \iota\) is injective, a set \(D\) (in fact an open interval) and a function \(k\), with \(c(\iota(z)) \in D\) and \(k(c(\iota(z))) = c'(\iota(z))\) for \(z \in V\), such that either \(k\) is strictly increasing on \(D\) and \(dc(v)\,dc'(v) > 0\), or \(k\) is strictly decreasing on \(D\) and \(dc(v)\,dc'(v) < 0\) Chapter5/LevelArcexists_transition.

Since \(d(c \circ \iota)_a(1) = dc(v) \neq 0\), the inverse function theorem (V1.1) makes \(c \circ \iota\) a local diffeomorphism \(\Phi\) near \(a\) Chapter1/InverseFunctionisLocalDiffeomorphAt_of_isInvertible_mfderiv. The function \(k = c' \circ \iota \circ \Phi^{-1}\) has derivative \(dc'(v)/dc(v)\) at \(c(\iota(a))\). The derivative is continuous, so of one sign on an interval \(D\), and the mean value theorem makes \(k\) strictly monotone there.

The invariant along an arc

An arc of \(A\), in the sense of the Appendix, is a homeomorphism \(\gamma\) from a bounded nontrivial interval \(J\) onto an open subset of \(A\), under which the points of \(B\) correspond to the endpoints of \(J\) that lie in \(J\) Appendix/OneManifoldArc. It is an arc from \(p\) if \(\gamma(0) = p\) and \(J \subseteq [0, \infty)\) Appendix/OneManifoldIsFrom. Nothing about \(\gamma\) is smooth.

Write \(\beta(x) = \operatorname{sign} d(f, g)_x\) Chapter5/ArcSignbdrySign. For \(t \in J\) choose a chart function \(c_t\) at \(\gamma(t)\) Chapter5/ArcSigncfAt and put \[\varepsilon(t) = \varepsilon_{c_t}(\gamma(t)) \cdot \mu_J(c_t \circ \gamma,\ t)\] Chapter5/ArcSignarcEps. Up to a constant sign, \(\varepsilon_c\) tells whether \(c\) increases in the positive direction of Milnor’s orientation of the arc, and \(\mu_J\) tells whether \(c\) increases with the parameter. The product compares that orientation with the parameter, and \(c\) drops out. This takes three steps.

  1. Any chart function will do. For every chart function \(c\) at \(\gamma(t)\), \(\ \varepsilon_c(\gamma(t))\,\mu_J(c \circ \gamma, t) = \varepsilon(t)\) Chapter5/ArcSignsign_mul_monoAt_eq. Near \(t\) the function \(c \circ \gamma\) is continuous and injective, hence strictly monotone Chapter5/ArcSignexists_ball_good, and \(c_t \circ \gamma = k \circ (c \circ \gamma)\) for the transition \(k\). If \(k\) increases, \(\mu_J\) is unchanged and \(\varepsilon_c = \varepsilon_{c_t}\) by the first fact about chart functions; if \(k\) decreases, both factors change sign.
  2. Local constancy. \(\varepsilon\) is constant near each \(t_0 \in J\) Chapter5/ArcSigneventually_arcEps_eq. Keep \(c = c_{t_0}\). For \(t\) near \(t_0\) it is a chart function at \(\gamma(t)\) with the same sign, by the second fact, and \(\mu_J(c \circ \gamma, t) = \mu_J(c \circ \gamma, t_0)\) because \(c \circ \gamma\) is strictly monotone around \(t_0\). Step 1 at \(t\) finishes.
  3. The ends. If the arc from \(p\) is closed, \(J = [0, T]\), then \(q = \gamma(T)\) lies in \(B\) and \(\beta(p) = -\beta(q)\) Chapter5/ArcSignbdrySign_end_eq_neg. Indeed \(\varepsilon\) is constant on the connected interval \(J\). At both ends use the chart function \(g\). Since \(g \ge 0\) on \(A\) and \(g(p) = g(q) = 0\), the function \(g \circ \gamma\) has its minimum at both ends of \(J\), so \(\mu_J(g \circ \gamma, 0) = 1\) and \(\mu_J(g \circ \gamma, T) = -1\). Hence \(\beta(p) = \varepsilon(0) = \varepsilon(T) = -\beta(q)\).

The proof of Lemma 1 as formalized

  1. \(S = f^{-1}(y)\) is a one-manifold (V2.2) Chapter2/LevelSetisSliceSubmanifold_preimage with tangent line \(K_x\) at \(x\) (V2.3) Chapter2/LevelSetmem_range_mfderiv_val_iff. Inside it, \(A = S \cap \{g \ge 0\}\) is a manifold with boundary \(B = S \cap \{g = 0\}\) (V2.6), all of whose charts send exactly \(B\) to \(0\) Chapter2/WithBoundaryisHalfSliceSubmanifold_levelSet Appendix/HalfSpaceIsHalfSliceSubmanifold.boundaryCompatible. It is compact by hypothesis.
  2. For \(p \in B\) the Appendix supplies a closed arc from \(p\), whose image is then the whole component of \(p\) Appendix/OneManifoldexists_closed_arc Appendix/OneManifoldIsFrom.source_eq_of_mem. That component meets \(B\) in exactly \(\{p, q\}\), with \(q = \gamma(T) \neq p\) Appendix/OneManifoldIsFrom.boundary_inter_component. The arc argument, with \(\iota\) the inclusion of \(S\), gives \(\beta(p) = -\beta(q)\).
  3. Choosing \(q\) for each \(p\) defines \(\pi : B \to B\). It is an involution: \(\pi(\pi(p))\) lies in the component of \(p\), hence in \(\{p, \pi(p)\}\), and it differs from \(\pi(p)\).
  4. \(B\) is finite: it is closed in the compact \(A\), and each arc at a boundary point meets \(B\) only there Appendix/OneManifoldfinite_boundary. As \(\pi\) permutes \(B\), \(\sum_B \beta = \sum_B \beta \circ \pi = -\sum_B \beta\), so the sum vanishes, and the inclusion carries it to \(M\).

Where the formal proof departs from Milnor. No orientation of the arc and no tangent field is constructed, and boundary points are paired by “the other end of my component” rather than by a decomposition into arcs and circles. Both changes come from the Appendix being proved for topological one-manifolds (V.A). The monotonicity sign is the price: two hundred lines of real analysis replace Milnor’s one-line observation about the unit tangent field.

V5.4 Theorem B at a common regular value (Milnor’s Lemma 2)

Theorem. Let \(M\) be compact, Hausdorff and second countable, \(N\) Hausdorff, \(\dim E = \dim F = n\) with \(E\) and \(F\) in a common universe, both oriented, \(\Phi : M \times \mathbb R \to N\) smooth, \(f_0 = \Phi(\cdot, 0)\), \(f_1 = \Phi(\cdot, 1)\), and \(y\) a regular value of \(f_0\) and of \(f_1\). Then \(\deg(f_0; y) = \deg(f_1; y)\) Chapter5/HomotopyInvdegAt_eq_of_homotopy.

In the book this is Lemma 2 of §5, Theorem B at a common regular value, from which Milnor derives both theorems; Theorem B for the degree itself is the second item of V5.7. The letters A and B here are Milnor’s (p. 28); the docstrings of the formal source use the opposite lettering. The section comes before Theorem A because the proof of A uses it, in the formal text as in the book.

The idea. Apply Lemma 1 to the cylinder \(M \times [0, 1] = \{t(1 - t) \ge 0\}\) in \(M \times \mathbb R\), whose boundary signs are \(\operatorname{sign} df_0\) and \(-\operatorname{sign} df_1\). A perturbation of \(y\) handles the general case.

The proof as formalized. 1. Suppose first that \(y\) is also a regular value of \(\Phi\) Chapter5/HomotopyInvdegAt_eq_of_homotopy_of_isRegularValue. Orient \(M \times \mathbb R\) by \(\hat o\) and take \(g(x, t) = t(1 - t)\), with \(dg_{(x,t)}(v, s) = (1 - 2t)s\) Chapter5/HomotopyInvmfd_cyl. At \((x, c) \in \Phi^{-1}(y)\) with \(c \in \{0, 1\}\), V4.2 gives a kernel vector of \(d\Phi\) with nonzero \(\mathbb R\)-component \(s\), on which \(dg = \pm s \neq 0\) Chapter4/Homotopycylinder_transversality. The set \(\Phi^{-1}(y) \cap (M \times [0, 1])\) is compact, so Lemma 1 applies. 2. The boundary set is the disjoint union of \(f_0^{-1}(y) \times \{0\}\) and \(f_1^{-1}(y) \times \{1\}\), both finite (V1.3). 3. Write \(f_c = \Phi(\cdot, c)\). At \((x, c)\) the derivative of \((\Phi, g)\) is \((v, s) \mapsto \bigl(d(f_c)_x v + s\,w,\ (1 - 2c)s\bigr)\) with \(w = d\Phi_{(x,c)}(0, 1)\) Chapter5/HomotopyInvmfd_prod_apply. The block formula gives the sign \(\operatorname{sign} d(f_c)_x \cdot \operatorname{sgn}(1 - 2c)\), and Lemma 1 reads \(\deg(f_0; y) - \deg(f_1; y) = 0\). 4. In general, V1.4 (strengthened) and V5.2 give a neighbourhood \(U\) of \(y\) consisting of regular values of \(f_0\) and \(f_1\) with the same signed counts Chapter1/RegularValueIsRegularValue.eventually_isRegularValue_and_ncard Chapter5/DegreeAtIsRegularValue.eventually_degAt_eq. Brown’s theorem (V3.3) gives a regular value of \(\Phi\) in \(U\) Chapter2/Browndense_regularValues, where steps 1–3 apply.

One function presents both ends of the cylinder, so the two-function Lemma 4 for the cylinder (V4.1), which served the degree modulo 2, is not needed. Second countability enters only in step 4, through Brown’s theorem, which is also stated for model spaces in a common universe.

V5.5 Isotopies preserve orientation

What the book leaves implicit. Milnor observes that a diffeomorphism isotopic to the identity preserves orientation. The formal proof needs every stage of the isotopy to be a diffeomorphism, and the Homogeneity Lemma (V4.4) was strengthened to supply it. Points \(y\), \(z\) are isotopic if there are a diffeomorphism \(h\) with \(h(y) = z\) and a smooth \(H : N \times \mathbb R \to N\) with \(H(\cdot, 0) = \mathrm{id}\), \(H(\cdot, 1) = h\) and every \(H(\cdot, t)\) a diffeomorphism Chapter4/HomogeneityIsotopic.

Theorem. Let \(\dim F = n\), \(N\) Hausdorff and oriented, and \(y\), \(z\) isotopic. Then there are a diffeomorphism \(h\) with \(h(y) = z\) and a smooth \(H : N \times \mathbb R \to N\) with \(H(\cdot, 0) = \mathrm{id}\) and \(H(\cdot, 1) = h\) such that \(\operatorname{sign} dh_x = 1\) for all \(x \in N\) Chapter5/Degreeexists_isotopy_signAt_eq_one.

The proof keeps the \(h\) and \(H\) of the isotopy and does not use the Hausdorff property. By the block formula with \(c = 1\), the sign at \((w, t)\) of \(G(w, t) = (H(w, t), t)\), a self-map of \(N \times \mathbb R\), is that of \(H(\cdot, t)\) at \(w\) Chapter5/OrientsignAt_prodReal. It is nonzero because \(H(\cdot, t)\) is a diffeomorphism Chapter4/Degreesurjective_mfderiv_diffeomorph. So V5.1 applies to \(G\) at every point, and \(t \mapsto \operatorname{sign} d(H(\cdot, t))_x\) is locally constant on \(\mathbb R\), hence constant, equal to its value \(1\) at the identity Chapter5/DegreesignAt_id.

V5.6 Theorem A: the signed count does not depend on the regular value

For smooth \(f : M \to N\) and \(h : N \to P\), with \(P\) an oriented manifold modelled like \(N\), \(\dim E = \dim F = n\) and \(E\), \(F\) in a common universe, the chain rule for signs holds: \(\operatorname{sign} d(h \circ f)_x = \operatorname{sign} dh_{f(x)} \cdot \operatorname{sign} df_x\) Chapter5/DegreesignAt_comp.

Theorem. Let \(M\) be compact, Hausdorff and second countable, \(N\) Hausdorff and preconnected, \(\dim E = \dim F = n\) with \(E\) and \(F\) in a common universe, both oriented, and \(f : M \to N\) smooth. For any two regular values \(y\), \(z\) of \(f\), \(\ \deg(f; y) = \deg(f; z)\) Chapter5/DegreedegAt_eq_of_isRegularValue.

The proof as formalized is Milnor’s. 1. By V4.4 and V5.5 there are \(h\) and \(H\) with \(h(y) = z\) and \(\operatorname{sign} dh = 1\) Chapter4/Homogeneityisotopic_of_preconnected. 2. \((h \circ f)^{-1}(z) = f^{-1}(y)\) Chapter4/Degreepreimage_diffeomorph_comp, and the chain rule makes the signs agree, so \(\deg(h \circ f; z) = \deg(f; y)\). 3. \((x, t) \mapsto H(f(x), t)\) is a smooth homotopy from \(f\) to \(h \circ f\). The point \(z\) is a regular value of \(f\) by hypothesis and of \(h \circ f\) by V4.5 Chapter4/DegreeIsRegularValue.diffeomorph_comp, so Lemma 2 (V5.4) gives \(\deg(f; z) = \deg(h \circ f; z)\).

“Preconnected” admits the empty manifold, harmlessly.

V5.7 The Brouwer degree

The degree of \(f\) is \(\deg(f; y_0)\) for a regular value \(y_0\) picked by choice, and \(0\) if there is none Chapter5/Degreedeg. It is a number for every map; the theorems say when it is Milnor’s. Under the hypotheses of V5.6:

  • \(\deg f = \deg(f; y)\) for every regular value \(y\), the final form of Theorem A Chapter5/Degreedeg_eq;
  • smoothly homotopic maps have the same degree, Theorem B as Milnor states it Chapter5/Degreedeg_eq_of_homotopy: for \(N \neq \emptyset\) the two ends have a common regular value, by Brown’s theorem and the openness of regular values (V1.4) Chapter4/Degreeexists_common_isRegularValue, where V5.4 applies, and for \(N = \emptyset\) both degrees are \(0\) by definition;
  • a map of nonzero degree is surjective, since a point outside the image is a regular value with empty preimage Chapter5/Degreedeg_eq_zero_of_notMem_range Chapter5/Degreesurjective_of_deg_ne_zero.

For \(N\) compact, Hausdorff, second countable, preconnected, nonempty and oriented, with \(\dim F = n\), the identity has degree \(1\) Chapter5/Degreedeg_id.

V5.8 The induced orientation of a level set

Let \(E\) have dimension \(n + 1\) and orientation \(a_0\), let \(\dim Z = n\), and let \(g : E \to \mathbb R\) be smooth with \(0\) a regular value. By V2.2, \(S = g^{-1}(0)\) is a manifold modelled on \(Z\); let \(d\iota_q : Z \to E\) be the derivative of its inclusion at \(q\).

  • The contraction of an \((n+1)\)-form \(\omega\) by \(\nu \in E\) along a linear \(T : Z \to E\) is the \(n\)-form \((z_1, \dots, z_n) \mapsto \omega(\nu, Tz_1, \dots, Tz_n)\) Chapter5/LevelOrientcontractForm. If \(T\) is injective with image in a hyperplane \(\ker\lambda\) and \(\lambda(\nu) \neq 0\), then \((\nu, Tu_1, \dots, Tu_n)\) is a basis of \(E\) for every basis \(u\) of \(Z\), so the contraction of \(\omega \neq 0\) vanishes on no basis Chapter5/LevelOrientcontractForm_basis_ne_zero. Its class does not depend on the representative of \(a_0\) Chapter5/LevelOrientcontractOr Chapter5/LevelOrientrayOfNeZero_contractForm. A vanishing contraction would give a default value, the orientation of the reference basis; this never happens on a level set.
  • The outward vector is \(\nu(x) = -\sum_i dg_x(e_i)\,e_i\) for the reference basis \(e\) of \(E\) Chapter5/LevelOrientoutward. It is continuous in \(x\), and \(dg_x(\nu(x)) = -\sum_i dg_x(e_i)^2 < 0\) when \(dg_x \neq 0\) Chapter5/LevelOrientcontinuous_outward Chapter5/LevelOrientfderiv_outward_neg.

Theorem. The contractions of \(a_0\) by \(\nu(q)\) along \(d\iota_q\), for \(q \in S\), form an orientation of \(S\) in the sense of V5.0 Chapter5/LevelOrientlevelOrient Chapter5/LevelOrientlevelOrient_cont.

A basis \(z\) is positive at \(q\) exactly when \((\nu(q), d\iota_q z_1, \dots, d\iota_q z_n)\) is positive for \(a_0\). As \(\nu\) points out of \(X = \{g \ge 0\}\), this is Milnor’s boundary orientation of \(\partial X\), outward normal first. Milnor allows any outward vector, while the formal definition fixes one. Any \(w\) with \(dg_q(w) < 0\) gives the same orientation, since \(w\) is a positive multiple of \(\nu(q)\) plus a tangent vector, which does not change the contraction; that lemma is proved in Chapter 6, where it is needed Chapter6/SignLemmascontractForm_eq_smul.

The idea. Near \(q_0\), compare every orientation with one fixed \(n\)-form on \(Z\), through a chart of \(S\).

The proof of continuity as formalized. Fix \(q_0\), the chart \(\psi_0\) of \(S\) at \(q_0\), and \(\psi = \iota \circ \psi_0^{-1}\). 1. The chain rule gives \(d\iota_q = d\psi_{\psi_0(q)} \circ D_q\), with \(D_q = d(\psi_0)_q\) invertible and \(D_{q_0} = \mathrm{id}\) Chapter5/LevelOrientmfd_extChartAt_self. 2. Let \(\Lambda(q)\) be the contraction of \(\omega = \epsilon_e(a_0)\det_e\) by \(\nu(q)\) along \(d\psi_{\psi_0(q)}\), an \(n\)-form on the fixed space \(Z\). On the reference basis \(u\) of \(Z\), \(\Lambda(q)(u)\) is a determinant whose columns are continuous in \(q\). 3. Top forms on \(Z\) are proportional, so \(\Lambda(q) = \kappa(q)\Lambda(q_0)\) with \(\kappa(q) = \Lambda(q)(u)/\Lambda(q_0)(u)\). This is continuous and equal to \(1\) at \(q_0\), hence positive nearby. 4. The orientations at \(q\) and \(q_0\) are represented by \(\Lambda(q) \circ D_q\) and \(\Lambda(q_0)\). Evaluating the sign of \(D_q\) on \(D_q^{-1}u\) gives \(\operatorname{sgn}\bigl(\kappa(q)\Lambda(q_0)(u)^2\bigr) = 1\).

This covers level sets in a vector space only; Chapter 6 repeats the construction inside an oriented manifold (V6.1).

V5.9 The sphere and the antipodal map

The sphere \(S^n\) is the level set \(g^{-1}(0)\) of \(g(x) = \langle x, x\rangle - 1\) on Euclidean \(\mathbb R^{n+1}\), where \(dg_x(v) = 2\langle x, v\rangle\) and \(0\) is a regular value Chapter5/HairyBallfderiv_sphG Chapter5/HairyBallisRegularValue_sphG. It is a compact manifold modelled on \(\mathbb R^n\) (V2.2), preconnected for \(n \ge 1\) Chapter5/HairyBallsphS Chapter5/HairyBallpreconnectedSpace.

How the orientation of \(S^n\) is chosen. It is the level-set orientation of V5.8 for the orientation of \(\mathbb R^{n+1}\) given by the reference basis \(e\) Chapter5/HairyBallsphOr. It does not come from Milnor’s convention for the sphere. Plainly: - The reference basis is produced by the axiom of choice, as an unspecified basis of a space of dimension \(n + 1\). It need not be the standard basis, and whether it is positive for the standard orientation is never decided. - The outward vector \(\nu(q) = -2\sum_i \langle q, e_i\rangle e_i\) has \(\langle q, \nu(q)\rangle < 0\): it points into the ball, and \(\{g \ge 0\}\) is the exterior of the ball. So even for the standard ambient orientation this would be the opposite of Milnor’s orientation of \(S^n = \partial D^{n+1}\).

The orientation is therefore one of the two, and the formalization does not know which. Nothing in this part depends on it: every statement here uses it on both source and target, and reversing both leaves every sign unchanged Chapter5/OrSignorSign_neg_left Chapter5/OrSignorSign_neg_right.

The antipodal map \(\alpha(q) = -q\) is smooth by corestriction (V2.8) Chapter5/HairyBallcontMDiff_antip.

Theorem. With this orientation on both sides: for every \(n\) and \(q \in S^n\), \(\ \operatorname{sign} d\alpha_q = (-1)^{n+1}\); for \(n \ge 1\), \(\ \deg \alpha = (-1)^{n+1}\) Chapter5/HairyBallsignAt_antip Chapter5/HairyBalldeg_antip.

Where the formal proof departs from Milnor. Milnor composes \(n + 1\) reflections of degree \(-1\). The formal proof reads the sign off the contracted form, using \(\nu(-x) = -\nu(x)\) and \(d\iota_{-q} \circ d\alpha_q = -d\iota_q\), which follows from \(\iota \circ \alpha = -\iota\) Chapter5/HairyBalloutward_neg Chapter5/HairyBallmfd_val_comp_antip. The form representing the orientation at \(-q\), pulled back by \(d\alpha_q\) and evaluated on the reference basis \(u\) of \(\mathbb R^n\), is \[\omega\bigl(-\nu(q), -d\iota_q u_1, \dots, -d\iota_q u_n\bigr) = (-1)^{n+1}\,\omega\bigl(\nu(q), d\iota_q u_1, \dots, d\iota_q u_n\bigr),\] so the sign is \((-1)^{n+1}\) times the sign of a square. Every point is then a regular value Chapter5/HairyBallisRegularValue_antip, the preimage of \(y\) is \(\{-y\}\), and V5.7 gives the degree.

V5.10 The hairy ball theorem

Theorem. Let \(n\) be even and positive, and let \(v : S^n \to \mathbb R^{n+1}\) be smooth with \(\langle q, v(q)\rangle = 0\) for all \(q\). Then \(v(q) = 0\) for some \(q\) Chapter5/HairyBallhairy_ball.

The proof as formalized is Milnor’s. Suppose that \(v\) has no zero. 1. \(w = v/|v|\) is a smooth tangent field of unit vectors, the norm being smooth away from \(0\). 2. \(F(q, t) = \cos(\pi t)\,q + \sin(\pi t)\,w(q)\) has \(|F|^2 = \cos^2(\pi t) + \sin^2(\pi t) = 1\) because \(\langle q, w(q)\rangle = 0\). It is smooth into \(\mathbb R^{n+1}\), hence into \(S^n\) Chapter2/CorestrictcontMDiff_codRestrict, with \(F(\cdot, 0) = \mathrm{id}\) and \(F(\cdot, 1) = \alpha\). 3. By V5.7 and V5.9, \(1 = \deg \mathrm{id} = \deg \alpha = (-1)^{n+1} = -1\).

The converse is proved too. For \(n\) odd, write \(n + 1 = 2(m + 1)\) and \(x = (a, b)\) with \(a\) the first and \(b\) the last \(m + 1\) coordinates. Then \(v(a, b) = (b, -a)\) is smooth, tangent because \(\langle x, v(x)\rangle = \sum_j a_j b_j - \sum_j b_j a_j = 0\), and of norm \(1\) Chapter5/HairyBallexists_nonvanishing_field. It pairs the two halves of the coordinates, not adjacent coordinates.

What the formalization taught us

  • Orientation through chart transitions. Near each point the transitions into the chart at that point must preserve the chosen orientations; this is the definition a reader must confirm Chapter5/OrientOrient.
  • Hidden hypotheses. \(M\) and \(N\) Hausdorff for the local constancy of the signed count Chapter5/DegreeAtIsRegularValue.eventually_degAt_eq; \(M\) Hausdorff in Lemma 1, for the Appendix Chapter5/LemmaOnelemmaOne_ambient'; \(M\) second countable in Theorems A and B, for Brown’s theorem Chapter5/HomotopyInvdegAt_eq_of_homotopy; from Lemma 1 on, \(E\) and \(F\) in a common universe, a formality. The Hausdorff property of \(N\) is assumed in Lemma 1 but not used there.
  • Lemma 1 is ambient. Its boundary signs are those of \((f, g)\), which differ from Milnor’s boundary-orientation signs by \((-1)^{n+1}\) Chapter6/LevelSignsignAt_levelOrient_eq'.
  • The arc argument is a third of the chapter. Topological arcs force Milnor’s tangent field to be replaced by the product of the sign of \((f, c)\) and the monotonicity sign of \(c\), shown to be independent of \(c\), locally constant, and opposite at the two ends Chapter5/ArcSignsign_mul_monoAt_eq Chapter5/ArcSignbdrySign_end_eq_neg.
  • Isotopies must be isotopies. Orientation preservation needs every stage to be a diffeomorphism, which forced a strengthening of the Homogeneity Lemma Chapter5/Degreeexists_isotopy_signAt_eq_one.
  • One cylinder function, \(t(1 - t)\), presents both ends in Lemma 2, the core of Theorem B Chapter5/HomotopyInvdegAt_eq_of_homotopy_of_isRegularValue.
  • The degree is total, \(0\) when there is no regular value Chapter5/Degreedeg.
  • The sphere’s orientation is unknown and irrelevant. It comes from a basis chosen by the axiom of choice and an outward vector pointing into the ball, and it is used on both sides of every statement of this part Chapter5/HairyBallsphOr.
  • Direct computations: the antipodal sign without reflections, and for odd \(n\) a field pairing the two halves of the coordinates Chapter5/HairyBallsignAt_antip Chapter5/HairyBallexists_nonvanishing_field.
