Part IV. Vector fields and the Poincaré–Hopf theorem (Milnor §6)

This part covers Milnor’s §6: the index of an isolated zero, its invariance under diffeomorphisms, Hopf’s lemma for compact regions of \(\mathbb R^{n+1}\), and the Poincaré–Hopf theorem for a compact submanifold \(N \subseteq \mathbb R^{K+1}\). The formal proof keeps Milnor’s architecture: every index computation reduces to Lemma 1 of §5 (a map that extends over a compact region has degree zero on its boundary) and to the homotopy invariance of the degree. It departs from the book in three places. Lemma 1 of §5 is extended, in boundary form, to level sets in manifolds and to maps smooth only on an open set, because \(v/|v|\) is smooth only where \(v \ne 0\). Milnor’s Lemma 2 (an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism of \(\mathbb R^m\) is smoothly isotopic to the identity, through its derivative and then through \(GL^+\)) is replaced by a sign computation built on one new lemma about maps between level sets (V6.2). And the \(\varepsilon\)-neighbourhood theorem, which Milnor quotes from §8, is proved here with the inverse function theorem. Because the index of a tangent field on \(N\) is defined through its extension to a tubular neighbourhood, the formal Poincaré–Hopf theorem does not use the invariance lemma.

Six sections at the end of the part, V6.10 to V6.15, close the remarks of §6 that the first pass left aside: Lemma 4, the index at a non-degenerate zero; Hadamard’s lemma; Lemma 2 itself, which is thus proved although the development has replaced it; Lemma 5 and the derivative of the retraction; Milnor’s own chart definition of the index, with its agreement with the definition used here at a non-degenerate zero; and the Euler number \(1 + (-1)^n\) of \(S^n\). One sentence of the section still cannot be written down, and V6.15 says which.

Map. The files, in logical order (all in Chapter6/):

  • LevelSign: level sets in a vector space; signs on the level set versus signs of the pair map \((f, G)\).
  • Index: the sphere map and the index; independence of the radius; homotopy invariance.
  • Opens: orientations and signs restricted to an open subset.
  • SignLemmas: the chain rule for signs; tangential changes of the outward vector do not matter.
  • LevelOrientM: the level-set orientation in an oriented manifold, and its continuity.
  • LevelSignM: level-set signs versus pair-map signs, in a manifold.
  • RegularOpen: openness of regular values for compact domains; common regular values.
  • LevelMap: the sign of a map between level sets (V6.2); degrees and bijections.
  • LevelZero: opposite orientations, the product rule, transversality, Lemma 1 of §5 on an open set.
  • Region: the region lemma (V6.3).
  • Extend: extension of a locally smooth field by a cut-off.
  • Compose: degrees under composition with bijections of constant sign.
  • Hopf: Hopf’s lemma (V6.4).
  • Tubular1: local parametrizations of a submanifold of \(\mathbb R^k\).
  • Tubular2: the nearest-point equation and the inverse function theorem.
  • Tubular3: the nearest-point retraction (V6.6).
  • Tubular4: the region \(N_{\varepsilon/2}\) and the extended field (V6.7).
  • PoincareHopf: germs, the index on \(N\) (V6.8), the theorem (V6.9).
  • DetSign: constancy of \(\operatorname{sgn}\det df\) on a ball.
  • Radial: the matrix determinant lemma; the sign of \(u \mapsto Au/|Au|\).
  • Invariance1: region functions, sphere parametrizations, transfer of regular values.
  • Invariance: invariance of the index under diffeomorphisms (V6.5).
  • Nondegenerate: the index at a non-degenerate zero, Milnor’s Lemma 4 (V6.10).
  • Hadamard: smoothness of a parametric integral, and Hadamard’s lemma (V6.11).
  • ChartIndex: the derivative of the retraction, Lemma 5, the chart index and the agreement (V6.13, V6.14).
  • EulerSphere: the Euler number of \(S^n\) (V6.15).
  • Chapter7/Isotopy: Lemma 2 of §6 (V6.12), which sits in Chapter 7 because its last step is the \(GL^+\) path proved there.

Conventions: spheres, signs and degrees

Except in V6.1 and V6.2, where \(E\) is any real normed space of dimension \(n + 1\), \(E = \mathbb R^{n+1}\) with its Euclidean norm; \(S^n = \{x : |x|^2 = 1\}\) is a compact submanifold, connected when \(n \ge 1\) Chapter5/HairyBallSph Chapter5/HairyBallpreconnectedSpace. For oriented manifolds of equal dimension, \(\operatorname{sign}_x f\) is \(\pm 1\) at a regular point and \(0\) at a critical one; \(\deg(f; y)\) sums the signs over \(f^{-1}(y)\); and \(\deg f\) is \(\deg(f; y)\) at a regular value \(y\) chosen by the axiom of choice, or \(0\) if there is none Chapter5/OrientsignAt Chapter5/DegreeAtdegAt Chapter5/Degreedeg. For a compact, Hausdorff, second countable domain and a preconnected Hausdorff target, \(\deg f = \deg(f; y)\) at every regular value, and smoothly homotopic maps have equal degrees Chapter5/Degreedeg_eq Chapter5/Degreedeg_eq_of_homotopy.

The reference orientation \(a_0\) of \(E\) is that of a basis chosen by the library, not provably the standard one; \(o_E\) is the constant orientation it defines on the manifold \(E\) Chapter6/LevelSignOrient.const. When \(0\) is a regular value of \(g\), the level-set orientation of \(g^{-1}(0)\) puts first an outward vector \(\nu_q\) with \(dg_q(\nu_q) < 0\): it is the boundary orientation of \(\{g \ge 0\}\). The sphere carries \(o_{S^n}\), the level-set orientation of \(|x|^2 - 1\) for \(a_0\) Chapter5/HairyBallsphOr. Its outward vector \(\nu_x = -2\sum_i \langle x, e_i\rangle e_i\), built from the reference basis \((e_i)\), satisfies \(\langle x, \nu_x\rangle < 0\) and so points into the ball: \(o_{S^n}\) is the boundary orientation of the complement of the ball, the opposite of Milnor’s convention for the same ambient orientation. Every degree below is taken between two orientations of the same kind, so the numbers are Milnor’s. Replacing \(a_0\) by \(-a_0\) reverses both orientations in each degree, so the library’s choice is immaterial; no proof needs this remark.

Write \(\hat y = y/|y|\). The formal normalization sends \(0\) to a fixed base point, so \(\hat v = v/|v|\) is defined everywhere and smooth where \(v \ne 0\) Chapter6/Regionnv0 Chapter6/RegioncontMDiff_nv0_comp. Homotopies are reparametrized by Mathlib’s smooth transition function \(\tau\) (\(0\) on \((-\infty, 0]\), \(1\) on \([1, \infty)\)), because the formal homotopy invariance asks for a smooth map on \(M \times \mathbb R\).

V6.0 The index of an isolated zero

For a smooth \(v : \mathbb R^{n+1} \to \mathbb R^{n+1}\), a point \(z\) and a real \(\varepsilon\), the sphere map is \[s_{v,z,\varepsilon} : S^n \to S^n, \qquad u \mapsto \frac{v(z + \varepsilon u)}{|v(z + \varepsilon u)|},\] with the value \(u\) where \(v(z + \varepsilon u) = 0\), and \(\operatorname{ind}_\varepsilon(v; z) := \deg s_{v,z,\varepsilon}\) for \(o_{S^n}\) on both sides Chapter6/IndexsphMap Chapter6/IndexindexAt. The point \(z\) is an isolated zero of radius \(r\) if \(v(z) = 0\) and \(v(x) \ne 0\) whenever \(0 < |x - z| \le r\) Chapter6/IndexIsolatedZero. The index \(\operatorname{ind}(v; z)\) is \(\operatorname{ind}_r(v; z)\) for some \(r > 0\) of this kind, chosen by the axiom of choice, and \(0\) if no such \(r\) exists Chapter6/Indexindex.

Theorem (V6.0). Let \(n \ge 1\) and let \(v : \mathbb R^{n+1} \to \mathbb R^{n+1}\) be smooth.

  1. If \(z\) is an isolated zero of \(v\) of radius \(r > 0\) and \(0 < \varepsilon \le r\), then \(\operatorname{ind}(v; z) = \operatorname{ind}_\varepsilon(v; z)\).

  2. If \(V : \mathbb R^{n+1} \times \mathbb R \to \mathbb R^{n+1}\) is smooth and \(V(z + \varepsilon u, t) \ne 0\) for all \(u \in S^n\) and \(t \in \mathbb R\), then \(\operatorname{ind}_\varepsilon(V(\cdot, 0); z) = \operatorname{ind}_\varepsilon(V(\cdot, 1); z)\).

  3. If \(w, w'\) are smooth, agree on a neighbourhood of \(z\), and \(z\) is an isolated zero of \(w\) of some radius \(r > 0\), then \(\operatorname{ind}(w; z) = \operatorname{ind}(w'; z)\).

The idea. All three statements are homotopy invariance of the degree of maps \(S^n \to S^n\), available because \(S^n\) is compact and, for \(n \ge 1\), connected.

The proof as formalized. If \(v\) has no zero on the spheres of radius \(\rho(t)\) for a smooth family of radii \(\rho\), then \((u, t) \mapsto s_{v,z,\rho(t)}(u)\) is a smooth map \(S^n \times \mathbb R \to S^n\): the formula is smooth into \(\mathbb R^{n+1}\), lands in the sphere, and the slice structure of \(S^n\) makes the corestriction smooth Chapter6/IndexcontMDiff_sphMap_family. For radii \(\varepsilon_1, \varepsilon_2 \in (0, r]\), the family \(\rho(t) = \varepsilon_1 + \tau(t)(\varepsilon_2 - \varepsilon_1)\) stays between \(\min(\varepsilon_1, \varepsilon_2)\) and \(r\), so the degrees at \(t = 0\) and \(t = 1\) agree Chapter6/IndexindexAt_eq_of_radii. Comparing both the chosen radius and \(\varepsilon\) with the smaller of the chosen radius and \(r\) gives (a) Chapter6/Indexindex_eq. For (b), \((u, t) \mapsto \widehat{V}(z + \varepsilon u, t)\) is the homotopy; this is Milnor’s remark on p. 33 Chapter6/IndexindexAt_eq_of_homotopy. For (c), if \(w = w'\) on the \(\delta\)-ball, then \(z\) is an isolated zero of \(w'\) of radius \(\varepsilon = \min(r, \delta/2)\), the two sphere maps of radius \(\varepsilon\) coincide, and (a) applies to both fields Chapter6/PoincareHopfindex_eq_of_eventuallyEq.

Where the formal statement departs from Milnor. Milnor’s field lives on an open set; the formal field is defined on all of \(\mathbb R^{n+1}\). By (c) nothing is lost: a map \(v\) smooth on an open \(W\) agrees near any compact \(K \subseteq W\) with the global smooth map equal to \(\chi v\) on \(W\) and to \(0\) elsewhere, where the smooth Urysohn function \(\chi\) is \(1\) near \(K\) and \(0\) near the complement of \(W\) Chapter6/Extendexists_extension. The tubular field of V6.7 becomes global this way.

V6.1 Level-set orientations in a manifold, and Lemma 1 of §5 in boundary form

The region lemma applies Lemma 1 of §5 to \(\hat v\) on the open set \(\{v \ne 0\}\), a manifold with charts in \(E\) but not a vector space, so the level-set orientation of Chapter 5 had to be rebuilt for manifolds.

Setting. \(M\) is a smooth manifold with charts in \(E\), \(\dim E = n + 1\), oriented by \(o_M\); \(g : M \to \mathbb R\) is smooth with \(0\) a regular value; \(S = g^{-1}(0)\) is a slice submanifold modelled on a space \(Z\) of dimension \(n\), with inclusion \(\iota\). For \(q \in S\) let \[\nu_q = -\sum_i dg_q(e_i)\, e_i, \qquad dg_q(\nu_q) = -\sum_i dg_q(e_i)^2 < 0,\] where \(dg_q\) is read in the chart of \(M\) at \(q\) and \((e_i)\) is the reference basis of \(E\) Chapter6/LevelOrientMoutwardM. The orientation of \(S\) at \(q\) is the class of the \(n\)-form \[(\zeta_1, \dots, \zeta_n) \mapsto \omega(\nu_q, d\iota_q \zeta_1, \dots, d\iota_q \zeta_n),\] \(\omega\) a representative of \(o_M(q)\) Chapter5/LevelOrientcontractOr Chapter6/LevelOrientMlevelOrientM. The form is nonzero: \(d\iota_q\) is injective with image \(\ker dg_q\) and \(dg_q(\nu_q) \ne 0\), so \((\nu_q, d\iota_q\zeta)\) is a basis of \(E\) whenever \(\zeta\) is a basis of \(Z\) Chapter6/LevelOrientMlevelOrientM_rep_ne_zero. For \(M = E\) with \(o_E\) this is the orientation of Chapter 5; in particular \(o_{S^n}\) is an instance Chapter6/LevelZerolevelOrient_eq_levelOrientM.

Theorem (V6.1, the orientation). These orientations vary continuously: for \(q\) near \(q_0\) in \(S\), the derivative at \(q\) of the chart of \(S\) at \(q_0\) carries the orientation at \(q\) to the orientation at \(q_0\). Chapter6/LevelOrientMlevelOrientM_cont

The idea. Read in fixed charts at \(q_0\), the orientation at a nearby \(q\) is a positive multiple of a form that depends continuously on \(q\) and has the right sign at \(q_0\).

The proof as formalized. 1. Fix the charts \(\varphi\) of \(M\) and \(c_0\) of \(S\) at \(q_0\) and a representative \(\omega_0\) of \(o_M(q_0)\). In these charts put \(\hat g = g \circ \varphi^{-1}\), \(\psi = \varphi \circ \iota \circ c_0^{-1}\), \(\hat\nu(q) = -\sum_i d\hat g_{\varphi(q)}(e_i)\, e_i\) and \(\Lambda(q)(\zeta) = \omega_0(\hat\nu(q), d\psi_{c_0(q)}\zeta)\). For a fixed basis \(u_0\) of \(Z\), \(q \mapsto \Lambda(q)(u_0)\) is continuous near \(q_0\), being a determinant with continuous entries. 2. Near \(q_0\) the derivative \(D\varphi_q\) of the fixed chart carries \(o_M(q)\) to \(o_M(q_0)\), because \(o_M\) is an orientation; so \(\omega_0 \circ D\varphi_q = \kappa\, \omega_q\) with \(\kappa > 0\), \(\omega_q\) the chosen representative of \(o_M(q)\) Chapter6/LevelOrientMexists_pos_smul_of_orSign_eq_one. Pullbacks move inside the contraction: contracting \(\omega \circ L\) with \((\nu, T)\) is contracting \(\omega\) with \((L\nu, L T)\) Chapter6/LevelOrientMcontractForm_pullback. Next, \(D\varphi_q(\nu_q) = a\, \hat\nu(q) + t\) with \(a = d\hat g(D\varphi_q\nu_q)/d\hat g(\hat\nu(q))\), which is positive because both values are negative, and with \(t \in \ker d\hat g\), which is the image \(D\varphi_q(d\iota_q Z)\) of the tangent space. A tangent summand contributes nothing, as \(n + 1\) vectors in an \(n\)-dimensional image are dependent Chapter6/SignLemmascontractForm_eq_smul. With the chain rule \(D\varphi_q \circ d\iota_q = d\psi_{c_0(q)} \circ Dc_0(q)\), the representative at \(q\) is a positive multiple of \(\Lambda(q) \circ Dc_0(q)\). 3. Top forms on \(Z\) form a line, so \(\Lambda(q) = \big(\Lambda(q)u_0/\Lambda(q_0)u_0\big)\Lambda(q_0)\), with a ratio that is positive near \(q_0\) by step 1. At \(q_0\) both chart derivatives are the identity. Evaluating the two representatives on \(Dc_0(q)^{-1}u_0\) gives positive factors times \((\Lambda(q_0)u_0)^2\), so the sign is \(+1\) Chapter6/LevelOrientMlevelOrientM_cont.

The bridge to pair maps. Let \(N\) be a smooth manifold without boundary modelled on a space \(F\) of dimension \(n\), with \(E\) and \(F\) in a common universe, oriented by \(o_N\), and \(f : M \to N\) differentiable at \(q \in S\). Then \[\operatorname{sign}_q(f|_S) = (-1)^{n+1} \operatorname{sign}_q(f, g),\] the left side for the level-set orientation and \(o_N\), the right side for \(o_M\) and the product orientation of \(N \times \mathbb R\) (a positive basis of \(TN\) followed by \(\partial_t\)) Chapter5/OrientOrient.prodReal Chapter6/LevelSignMsignAt_levelOrientM_eq'. Both signs are evaluated on the basis \((\nu_q, d\iota_q u_0)\) of \(E\). On the left one gets the sign of \(\eta(df_q\, d\iota_q u_0) \cdot \omega(\nu_q, d\iota_q u_0)\), with \(\eta\) representing \(o_N(f(q))\). On the right, the matrix of \(d(f, g)_q\) on that basis has last row \((dg_q\nu_q, 0, \dots, 0)\) because \(dg_q \circ d\iota_q = 0\). Expanding along that row gives \((-1)^n dg_q(\nu_q) \det(df_q\, d\iota_q u_0)\), and \(dg_q(\nu_q) < 0\) supplies the last factor \(-1\). The same computation in a vector space is Chapter6/LevelSignsignAt_levelOrient_eq'.

Theorem (V6.1, Lemma 1 of §5 on an open set). In the setting above, with \(N\), \(F\) as in the bridge (\(E\) and \(F\) in a common universe), let \(M\) and \(N\) be Hausdorff, \(U \subseteq M\) open with \(g^{-1}(0) \subseteq U\), \(f\) smooth on \(U\), and \(y\) a regular value of \(f|_U\). Assume transversality: for every \(x \in g^{-1}(0)\) with \(f(x) = y\) there is \(w\) with \(df_x w = 0\) and \(dg_x w \ne 0\). If \(\{x \in U : f(x) = y,\ g(x) \ge 0\}\) is compact, then \((f|_S)^{-1}(y)\) is finite and \(\deg(f|_S; y) = 0\) for the level-set orientation. Chapter6/LevelZerodegAt_level_eq_zero_of_opens

The proof as formalized. Chapter 5’s ambient Lemma 1 says that the signed count of \(f^{-1}(y) \cap g^{-1}(0)\), with the signs of the pair map \((f, g)\), is finite and vanishes Chapter5/LemmaOnelemmaOne_ambient'. It is applied to the manifold \(U\) with the restricted orientation Chapter6/OpensOrient.restrict. The inclusion of \(U\) has identity derivative in the restricted charts, so signs in \(U\) and in \(M\) agree Chapter6/OpenssignAt_restrict. Since \(g^{-1}(0) \subseteq U\), the sum over \(U\) is the sum over \(M\), and the bridge turns each pair-map sign into \((-1)^{n+1}\) times a level-set sign.

Transversality is how the formal Lemma 1 says that \(y\) is a regular value of \(f\) on the boundary. In the region lemma (V6.3) it is derived from regularity of the restriction: if \(f|_S\) is regular at \(q\), a nonzero vector of \(\ker df_q\) (one exists by counting dimensions) cannot be tangent to \(S\), for \(f|_S\) would kill its preimage Chapter6/LevelZeroexists_mfd_eq_zero_of_isRegularPoint_level. That lemma also assumes \(f\) regular at \(q\), which its proof never uses.

V6.2 The sign of a map between level sets

Theorem (V6.2). Let \(M, M'\) be smooth manifolds with charts in \(E\), \(\dim E = n + 1\), oriented by \(o_M, o_{M'}\), and let \(G : M \to \mathbb R\), \(G' : M' \to \mathbb R\) be smooth with \(0\) as a regular value, both level sets being modelled on a space \(Z\) of dimension \(n\) as in V6.1. Let \(\Phi : M \to M'\) map \(G^{-1}(0)\) into \(G'^{-1}(0)\), with \(\Phi|_{G^{-1}(0)} : G^{-1}(0) \to M'\) smooth and \(\Phi\) differentiable at \(q \in G^{-1}(0)\). If \(dG'_{\Phi(q)} \circ d\Phi_q = c\, dG_q\) with \(c \ne 0\), then \[\operatorname{sign}_q\big(\Phi : G^{-1}(0) \to G'^{-1}(0)\big) = \operatorname{sgn}(c)\, \operatorname{sign}_q \Phi,\] with the level-set orientations on the left and \(o_M, o_{M'}\) on the right. Chapter6/LevelMapsignAt_levelOrientM_map'

The case \(c > 0\) is stated separately Chapter6/LevelMapsignAt_levelOrientM_map.

The idea. \(d\Phi_q\) sends the outward vector at \(q\) to \(a\) times the outward vector at \(\Phi(q)\) plus a tangent vector, with \(\operatorname{sgn} a = \operatorname{sgn} c\), and tangent vectors are invisible to the contracted form.

The proof as formalized. Let \(T, T'\) be the derivatives of the two inclusions and \(\Phi_S\) the restricted map, so that \(T' \circ d\Phi_S = d\Phi_q \circ T\). Write \(d\Phi_q(\nu) = a\nu' + t\) with \(a = dG'(d\Phi_q \nu)/dG'(\nu')\); then \(dG'(t) = 0\), so \(t\) lies in the image of \(T'\). Since \(dG'(d\Phi_q\nu) = c\, dG(\nu)\) and both \(dG(\nu)\) and \(dG'(\nu')\) are negative, \(\operatorname{sgn} a = \operatorname{sgn} c\). With \(\omega' \circ d\Phi_q = c'\omega\), so that \(\operatorname{sign}_q \Phi = \operatorname{sgn} c'\), \[\omega'(\nu', T' d\Phi_S \zeta) = a^{-1}\omega'(d\Phi_q \nu, d\Phi_q T\zeta) = a^{-1}c'\, \omega(\nu, T\zeta).\] The first equality drops \(t\), because \(t\) and all the \(d\Phi_q T\zeta\) lie in the \(n\)-dimensional image of \(T'\) Chapter6/LevelMapcontractForm_eq_smul_of_mem. The sign is therefore \(\operatorname{sgn}(a^{-1}c') = \operatorname{sgn}(c) \operatorname{sign}_q\Phi\).

This lemma has no counterpart in the book. It is the single tool through which the formalization moves degrees between level sets, applied to four kinds of map: to the inclusion of a boundary component (\(\Phi = \mathrm{id}\), \(c\) the product of the other factors), to the parametrization \(u \mapsto z + \varepsilon u\) of a sphere (\(c = 1\)), to a diffeomorphism \(f\) (\(c = -r^2\)) and to the radial map \(\Theta\) (\(c = 1\)), the last two in V6.5. Ambient signs come from one fact: for a self-map of an oriented vector space the sign is \(\operatorname{sgn}\det\) Chapter6/LevelMaporSign_self_eq_sgn_det. For the degrees, composing on either side with a bijection of constant sign \(\sigma = \pm 1\) multiplies \(\deg(\cdot\,; y)\) by \(\sigma\), the point \(y\) being moved by the bijection when it acts on the left Chapter6/LevelMapdegAt_comp_bij Chapter6/ComposedegAt_comp_bij' Chapter6/ComposedegAt_comp_bij_left.

V6.3 The region lemma

Theorem (V6.3). Let \(n \ge 1\) and \(v : \mathbb R^{n+1} \to \mathbb R^{n+1}\) smooth. Let \(G : \mathbb R^{n+1} \to \mathbb R\) be smooth with \(0\) a regular value and \(X = \{G \ge 0\}\) compact. Let \(\varepsilon > 0\) and \(z_1, \dots, z_k\) be points with \(G > 0\) on each closed ball \(\bar B_\varepsilon(z_i)\) and \(|z_i - z_j| > 2\varepsilon\) for \(i \ne j\), and suppose every zero of \(v\) in \(X\) is one of the \(z_i\). Then \[\sum_{i=1}^k \operatorname{ind}_\varepsilon(v; z_i) = \deg\big(\hat v : G^{-1}(0) \to S^n\big),\] where \(G^{-1}(0)\) carries the level-set orientation for \(o_E\), reversed, and \(S^n\) carries \(o_{S^n}\). Chapter6/Regionsum_indexAt_eq_deg

Milnor assumes the zeros in \(X\) are exactly the \(z_i\); the formal statement needs only that they lie among them.

The idea. As in Milnor’s proof of Hopf’s lemma (his Lemma 3): delete small open balls around the zeros, apply Lemma 1 of §5 to \(\hat v\) on what remains, and split the boundary into \(\partial X\) and the small spheres, each of which contributes an index.

The proof as formalized. 1. The region with holes as one sublevel set. Put \(G_i(x) = |x - z_i|^2/\varepsilon^2 - 1\) and \(g = G \prod_i G_i\) Chapter6/RegionGsph Chapter6/RegiongProd. At a zero of one factor every other factor is positive, because the balls are disjoint and lie in \(\{G > 0\}\) Chapter6/RegionGf_pos_of_ne. So \(g^{-1}(0)\) is the disjoint union of \(G^{-1}(0)\) and the spheres \(S_\varepsilon(z_i)\). At a zero of one factor, \(dg\) is the derivative of that factor times the product of the others, a positive coefficient Chapter6/LevelZeromfd_prod_of_eq_zero, so \(0\) is a regular value of \(g\). Moreover \(g \ge 0\) forces \(G \ge 0\) and \(|x - z_i| \ge \varepsilon\) for all \(i\) Chapter6/Regionmem_K_of_gProd_nonneg, and \(v \ne 0\) on \(g^{-1}(0)\) Chapter6/Regionne_zero_of_gProd_eq_zero. 2. A common regular value. The proof picks \(y \in S^n\) regular for \(\hat v\) on the open set \(U = \{v \ne 0\}\), for \(\hat v\) on \(G^{-1}(0)\), and for each sphere map \(s_{v, z_i, \varepsilon}\). The first set of regular values is dense by Brown’s theorem Chapter2/Browndense_regularValues. The others are open and dense because the domains are compact: the critical points form a closed set, since the sign is locally constant near a regular point, and their image is compact Chapter6/RegularOpenisOpen_regularValues. A dense set meets finitely many open dense sets in the Baire space \(S^n\) Chapter6/RegularOpenexists_mem_of_dense_of_isOpen. Regularity of \(\hat v\) on \(S_\varepsilon(z_i)\) follows from that of \(s_{v,z_i,\varepsilon} = \hat v|_{S_\varepsilon(z_i)} \circ \psi_i\), where \(\psi_i(u) = z_i + \varepsilon u\). 3. Transversality and compactness. A point \(x \in g^{-1}(0)\) with \(\hat v(x) = y\) lies on exactly one component, the zero set of one factor \(G_\ast\) (either \(G\) or some \(G_i\)), where both \(\hat v\) and its restriction are regular. The transversality lemma of V6.1 gives \(w \in \ker d\hat v_x\) with \(dG_\ast(w) \ne 0\), hence \(dg(w) \ne 0\). The set \(\{x \in U : \hat v(x) = y,\ g(x) \ge 0\}\) is closed in the compact set \(X \cap \bigcap_i \{|x - z_i| \ge \varepsilon\}\), on which \(v\) has no zero. 4. Lemma 1. V6.1 on \(M = \mathbb R^{n+1}\) with \(o_E\) and the open set \(U\) gives \(\deg(\hat v|_{g^{-1}(0)}; y) = 0\) for the level-set orientation of \(g\). 5. Splitting. By V6.2 with \(\Phi = \mathrm{id}\) and \(c > 0\) the product of the other factors, the inclusion of each component \(G^{-1}(0)\) or \(G_i^{-1}(0)\) into \(g^{-1}(0)\) has sign \(+1\) everywhere. By the chain rule for signs Chapter6/SignLemmassignAt_comp', the vanishing count splits as \[0 = \deg(\hat v|_{G^{-1}(0)}; y) + \sum_i \deg(\hat v|_{S_\varepsilon(z_i)}; y),\] each component carrying the level-set orientation of its own function. 6. The pieces. The first term is \(\deg(\hat v|_{G^{-1}(0)})\), since \(G^{-1}(0)\) is compact. On the sphere \(S_\varepsilon(z_i) = G_i^{-1}(0)\), the bijection \(\psi_i\) from \(S^n\) has sign \(+1\) by V6.2 with \(c = 1\): \(G_i \circ \psi_i\) is exactly \(|u|^2 - 1\), and the ambient sign of \(u \mapsto z_i + \varepsilon u\) is \(\operatorname{sgn}\varepsilon^{n+1} = 1\) Chapter6/RegionsignAt_aff. So the \(i\)-th term is \(\deg(s_{v,z_i,\varepsilon}; y) = \operatorname{ind}_\varepsilon(v; z_i)\). Hence \(\sum_i \operatorname{ind}_\varepsilon(v; z_i) = -\deg(\hat v|_{G^{-1}(0)})\), the degree for the reversed orientation Chapter6/LevelZeroOrient.neg Chapter6/LevelZerodeg_neg_left.

Where the formal proof departs from Milnor. In both proofs the small spheres, as part of \(\partial X'\), carry the orientation opposite to that of boundaries of balls: here each is a component of \(g^{-1}(0)\) with the level-set orientation of \(G_i\). Milnor’s index uses the ball convention, so he moves the spheres to the other side of the equation. The formal index uses \(o_{S^n}\), which has the complement convention as well; the level-set orientation of \(G_i\) is \(o_{S^n}\) transported by \(\psi_i\), the spheres keep their sign, and the reversal lands on \(\partial X\) instead.

What the book leaves implicit. Milnor uses one regular value for all these maps at once. Its existence needs the openness of regular values for compact domains. Chapter 4 already had it, through V1.4 Chapter4/DegreeisOpen_isRegularValue; the proof here uses a second version, proved through the local constancy of the sign and therefore stated for oriented manifolds Chapter6/RegularOpenisOpen_regularPoints Chapter6/RegularOpenisOpen_regularValues.

V6.4 Hopf’s lemma

Theorem (V6.4). Under the hypotheses of V6.3 (with \(G\) smooth), suppose also that \(dG_x(v(x)) < 0\) whenever \(G(x) = 0\). Then \[\sum_{i=1}^k \operatorname{ind}_\varepsilon(v; z_i) = \deg\Big(x \mapsto \frac{-\nabla G(x)}{|\nabla G(x)|} : G^{-1}(0) \to S^n\Big),\] with the orientations of V6.3. Chapter6/Hopfhopf_lemma

The right-hand side does not involve \(v\).

The proof as formalized. V6.3 rewrites the left side as the degree of \(\hat v\) on \(G^{-1}(0)\). On \(G^{-1}(0) \times \mathbb R\) put \(w(q, t) = (1 - \tau(t))\, v(q) + \tau(t)(-\nabla G(q))\). Since \(dG_q(h) = \langle \nabla G(q), h\rangle\) Chapter6/Hopffderiv_apply_eq_inner_gradient, \[dG_q(w(q,t)) = (1 - \tau)\, dG_q(v(q)) - \tau\, |\nabla G(q)|^2 < 0,\] because both terms are \(\le 0\) and one is negative: the first when \(\tau \le 1/2\), the second when \(\tau > 1/2\), as \(\nabla G \ne 0\) on \(G^{-1}(0)\) by regularity. So \(\hat w\) is a smooth homotopy on the compact manifold \(G^{-1}(0)\) from \(\hat v\) to the Gauss map, and the degrees agree. This is Milnor’s proof of Lemma 3 (p. 35); the reparametrization by \(\tau\) lets the homotopy be defined for all times.

V6.5 Invariance of the index under diffeomorphisms (Milnor’s Lemma 1)

Theorem (V6.5). Let \(n \ge 1\), \(U, U' \subseteq \mathbb R^{n+1}\) open, and \(f, g : \mathbb R^{n+1} \to \mathbb R^{n+1}\) with \(f\) smooth on \(U\), \(f(U) \subseteq U'\), \(g\) smooth on \(U'\), \(g(U') \subseteq U\), \(g \circ f = \mathrm{id}\) on \(U\) and \(f \circ g = \mathrm{id}\) on \(U'\). Let \(v\) be smooth on \(\mathbb R^{n+1}\) with an isolated zero at \(z\) of radius \(r > 0\), where \(\bar B_r(z) \subseteq U\). Let \(w\) be smooth on \(\mathbb R^{n+1}\) with \(w(y) = df_{g(y)}\big(v(g(y))\big)\) for \(y \in f(\bar B_r(z))\). Then \(\operatorname{ind}(w; f(z)) = \operatorname{ind}(v; z)\). Chapter6/Invarianceindex_eq_of_diffeo

The formal Poincaré–Hopf theorem (V6.9) does not use this result.

The idea. Milnor derives the lemma from his Lemma 2, that an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism of \(\mathbb R^m\) is smoothly isotopic to the identity (first through \(f(tx)/t\) to its derivative, then through \(GL^+\)), and treats reflections directly. The formal proof instead tracks signs. The region lemma turns \(\operatorname{ind}(w; f(z))\) into a degree over \(f(S_r(z))\); pulling back by \(f\) costs \(-\sigma\), with \(\sigma = \operatorname{sgn}\det df\); a homotopy freezes the derivative at \(z\); and \(A = df_z\) acts on directions with sign \(\sigma\). The two factors \(\sigma\) cancel.

The proof as formalized. 1. Linear algebra of \(f\). The relations \(dg_{f(x)} \circ df_x = \mathrm{id}\) on \(U\) and \(df_{g(y)} \circ dg_y = \mathrm{id}\) on \(U'\) make \(df_x\) bijective on \(U\). Let \(\sigma = \operatorname{sgn}\det df_z\). It is also the sign of \(\det df_x\) for every \(x \in \bar B_r(z)\): along the segment from \(z\) to \(x\) the determinant is continuous and never zero, so the intermediate value theorem applies Chapter6/DetSigncontinuous_det_clm Chapter6/DetSignsgn_det_fderiv_eq. 2. The image region. \(G_0(y) = r^2 - |g(y) - z|^2\) is smooth on \(U'\), and \(f(\bar B_r(z)) = \{y \in U' : G_0(y) \ge 0\}\). With a cut-off \(\chi\) equal to \(1\) near this compact set and \(0\) near the complement of \(U'\), the function \(G' = \chi G_0 + (\chi - 1)\) on \(U'\), \(G' = -1\) elsewhere, is smooth, with \(\{G' \ge 0\} = f(\bar B_r(z))\) and \(G' = G_0\) nearby Chapter6/Invariance1exists_region_fun. Its zero set is \(f(S_r(z))\), and \(0\) is a regular value because \(dG_0(df_x(x - z)) = -2|x - z|^2 \ne 0\). 3. The index of \(w\) by the region lemma. Since \(w(f(x)) = df_x(v(x))\), the only zero of \(w\) in \(f(\bar B_r(z))\) is \(f(z)\). The set \(f(B_r(z)) = U' \cap g^{-1}(B_r(z))\) is open, so it contains a closed ball about \(f(z)\) of some radius \(\varepsilon\), on which \(G' > 0\). V6.3 with \(k = 1\) gives \(\operatorname{ind}_\varepsilon(w; f(z)) = -\deg(\hat w|_{f(S_r(z))})\) for the level-set orientation of \(G'\). 4. Pulling back by \(f\) and \(\psi\). The restriction \(f_S : S_r(z) \to f(S_r(z))\) is a bijection with sign \(-\sigma\) at every point, by V6.2 with \(c = -r^2\): near the sphere \(G'(f(x)) = r^2 - |x - z|^2 = -r^2(|x - z|^2/r^2 - 1)\), and the ambient sign of \(f\) is \(\sigma\). The parametrization \(\psi(u) = z + ru\) of \(S_r(z)\) has sign \(+1\) Chapter6/Invariance1ψaff Chapter6/Invariance1signAt_ψaff. A regular value \(y\) of \(\hat w|_{f(S_r(z))}\) (Brown) stays regular after precomposition with maps whose derivatives are surjective Chapter6/Invariance1IsRegularValue.comp_of_surjective. So \(\deg(u \mapsto \hat w(f(z + ru))) = -\sigma \deg(\hat w|_{f(S_r(z))}; y)\). 5. Freezing the derivative. \(H(u, t) = df_{z + \tau(t) r u}\big(v(z + ru)\big)\) never vanishes, since \(v \ne 0\) on the sphere and \(df\) is invertible on the ball. At \(t = 1\) it equals \(w(f(z + ru))\). At \(t = 0\) it is \(A\,v(z + ru)\) with \(A = df_z\), whose normalization is \(h(s_{v,z,r}(u))\) for \(h(u) = Au/|Au|\), because normalization ignores positive factors Chapter6/Invariance1nv0_smul. Homotopy invariance equates the two degrees. 6. The linear end. \(h\) is a bijection of \(S^n\), with inverse \(u \mapsto \widehat{A^{-1}u}\), of sign \(\sigma\) at every point (next subsection). For a regular value \(y''\) of \(h \circ s_{v,z,r}\), the point \(y_0 = h^{-1}(y'')\) is regular for \(s_{v,z,r}\) because \(dh\) is injective Chapter6/Invariance1IsRegularValue.of_comp_injective, and \(\deg(h \circ s_{v,z,r}) = \sigma \deg(s_{v,z,r}; y_0) = \sigma \operatorname{ind}_r(v; z)\). 7. Assembly. Steps 4–6 give \(-\sigma \deg(\hat w|_{f(S_r(z))}; y) = \sigma \operatorname{ind}_r(v; z)\), and \(\sigma^2 = 1\). As \(f(z)\) is an isolated zero of \(w\) of radius \(\varepsilon\), \(\operatorname{ind}(w; f(z)) = \operatorname{ind}_\varepsilon(w; f(z)) = -\deg(\hat w|_{f(S_r(z))}) = \operatorname{ind}_r(v; z) = \operatorname{ind}(v; z)\).

Replacing Lemma 2: the radial map

Proposition. For a bijective linear map \(A\) of \(\mathbb R^{n+1}\) and every \(u \in S^n\), the sign at \(u\) of \(u \mapsto Au/|Au|\), for \(o_{S^n}\) on both sides, is \(\operatorname{sgn}\det A\). Chapter6/RadialsignAt_nv0_linear

The proof as formalized. The map is the restriction to \(S^n\) of \(\Theta(x) = \lambda(x)\,Ax\) with \(\lambda(x) = |x|/|Ax|\) Chapter6/Radiallam Chapter6/RadialΘ. \(\Theta\) preserves \(|x|\), hence the defining function \(|x|^2 - 1\) Chapter6/RadialsphG_Θ, so V6.2 with \(c = 1\) makes the sign on the sphere equal to \(\operatorname{sgn}\det d\Theta_u\). Now \[d\Theta_u = \lambda(u)A + d\lambda_u \otimes Au = \big(\lambda(u)\,\mathrm{id} + \mu \otimes Au\big) \circ A, \qquad \mu = d\lambda_u \circ A^{-1}.\] Because \(\lambda\) is homogeneous of degree \(0\), Euler’s identity \(d\lambda_u(u) = 0\) holds Chapter6/Radialfderiv_lam_self, that is, \(\mu(Au) = 0\). The matrix determinant lemma \(\det(\mathrm{id} + \mu \otimes p) = 1 + \mu(p)\) Chapter6/Radialdet_id_add_smulRight gives \(\det(c\,\mathrm{id} + \mu \otimes p) = c^{n+1}\) when \(\mu(p) = 0\) Chapter6/Radialdet_smul_id_add_smulRight. Hence \(\det d\Theta_u = \lambda(u)^{n+1}\det A\) with \(\lambda(u) > 0\) Chapter6/Radialdet_fderiv_Θ.

Where the formal proof departs from Milnor. Neither deformation of Lemma 2 is used. The deformation of \(f\) through \(f(tx)/t\) into \(df_z\) is replaced by the homotopy of step 5, which moves only the base point of the derivative, and the isotopy of \(df_z\) through \(GL^+\) by the sign computation above. That \(GL^+\) is connected by smooth paths is proved only later, for §7 Chapter7/GLplusexists_glPath. Lemma 2 itself is a theorem of this development (V6.12 below), reached through Hadamard’s lemma (V6.11); nothing depends on it, and this proof does not go through it.

V6.6 The ε-neighbourhood theorem

Theorem (V6.6). Let \(N \subseteq \mathbb R^k\) be a slice submanifold with model \(\mathbb R^n\) and complement \(\mathbb R^m\), compact and nonempty. There are \(\varepsilon > 0\) and \(r : \mathbb R^k \to N\) such that:

  1. \(|x - r(x)| = \operatorname{dist}(x, N)\) for every \(x\);

  2. if \(\operatorname{dist}(x, N) < \varepsilon\), every nearest point of \(N\) to \(x\) equals \(r(x)\);

  3. \(r(x) = x\) for \(x \in N\);

and for every \(x\) with \(\operatorname{dist}(x, N) < \varepsilon\):

  1. \(r\) is smooth at \(x\);

  2. \(x - r(x) \perp T_{r(x)}N\);

  3. \(dr_x\) takes values in \(T_{r(x)}N\);

finally, (vii) if \(x \in N\) and \(v \perp T_xN\), then \(r(x + sv) = x\) for all \(s\) near \(0\). Chapter6/Tubular3tubular

Here \(T_qN\) is the image of the derivative of the inclusion in the slice charts Chapter2/SubmanifoldIsSliceSubmanifold. Milnor quotes the theorem from §8 (Problems 11 and 12), where it comes from the normal bundle; the formal proof uses nearest points.

The idea. A nearest point \(\varphi(z)\) of \(x\) satisfies \((d\varphi_z)^*(x - \varphi(z)) = 0\). The inverse function theorem solves this equation uniquely and smoothly near each point of \(N\), and compactness makes the radius uniform.

The proof as formalized. 1. Parametrizations. For \(p \in N\) choose a slice chart \(\sigma_p\) containing \(p\) Chapter6/Tubular1σ, and let \(\Omega_p = \{z \in \mathbb R^n : (z, 0) \in \operatorname{target}\}\) Chapter6/Tubular1Ω. Put \(\varphi_p(z) = \sigma_p^{-1}(z, 0) \in N\) Chapter6/Tubular1φ, and let \(c_p(q)\) be the first component of \(\sigma_p(q)\) Chapter6/Tubular1c. Since \(\sigma_p \circ \varphi_p\) is \(z \mapsto (z, 0)\), \(d\varphi_p\) is injective Chapter6/Tubular1injective_fderiv_φ, and \(T_qN\) is the image of \(d\varphi_p\) at \(c_p(q)\) Chapter6/Tubular1range_mfd_val. 2. The equation. \(F(z, x) = (d\varphi_z)^*(x - \varphi(z))\) Chapter6/Tubular2A Chapter6/Tubular2Fn. If \(q = \varphi(c_p(q))\) is a nearest point to \(x\), then \(z \mapsto |x - \varphi(z)|^2\) has a local minimum at \(c_p(q)\), so \(\langle x - \varphi(z), d\varphi_z a\rangle = 0\) for all \(a\), which is \(F(c_p(q), x) = 0\) Chapter6/Tubular2Fn_eq_zero_of_nearest. 3. The inverse function theorem. \(\Phi(z, x) = (F(z, x), x)\) Chapter6/Tubular2Φ has derivative \((a, b) \mapsto \big((d\varphi_{z_0})^*(b - d\varphi_{z_0}a),\, b\big)\) at \((z_0, \varphi(z_0))\); the term from differentiating \(z \mapsto (d\varphi_z)^*\) is multiplied by \(x - \varphi(z_0) = 0\) Chapter6/Tubular2hasFDerivAt_Φ. It is injective, since \(b = 0\) and \((d\varphi)^*d\varphi\, a = 0\) give \(|d\varphi\, a|^2 = 0\), hence \(a = 0\) by step 1 Chapter6/Tubular2injective_DΦ. Let \(U(x)\) be the first component of \(\Phi^{-1}(0, x)\) Chapter6/Tubular2U. Then \(F(U(x), x) = 0\) for \(x\) near \(\varphi(z_0)\) Chapter6/Tubular2eventually_Fn_U, and every solution near \((z_0, \varphi(z_0))\) has \(z = U(x)\) Chapter6/Tubular2eventually_eq_U. The library’s inverse function theorem gives smoothness of the local inverse only at the one image point; smoothness on a neighbourhood follows because invertibility of \(d\Phi\) is an open condition and the inverse is smooth wherever it holds Chapter6/Tubular2exists_contDiffOn_U. 4. A good radius at each point. For each \(p \in N\) there is \(\delta_p > 0\) such that, for \(|x - p| < \delta_p\), every nearest point of \(x\) is \(\varphi_p(U_p(x))\), and \(U_p\) solves the equation and is smooth at \(x\). A nearest point \(q\) satisfies \(|q - p| \le 2|x - p|\), so it lies in the chart with \(c_p(q)\) near \(z_0\), and Fermat’s condition with uniqueness gives \(c_p(q) = U_p(x)\) Chapter6/Tubular3exists_good. 5. A uniform radius. Some \(\varepsilon > 0\) has the property that \(\operatorname{dist}(x, N) < \varepsilon\) implies \(|x - p| < \delta_p\) for some \(p \in N\) Chapter6/Tubular3exists_eps. Otherwise there are \(x_j\) with \(\operatorname{dist}(x_j, N) < 1/(j+1)\) and \(|x_j - p| \ge \delta_p\) for all \(p\). Their nearest points have a subsequence converging to some \(p \in N\), along which \(x_j \to p\): a contradiction. The radii \(\delta_p\) are chosen with no continuity in \(p\), and the sequential argument needs none. 6. Conclusion. \(r(x)\) is a nearest point chosen for every \(x\), using compactness and nonemptiness Chapter6/Tubular3nearestPt. Near any \(x\) with \(\operatorname{dist}(x, N) < \varepsilon\), \(r = \varphi_p \circ U_p\), which gives (ii) and (iv); (v) is \(\langle x - \varphi(U(x)), d\varphi\, a\rangle = \langle F(U(x), x), a\rangle = 0\), and (vi) is \(dr_x = d\varphi \circ dU_x\). For (vii), \(F(z_0, x + sv) = s\,(d\varphi_{z_0})^*v = 0\), and uniqueness gives \(U(x + sv) = z_0\). Clause (vii) serves Chapter 7, not this chapter.

Hidden hypotheses. \(N\) is nonempty, and the model and complement are Euclidean spaces, so that adjoints exist.

V6.7 The region \(N_{\varepsilon/2}\) and the extended field

Take \(N \subseteq \mathbb R^{K+1}\) and fix \(\varepsilon\) and \(r\) from V6.6, chosen by the axiom of choice Chapter6/Tubular4tubε Chapter6/Tubular4tubr. Let \(N_\varepsilon = \{\operatorname{dist}(\cdot, N) < \varepsilon\}\) Chapter6/Tubular4Nε and \(X = \{\operatorname{dist}(\cdot, N) \le \varepsilon/2\}\), compact because closed and bounded Chapter6/Tubular4X Chapter6/Tubular4isCompact_X. A tangent field is a smooth \(v : N \to \mathbb R^{K+1}\) with \(v(q) \in T_qN\) for all \(q\).

Theorem (V6.7). (a) There is a smooth \(G : \mathbb R^{K+1} \to \mathbb R\) with \(\{G \ge 0\} = X\), \(G = G_0 := (\varepsilon/2)^2 - |x - r(x)|^2\) near \(X\), and \(0\) a regular value Chapter6/Tubular4exists_G Chapter6/Tubular4isRegularValue_G. (b) For a smooth \(v : N \to \mathbb R^{K+1}\), the field \(w(x) = v(r(x)) + (x - r(x))\) Chapter6/Tubular4w₀ is smooth on \(N_\varepsilon\) and equals \(v\) on \(N\). If \(v\) is a tangent field, the zeros of \(w\) in \(N_\varepsilon\) are the zeros of \(v\), and \(dG_0(w(x)) = -2|x - r(x)|^2\) on \(N_\varepsilon\).

The proof as formalized. On \(N_\varepsilon\), \(dG_0(h) = -2\langle x - r(x), h - dr_x h\rangle = -2\langle x - r(x), h\rangle\), because \(dr_x h \in T_{r(x)}N\) is orthogonal to \(x - r(x)\) Chapter6/Tubular4fderiv_G₀_apply. This is Milnor’s “easy computation” \(\operatorname{grad}\varphi = 2(x - r(x))\) on p. 38. The function \(G\) is \(\chi G_0 + (\chi - 1)\) on \(N_\varepsilon\) and \(-1\) elsewhere, with \(\chi\) smooth, \(1\) near \(X\) and \(0\) near the complement of \(N_\varepsilon\). Outside \(X\), \(G \ge 0\) would force \(\chi = 1\) and then \(G = G_0 < 0\). At a zero of \(G\), \(|x - r(x)| = \varepsilon/2\) and \(dG(x - r(x)) = -2|x - r(x)|^2 \ne 0\). On \(N\) the retraction is the identity, so \(w = v\) there Chapter6/Tubular4w₀_of_mem. For a tangent field \(v\), \(v(r(x))\) is tangent at \(r(x)\), hence orthogonal to \(x - r(x)\), so \(\langle w(x), x - r(x)\rangle = |x - r(x)|^2\), and a zero of \(w\) has \(x = r(x) \in N\) and \(v(x) = 0\) Chapter6/Tubular4w₀_eq_zero. The same orthogonality gives \(dG_0(w)\) Chapter6/Tubular4fderiv_G₀_w₀. Smoothness holds because \(r\) is smooth from \(N_\varepsilon\) into the manifold \(N\) Chapter6/Tubular4contMDiffOn_w₀.

V6.8 The index of a tangent field on \(N\)

For a smooth \(v : N \to \mathbb R^{K+1}\), let \(\tilde w\) be a global smooth field that agrees with \(w\) near \(X\), chosen through the cut-off lemma Chapter6/PoincareHopfwext. The index of \(v\) at \(q \in N\) is defined as \(\operatorname{ind}_N(v; q) := \operatorname{ind}(\tilde w; q)\) Chapter6/PoincareHopfindexN.

Proposition (V6.8). Let \(K \ge 1\), \(v : N \to \mathbb R^{K+1}\) smooth and \(q \in N\). If \(w'\) is smooth on \(\mathbb R^{K+1}\) and agrees with \(w\) near \(q\), and \(q\) is an isolated zero of \(\tilde w\) of some radius \(r > 0\), then \(\operatorname{ind}_N(v; q) = \operatorname{ind}(w'; q)\). Chapter6/PoincareHopfindexN_eq

Indeed \(\tilde w = w\) near \(q\), because \(q \in N \subseteq X\), and V6.0(c) applies. So \(\operatorname{ind}_N\) depends only on the germ of \(w\) at \(q\), which is determined by \(v\) and by the nearest-point retraction, canonical on \(N_\varepsilon\).

Where the formal definition departs from Milnor. Milnor defines the index through a chart, needs his Lemma 1 (V6.5) for it to be well defined, and remarks on p. 38 that it equals the index of \(w\). Here the second quantity is the definition, and the theorem below is proved for it. The chart definition is formalized too, and the two are proved equal at a non-degenerate zero (V6.14), which is Milnor’s Lemma 5 and is what his own arguments use. At an arbitrary isolated zero the agreement is not proved and cannot be with what this development has; V6.14 says what it would need, and Milnor does not prove it either. For the theorem below the difference does not arise, its content being the independence of the index sum from \(v\).

V6.9 The Poincaré–Hopf theorem

Theorem (V6.9). Let \(N \subseteq \mathbb R^{K+1}\), \(K \ge 1\), be a slice submanifold with model \(\mathbb R^n\) and complement \(\mathbb R^m\), compact and nonempty. There is an integer \(\chi\) with the following property. Let \(v : N \to \mathbb R^{K+1}\) be smooth with \(v(q) \in T_qN\) for all \(q\), and let \(z_1, \dots, z_j\) be distinct points of \(N\) with \(\{q : v(q) = 0\} = \{z_1, \dots, z_j\}\). Then \[\sum_{i=1}^j \operatorname{ind}_N(v; z_i) = \chi.\] Chapter6/PoincareHopfpoincare_hopf

The idea. As on Milnor’s p. 38: the extended field points outward along \(\partial N_{\varepsilon/2}\), so Hopf’s lemma computes its index sum as the degree of a Gauss map that does not involve \(v\).

The proof as formalized. 1. With \(G\) from V6.7, let \(\chi\) be the degree of \(x \mapsto -\nabla G(x)/|\nabla G(x)|\) on \(G^{-1}(0) = \partial X\), with the reversed level-set orientation and \(o_{S^K}\) on the target. It is defined before \(v\) is given. 2. Given \(v\) and its zeros, let \(d\) be the least distance between two distinct zeros (\(d = 1\) if there are fewer than two), and \(\varepsilon' = \min(\varepsilon/4, d/4)\). 3. Hopf’s lemma applies to \(\tilde w\), \(X = \{G \ge 0\}\), the centres \(z_i\) and the radius \(\varepsilon'\). A point within \(\varepsilon'\) of \(z_i\) lies within \(\varepsilon/4\) of \(N\), hence in \(X\), where \(G = G_0 = (\varepsilon/2)^2 - \operatorname{dist}(x, N)^2 > 0\). Next, \(2\varepsilon' < d \le |z_i - z_{i'}|\). A zero of \(\tilde w\) in \(X\) is a zero of \(w\), hence of \(v\), hence one of the \(z_i\). On \(\partial X\), \(dG(\tilde w) = -2|x - r(x)|^2 < 0\). 4. Hopf’s lemma gives \(\sum_i \operatorname{ind}_{\varepsilon'}(\tilde w; z_i) = \chi\). 5. Each \(z_i\) is an isolated zero of \(\tilde w\) of radius \(\varepsilon'\): \(\tilde w(z_i) = v(z_i) = 0\), and any other zero in the ball would be some \(z_{i'}\) at distance more than \(2\varepsilon'\). So \(\operatorname{ind}_N(v; z_i) = \operatorname{ind}_{\varepsilon'}(\tilde w; z_i)\) by V6.0(a).

Not formalized. The identification of \(\chi\) with the Euler characteristic, which Milnor quotes; and manifolds not given inside a Euclidean space, which would need Whitney’s embedding theorem (Milnor also works with \(N \subseteq \mathbb R^k\)). For \(N = S^n\) the integer is computed: it is \(1 + (-1)^n\) (V6.15).

V6.10 The index of a non-degenerate zero (Milnor’s Lemma 4)

Theorem (V6.10). Let \(n \ge 1\) and let \(v : \mathbb R^{n+1} \to \mathbb R^{n+1}\) be smooth with \(v(z) = 0\) and \(dv_z\) bijective. Then \[\operatorname{ind}(v; z) = \operatorname{sgn}\det dv_z,\] so the index is \(+1\) or \(-1\) according as the determinant is positive or negative, which is Milnor’s own form of the lemma. Chapter6/Nondegenerateindex_eq_sgn_det Chapter6/Nondegenerateindex_nondegenerate

That \(z\) is an isolated zero is not assumed; it is part of what is proved.

The idea is Milnor’s. Deform \(v\) to its linear part along a straight line, which changes nothing by V6.0(b), and read off the sign of the resulting linear field from the radial computation of V6.5.

The proof as formalized. Write \(A = dv_z\).

  1. One estimate does two jobs. A bijective linear map is bounded below, \(\|Ay\| \ge c\|y\|\) with \(c > 0\) Chapter6/Nondegenerateexists_lower_bound_of_bijective, and \(v(x) = A(x - z) + o(|x - z|)\). So there is a radius \(r > 0\) on which no combination \[A(x - z) + b\,\big(v(x) - A(x - z)\big), \qquad 0 \le b \le 1,\] vanishes off \(z\) Chapter6/Nondegenerateexists_radius_of_nondegenerate. The case \(b = 1\) says that \(z\) is an isolated zero of radius \(r\); the whole range says that the straight-line homotopy from the linear field to \(v\) keeps the \(r\)-sphere free of zeros Chapter6/NondegeneratelinHomotopy. By V6.0(b) and V6.0(a) the index of \(v\) at \(z\) is the index at \(z\) of \(x \mapsto A(x - z)\). Milnor takes both steps in one phrase.
  2. From a constant sign to a degree. The sphere map of the linear field is \(u \mapsto Au/|Au|\), whose sign at every point of \(S^n\) is \(\operatorname{sgn}\det A\) — the proposition of V6.5, which is what stands in this development for Milnor’s appeal to Lemma 2. A constant pointwise sign is not yet a degree, and the passage is new here: the map is a bijection of \(S^n\), so every point is a regular value with exactly one preimage, and the degree is that one sign Chapter6/Nondegeneratedeg_nv0_linear.

Hidden hypothesis. \(n \ge 1\), as everywhere in this part, the index being a degree on \(S^n\).

V6.11 Hadamard’s lemma, and a parametric integral

Milnor’s isotopy in Lemma 2 of §6 is \(F(x, t) = f(tx)/t\), and the whole difficulty is smoothness at \(t = 0\). It rests on a factorization \(f(x) = L(x)\,x\) with \(L\) smooth, and that rests on a fact Mathlib does not have.

Theorem (V6.11). Let \(E\) and \(F\) be real normed spaces with \(F\) complete.

  1. If \(h : E \times \mathbb R \to F\) is of class \(C^n\), then so is \(x \mapsto \int_0^1 h(x, t)\,dt\); likewise for \(C^\infty\). Chapter6/HadamardcontDiff_intervalIntegral Chapter6/HadamardcontDiff_intervalIntegral_infty

  2. Hadamard’s lemma. A smooth \(f : E \to F\) with \(f(0) = 0\) factors as \(f(x) = L(x)\,x\) with \(L(x) = \int_0^1 df_{tx}\,dt\) smooth and \(L(0) = df_0\). Chapter6/Hadamardexists_hadamard

  3. Hence \(t^{-1}f(tx)\) extends to a smooth map of \(E \times \mathbb R\) with value \(df_0(x)\) at \(t = 0\) — as an existence statement, and for the explicit formula “\(df_0(x)\) if \(t = 0\), else \(t^{-1}f(tx)\)” in which the isotopy is written. Chapter6/Hadamardexists_contDiff_extension Chapter6/HadamardcontDiff_ite_smul_inv

The idea. Mathlib has the integral form of Taylor’s theorem but no theorem saying that an integral over a fixed interval depends smoothly on a parameter, so (a) comes first. It is proved by induction on \(n\), differentiating under the integral sign and dominating on a tube around the compact segment \(\{x\} \times [0,1]\); the template is Mathlib’s convolution file. Because the domination is on a tube and not on a compact set of the parameter, neither finite dimension nor local compactness is needed. Then (b) is the fundamental theorem of calculus along the segment from \(0\) to \(x\), \(f(x) = \int_0^1 \frac{d}{dt}f(tx)\,dt = \int_0^1 df_{tx}(x)\,dt\), with (a) supplying the smoothness of the result in \(x\); and (c) is (b) applied at \(tx\).

The one hypothesis Milnor would not state is completeness of the target, so that the Bochner integrals exist; his spaces are \(\mathbb R^m\). Otherwise the statements are more general than the book’s, being about smooth maps between real normed spaces.

V6.12 Lemma 2 of §6: an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism is isotopic to the identity

Theorem (V6.12). Every diffeomorphism \(f\) of \(\mathbb R^m\) — and more generally of a finite-dimensional real normed space \(E\) — whose Jacobian determinant is positive at one point is smoothly isotopic to the identity. Chapter7/Isotopylemma2_of_sec6 Chapter7/IsotopysmoothIsotopicMap_id

A diffeomorphism is given unbundled, as a smooth map with a smooth two-sided inverse, as in V6.5 Chapter7/IsotopyIsDiffeoSelf; an isotopy is a smooth \(H : E \times \mathbb R \to E\) with \(H(\cdot, 0) = f\), \(H(\cdot, 1) = \mathrm{id}\) and every time slice a diffeomorphism, the shape already used in V4.4 Chapter7/IsotopySmoothIsotopicMap. Positivity of the Jacobian at one point is positivity at every point, the sign of the determinant of the derivative of a diffeomorphism being constant Chapter7/IsotopyIsDiffeoSelf.sgn_det_fderiv_const.

Nothing in the development depends on this lemma. §6 replaced Milnor’s appeal to it by the sign computation of V6.5, and it is formalized because it is a theorem of the book. The Lean file sits in Chapter7/ because its last step is the \(GL^+\) path of Chapter 7 and Chapter 6 may not import Chapter 7.

The proof as formalized is Milnor’s, in three steps composed by transitivity. Translation carries \(f\) to \(x \mapsto f(x) - f(0)\) Chapter7/IsotopysmoothIsotopicMap_sub_apply_zero. A diffeomorphism fixing the origin is isotopic to its derivative there by \(F(x, t) = f(tx)/t\), smooth by V6.11(c) Chapter7/IsotopysmoothIsotopicMap_fderiv. And a linear automorphism of positive determinant is isotopic to the identity along the \(GL^+\) path of V7.3 Chapter7/IsotopysmoothIsotopicMap_id_of_det_pos Chapter7/GLplusexists_glPath.

Three things Milnor passes over. Transitivity of isotopy needs the two isotopies made constant near the join before they are glued Chapter7/IsotopySmoothIsotopicMap.trans. The slices at negative times must be diffeomorphisms too, because the definition asks for every real time. And invertibility of the derivative, which the first two steps use, comes from the chain rule applied to the two-sided inverse Chapter7/IsotopyIsDiffeoSelf.bijective_fderiv.

Stronger than the book. The statement is for any finite-dimensional real normed space, and positivity of the dimension is not needed.

V6.13 Lemma 5, and the derivative of the retraction

Let \(N \subseteq \mathbb R^{K+1}\) be a compact nonempty submanifold of dimension \(n\), and \(r\) the nearest-point retraction of V6.6.

Theorem (V6.13).

  1. At \(q \in N\) the derivative \(dr_q\) is the orthogonal projection of \(\mathbb R^{K+1}\) onto \(T_qN\): it is the identity on \(T_qN\), its image is \(T_qN\), it is idempotent, and its kernel is exactly \((T_qN)^\perp\). Chapter6/ChartIndexTub.dret Chapter6/ChartIndexTub.dret_apply_of_mem_tanN Chapter6/ChartIndexTub.ker_dret

  2. Milnor’s Lemma 5. If \(v\) is a smooth tangent field on \(N\) with \(v(q) = 0\), the derivative of \(v\) at \(q\) carries \(T_qN\) into itself — both in the ambient reading, the derivative at \(q\) of \(x \mapsto v(r(x))\), and in the intrinsic one, the derivative of \(v : N \to \mathbb R^{K+1}\) on the image of the derivative of the inclusion. Chapter6/ChartIndexTub.dvr_mem_tanN Chapter6/ChartIndexTub.mfd_mem_tanN

  3. Hence, at a zero of \(v\), the derivative of the extended field \(w = v \circ r + (\mathrm{id} - r)\) of V6.7 is \(dv_q \circ dr_q + (\mathrm{id} - dr_q)\), which in the splitting \(\mathbb R^{K+1} = T_qN \oplus (T_qN)^\perp\) is \(dv_q\) on the tangent part and the identity on the normal one. So \(\det dw_q\) is the determinant of the restriction \(dv_q|_{T_qN}\), and \(dw_q\) is invertible exactly when that restriction is. Chapter6/ChartIndexTub.dvT Chapter6/ChartIndexTub.det_fderiv_w₀ Chapter6/ChartIndexTub.bijective_fderiv_w₀_iff

The idea. V6.6 gives \(x - r(x) \perp T_{r(x)}N\) and \(dr_x\) with values in \(T_{r(x)}N\); differentiating those two facts at a point of \(N\), where \(r\) is the identity, yields (a). For (b), differentiate the identity \((\mathrm{id} - dr)(v \circ r) = 0\) rather than the field itself.

Where the route differs from Milnor’s. Milnor proves Lemma 5 by writing the field in a basis of coefficient fields and differentiating, which presumes the smoothness of the coefficients. Here nothing is written in coordinates: the identity \((\mathrm{id} - dr)(v \circ r) = 0\) holds because \(v \circ r\) takes values in the tangent spaces, and differentiating it at a zero of \(v\) kills the term in which \(dr\) is differentiated, because it is multiplied by \(v(q) = 0\).

What Milnor leaves implicit is what “the derivative of a field on a submanifold” means at all. Both readings are given, and their agreement is a theorem, not a convention.

Hidden hypotheses. \(N\) compact and nonempty, because the retraction of V6.6 exists only then; Lemma 5 itself needs no compactness. The hypothesis \(v(q) = 0\) is essential in (b) and is Milnor’s: without it the derivative of \(v\) at \(q\) has no invariant meaning as an endomorphism of \(T_qN\).

V6.14 The chart definition of the index, and the agreement of the two

Milnor defines the index of a zero of a field on a manifold through a parametrization (p. 33): a local parametrization \(\psi : \Omega \to N\), with \(\Omega \subseteq \mathbb R^n\) open and \(\psi(u_0) = q\), pulls \(v\) back to a field on \(\Omega\), and the index of \(v\) at \(q\) is the index of the pull-back at \(u_0\). The formal version pulls back through the slice-chart parametrization of V6.6, extends the result to a global field by the cut-off of V6.0, and takes its index Chapter6/ChartIndexTub.chartField Chapter6/ChartIndexTub.chartIndexN.

Theorem (V6.14). Let \(N \subseteq \mathbb R^{K+1}\) be compact and nonempty, of dimension \(n\).

  1. The chart index depends neither on the parametrization nor on the extension. For any smooth local parametrization \(\psi\) of \(N\) at \(q\) with a smooth ambient left inverse \(\chi\) and with \(d\psi_u\) spanning the tangent space, and any globally smooth field on \(\mathbb R^n\) that agrees near \(u_0\) with the pull-back and has an isolated zero there, the index at \(u_0\) is the chart index of \(v\) at \(q\). Chapter6/ChartIndexTub.index_eq_chartIndexN

  2. At a non-degenerate zero both definitions are the sign of one determinant: the index of the extended field is \(\operatorname{sgn}\det(dv_q|_{T_qN})\) by V6.13(c) and V6.10, and so is the chart index, because \(d\varphi_q\) conjugates the derivative of the pulled-back field into that restriction. Chapter6/ChartIndexTub.indexN_eq_sgn_det Chapter6/ChartIndexTub.chartIndexN_eq_sgn_det

  3. Hence the chart definition agrees with the definition of V6.8 at every non-degenerate zero (Milnor, pp. 33 and 37). Chapter6/ChartIndexTub.chartIndexN_eq_indexN

Part (a) is Milnor’s Lemma 1 (V6.5) applied to the transition \(\chi_q \circ \psi\) between two parametrizations; it is what makes the chart index well defined, and it is exactly the use Milnor makes of his Lemma 1.

Hidden hypotheses, and they are two. The ambient index needs \(K \ge 1\) and the chart index needs \(n \ge 2\), because the two are degrees on spheres of different dimensions, \(S^K\) and \(S^{n-1}\); also \(N\) compact and nonempty, as in V6.13.

What is not proved, and why it is not a matter of effort. The agreement at an arbitrary isolated zero. Since the two numbers are degrees of maps of spheres of different dimensions, no appeal to invariance under diffeomorphisms compares them. What is needed first is a suspension formula — that the index of a field of the shape \((u, y) \mapsto (\tilde v(u), y)\) on \(\mathbb R^n \times \mathbb R^{K+1-n}\) is the index of \(\tilde v\) — which this development does not have and which Milnor does not prove either. At a non-degenerate zero the question does not arise, and that is the case his arguments use.

V6.15 The Euler number of the sphere

Theorem (V6.15). Let \(n \ge 1\). For every smooth tangent field \(v\) on \(S^n\) whose zeros are finitely many distinct points \(z_1, \dots, z_j\), \[\sum_{i=1}^j \operatorname{ind}_{S^n}(v; z_i) = 1 + (-1)^n,\] which is \(2\) for \(n\) even and \(0\) for \(n\) odd. Chapter6/EulerSphereSphere.indexSum_sph Chapter6/EulerSphereSphere.indexSum_sph_even Chapter6/EulerSphereSphere.indexSum_sph_odd

This is Milnor’s example on p. 39, with pp. 32–33. The integer of V6.9 is thereby not merely bounded but pinned down: any integer with the property that V6.9 asserts of \(\chi\) equals \(1 + (-1)^n\) Chapter6/EulerSphereSphere.eq_of_indexSum_sph Chapter6/EulerSphereSphere.poincare_hopf_sph.

The proof as formalized is Milnor’s. The field is the gradient on \(S^n\) of the height function, \(v(x) = e - \langle e, x\rangle x\) for a unit vector \(e\) Chapter6/EulerSphereSphere.gradHeight Chapter6/EulerSphereSphere.gradSph, whose zeros are exactly the two poles \(e\) and \(-e\). By V6.13 the derivative on the tangent space is minus the identity at \(e\), of determinant \((-1)^n\), and the identity at \(-e\), of determinant \(1\) Chapter6/EulerSphereSphere.dvT_gradSph_pos Chapter6/EulerSphereSphere.dvT_gradSph_neg, so V6.10 and V6.14 give the indices \((-1)^n\) and \(1\) Chapter6/EulerSphereSphere.indexSum_gradSph, and V6.9 transfers their sum to every field.

The odd case is checked a second way. For \(n\) odd the sphere carries a nowhere-zero field, by the converse half of V5.10 rebuilt here Chapter6/EulerSphereSphere.exists_perp_linear Chapter6/EulerSphereSphere.exists_nonvanishing_tangent, so the index sum is an empty sum and the integer is \(0\) Chapter6/EulerSphereSphere.indexSum_sph_of_nonvanishing; a third theorem derives \(1 + (-1)^n = 0\) from the two computations, as it must Chapter6/EulerSphereSphere.indexSum_sph_odd_agree.

What had to be added. §6’s tubular machinery is written for slice charts whose complement model is a Euclidean space \(\mathbb R^m\), whereas Chapter 5 presents \(S^n\) as the level set of a real-valued function and so with the line itself as complement. The two are isomorphic but not the same model, so the presentation was redone with complement model \(\mathbb R^1\) Chapter6/EulerSphereSphere.sphSub, together with the tangent space at \(q\) as \(q^\perp\) for that structure Chapter6/EulerSphereSphere.mem_tanN_iff and the derivative through the retraction of a field coming from the ambient space Chapter6/EulerSpheredvr_of_ambient. For the same reason the nowhere-zero field of V5.10 had to be rebuilt here as an ambient linear map, some forty duplicated lines. A general lemma saying that two slice structures on the same set have the same smooth maps would remove them, and the project has none.

Not formalized, and not writable. That this integer is the Euler characteristic of \(S^n\). This is a gap in vocabulary, not in effort: Mathlib has no Euler characteristic of a space, no Betti numbers and no cellular homology, so the sentence \(\chi(S^n) = 1 + (-1)^n\) cannot be formed at all. Every statement here is about index sums of vector fields, and Milnor himself proves no more, referring to Hopf’s theorem and to the literature. It is the one place where this edition is further from the book than a page count suggests.

What the formalization taught us

  • The index is a total function: \(0\) at a point that is not an isolated zero, with junk values for the sphere map and the normalization where \(v\) vanishes. Every theorem assumes the nonvanishing it needs, so these values never enter a result Chapter6/Indexindex Chapter6/IndexsphMap.
  • The sphere carries the complement convention, so the region lemma reverses the orientation of \(\partial X\), and the numbers are Milnor’s Chapter5/HairyBallsphOr Chapter6/Regionsum_indexAt_eq_deg.
  • Lemma 1 of §5 was generalized twice, to level sets in manifolds and to maps smooth only on an open set, at the price of a chart-level continuity proof Chapter6/LevelOrientMlevelOrientM_cont Chapter6/LevelZerodegAt_level_eq_zero_of_opens.
  • A common regular value is not free. It takes Brown’s theorem, openness of regular values for compact domains (re-proved here through the sign, hence for oriented manifolds, although V1.4 already gives it), and the Baire property of \(S^n\) Chapter6/RegularOpenisOpen_regularPoints Chapter6/RegularOpenexists_mem_of_dense_of_isOpen.
  • One transport lemma replaces an isotopy. V6.2 handles inclusions, affine parametrizations, the diffeomorphism and the radial map Chapter6/LevelMapsignAt_levelOrientM_map'.
  • Milnor’s Lemma 2 is not needed. A homogeneous radial map, Euler’s identity and the matrix determinant lemma compute the sign directly, and the intermediate value theorem keeps \(\operatorname{sgn}\det df\) constant on a ball Chapter6/RadialsignAt_nv0_linear Chapter6/DetSignsgn_det_fderiv_eq. The lemma is nonetheless proved, and its cost is almost all in one fact Mathlib lacks: that an integral over a fixed interval depends smoothly on a parameter Chapter6/HadamardcontDiff_intervalIntegral Chapter7/Isotopylemma2_of_sec6.
  • The derivative of the retraction is the orthogonal projection. That one identification carries Lemma 5, the determinant of the extended field, and both index computations of V6.14 Chapter6/ChartIndexTub.ker_dret Chapter6/ChartIndexTub.det_fderiv_w₀.
  • Two indices, two sphere dimensions. The extended field gives a degree on \(S^K\) and a parametrization a degree on \(S^{n-1}\), which is why the two definitions can be compared at a non-degenerate zero and not, as yet, anywhere else Chapter6/ChartIndexTub.chartIndexN_eq_indexN.
  • The \(\varepsilon\)-neighbourhood theorem is proved, not quoted. It needs \(N\) nonempty, a separate proof that the local inverse is smooth on a neighbourhood, and a sequential compactness argument for the uniform radius Chapter6/Tubular2exists_contDiffOn_U Chapter6/Tubular3exists_eps.
  • The index on \(N\) is defined through the extension, so Poincaré–Hopf does not depend on the invariance lemma; Milnor’s chart definition is formalized beside it, and the two agree wherever his own arguments compare them Chapter6/PoincareHopfindexN Chapter6/ChartIndexTub.chartIndexN.
  • The exact hypotheses of Poincaré–Hopf: ambient dimension at least \(2\), \(N\) compact and nonempty, finitely many zeros listed without repetition. The integer \(\chi\) is a degree; for \(S^n\) it is computed to be \(1 + (-1)^n\), and calling it the Euler characteristic is a sentence this library cannot yet form Chapter6/PoincareHopfpoincare_hopf Chapter6/EulerSphereSphere.indexSum_sph.
  • Two statements are slightly stronger than the book’s, one hypothesis is idle. The region lemma and Hopf’s lemma need the zeros only to lie among the \(z_i\); the transversality lemma assumes a regularity of \(f\) that its proof never uses Chapter6/Hopfhopf_lemma Chapter6/LevelZeroexists_mfd_eq_zero_of_isRegularPoint_level.

Part V. Framed cobordism, Theorem A and the first half of Theorem B (Milnor §7)

This part runs from framed submanifolds to Milnor’s Theorem A and the first half of his Theorem B. Theorem A says the framed cobordism class of the Pontryagin manifold depends on neither the regular value nor the positive basis. The first half of Theorem B says smoothly homotopic maps \(M \to S^p\) have framed cobordant Pontryagin manifolds. The formal text spends seventeen files on this, partly because it proves four facts the book quotes. Framed cobordism is symmetric and transitive; regular values form an open set; \(GL^+(p,\mathbb R)\) is smoothly path connected; and a homotopy can be made constant near its ends without losing a regular value. Two definitional choices shape everything. A cobordism is a boundaryless submanifold of \(M \times \mathbb R\). Every framing built from a map is an explicit formula, a pseudo-inverse of an ambient derivative, so its smoothness reduces to that of the ingredients.

Map. Paths are relative to Milnor/.

  • Chapter7/Transition: a time change \(\rho\), \(0\) below \(\varepsilon\), \(1\) above \(1-\varepsilon\), \(\rho' > 0\) between.
  • Chapter7/Framed: ambient tangent spaces, framed submanifolds, framed cobordisms.
  • Chapter7/Pontryagin: the pseudo-inverse, the extension \(\tilde F = c_y \circ f \circ r\), the Pontryagin manifold.
  • Chapter7/AdjXR: adjoint and pseudo-inverse on \(\mathbb R^{K+1} \times \mathbb R\).
  • Chapter7/Reparam: a homotopy made constant near its ends.
  • Chapter7/Cobordism: the cobordism \(F^{-1}(z)\) inside Lemmas 2 and 3.
  • Chapter7/GLplus: smooth paths in \(GL^+(p,\mathbb R)\).
  • Chapter7/BasisPath: smooth paths of bases.
  • Chapter7/Lemma1: Lemma 1, general form.
  • Chapter7/RegOpen: regular values of \(M \to S^p\) form an open set.
  • Chapter7/Rotation: planar rotations of \(S^p\).
  • Chapter7/Transport: time changes, locality of tangent spaces, gluing.
  • Chapter7/Equiv: symmetry and transitivity.
  • Chapter7/Compose: composing with a map of the sphere.
  • Chapter7/RotHomotopy: rotating the target.
  • Chapter7/Lemma2: Lemma 2 along an arc, then Theorem A.
  • Chapter7/ThmA: the first half of Theorem B.

Letters follow Milnor. The file names, the project’s docstrings and the verified edition use an older lettering: their “Lemma 2” is Theorem A, their “Lemma 3” is the construction of V7.2, their “Theorem A, first half” is the first half of Theorem B, their “Theorem B” is Theorem C, and their “Theorem C” is Milnor’s unlettered product neighbourhood theorem.

Standing conventions

\(M \subseteq \mathbb R^{K+1}\) is a slice submanifold modelled on \(\mathbb R^m\) (normal model \(\mathbb R^w\)), with the manifold structure induced by its slice charts Chapter2/SubmanifoldIsSliceSubmanifold. The standing hypotheses add that \(M\) is compact and nonempty and that \(n + p = m\). Nonemptiness is required by the tubular neighbourhood of Chapter 6, on which every framing is built. Hausdorffness and second countability come free for a subset of Euclidean space. Tangent spaces are subspaces of the ambient space: \(T_xM \subseteq \mathbb R^{K+1}\) is the range of the derivative of the inclusion, and likewise for \(N \subseteq M\) and, inside \(\mathbb R^{K+1} \times \mathbb R\), for \(S \subseteq M \times \mathbb R\) Chapter7/FramedtangentM Chapter7/FramedtangentN Chapter7/FramedtangentS. \(S^p \subseteq \mathbb R^{p+1}\) is the zero set of \(|x|^2 - 1\) with the slice structure of Chapter 2 and the orientation of Chapter 5 Chapter5/HairyBallSph Chapter5/HairyBallsphOr. Derivatives into \(S^p\) are read in charts. So a “basis of \(T_yS^p\)” is a basis of the model space \(\mathbb R^p\). It is positive at \(y\) when its orientation equals the orientation of the sphere read in the chart \(c_y\) at \(y\).

V7.0 Framed submanifolds and framed cobordism

Definition (framed submanifold). Let \(M \subseteq \mathbb R^k\) be a slice submanifold modelled on \(\mathbb R^m\). A framed submanifold of dimension \(n\) and codimension \(p\) is a set \(N \subseteq M\) together with maps \(v_1, \dots, v_p : N \to \mathbb R^k\) such that:

  • \(N\) is a slice submanifold of \(M\) modelled on \(\mathbb R^n\) with normal model \(\mathbb R^p\);
  • \(n + p = m\), and \(N\) is compact;
  • each \(v_i\) is smooth for the induced structure on \(N\);
  • for every \(x \in N\), \(v_i(x) \in T_xM\) and \(\langle v_i(x), w\rangle = 0\) for all \(w \in T_xN\);
  • \(v_1(x), \dots, v_p(x)\) are linearly independent Chapter7/FramedFramedSub.

Only independence is asked; that the \(v_i(x)\) then span the normal space of \(N\) in \(M\) follows by counting dimensions.

Definition (framed cobordism). Let \((N_0, v^0)\) and \((N_1, v^1)\) be framed submanifolds of \(M\) of dimension \(n\) and codimension \(p\). A framed cobordism from the first to the second consists of the following data.

  1. A slice submanifold \(S\) of the product manifold \(M \times \mathbb R\), modelled on \(\mathbb R^{n+1}\) with normal model \(\mathbb R^p\).
  2. A number \(\varepsilon\) with \(0 < \varepsilon < \tfrac12\). For \(t < \varepsilon\), \((x,t) \in S\) if and only if \(x \in N_0\). For \(t > 1 - \varepsilon\), \((x,t) \in S\) if and only if \(x \in N_1\).
  3. \(S \cap (M \times [0,1])\) is compact.
  4. Smooth maps \(u_1, \dots, u_p : S \to \mathbb R^k \times \mathbb R\). At \(q = (x,t)\), the \(\mathbb R^k\)-component of each \(u_i(q)\) lies in \(T_xM\). The \(u_i(q)\) are orthogonal to \(T_qS\) for \(\langle (a,s),(b,t)\rangle = \langle a,b\rangle + st\) and linearly independent.
  5. \(u_i(x,t) = (v^0_i(x), 0)\) when \(x \in N_0\) and \(t < \varepsilon\), and \(u_i(x,t) = (v^1_i(x), 0)\) when \(x \in N_1\) and \(t > 1-\varepsilon\).

Two framed submanifolds are framed cobordant if a framed cobordism exists Chapter7/FramedFramedCob Chapter7/FramedFramedCobordant. The inner product on \(\mathbb R^k \times \mathbb R\) is written out by hand, because Mathlib gives the product the sup norm and no inner product structure Chapter7/FramedipXR.

Where the formal definition departs from Milnor. Milnor’s cobordism is a compact manifold with boundary \(X \subseteq M \times [0,1]\), a product near both ends. The formal \(S\) has no boundary and lives for all times. Milnor’s \(X\) is \(S \cap (M \times [0,1])\), and nothing here ever needs \(X\) to be a manifold with boundary. The choice pays off twice and costs nothing.

  • Cobordisms built from maps are level sets, which the regular value theorem of Chapter 2 makes slice submanifolds of a boundaryless manifold Chapter2/LevelSetisSliceSubmanifold_preimage. V7.2 uses \(F^{-1}(z)\) for a homotopy on all of \(M \times \mathbb R\). Lemma 1 uses \(f^{-1}(y) \times \mathbb R\), realized as \((f \circ \mathrm{pr}_1)^{-1}(y)\).
  • Symmetry and transitivity become preimages under \((x,t) \mapsto (x, at+c)\) and gluing along an open strip. With boundaries, gluing end to end is exactly where collars are needed.
  • Nothing is lost: below \(\varepsilon\), \(S\) is exactly \(N_0 \times (-\infty,\varepsilon)\), and above \(1-\varepsilon\) exactly \(N_1 \times (1-\varepsilon,\infty)\). Milnor’s assumed product structure is built in.

V7.1 The Pontryagin manifold

Construction. Assume the standing hypotheses. Let \(f : M \to S^p\) be smooth, let \(y\) be a regular value of \(f\), and let \(b_1, \dots, b_p \in \mathbb R^p\) be linearly independent. The Pontryagin manifold \((f^{-1}(y), f^*b)\) is the framed submanifold of dimension \(n\) and codimension \(p\) with underlying set \(f^{-1}(y)\) and framing \[v_i(x) = A_x^*(A_xA_x^*)^{-1}b_i, \qquad A_x = d\tilde F_x, \qquad \tilde F = c_y \circ f \circ r,\] where \(r\) is the nearest-point retraction onto \(M\) and \(c_y\) the chart of \(S^p\) at \(y\). It satisfies \(A_xv_i(x) = b_i\) Chapter7/Pontryaginpontryagin Chapter7/PontryaginAt_pontV. The basis need not be positive: orientations of bases enter with Lemma 1, and positivity with Theorem A.

The idea. Milnor takes the unique normal vector \(v\) with \(df_x(v) = b_i\) and leaves its smoothness to the reader; the formal text writes it as a formula. Extended off \(M\) through \(r\), the ambient derivative \(A_x\) kills the normal space of \(M\) and the tangent space of \(N\). So the minimal-norm solution of \(A_xv = b_i\) is tangent to \(M\) and normal to \(N\), and it is smooth because each ingredient is.

The proof as formalized.

  1. Linear algebra. For a surjective linear map \(A : E \to F\) of finite-dimensional inner product spaces, \(AA^*\) is invertible. If \(AA^*c = 0\), then \(|A^*c|^2 = \langle c, AA^*c\rangle = 0\), and writing \(c = Av\) gives \(|Av|^2 = \langle v, A^*c\rangle = 0\). So \(AA^*\) is injective, hence bijective Chapter7/PontryaginisUnit_comp_adjoint. Put \(A^+ = A^*(AA^*)^{-1}\) Chapter7/Pontryaginpinv. Then \(AA^+c = c\) Chapter7/Pontryagincomp_pinv. Also \(\langle A^+c, v\rangle = \langle (AA^*)^{-1}c, Av\rangle = 0\) whenever \(Av = 0\) Chapter7/Pontryagininner_pinv_eq_zero.
  2. The extension. Chapter 6 supplies \(\varepsilon_M > 0\) and a map \(r : \mathbb R^{K+1} \to M\). It is the identity on \(M\) and smooth on \(N_\varepsilon = \{\operatorname{dist}(\cdot, M) < \varepsilon_M\}\). It is also constant along short normal segments: if \(x \in M\) and \(v \perp T_xM\), then \(r(x+sv) = x\) for \(s\) near \(0\) Chapter6/Tubular4tubr_spec. Put \(\tilde F(z) = c_y(f(r(z)))\). It is smooth on the open set \(\tilde W\) of \(z \in N_\varepsilon\) with \(f(r(z))\) in the domain of \(c_y\), and equals \(c_y \circ f\) on \(M\) Chapter7/PontryaginFt Chapter7/PontryagincontDiffOn_Ft Chapter7/PontryaginFt_of_mem. Let \(A_z\) be its derivative at \(z\) Chapter7/PontryaginAt.
  3. Four facts at \(x \in N = f^{-1}(y)\).
      1. The chain rule along \(M\) gives \(A_x \circ d(\iota)_x = d(c_y)_{f(x)} \circ df_x\), where \(\iota\) is the inclusion Chapter7/PontryaginAt_comp_mfd_val.
      1. Hence \(A_x\) is surjective, since \(df_x\) is and the chart derivative is invertible Chapter7/Pontryaginsurjective_At.
      1. \(A_x\) vanishes on \((T_xM)^\perp\), because \(s \mapsto \tilde F(x+sv)\) is constant near \(0\) Chapter7/PontryaginAt_normal_eq_zero.
      1. \(A_x\) vanishes on \(T_xN\), because \(\tilde F\) is constant on \(N\) Chapter7/PontryaginAt_tangentN_eq_zero.
  4. The framing \(v_i(x) = A_x^+b_i\) Chapter7/PontryaginpontV. Step 1 gives \(A_xv_i = b_i\), so the \(v_i\) are independent because their images are Chapter7/PontryaginpontV_indep. Orthogonality to \(T_xN\) follows from (d) Chapter7/PontryaginpontV_normal. For tangency, \(v_i \in (\ker A_x)^\perp \subseteq ((T_xM)^\perp)^\perp = T_xM\) by (c) Chapter7/PontryaginpontV_tangent.
  5. Smoothness. \(z \mapsto A_z\) is smooth on \(\tilde W\). Adjoints are a continuous linear operation, and inversion is smooth near an invertible operator. So \(z \mapsto A_z^+b_i\) is smooth near \(N\), and \(v_i\) is its composite with the inclusion \(N \to \mathbb R^{K+1}\) Chapter7/PontryagincontMDiff_pontV.
  6. The set. \(N\) is a slice submanifold of codimension \(p\) by the regular value theorem, and compact as a closed subset of \(M\) Chapter7/PontryaginisSliceSubmanifold_level Chapter7/PontryaginisCompact_level.

V7.2 The cobordism \(F^{-1}(z)\): the construction inside Lemmas 2 and 3

Theorem. Assume the standing hypotheses and let \(0 < \varepsilon < \tfrac12\). Let \(F : M \times \mathbb R \to S^p\) be smooth with regular value \(z\). Let \(f, g : M \to S^p\) be smooth, each with regular value \(z\), such that \(F(x,t) = f(x)\) for \(t \le \varepsilon\) and \(F(x,t) = g(x)\) for \(t \ge 1-\varepsilon\). Let \(b_1, \dots, b_p \in \mathbb R^p\) be linearly independent. Then \((f^{-1}(z), f^*b)\) and \((g^{-1}(z), g^*b)\) are framed cobordant Chapter7/CobordismframedCobordant_of_homotopy.

The idea. Frame \(S = F^{-1}(z)\) by the construction of V7.1 one dimension up. Near the ends \(F\) ignores \(t\), so there the framing is the Pontryagin framing of \(f\) or \(g\) with time component \(0\).

The adjoint on \(\mathbb R^{K+1} \times \mathbb R\). For \(A : \mathbb R^{K+1} \times \mathbb R \to \mathbb R^p\) with partial maps \(A_1 = A(\cdot, 0)\) and \(A_2 = A(0, \cdot)\), set \(A^\dagger c = (A_1^*c, A_2^*c)\). Then \(\langle A^\dagger c, v\rangle = \langle c, Av\rangle\) for the product inner product Chapter7/AdjXRadjXR Chapter7/AdjXRipXR_adjXR. The pseudo-inverse \(A^\dagger(AA^\dagger)^{-1}\) has the properties of step 1 of V7.1 Chapter7/AdjXRisUnit_comp_adjXR Chapter7/AdjXRcomp_pinvXR Chapter7/AdjXRipXR_pinvXR_eq_zero. It has one more, which makes the ends work: if \(A = B \circ \mathrm{pr}_1\) ignores time, it sends \(c\) to \((B^+c, 0)\) Chapter7/AdjXRpinvXR_comp_fst.

The proof as formalized.

  1. \(S = F^{-1}(z)\) is a slice submanifold of \(M \times \mathbb R\) modelled on \(\mathbb R^{n+1}\), by the regular value theorem and \((n+1) + p = m + 1\) Chapter7/CobordismlevelDimXR Chapter7/CobordismisSliceSubmanifold_levelXR.
  2. Extend by \(\hat F(z', t) = c_z(F(r(z'), t))\), smooth where \(z' \in N_\varepsilon\) and \(F(r(z'),t)\) lies in the domain of \(c_z\). Let \(\hat A_q : \mathbb R^{K+1} \times \mathbb R \to \mathbb R^p\) be its derivative Chapter7/CobordismFh Chapter7/CobordismAh. Facts (a)–(c) of V7.1 carry over: the chain rule along \(M \times \mathbb R\), surjectivity on \(S\), and \(\hat A_q(v, 0) = 0\) for \(v \perp T_xM\) Chapter7/CobordismAh_comp_mfd_embXR Chapter7/Cobordismsurjective_Ah Chapter7/CobordismAh_normal_eq_zero. So does (d): \(\hat A_q\) vanishes on \(T_qS\) Chapter7/CobordismAh_tangentS_eq_zero.
  3. The framing is \(u_i(q) = \hat A_q^\dagger(\hat A_q\hat A_q^\dagger)^{-1}b_i\) Chapter7/Cobordismuh. It is normal to \(T_qS\), independent and smooth, as in V7.1 Chapter7/Cobordismuh_normal Chapter7/Cobordismuh_indep Chapter7/CobordismcontMDiff_uh. Its \(\mathbb R^{K+1}\)-component lies in \(T_xM\), since for \(v \perp T_xM\) it pairs with \(v\) to \(\langle u_i, (v,0)\rangle = 0\) Chapter7/Cobordismuh_tangent.
  4. The ends. If \(F(x,t) = f(x)\) for \(t\) in an open set \(O\), then on \(\mathbb R^{K+1} \times O\) the extension \(\hat F\) equals \(\tilde F_f \circ \mathrm{pr}_1\), with \(\tilde F_f\) the extension of \(f\) for the same chart. Hence \(\hat A_{(x,t)} = A_x \circ \mathrm{pr}_1\) when \(t \in O\) and \(f(x) = z\) Chapter7/CobordismAh_eq_At_of_const. The extra property of the pseudo-inverse then gives \(u_i(x,t) = (v_i(x), 0)\), with \(v\) the Pontryagin framing of \(f\) Chapter7/Cobordismuh_end. Take \(O = (-\infty, \varepsilon)\) and \(O = (1-\varepsilon, \infty)\).
  5. For \(t < \varepsilon\), \(F(x,t) = z\) if and only if \(f(x) = z\), and likewise for \(g\) at the top. \(S \cap (M \times [0,1])\) is closed in the compact \(M \times [0,1]\) Chapter7/CobordismframedCobordant_of_homotopy.

Where the formal proof departs from Milnor. This step is the heart of Milnor’s proofs of Lemmas 2 and 3. His Lemma 3 starts from a value \(y\) regular for \(f\) and \(g\) and moves, by Lemma 2, to a nearby regular value \(z\) of the homotopy. Here \(z\) is given; the moving happens in V7.5 and V7.6, and Lemma 3 is the case \(y = z\) of V7.6. Regularity for \(f\) and \(g\) is assumed because the Pontryagin manifolds need it, though it follows from regularity for \(F\).

Making a homotopy constant near its ends

Proposition. Let \(M \subseteq \mathbb R^k\) be a slice submanifold modelled on \(\mathbb R^m\); compactness is not needed. Let \(F : M \times \mathbb R \to S^p\) be smooth, let \(z\) be a regular value of \(F\), of \(F(\cdot,0)\) and of \(F(\cdot,1)\), and let \(0 < \varepsilon < \tfrac12\). Then there is a smooth \(F' : M \times \mathbb R \to S^p\) such that:

  • \(F'(x,t) = F(x,0)\) for \(t \le \varepsilon\);
  • \(F'(x,t) = F(x,1)\) for \(t \ge 1-\varepsilon\);
  • \(z\) is a regular value of \(F'\) Chapter7/Reparamexists_reparam.

The proof as formalized. Put \(F'(x,t) = F(x, \rho(t))\) with \(\rho(t) = \sigma\big((t-\varepsilon)/(1-2\varepsilon)\big)\), where \(\sigma(s) = \psi(s)/(\psi(s) + \psi(1-s))\) is Mathlib’s transition function and \(\psi(s) = e^{-1/s}\) for \(s > 0\), \(\psi(s) = 0\) otherwise.
