From \(\psi'(s) = s^{-2}\psi(s)\) the formal text computes \[\sigma'(s) = \frac{\psi'(s)\psi(1-s) + \psi(s)\psi'(1-s)}{(\psi(s)+\psi(1-s))^2},\] which is positive on \((0,1)\) Chapter7/TransitionhasDerivAt_smoothTransition Chapter7/Transitionderiv_smoothTransition_pos. So \(\rho\) is \(0\) for \(t \le \varepsilon\), \(1\) for \(t \ge 1-\varepsilon\), takes values in \([0,1]\), and has \(\rho' > 0\) on \((\varepsilon, 1-\varepsilon)\) Chapter7/Transitionexists_timeTransition. At a point with \(F'(x,t) = z\), \[dF'_{(x,t)}(a,s) = dF_{(x,\rho(t))}(a, \rho'(t)s).\] If \(\rho(t) \in \{0,1\}\), the vectors \((a,0)\) already suffice, because the \(x\)-derivative is that of \(F(\cdot,0)\) or \(F(\cdot,1)\). Otherwise \(\varepsilon < t < 1-\varepsilon\) and \(\rho'(t) > 0\), so \((a,s) \mapsto (a, \rho'(t)s)\) is bijective and the surjectivity of \(dF\) transfers Chapter7/Reparamexists_reparam.

Why these hypotheses. The lemma keeps a regular value chosen before the time change. A transition function merely constant near the ends could have \(\rho' = 0\) at an interior point where only the time direction made \(dF\) onto; hence \(\rho' > 0\). For \(t \le \varepsilon\) and \(t \ge 1-\varepsilon\), where \(\rho' = 0\), the time direction is lost, so the end maps must be regular themselves. Milnor reparametrizes first and then chooses the regular value, which makes regularity at the ends automatic; the formal proof of V7.6 takes the other order.

V7.3 Lemma 1: the basis does not matter

Theorem (Lemma 1, general form). Assume the standing hypotheses. Let \(f, g : M \to S^p\) be smooth, with \(y\) a regular value of \(f\) and \(z\) a regular value of \(g\). Let \(b\) and \(c\) be linearly independent \(p\)-tuples in \(\mathbb R^p\), and let \(A\) be a \(p \times p\) matrix with \(\det A > 0\). Suppose \(g^{-1}(z) = f^{-1}(y)\) and \(g^*c = f^*(A\cdot b)\) at every point of this set, where \((A \cdot b)_j = \sum_i A_{ij}b_i\). Then \((g^{-1}(z), g^*c)\) and \((f^{-1}(y), f^*b)\) are framed cobordant Chapter7/Lemma1framedCobordant_of_det_pos'.

With \(g = f\), \(z = y\) and \(c = b' = A\cdot b\) it gives \((f^{-1}(y), f^*b') \sim (f^{-1}(y), f^*b)\). Bases \(b, b'\) with the same orientation are related by such an \(A\), and this is Milnor’s Lemma 1 Chapter7/Lemma1framedCobordant_of_det_pos Chapter7/Lemma1framedCobordant_of_orientation_eq. The general form serves V7.5, where the Pontryagin manifold of \(r \circ f\) at \(r(y)\), for a rotation \(r\), has the same underlying set as that of \(f\) at \(y\) and a framing of the form \(f^*(\cdot)\).

The idea. Join \(A \cdot b\) to \(b\) by a smooth path of bases \(B(t)\), and frame \(f^{-1}(y) \times \mathbb R\) by \(f^*B(t)\) at time \(t\). Milnor quotes the connectedness of \(GL^+\); the formal text builds the path.

Smooth paths in \(GL^+(p, \mathbb R)\)

Theorem. Every real \(p \times p\) matrix \(A\) with \(\det A > 0\) is joined to the identity by a map \(G : \mathbb R \to M_p(\mathbb R)\) with smooth entries, \(G(0) = A\), \(G(1) = I\), and \(\det G(t) > 0\) for \(0 \le t \le 1\) Chapter7/GLplusexists_glPath.

The proof as formalized.

  1. Mathlib’s Gaussian elimination gives \(A = L\,D\,L'\), with \(L, L'\) products of transvections \(I + cE_{ij}\) (\(i \ne j\)) and \(D = \operatorname{diag}(d_1, \dots, d_p)\). Each transvection is joined to \(I\) by \(I + tcE_{ij}\), of determinant \(1\). Multiplying along the lists joins \(L\) and \(L'\) to \(I\) within determinant \(1\) Chapter7/GLplustransPath Chapter7/GLpluslistPath Chapter7/GLplusdet_listPath.
  2. Since \(\det D = \det A > 0\), the \(d_i\) are nonzero and evenly many are negative Chapter7/GLpluseven_card_neg. The negative indices are paired off Chapter7/GLplusexists_matching.
  3. The rotation \(R_{ij}(\theta) = I + (\cos\theta - 1)(E_{ii} + E_{jj}) + \sin\theta\,(E_{ji} - E_{ij})\) Chapter7/GLplusrot is \(I + P(CP^{T})\), with \(P\) the \(p \times 2\) matrix with columns \(e_i, e_j\) and \(C = \begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta - 1 & -\sin\theta\\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta - 1\end{pmatrix}\). As \(P^TP = I_2\), \(\det(I + XY) = \det(I + YX)\) gives \(\det R_{ij}(\theta) = \det(I_2 + C) = \cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta = 1\) Chapter7/GLplusdet_rot. And \(R_{ij}(\pi)\) is diagonal with \(-1\) exactly at \(i\) and \(j\) Chapter7/GLplusrot_pi.
  4. The diagonal path is \(\prod_{\text{pairs}} R_{ij}(\pi t) \cdot \operatorname{diag}\big((1-t)d_i + t\operatorname{sgn} d_i\big)\) Chapter7/GLplusdiagPath. It is \(D\) at \(t = 0\), and \(I\) at \(t = 1\) because each negative index lies in exactly one pair Chapter7/GLplusdiagPath_one. Its determinant is \(\prod_i\big((1-t)d_i + t\operatorname{sgn}d_i\big)\), positive for \(0 \le t \le 1\) since each factor keeps the sign of \(d_i\) Chapter7/GLplusdet_diagPath Chapter7/GLplusprod_diagScale_pos.
  5. \(G(t)\) is the \(L\)-path at \(1-t\), times the diagonal path at \(t\), times the \(L'\)-path at \(1-t\) Chapter7/GLplusexists_glPath.

The determinant is known to be positive only on \([0,1]\), so the path of bases composes \(G\) with the transition function \(\rho\), whose values lie in \([0,1]\). For \(b\) independent, \(\det A > 0\) and \(0 < \varepsilon < \tfrac12\), the map \(B(t) = G(\rho(t)) \cdot b\) is smooth and independent for every \(t\). It equals \(A\cdot b\) for \(t \le \varepsilon\) and \(b\) for \(t \ge 1-\varepsilon\) Chapter7/BasisPathexists_basisPath Chapter7/BasisPathlinearIndependent_mulTuple. Bases with the same orientation differ by a change-of-basis matrix of positive determinant Chapter7/BasisPathexists_det_pos_of_orientation_eq.

The cobordism

The proof as formalized.

  1. The cobordism is \(f^{-1}(y) \times \mathbb R\), the level set of \((x,t) \mapsto f(x)\), for which \(y\) is again regular Chapter7/Lemma1isRegularValue_comp_fst. Take \(\varepsilon = \tfrac14\).
  2. The framing is \(u_i(x,t) = \hat A^\dagger(\hat A\hat A^\dagger)^{-1}B(t)_i\), with \(\hat A\) the derivative of the extension of \((x,t) \mapsto f(x)\) Chapter7/Lemma1uht. Pointwise it is the framing of V7.2 with the basis frozen at \(B(t)\), so tangency, normality and independence are quoted. Only smoothness uses the variation of \(B\) Chapter7/Lemma1contMDiff_uht.
  3. The ends. For \(t < \tfrac14\) the end lemma of V7.2 gives \(u_i = (f^*(A \cdot b)_i, 0) = (g^*c_i, 0)\), and \(S\) matches \(g^{-1}(z) = f^{-1}(y)\). For \(t > \tfrac34\) it gives \(u_i = (f^*b_i, 0)\) Chapter7/Lemma1framedCobordant_of_det_pos'.

V7.4 Framed cobordism is symmetric and transitive

Theorem. Let \(M \subseteq \mathbb R^{K+1}\) be a slice submanifold modelled on \(\mathbb R^m\); compactness is not needed. Let \(F_0, F_1, F_2\) be framed submanifolds of \(M\) of dimension \(n\) and codimension \(p\). If \(F_0\) is framed cobordant to \(F_1\), then \(F_1\) is framed cobordant to \(F_0\). If moreover \(F_1\) is framed cobordant to \(F_2\), then \(F_0\) is framed cobordant to \(F_2\) Chapter7/EquivFramedCobordant.symm Chapter7/EquivFramedCobordant.trans.

Reflexivity is not proved here, and this part does not need it. In general it comes only in Chapter 8, by a detour: Theorem C writes \(F\) as a Pontryagin manifold, and V7.2 applies to the constant homotopy Chapter8/FramedOpsframedCobordant_refl. For framed points the same detour is taken later in Chapter 7 Chapter7/ReachFramedCobordant.refl'.

The idea. Symmetry reverses time. Transitivity shifts the second cobordism to \([1,2]\), glues along the common product strip at \(t = 1\), and compresses \([0,2]\) to \([0,1]\). Milnor asserts all this without proof. The formal work is to show each operation yields a slice submanifold and a framing.

Transport and gluing

  1. Preimages. The preimage of a slice submanifold under an ambient diffeomorphism \(\tau\) is a slice submanifold: compose its slice charts with \(\tau\) Chapter7/TransportisSliceSubmanifold_preimage_diffeomorph. The time changes \(\tau(x,t) = (x, at+c)\), \(a \neq 0\), are diffeomorphisms of \(M \times \mathbb R\) Chapter7/TransportaffineXR Chapter7/TransportisSliceSubmanifold_preimage_affine.
  2. Tangent spaces. With \(D_a(v,s) = (v, as)\), \(T_{\tau(q)}S = D_a\big(T_q\,\tau^{-1}(S)\big)\) Chapter7/TransportdtXR Chapter7/TransporttangentS_affine. This follows from the chain rule, since the derivative of \(\tau^{-1}(S) \to S\) is surjective, the map having a smooth inverse Chapter7/Transportsurjective_mfd_ιaff.
  3. Locality. If \(S \cap U = T \cap U\) with \(U\) open, then \(S\) and \(T\) have the same tangent spaces on \(U\) Chapter7/TransporttangentS_eq_of_inter_eq.
  4. Gluing. If \(S_1, S_2\) agree on the strip \(c' < t < c\), then \((S_1 \cap \{t < c\}) \cup (S_2 \cap \{t > c'\})\) is a slice submanifold. Slice charts of \(S_1\) restrict to \(\{t < c\}\), and those of \(S_2\) to \(\{t > c'\}\) Chapter7/TransportglueS Chapter7/TransportisSliceSubmanifold_glueS.

A framing without end conditions Chapter7/EquivFraming is transported by \(u'_i(q) = D_a u_i(\tau(q))\) Chapter7/EquivFraming.transport. Tangent vectors come back from \(\tau(q)\) to \(q\) by \(D_a^{-1}\); normal vectors come back by the transpose of \(D_a\), and \(D_a\) is its own transpose, \(\langle D_au, w\rangle = \langle u, D_aw\rangle\) Chapter7/EquivipXR_dtXR. So if \(u \perp T_{\tau(q)}S\) and \(w \in T_q\tau^{-1}(S)\), then \(D_aw \in T_{\tau(q)}S\) and \(\langle D_au, w\rangle = \langle u, D_aw\rangle = 0\). \(D_a\) is injective and fixes the \(\mathbb R^{K+1}\)-component, so independence and tangency survive. Framings agreeing on the strip glue with a cut at \(c_0 \in (c', c)\): \(u_1\) below \(c_0\), \(u_2\) from \(c_0\) on Chapter7/EquivglueU. The result is \(u_1\) on the open set \(\{t < c_0\}\) and \(u_2\) on the open set \(\{t > c'\}\), hence smooth, and it is normal by locality Chapter7/EquivFraming.glue.

Symmetry and transitivity

Symmetry. Take \(\tau^{-1}(S)\) for \(\tau(x,t) = (x, 1-t)\), with the same \(\varepsilon\). Time components of the framing change sign, which leaves the end framings \((v_i, 0)\) alone. The middle piece is the image of the old one under \(\tau\) Chapter7/EquivFramedCobordant.symm.

Transitivity. Let \(X\) run from \(F_0\) to \(F_1\) with margin \(\varepsilon_X\), and \(Y\) from \(F_1\) to \(F_2\) with \(\varepsilon_Y\).

  1. Shift \(Y\) to \([1,2]\): take its preimage under \((x,t) \mapsto (x, t-1)\).
  2. On \(1 - \varepsilon_X < t < 1 + \varepsilon_Y\), both \(X\) and the shifted \(Y\) are \(N_1 \times\) strip, framed by \((v^1_i, 0)\). Glue with \(c_0 = 1\).
  3. Compress: take the preimage under \((x,t) \mapsto (x, 2t)\). This doubles the time components of the framing; the new margin is \(\varepsilon = \min(\varepsilon_X, \varepsilon_Y)/2\).
  4. The glued piece over \([0,2]\) is \(X \cap (M \times [0,1])\) together with the shifted \(Y \cap (M \times [0,1])\), hence compact Chapter7/EquivFramedCobordant.trans.

V7.5 Theorem A: neither the regular value nor the positive basis matters

Theorem (Theorem A). Assume the standing hypotheses and \(p \ge 1\). Let \(f : M \to S^p\) be smooth and let \(y, z\) be regular values of \(f\). Let \(e_0\) be a positive basis at \(y\) and \(e\) a positive basis at \(z\). Then \((f^{-1}(y), f^*e_0)\) and \((f^{-1}(z), f^*e)\) are framed cobordant Chapter7/Lemma2framedCobordant_of_regularValues.

Milnor’s Lemma 2 is the local case, \(z\) near \(y\), proved by rotating the sphere. His proof of Theorem A takes one rotation \(r\) with \(r(y) = z\) and applies Lemma 3 to \(f \simeq r \circ f\); Lemma 3 in turn moves regular values by Lemma 2. The formal proof builds four tools, proves Lemma 2 along an arc, and runs the rest as one explicit chain.

The regular values form an open set

Proposition. Let \(M\) be compact and nonempty, as in the standing hypotheses, and let \(f : M \to S^p\) be smooth. Then the regular points of \(f\) form an open subset of \(M\), and the regular values form an open subset of \(S^p\) Chapter7/RegOpenisOpen_regularPoints_sph Chapter7/RegOpenisOpen_regularValues_sph.

The idea. \(df_x\) is read in the chart at \(f(x)\), which moves with \(x\), so there is no continuous family to perturb. Fix instead \(y = f(x_0)\) and the extension \(\tilde F\) of V7.1 for the chart \(c_y\). Then \(x \mapsto A_x\) is continuous.

The proof as formalized.

  1. For \(x \in M\) with \(f(x)\) in the domain of \(c_y\), \(df_x\) is onto if and only if \(A_x\) is Chapter7/RegOpensurjective_At_of_isRegularPoint. For the converse, write \(v = t + \nu\) with \(t \in T_xM\) and \(\nu \perp T_xM\); then \(A_x\nu = 0\), and the chart derivative is injective Chapter7/RegOpenisRegularPoint_of_surjective_At.
  2. \(A\) is onto if and only if \(AA^*\) is invertible, and invertible operators form an open set Chapter7/RegOpensurjective_iff_isUnit_comp_adjoint Chapter7/RegOpenisOpen_surjective.
  3. So regular points form an open set. Critical points are closed in the compact \(M\), hence compact, and so the critical values are compact and closed.

Planar rotations of the sphere

For orthonormal \(u, v \in \mathbb R^{p+1}\) let \[R_\theta x = x + (\cos\theta - 1)\big(\langle u,x\rangle u + \langle v,x\rangle v\big) + \sin\theta\big(\langle u,x\rangle v - \langle v,x\rangle u\big)\] Chapter7/RotationrotCLM. These form a one-parameter group of isometries Chapter7/RotationrotCLM_add Chapter7/Rotationnorm_rotCLM. Each has positive determinant, by continuity: \(\theta \mapsto \det R_\theta\) never vanishes, since \(\det R_{-\theta}\det R_\theta = 1\), and equals \(1\) at \(0\) Chapter7/Rotationdet_rotCLM_pos. The induced map \(r_\theta\) of \(S^p\) is defined by normalizing, so it needs no hypotheses. For orthonormal \(u, v\) it is the restriction of \(R_\theta\) Chapter7/RotationrotS Chapter7/RotationrotS_val. The family \((x,t) \mapsto r_{\rho(t)}(x)\) is smooth for smooth \(\rho\) Chapter7/RotationcontMDiff_rotS_family. Each \(r_\theta\) has sign \(+1\) everywhere, by Chapter 6’s formula \(\operatorname{sgn}\det\) for normalized linear maps Chapter7/RotationsignAt_rotS Chapter6/RadialsignAt_nv0_linear.

Lemma (rotation paths). Let \(p \ge 1\) and \(y, y' \in S^p\). There are orthonormal \(u, v\) and \(\theta_0 \in [0,\pi]\) with \(R_{\theta_0}y = y'\) and \(|R_{t\theta_0}y - y| \le |y' - y|\) for \(0 \le t \le 1\) Chapter7/Rotationexists_rotation_path.

The proof as formalized. Take \(u = y\), \(a = \langle y, y'\rangle\) and \(w = y' - ay\), so that \(w \perp y\) and \(|w|^2 = 1 - a^2\). Let \(v = w/|w|\) if \(w \ne 0\), and otherwise any unit vector orthogonal to \(y\), which exists because \(p \ge 1\) Chapter7/Rotationexists_unit_orthogonal. With \(\theta_0 = \arccos a\), \(R_{\theta_0}y = ay + |w|v = y'\). The chord \(|R_\theta y - y|^2 = 2 - 2\cos\theta\) increases on \([0,\pi]\) Chapter7/Rotationdist_rotCLM_u_sq Chapter7/Rotationdist_rotCLM_u.

Composing with a map of the sphere

Proposition. Assume the standing hypotheses. Let \(f\) be smooth with regular value \(y\). Let \(r : S^p \to S^p\) be smooth with \(dr_y\) bijective and of sign \(+1\), and such that \(r(f(x)) = r(y)\) implies \(f(x) = y\). Let \(e\) be positive at \(r(y)\) and \(e_0\) positive at \(y\). Then \(r(y)\) is a regular value of \(r \circ f\), and \(((r\circ f)^{-1}(r(y)), (r \circ f)^*e)\) is framed cobordant to \((f^{-1}(y), f^*e_0)\) Chapter7/ComposeisRegularValue_comp Chapter7/ComposeframedCobordant_comp.

\(r\) need not be a diffeomorphism; only conditions at \(y\) and on the fibre are asked.

The proof as formalized.

  1. Near \(x \in f^{-1}(y)\) the extension of \(r \circ f\) is \((c_{r(y)} \circ r \circ c_y^{-1}) \circ \tilde F_f\). Hence \(A^{r\circ f}_x = dr_y \circ A^f_x\), with \(dr_y\) read in charts Chapter7/ComposehasFDerivAt_written Chapter7/ComposeAt_comp.
  2. For surjective \(A\) and bijective \(D\), \((DA)^+c = A^+(D^{-1}c)\). Indeed \(A^+c\) is the unique vector in the range of \(A^*\) mapped to \(c\), and \((DA)^*\) has the range of \(A^*\) Chapter7/Composepinv_unique Chapter7/Composepinv_comp. So \((r \circ f)^*e = f^*(dr_y^{-1}e)\) Chapter7/ComposepontV_comp.
  3. Sign \(+1\) means \(dr_y\) carries the orientation at \(y\) to that at \(r(y)\) Chapter7/Composeorientation_map_of_orSign_eq_one. So \(dr_y^{-1}e = A \cdot e_0\) with \(\det A > 0\), and the general Lemma 1 applies: the level sets coincide by the fibre hypothesis, the framings by step 2 Chapter7/ComposeframedCobordant_comp.

Rotating the target

Proposition. Let \(M \subseteq \mathbb R^{K+1}\) be a slice submanifold modelled on \(\mathbb R^m\). Let \(f : M \to S^p\) be smooth, let \(u, v\) be orthonormal, let \(\theta_0 \in \mathbb R\) and \(0 < \varepsilon < \tfrac12\). Then there is a smooth \(F : M \times \mathbb R \to S^p\) such that:

  • \(F(x,t) = f(x)\) for \(t \le \varepsilon\);
  • \(F(x,t) = r_{\theta_0}(f(x))\) for \(t \ge 1-\varepsilon\);
  • for every \(y\), if \(\theta_0 \ge 0\) and every \(r_\tau(y)\) with \(0 \le \tau \le \theta_0\) is a regular value of \(f\), then \(r_{\theta_0}(y)\) is a regular value of \(F\) Chapter7/RotHomotopyexists_rotHomotopy.

The proof as formalized. Put \(F(x,t) = r_{\theta_0\rho(t)}(f(x))\). If \(F(x,t) = r_{\theta_0}(y)\), then \(f(x) = r_{\theta_0(1-\rho(t))}(y)\) lies on the arc Chapter7/RotHomotopyrotS_add. So \(df_x\) is onto, and so is \(dr \circ df_x\), which is \(dF\) on vectors \((a,0)\). Only space directions are used; the monotonicity of \(\rho\) plays no role.

Lemma 2 along an arc, then Theorem A

Proposition (Lemma 2). Assume the standing hypotheses. Let \(f\) be smooth, \(u, v\) orthonormal and \(\theta_0 \ge 0\). Suppose \(y\), every \(r_\tau(y)\) with \(\tau \in [0,\theta_0]\), and \(r_{\theta_0}(y)\) are regular values of \(f\). Let \(e\) be positive at \(r_{\theta_0}(y)\) and \(e_0\) positive at \(y\). Then \((f^{-1}(r_{\theta_0}(y)), f^*e)\) and \((f^{-1}(y), f^*e_0)\) are framed cobordant Chapter7/Lemma2framedCobordant_arc.

The proof is Milnor’s. Take the rotation homotopy with \(\varepsilon = \tfrac14\). V7.2 at \(z = r_{\theta_0}(y)\) joins \(f^{-1}(z)\) to \((r_{\theta_0} \circ f)^{-1}(z)\), and the composition rule joins that to \(f^{-1}(y)\).

Proof of Theorem A as formalized.

  1. The regular values of \(f\) contain balls of radius \(\delta\) around \(y\) and \(z\) Chapter7/RegOpenisOpen_regularValues_sph. Take a rotation \(r = r_{\theta_0}\) with \(r(y) = z\) and the rotation homotopy \(F\) from \(f\) to \(r \circ f\); its regularity clause is not used.
  2. By Brown’s theorem the regular values of \(F\), \(f\) and \(r \circ f\) are dense, and the last two sets are open Chapter2/Browndense_regularValues. So their intersection is dense and contains some \(z'\) with \(|z' - z| < \delta\).
  3. Put \(y' = r^{-1}(z')\). Then \(|y' - y| = |z' - z| < \delta\), so \(y'\) is regular Chapter7/RotHomotopydist_rotS. Pick positive bases \(e_1\) at \(y'\) and \(e_2\) at \(z'\) Chapter7/Lemma2exists_posBasis.
  4. Chain four framed cobordisms:
    • \(f^{-1}(y) \sim f^{-1}(y')\), by Lemma 2 along a rotation path that stays in the ball Chapter7/Lemma2arc_bound;
    • \(f^{-1}(y') \sim (r \circ f)^{-1}(z')\), by the composition rule;
    • \((r \circ f)^{-1}(z') \sim f^{-1}(z')\), by V7.2 for \(F\);
    • \(f^{-1}(z') \sim f^{-1}(z)\), by Lemma 2 from \(z\) to \(z'\).
    Symmetry and transitivity combine them. A bookkeeping lemma rewrites Pontryagin manifolds along equalities such as \(r(y') = z'\) Chapter7/Lemma2pontryagin_congr.

Unlike the book, the chain applies Lemma 2 only to \(f\): it moves from \(y\) to \(y' = r^{-1}(z')\) before composing with \(r\), where the book, inside Lemma 3, moves along an arc for \(r \circ f\).

Where \(p \ge 1\) enters. It enters twice. Every rotation path is built from a unit vector orthogonal to its starting point; when the two ends are equal or antipodal they determine no such vector, and one exists only because \(p \ge 1\) Chapter7/Rotationexists_unit_orthogonal. And positive bases must be found at \(y'\) and \(z'\) Chapter7/Lemma2exists_posBasis. The hypothesis serves the proof rather than the statement. For \(p = 0\) the outward vectors at the two points of \(S^0\) are opposite Chapter5/HairyBalloutward_neg, so the sphere’s orientation differs at the two points and the empty basis of \(\mathbb R^0\) is positive at exactly one of them. Positive bases at \(y\) and \(z\) then force \(y = z\), and the claim becomes that a Pontryagin manifold is framed cobordant to itself, which V7.2 gives for the constant homotopy Chapter7/CobordismframedCobordant_of_homotopy. This is an observation about the definitions, not a formal theorem.

V7.6 Theorem B, first half: homotopic maps have cobordant Pontryagin manifolds

Theorem. Assume the standing hypotheses and \(p \ge 1\). Let \(F : M \times \mathbb R \to S^p\) be smooth, and write \(f = F(\cdot,0)\), \(g = F(\cdot,1)\). The statement also assumes \(f\) and \(g\) smooth, which already follows. Let \(y\) be a regular value of \(f\) and \(z\) one of \(g\), with \(e_0\) positive at \(y\) and \(e\) positive at \(z\). Then \((f^{-1}(y), f^*e_0)\) and \((g^{-1}(z), g^*e)\) are framed cobordant Chapter7/ThmAframedCobordant_of_homotopic.

Milnor’s Lemma 3 is the case \(y = z\), \(e_0 = e\).

The proof as formalized.

  1. A common regular value \(z'\) of \(F\), \(f\) and \(g\). By Brown’s theorem each set of regular values is dense Chapter2/Browndense_regularValues. Those of \(f\) and \(g\) are open Chapter7/RegOpenisOpen_regularValues_sph. Those of \(F\) need not be, as \(M \times \mathbb R\) is not compact. A dense set meets a dense open set in a dense set, so the triple intersection is nonempty.
  2. Reparametrize \(F\) at \(z'\) with \(\varepsilon = \tfrac14\) Chapter7/Reparamexists_reparam, and pick a positive basis \(e'\) at \(z'\).
  3. V7.2 gives \((f^{-1}(z'), f^*e') \sim (g^{-1}(z'), g^*e')\) Chapter7/CobordismframedCobordant_of_homotopy.
  4. Theorem A for \(f\) (from \(y\) to \(z'\)) and for \(g\) (from \(z'\) to \(z\)) completes the chain Chapter7/Lemma2framedCobordant_of_regularValues Chapter7/EquivFramedCobordant.trans.

Where the formal proof departs from Milnor. Milnor reparametrizes first; here \(z'\) is chosen for the original homotopy and kept through the reparametrization, which is why that lemma needs regular end maps and \(\rho' > 0\). Openness of regular values is what makes the three dense sets meet.

What the formalization taught us

  • Cobordisms without boundary. Product ends are built in, and level sets, reversal and gluing need no boundary theory Chapter7/FramedFramedCob.
  • Framings as formulas. Every framing built from a map is \(A^*(AA^*)^{-1}b\) for an ambient derivative \(A\), with a hand-built adjoint on \(\mathbb R^{K+1} \times \mathbb R\) Chapter7/PontryaginpontV Chapter7/AdjXRadjXR.
  • Reparametrization. It needs \(\rho' > 0\) in the middle and regular end maps Chapter7/Reparamexists_reparam.
  • Openness, twice. It supplies Lemma 2’s arcs and makes dense sets of regular values meet; its proof uses the ambient derivative, since \(df_x\) moves with its chart Chapter7/RegOpenisOpen_regularValues_sph Chapter7/ThmAframedCobordant_of_homotopic.
  • \(GL^+\) made explicit. Transvections, rotations by \(\pi\) and a scaling give a path whose determinant is known to be positive only on \([0,1]\) Chapter7/GLplusexists_glPath.
  • Self-adjoint transport. Under a time change, framings are pulled back by \(D_a\) itself, its own transpose: normal time components scale by \(a\) while tangent ones scale by \(1/a\) Chapter7/EquivFraming.transport Chapter7/TransporttangentS_affine.
  • Reflexivity absent. In general it comes only in Chapter 8, through Theorem C Chapter8/FramedOpsframedCobordant_refl.
  • Weak composition hypotheses. Sign \(+1\) at one point and a fibre condition suffice Chapter7/ComposeframedCobordant_comp.
  • Hidden and redundant hypotheses. \(M\) must be nonempty, since the retraction on which every framing is built is a map into \(M\) Chapter6/Tubular4tubr. The proof of Theorem A uses \(p \ge 1\), though its statement would survive without it Chapter7/Rotationexists_unit_orthogonal Chapter7/Lemma2exists_posBasis. Smooth end maps in V7.6, and smooth and regular end maps in V7.2, are implied by the other hypotheses Chapter7/ThmAframedCobordant_of_homotopic Chapter7/CobordismframedCobordant_of_homotopy.
  • Milnor rearranged. V7.2 takes the good regular value as given; all moves between regular values happen in explicit chains Chapter7/Lemma2framedCobordant_of_regularValues.
← Part IV. Vector fields and the Poincaré–Hopf theorem (Milnor §6)Part VI. The product neighbourhood, Theorem C and the second half of Theorem B (Milnor §7) →

Part VI. The product neighbourhood, Theorem C and the second half of Theorem B (Milnor §7)

This part runs Pontryagin’s construction backwards: a framed submanifold becomes a map to the sphere (Theorem C), a framed cobordism becomes a homotopy, and with the lemmas of Part V this gives the second half of Theorem B: maps with framed cobordant Pontryagin manifolds are homotopic. Milnor’s pages 46–49 rest on three constructions he sketches or takes for granted: a product neighbourhood, a map \(\mathbb R^p \to S^p\) collapsing the outside of a ball, and the smoothness of maps given by a formula near \(N\) and a constant elsewhere. All three are built here. The product neighbourhood theorem is proved once, for an abstract map and a compact set outside which injectivity is known, so that it also serves the non-compact cobordisms of the formal definition. Because the collapse map is fixed, Theorem C realises the framing only for a multiple \(c\,b\), \(c > 0\), of the chosen basis. Lemma 4 is proved by another route, with a first-order estimate in place of Milnor’s second-order Taylor bound. (Letters follow Milnor: Theorem B is the homotopy classification, Theorem C the realisation, and the product neighbourhood theorem is unlettered. The file names, the project’s docstrings and the verified edition use an older lettering, in which the realisation is Theorem B, the classification Theorem A and the product neighbourhood theorem Theorem C.)

The files, in logical order:

  • Chapter7/StdMap: the standard collapse map \(\pi : \mathbb R^p \to S^p\).
  • Chapter7/ProdNbhd: local injectivity and a uniform injectivity radius for an abstract \(G : N \times \mathbb R^p \to X\).
  • Chapter7/ProdNbhd2: bijectivity of \(dG\) on a tube, open image, smooth inverse.
  • Chapter7/Clamp: a smooth radial clamp.
  • Chapter7/ProdNbhdM: the tube map of a framed \(N \subseteq M\) and its derivative along \(N\).
  • Chapter7/PontFrame: the kernel of \(d\tilde F_x\) and a characterisation of the Pontryagin framing.
  • Chapter7/Collapse: the collapse map with prescribed derivative.
  • Chapter7/ThmB: Theorem C, every framed submanifold is a Pontryagin manifold.
  • Chapter7/Stereo: the straight-line homotopy in stereographic coordinates.
  • Chapter7/Taylor: a uniform first-order estimate on a tube.
  • Chapter7/Homotopy: smooth homotopy is an equivalence relation.
  • Chapter7/TubeData: the product neighbourhood of \((N, v)\), packaged for reuse.
  • Chapter7/Deform: the deformation lemma.
  • Chapter7/ProdNbhdS: the tube map of a framed cobordism \(S \subseteq M \times \mathbb R\).
  • Chapter7/SamePont: maps with the same Pontryagin manifold are homotopic (Lemma 4).
  • Chapter7/Identify: recognising a Pontryagin manifold from its values along the framing.
  • Chapter7/CobMap: the map of a framed cobordism.
  • Chapter7/ThmAconv: the second half of Theorem B.

Setting

Throughout, \(M \subseteq \mathbb R^{K+1}\) is a compact, nonempty slice submanifold of dimension \(m\) with its induced structure. Chapter 6 provides \(\varepsilon_M > 0\) and the nearest-point retraction \(r : \mathbb R^{K+1} \to M\): smooth on \(U_M = \{z : \operatorname{dist}(z, M) < \varepsilon_M\}\), the identity on \(M\), and constant on short normal segments, \(r(x + sw) = x\) for small \(s\) when \(x \in M\) and \(w \perp T_xM\) Chapter6/Tubular4tubr_spec. A framed submanifold \((N, v)\) has dimension \(n\) and codimension \(p\) with \(n + p = m\); \(N\) is compact, and \(v_1, \dots, v_p\) are smooth, tangent to \(M\), orthogonal to \(N\) and independent at each point Chapter7/FramedFramedSub. Tangent spaces are subspaces of \(\mathbb R^{K+1}\), images of derivatives of inclusions Chapter7/FramedtangentN.

The Pontryagin manifold is defined through an extension (Part V). For \(f : M \to S^p\) smooth, \(y\) a regular value and \(\varphi_y\) the chart of \(S^p\) at \(y\), put \(\tilde F = \varphi_y \circ f \circ r\) and \(A_x = d\tilde F_x\) Chapter7/PontryaginFt Chapter7/PontryaginAt. For a linearly independent family \(b = (b_1, \dots, b_p)\) in \(\mathbb R^p\) the framing is \(f^*b_i(x) = A_x^*(A_xA_x^*)^{-1}b_i\) Chapter7/PontryaginpontV, and the Pontryagin manifold is \((f^{-1}(y), f^*b)\) Chapter7/Pontryaginpontryagin. Two framed submanifolds with the same set and the same fields are equal Chapter7/ThmBFramedSub.ext', and every “is the Pontryagin manifold” below is such a literal equality. The north pole of \(S^p \subseteq \mathbb R^{p+1}\) is the last basis vector \(e_{p+1}\), the south pole is \(-e_{p+1}\) Chapter7/StdMapnorth. A basis of \(\mathbb R^p\) is positive at \(y\) if its orientation is that of \(S^p\) at \(y\) Chapter5/HairyBallsphOr. \(B_\varepsilon\) and \(\bar B_\varepsilon\) are the open and closed balls about \(0\) in \(\mathbb R^p\).

V7.9, first part: the collapse map \(\pi : \mathbb R^p \to S^p\)

Milnor’s proof of Theorem C uses a map \(\mathbb R^p \to S^p\) sending the outside of the unit ball to a point and the open ball diffeomorphically onto the rest of the sphere. The formal proof needs less: one explicit map, never required to be injective.

Proposition (the standard map). Let \(\tau\) be Mathlib’s smooth transition function (\(0\) on \((-\infty, 0]\), \(1\) on \([1, \infty)\)) and \(\psi(s) = 1 - \tau\bigl((16s - 1)/3\bigr)\), so \(0 \le \psi \le 1\), \(\psi = 1\) on \((-\infty, \tfrac1{16}]\), and \(\psi(s) = 0\) exactly when \(s \ge \tfrac14\). For \(t \in \mathbb R^p\) put \[W(t) = \psi(|t|^2)\,(t, 0) + \bigl(2\psi(|t|^2) - 1\bigr)\,e_{p+1}, \qquad \pi(t) = W(t)/|W(t)|.\] Then \(W\) never vanishes and \(\pi\) is smooth; \(\pi(t) = (t, 1)/|(t, 1)|\) for \(|t| \le \tfrac14\); \(\pi(t)\) is north if and only if \(t = 0\) and south if and only if \(|t| \ge \tfrac12\); \(d\pi_0\) is bijective; and north is a regular value of \(\pi\) Chapter7/StdMapstdMap.

Proof. The vertical component of \(W\) is \(2\psi - 1\), the horizontal one \(\psi\,t\); both vanish only if \(\psi = \tfrac12\) and \(t = 0\), impossible since \(\psi(0) = 1\) Chapter7/StdMapstdW_ne_zero. So \(\pi\), the normalisation of a smooth nonvanishing map, is smooth Chapter7/StdMapcontMDiff_stdMap. The same components decide the level sets: \(\pi(t)\) is a pole only if \(\psi(|t|^2)\,|t|^2 = 0\), so \(t = 0\) (north) or \(|t| \ge \tfrac12\) (south) Chapter7/StdMapstdMap_eq_north_iff Chapter7/StdMapstdMap_eq_south_iff. Near \(0\), \(\pi\) is the central projection of the tangent plane at the north pole Chapter7/StdMapstdMap_eq_of_small, and since \((t, 0) \perp e_{p+1}\) its derivative into \(\mathbb R^{p+1}\) is \(t \mapsto (t, 0)\) Chapter7/StdMaphasFDerivAt_stdMap_val_zero. So \(d\pi_0\) is injective, hence bijective, and north is a regular value because \(0\) is its only preimage Chapter7/StdMapmfd_stdMap_zero_bijective Chapter7/StdMapisRegularValue_stdMap_north.

The collapse map with prescribed derivative. For linearly independent \(b\) let \(Bs = \sum_i s_i b_i\) Chapter7/CollapsebasisCLM and \(A = (d\pi_0)^{-1} \circ B\) Chapter7/CollapseAe, and for \(c \in \mathbb R\) put \(\pi_c(t) = \pi(c\,At)\) Chapter7/Collapsecollapse. Then \(\pi_c\) is smooth Chapter7/CollapsecontMDiff_collapse, for \(c \ne 0\) it takes the value north exactly at \(t = 0\) Chapter7/Collapsecollapse_eq_north_iff, and in the chart at the north pole \[\frac{d}{ds}\Big|_{s=0} \varphi_{\mathrm{north}}\bigl(\pi_c(sw)\bigr) = c\,Bw\] Chapter7/CollapsehasDerivAt_chart_collapse. For every \(\varepsilon > 0\), the constant \(c = 2(\|A^{-1}\| + 1)/\varepsilon\) makes \(\pi_c\) the south pole outside \(B_{\varepsilon/2}\), because then \(|cAt| \ge \tfrac12\) there Chapter7/Collapseexists_scale.

This is the origin of the scalar \(c\) in Theorem C. The product neighbourhood exists only over some ball \(B_\varepsilon\), and squeezing the fixed map \(\pi\) into \(B_{\varepsilon/2}\) by a linear rescaling multiplies its derivative at \(0\) by \(c\). Milnor avoids this by parametrising his product neighbourhood by all of \(\mathbb R^p\).

V7.7 The product neighbourhood theorem

Milnor’s statement: a neighbourhood of \(N\) in \(M\) is diffeomorphic to \(N \times \mathbb R^p\), with \(x\) corresponding to \((x, 0)\) and the frame to the standard basis. The formal proof separates an abstract theorem from the concrete tube maps.

The abstract theorem

Theorem (uniform injectivity radius). Let \(N\) be a smooth manifold modelled on \(\mathbb R^n\) with first countable topology, and \(X\) a Hausdorff smooth manifold modelled, without boundary, on a finite-dimensional (hence complete) real normed space. Let \(G : N \times \mathbb R^p \to X\) be smooth, \(K \subseteq N\) compact and \(\varepsilon_0 > 0\), and assume:

  1. \(dG_{(x,0)}\) is bijective for every \(x \in K\);
  2. \(G(x, 0) = G(x', 0)\) implies \(x = x'\), for all \(x, x' \in N\);
  3. if \(|s|, |s'| < \varepsilon_0\), \(x \notin K\) and \(G(x, s) = G(x', s')\), then \((x, s) = (x', s')\).

Then there is \(\varepsilon\) with \(0 < \varepsilon \le \varepsilon_0\) such that \(G\) is injective on \(N \times B_\varepsilon\) Chapter7/ProdNbhdexists_injOn.

Theorem (tube, open image, smooth inverse). In the same setting:

    1. if \(dG_{(x,0)}\) is bijective for all \(x\) in a compact \(K\), then for some \(\varepsilon > 0\), \(dG_{(x,t)}\) is bijective for \(x \in K\), \(|t| < \varepsilon\) Chapter7/ProdNbhd2exists_ball_bijective;
    1. if \(dG\) is bijective on \(N \times B_\varepsilon\), then \(G(N \times B_\varepsilon)\) is open Chapter7/ProdNbhd2isOpen_image_tube;
    1. if moreover \(N \ne \emptyset\) and \(G\) is injective on \(N \times B_\varepsilon\), then the inverse \(G^{-1} : X \to N \times \mathbb R^p\) (the preimage in the tube on the image, an arbitrary point elsewhere) is smooth at every point of \(G(N \times B_\varepsilon)\) Chapter7/ProdNbhd2Ginv Chapter7/ProdNbhd2contMDiffAt_Ginv.

The idea. Locally this is the inverse function theorem in charts. The uniform radius is Milnor’s compactness argument run with sequences; hypothesis 3 lets the compact set be smaller than \(N\), as the non-compact cobordism of V7.10(c) requires.

The proof as formalized.

  1. Local injectivity. Let \(w = \phi' \circ G \circ \phi^{-1}\) be the representative of \(G\) in the charts \(\phi\) at \(q_0\) and \(\phi'\) at \(G(q_0)\) Chapter7/ProdNbhdwr. As the model of \(X\) has no boundary, \(w\) is an ordinary map of vector spaces near \(\phi(q_0)\), and if \(dG_{q_0}\) is bijective the inverse function theorem gives \(w'\) with \(w'(w(\xi)) = \xi\) on a ball around \(\phi(q_0)\). On the part of the chart domain mapped into that ball, \(G(q) = G(q')\) gives \(w(\phi q) = w(\phi q')\), so \(\phi q = \phi q'\) and \(q = q'\) Chapter7/ProdNbhdexists_injOn_nhds.
  2. The uniform radius. If no \(\varepsilon\) works, there are \(q_k \ne q'_k\) with \(G(q_k) = G(q'_k)\) and second coordinates of norm below \(\min(\varepsilon_0, 1/(k+1))\). By hypothesis 3 their first coordinates lie in \(K\), so a subsequence of the pairs converges in the compact set \((K \times \bar B_{\varepsilon_0})^2\), to \((l, l')\) say; extracting it uses sequential compactness, hence first countability of \(N\). The second coordinates tend to \(0\), \(G(l) = G(l')\) because limits in the Hausdorff space \(X\) are unique, and hypothesis 2 gives \(l = l'\). For large \(k\), \(q_k\) and \(q'_k\) then lie in the neighbourhood of \(l\) where step 1 (with hypothesis 1) makes \(G\) injective: a contradiction Chapter7/ProdNbhdexists_injOn.
  3. Bijectivity on a tube. Bijective linear maps between finite-dimensional spaces form an open set Chapter7/ProdNbhd2isOpen_bijective_clm. Near \(q_0\), the derivative of \(w\) at \(\phi(q)\) is \(dG_q\) composed on both sides with invertible chart derivatives Chapter7/ProdNbhd2fderiv_wr_eq, and it is continuous in \(q\). So bijectivity of \(dG\) is an open condition Chapter7/ProdNbhd2isOpen_bijective_mfd, and the tube lemma around \(K \times \{0\}\) gives (a).
  4. Open image. Near \(G(q_0)\), \(q_0\) in the tube, the map \(\mathcal L = \phi^{-1} \circ w' \circ \phi'\) is a right inverse of \(G\) with values in the tube Chapter7/ProdNbhd2eventually_L. So the image is a neighbourhood of each of its points.
  5. Smooth inverse. \(G^{-1}\) is chosen as an inverse of \(G\) on the tube, and choosing needs a point of \(N\) Chapter7/ProdNbhd2Ginv. By injectivity on the tube, \(G^{-1}(z) = G^{-1}(G(\mathcal L z)) = \mathcal L z\) near \(G(q_0)\), so \(G^{-1}\) is smooth there Chapter7/ProdNbhd2contMDiffAt_Ginv.

What the book leaves implicit. Milnor’s argument is step 2 with \(K = N\); the hypotheses on \(N\) and \(X\) are the ones it uses without saying so.

The tube map of a framed submanifold

The point \(x + \sum_i s_i v_i(x)\) stays in the domain \(U_M\) of \(r\) only for small \(s\), so the formal proof clamps \(s\).

Lemma (the clamp). Let \(E\) be a real inner product space, \(a > 0\) and \(2a \le b\). There is a smooth \(\lambda : E \to E\) with \(\lambda(t) = t\) for \(|t| \le a\), \(|\lambda(t)| \le b\), and \(\lambda(t) = \gamma(t)\,t\) with \(0 < \gamma(t) \le 1\); namely \(\lambda(t) = g(t)^{-1/2}\,t\) with \(g(t) = 1 + \theta(|t|^2)\,|t|^2/b^2\), where \(\theta(s) = \tau\bigl((s - a^2)/(3a^2)\bigr)\) Chapter7/Clampexists_clamp.

Theorem (product neighbourhood of a framed submanifold). Let \((N, v)\) be a framed submanifold of \(M\), \(a_0 > 0\), and \(\lambda : \mathbb R^p \to \mathbb R^p\) smooth with \(\lambda(t) = t\) for \(|t| \le a_0\) and \(x + \sum_i \lambda(t)_i v_i(x) \in U_M\) for all \(x \in N\), \(t \in \mathbb R^p\). Put \[G(x, t) = r\Bigl(x + \sum_i \lambda(t)_i\,v_i(x)\Bigr).\] Then \(G : N \times \mathbb R^p \to M\) is smooth, \(G(x, 0) = x\), and there is \(\varepsilon\) with \(0 < \varepsilon \le a_0\) such that \(G\) is injective and \(dG\) is bijective on \(N \times B_\varepsilon\) Chapter7/TubeDataexists_tubeData_of_lam. Such \(a_0\) and \(\lambda\) exist Chapter7/TubeDataexists_tubeData. Hence \(V = G(N \times B_\varepsilon)\) is an open neighbourhood of \(N\), and for \(N \ne \emptyset\), \(G^{-1}\) is smooth on \(V\) Chapter7/TubeDataisOpen_V Chapter7/TubeDatacontMDiffAt_Ginv.

On \(N \times B_\varepsilon\) the clamp is the identity, so there \(G(x, s) = r(x + \sum_i s_i v_i(x))\).

The proof as formalized.

  1. The clamp exists. By compactness, \(|v_i(x)| \le C\) for some \(C > 0\) Chapter7/ProdNbhdMexists_bound_v. With \(a_0 = \varepsilon_M/(8(pC + 1))\) and the clamp for \(a = a_0\), \(b = 2a_0\), the displacement is at most \(p\,|\lambda(t)|\,C \le 2pa_0C < \varepsilon_M\) Chapter7/ProdNbhdMGamb_mem_Nε. So \(G\) is smooth Chapter7/ProdNbhdMcontMDiff_Gx and \(G(x, 0) = r(x) = x\) Chapter7/ProdNbhdMGx_zero.
  2. The ambient derivative. As \(\lambda\) is the identity near \(0\), \((x, t) \mapsto x + \sum_i \lambda(t)_i v_i(x)\) has derivative \(D(a, s) = d\iota_x(a) + \sum_i s_i v_i(x)\) at \((x, 0)\), with \(\iota : N \to \mathbb R^{K+1}\) the inclusion Chapter7/ProdNbhdMhasMFDerivAt_Gamb_zero. \(D\) is injective, since its summands are orthogonal (the \(v_i\) are normal to \(N\)) and injective in \(a\) and in \(s\) respectively Chapter7/ProdNbhdMDg_injective; its values lie in \(T_xM\) Chapter7/ProdNbhdMDg_mem_tangentM.
  3. The retraction fixes tangent vectors. Differentiating \(r \circ \iota_M = \iota_M\) gives \(dr_x w = w\) for \(w \in T_xM\) Chapter7/ProdNbhdMfderiv_tubr_of_mem. So \(dG_{(x,0)}\), followed by the inclusion of \(M\), is \(dr_x \circ D = D\) Chapter7/ProdNbhdMmfd_val_Gx_zero. Hence \(dG_{(x,0)}\) is injective, and bijective since \(n + p = m\) Chapter7/ProdNbhdMbijective_mfd_Gx_zero.
  4. The abstract theorem with \(K = N\): hypothesis 3 is vacuous, and \(G(x, 0) = x\) gives hypothesis 2. Part (a) gives \(\varepsilon_1\), and the uniform radius with \(\varepsilon_0 = \min(\varepsilon_1, a_0)\) gives \(\varepsilon\) Chapter7/TubeDataexists_tubeData_of_lam.

The data \((\lambda, a_0, \varepsilon, G)\) form a structure, reused by the deformation lemma and the cobordism with a prescribed clamp Chapter7/TubeDataTubeData.

Where the formal proof departs from Milnor. The book’s diffeomorphism \(N \times \mathbb R^p \to V\) becomes a map that is smooth everywhere but a diffeomorphism only from the tube \(N \times B_\varepsilon\) onto \(V\). Nothing later needs more.

The tube map of a framed cobordism

A framed cobordism between \((N_0, v^0)\) and \((N_1, v^1)\) is a submanifold \(S \subseteq M \times \mathbb R\) of dimension \(n + 1\), with a constant \(0 < \varepsilon_S < \tfrac12\), such that \(S\) agrees with \(N_0 \times \mathbb R\) for \(t < \varepsilon_S\) and with \(N_1 \times \mathbb R\) for \(t > 1 - \varepsilon_S\), its part over \([0, 1]\) is compact, and its framing \(u_i\) in \(\mathbb R^{K+1} \times \mathbb R\) (smooth, normal to \(S\), independent, with first component tangent to \(M\)) is \((v^0_i, 0)\), resp. \((v^1_i, 0)\), on the ends Chapter7/FramedFramedCob. Its tube map is \[G_S(q, t) = (r \times \mathrm{id})\Bigl(q + \sum_i \lambda(t)_i\,u_i(q)\Bigr), \qquad q \in S\] Chapter7/ProdNbhdSGxS. The facts about \(N\) carry over, each with a twist.

  • Boundedness. \(S\) is not compact, but \(u\) is bounded, being the framing of \(N_0\) or \(N_1\) on the ends and living on a compact set in between Chapter7/ProdNbhdSexists_bound_u.
  • The derivative. \(dG_S\) is bijective at \((q, 0)\), by steps 2–3 with the inner product \(\langle a, b\rangle + a_t b_t\) on \(\mathbb R^{K+1} \times \mathbb R\), since \(d(r \times \mathrm{id})\) fixes vectors whose first component is tangent to \(M\) Chapter7/ProdNbhdSDgS_injective Chapter7/ProdNbhdSfderiv_tubr'_of_mem Chapter7/ProdNbhdSbijective_mfd_GxS_zero.
  • The ends. Where \(u_i = (v_i, 0)\), \(G_S\) is the tube map of \(N_0\) or \(N_1\) times the identity in time Chapter7/CobMapGxS_end0; everywhere it shifts time by at most \(p\,|\lambda(t)|\,C\) Chapter7/CobMapabs_snd_GxS_sub_le. And \(S \cap (M \times [a, b])\) is compact for \(a \le 0\), \(b \ge 1\): it is \(N_0 \times [a, 0]\), the compact middle and \(N_1 \times [1, b]\) Chapter7/CobMapisCompact_S_Icc.

Theorem (injectivity radius of a cobordism). Let \(a_0 > 0\) and \(\lambda\) be smooth with \(\lambda(t) = t\) for \(|t| \le a_0\), such that the \(\mathbb R^{K+1}\)-component of \(q + \sum_i \lambda(t)_i u_i(q)\) always lies in \(U_M\). Let \(C > 0\) bound all \(|u_i|\), and let the ends have product-neighbourhood data built with the same \(\lambda\), with radii \(\varepsilon^{(0)}\), \(\varepsilon^{(1)}\). Then there is \(\varepsilon > 0\) with \(\varepsilon \le a_0\), \(\varepsilon \le \varepsilon^{(0)}, \varepsilon^{(1)}\) and \(p\,\varepsilon\,C < \varepsilon_S/4\), such that \(G_S\) is injective on \(S \times B_\varepsilon\) and \(dG_S\) is bijective at every \((q, t)\) with \(|t| < \varepsilon\) and the time of \(q\) in \([-3, 4]\) Chapter7/CobMapexists_injRadius_S.

Proof. Apply the abstract theorem with \(K = S \cap (M \times [-3, 4])\), compact as noted above, and \(\varepsilon_0 = \min(\varepsilon^{(0)}, \varepsilon^{(1)}, a_0, \varepsilon_S/(8(pC+1)))\), so that no point moves in time by as much as \(\varepsilon_S/4\); part (a), with the same \(K\), supplies the bijectivity. The ends enter through hypothesis 3. If \(q\) has time below \(-3\) and \(G_S(q, s) = G_S(q', s')\), both points have time below \(\varepsilon_S\), where \(G_S\) is the tube map of \(N_0\) times the identity, injective on its tube Chapter7/CobMapeq_of_GxS_eq_end0; above time \(4\) one uses \(N_1\) Chapter7/CobMapeq_of_GxS_eq_end1.

Bijectivity of \(dG_S\) on the whole tube is not obtained, since the tube lemma needs a compact set; V7.10(c) restricts \(G_S\) to an open piece of \(S\) instead.

V7.8 Identification of the framing

Proposition. Let \(f : M \to S^p\) be smooth, \(y\) a regular value, \(n + p = m\), \(N = f^{-1}(y)\) and \(x \in N\). Then \[\ker A_x = T_xN + (T_xM)^\perp.\] Consequently, if \(v \in T_xM\), \(v \perp T_xN\) and \(A_x v = b_i\), then \(v = f^*b_i(x)\) Chapter7/PontFrameker_At_eq Chapter7/PontFramepontV_eq_of.

Proof. Both summands lie in the kernel, since \(\tilde F\) is constant on \(N\) and, like \(r\), on short normal segments to \(M\) Chapter7/PontryaginAt_tangentN_eq_zero Chapter7/PontryaginAt_normal_eq_zero. Equality is a dimension count: \(A_x\) is onto \(\mathbb R^p\) Chapter7/Pontryaginsurjective_At, so its kernel has dimension \(K + 1 - p\), while the summands meet only in \(0\) (as \(T_xN \subseteq T_xM\)) and have dimensions \(n\) and \(K + 1 - m\) Chapter7/PontFramefinrank_tangentN_level. For the consequence, \(\operatorname{range} A_x^* = (\ker A_x)^\perp\) Chapter7/PontFramerange_adjoint_eq contains \(v\), and \(A_x^*(A_xA_x^*)^{-1}b_i\) is the only vector of that range mapped to \(b_i\) Chapter7/Composepinv_unique.

This links Milnor’s definition (the unique normal vector with prescribed image) to the formula for the framing. Theorem C applies it directly; the map of a cobordism uses it through a corollary.

Corollary. Let \((N, v)\) be a framed submanifold, \(k : M \to S^p\) smooth with \(k^{-1}(\mathrm{north}) = N\), \(b\) linearly independent, \(c > 0\) and \(\varepsilon' > 0\), and suppose \[k\bigl(r(x + s\,v_i(x))\bigr) = \pi_c(s\,e_i) \qquad (x \in N,\ |s| < \varepsilon',\ i = 1, \dots, p).\] Then north is a regular value of \(k\), and the Pontryagin manifold of \(k\) at north with basis \(c\,b\) is \((N, v)\) Chapter7/Identifypontryagin_eq_of_collapse.

Proof. Differentiating \(s \mapsto \tilde F(x + s\,v_i(x)) = \varphi_{\mathrm{north}}(\pi_c(s e_i))\) at \(0\) gives \(A_x v_i(x) = c\,b_i\). So \(A_x\) is onto, and \(x\) is a regular point of \(k\) Chapter7/RegOpenisRegularPoint_of_surjective_At. The \(v_i(x)\) are tangent to \(M\) and normal to \(N\), whose tangent space is that of \(k^{-1}(\mathrm{north})\) Chapter7/ThmBtangentN_congr, and the proposition identifies them with the Pontryagin framing.

V7.9 Theorem C: every framed submanifold is a Pontryagin manifold

Theorem C. Let \((N, v)\) be a framed submanifold of \(M\) of dimension \(n\) and codimension \(p\), and \(b = (b_1, \dots, b_p)\) linearly independent in \(\mathbb R^p\). There are a smooth \(f : M \to S^p\) with north as a regular value and a constant \(c > 0\) such that the Pontryagin manifold of \(f\) at north with basis \(c\,b\) is \((N, v)\) Chapter7/ThmBexists_map_of_framedSub.

The idea. Take the product neighbourhood on its injectivity tube \(N \times B_\varepsilon\), choose \(c\) so that \(\pi_c\) collapses outside \(B_{\varepsilon/2}\), and set \(f = \pi_c \circ \mathrm{pr}_2 \circ G^{-1}\) on \(V\), south elsewhere. Along the framing line \(x + s\,v_i(x)\) the map is \(\pi_c(s e_i)\), and V7.8 does the rest.

The proof as formalized.

  1. The empty case. If \(N = \emptyset\), the constant map south works with \(c = 1\): north has no preimage, so it is a regular value Chapter7/ThmBsouth_ne_north.
  2. The tube. The four steps of V7.7, carried out inline, give \(\varepsilon \le a_0\) with \(G\) injective and \(dG\) bijective on \(N \times B_\varepsilon\), so \(V\) is open and \(G^{-1}\) is smooth on \(V\) Chapter7/ProdNbhd2isOpen_image_tube Chapter7/ProdNbhd2contMDiffAt_Ginv.
  3. The map. Take \(c > 0\) with \(\pi_c = \mathrm{south}\) outside \(B_{\varepsilon/2}\) Chapter7/Collapseexists_scale, and let \(f(z) = \pi_c(\mathrm{pr}_2\,G^{-1}(z))\) for \(z \in V\), \(f(z) = \mathrm{south}\) otherwise.
  4. Smoothness. On \(V\), \(f\) is a composite of smooth maps. The compact set \(G(N \times \bar B_{\varepsilon/2})\) lies in \(V\), and \(f\) is the south pole off it, so \(f\) is locally constant at points outside \(V\). This closed-core argument replaces Milnor’s one-line assertion that \(f\) is smooth.
  5. The level set. \(f(z) = \mathrm{north}\) forces \(z \in V\) and \(\mathrm{pr}_2\,G^{-1}(z) = 0\), so \(z = G(x, 0) = x \in N\); conversely \(G^{-1}(x) = (x, 0)\) for \(x \in N\).
  6. The framing. For \(|s| < \min(a_0, \varepsilon)\) the clamp is the identity, so \(f(r(x + s\,v_i(x))) = f(G(x, s e_i)) = \pi_c(s e_i)\). Differentiating in the chart at north gives \(A_x v_i(x) = c\,b_i\). Hence north is a regular value, and V7.8 identifies the framing Chapter7/PontFramepontV_eq_of Chapter7/ThmBexists_map_of_framedSub.

Step 6, with the level set of step 5 as a hypothesis, is what the corollary of V7.8 packages for the two ends of a cobordism Chapter7/Identifypontryagin_eq_of_collapse.

Where the formal proof departs from Milnor. The basis \(b\) is arbitrary, not necessarily positive, but it is realised only up to the factor \(c > 0\). As \(c\,b\) and \(b\) have the same orientation, nothing is lost: Lemma 4 is proved for proportional bases.

Three tools for V7.10 and V7.11

The straight line in stereographic coordinates. Let \(\sigma_y(u) = (1 - \langle u, y\rangle)^{-1}\bigl(u - \langle u, y\rangle\,y\bigr)\) be stereographic projection from \(y \in S^p\) onto \(y^\perp\), with inverse \(\sigma_y^{-1}(w) = \bigl(2w + (|w|^2 - 1)\,y\bigr)/(|w|^2 + 1)\) Chapter7/Stereostereo Chapter7/StereostereoInv.

Proposition. Let \(X\) be a smooth manifold (any model), \(f, g : X \to S^p\) smooth, and \(U \subseteq X\) open with \(f = g\) on \(U\), and suppose \(f(x) \ne y \ne g(x)\) for \(x \notin U\). Then there is a smooth \(H : X \times \mathbb R \to S^p\) with \(H(\cdot, 0) = f\), \(H(\cdot, 1) = g\) and \(H(x, t) = f(x)\) for \(x \in U\), \(t \in \mathbb R\) Chapter7/Stereoexists_homotopy_of_eqOn.

Proof. Put \(H(x, t) = f(x)\) for \(x \in U\) and \(H(x, t) = \sigma_y^{-1}\bigl((1 - t)\,\sigma_y(f(x)) + t\,\sigma_y(g(x))\bigr)\) otherwise. The segment lies in \(y^\perp\), so \(\sigma_y^{-1}\) puts it on the sphere for every real \(t\), and \(\sigma_y^{-1}\sigma_y = \mathrm{id}\) away from \(y\) gives the end values Chapter7/StereostereoInv_stereo. Smoothness is checked on two open sets. On \(U \times \mathbb R\), \(H = f \circ \mathrm{pr}_1\). On \(\{f \ne y,\ g \ne y\} \times \mathbb R\), which contains every point with \(x \notin U\), \(H\) is given by the stereographic formula (at points of \(U\) the segment is constant), and \(\sigma_y\) is smooth where \(\langle u, y\rangle < 1\) Chapter7/StereocontDiffAt_stereo. This is the first step of Milnor’s proof of Lemma 4, with the two open sets made explicit.

Smooth homotopy. \(f \simeq g\) means a smooth \(H : X \times \mathbb R \to Y\) with \(H(\cdot, 0) = f\), \(H(\cdot, 1) = g\) Chapter7/HomotopySmoothHomotopic. The relation is reflexive on smooth maps and symmetric by \(t \mapsto 1 - t\) Chapter7/HomotopySmoothHomotopic.refl Chapter7/HomotopySmoothHomotopic.symm. For transitivity, a smooth step (\(0\) for \(t \le \tfrac14\), \(1\) for \(t \ge \tfrac34\)) makes both homotopies constant near the ends Chapter7/HomotopySmoothHomotopic.exists_const_near_ends; then \(H_1(x, 2t)\) for \(t \le \tfrac12\) is glued to \(H_2(x, 2t - 1)\) for \(t > \tfrac12\), and the result equals the first formula for \(t < \tfrac58\) and the second for \(t > \tfrac38\) Chapter7/HomotopySmoothHomotopic.trans.

Lemma (uniform first-order estimate). Let \(N\) be a compact smooth manifold (any model), \(P\) a finite-dimensional and \(F\) an arbitrary real normed space, and \(W \subseteq N \times P\) open with \(N \times \{0\} \subseteq W\). Let \(\Phi : N \times P \to F\) be smooth on \(W\) with \(\Phi(x, 0) = 0\), and let \(s \mapsto \Phi(x, s)\) have derivative \(L\) at \(0\) for every \(x\) (one fixed linear \(L\)). Then for every \(\kappa > 0\) there is \(\delta > 0\) with \[|\Phi(x, s) - Ls| \le \kappa\,|s| \qquad (x \in N,\ |s| < \delta)\] Chapter7/Taylorexists_uniform_taylor.

Proof. The \(s\)-derivative of \(R(x, s) = \Phi(x, s) - Ls\) is jointly continuous on \(W\), as the derivative of a smooth family, and vanishes on \(N \times \{0\}\). So \(\{|\partial_s R| < \kappa\}\) is an open set containing \(N \times \{0\}\), hence, by the tube lemma, some \(N \times B_\delta\). The mean value inequality on the convex ball \(B_\delta\) finishes. No second derivatives appear, whereas Milnor’s bound \(|F(x, u) - u| \le c_1|u|^2\) needs them bounded on a compact set.

V7.10 Lemma 4 and the map of a cobordism

(a) The deformation lemma

Lemma (deformation). Let \((N, v)\) be a framed submanifold with \(N \ne \emptyset\) and product-neighbourhood data \((\lambda, a_0, \varepsilon, G)\) as in V7.7. Let \(y \in S^p\) with chart \(\varphi = \varphi_y\), and \(k : M \to S^p\) smooth with \(k^{-1}(y) = N\). Let \(b\) be linearly independent, \(c > 0\), and \(A_x v_i(x) = c\,b_i\) for all \(x \in N\) and all \(i\), where \(A_x = d\tilde F_x\) is formed with \(k\) and \(y\). Then there are a smooth \(H : M \times \mathbb R \to S^p\) and \(\delta\) with \(0 < \delta \le \varepsilon\) such that

  • \(H(z, 0) = k(z)\) for all \(z \in M\);
  • \(H(G(x, s), 1) = \varphi^{-1}\bigl(\varphi(y) + Bs\bigr)\) for \(x \in N\), \(|s| < \delta\), where \(Bs = \sum_i s_i b_i\);
  • \(H(z, 1) \ne y\) for \(z \notin N\)

Chapter7/Deformexists_deform.

The idea. In the chart at \(y\) and the coordinates \(G\), \(k\) becomes \(\Phi(x, s) \approx c\,Bs\), uniformly in \(x\). Interpolate from \(\Phi\) to \(Bs\) by a bump in \(s\) and a step in time; each interpolant is within \(\kappa|s|\) of a multiple of \(Bs\) of size at least \(2\kappa|s|\), so no zeros appear off \(N\).

The proof as formalized.

  1. Coordinates. \(W_0 = \{(x, s) \in N \times B_\varepsilon : k(G(x, s)) \in \operatorname{dom}\varphi\}\) is open and contains \(N \times \{0\}\), hence, \(N\) being compact, a tube \(N \times B_{\delta_0}\) Chapter7/Deformexists_tube_subset. On \(W_0\) put \(\Phi(x, s) = \varphi(k(G(x, s))) - \varphi(y)\), smooth with \(\Phi(x, 0) = 0\).
  2. The fibre derivative is \(c\,B\). It suffices to check basis vectors. For \(|s| \le a_0\), \(G(x, s e_i) = r(x + s\,v_i(x))\) Chapter7/TubeDataG_line, so \(\Phi(x, s e_i) = \tilde F(x + s\,v_i(x)) - \varphi(y)\), with derivative \(A_x v_i(x) = c\,b_i\) at \(0\).
  3. Constants. \(|Bs| \ge m_0|s|\) with \(m_0 = 1/(\|B^{-1}\| + 1)\). Let \(\kappa = \min(1, c)\,m_0/2\), and take \(\delta_1\) from the uniform estimate: \(|\Phi(x, s) - cBs| \le \kappa|s|\) for \(|s| < \delta_1\). If the chart target contains the ball of radius \(\varrho\) about \(\varphi(y)\), put \(\delta_2 = \varrho/(\kappa + c\|B\| + \|B\| + 1)\) and \(\delta^* = \min(\delta_0, \delta_1, \delta_2, \varepsilon)\); then \(|\Phi(x, s)| < \varrho\) and \(|Bs| < \varrho\) for \(|s| < \delta^*\).
  4. The homotopy. Let \(\chi : \mathbb R^p \to [0, 1]\) be a smooth bump, \(1\) on \(\bar B_{\delta^*/4}\) and \(0\) outside \(B_{\delta^*/2}\), and \(\rho : \mathbb R \to [0, 1]\) a smooth step, \(0\) for \(\tau \le \tfrac14\) and \(1\) for \(\tau \ge \tfrac34\) Chapter7/Transitionexists_timeTransition. With \(\theta = \rho(\tau)\,\chi(s)\) put \[\Psi(x, s, \tau) = \Phi(x, s) + \theta\,\bigl(Bs - \Phi(x, s)\bigr) = (1 - \theta)\,\Phi(x, s) + \theta\,Bs,\] of norm below \(\varrho\) for \(|s| < \delta^*\). Let \(H(z, \tau) = \varphi^{-1}\bigl(\varphi(y) + \Psi(G^{-1}(z), \tau)\bigr)\) on \(V_{\delta^*} = G(N \times B_{\delta^*})\) and \(H(z, \tau) = k(z)\) elsewhere.
  5. Smoothness, \(\tau = 0\) and \(\tau = 1\). On \(V_{\delta^*} \times \mathbb R\) the formula is smooth. Off the compact set \(G(N \times \bar B_{\delta^*/2})\), \(\chi = 0\) and \(H(z, \tau) = k(z)\), which settles the points outside \(V_{\delta^*}\). At \(\tau = 0\), \(\rho = 0\) and \(H = k\); at \(\tau = 1\) and \(|s| < \delta^*/4\), \(\Psi = Bs\). The lemma’s \(\delta\) is \(\delta^*/4\).
  6. No new preimages. Let \(z \notin N\) with \(H(z, 1) = y\). Then \(z \in V_{\delta^*}\), since elsewhere \(H(z, 1) = k(z) \ne y\), and \(G^{-1}(z) = (x, s)\) with \(s \ne 0\), since \(s = 0\) gives \(z = x \in N\). Then \(\Psi = 0\), that is, \[\bigl((1 - \theta)\,c + \theta\bigr)\,Bs = -(1 - \theta)\,\bigl(\Phi(x, s) - cBs\bigr).\] The left side has norm at least \(\min(1, c)\,m_0|s| = 2\kappa|s|\), the right side at most \(\kappa|s|\), which is impossible for \(s \ne 0\) Chapter7/Deformexists_deform.

Where the formal proof departs from Milnor. Milnor deforms \(f\) until it agrees with \(g\) near \(N\), interpolating between their expressions in stereographic coordinates from the antipode of \(y\), kept in a common half-space by a second-order Taylor bound. The formal proof deforms each map separately to a standard form fixed by \(B\), which allows the derivatives \(b\) and \(c\,b\); it works in the chart at \(y\) and needs only the first-order estimate. Its statement controls the zero set only at time \(1\), which is all that is used.

(b) Same Pontryagin manifold, homotopic maps

Theorem (Lemma 4). Let \(n + p = m\), \(f, g : M \to S^p\) smooth with a common regular value \(y\), \(b\) linearly independent and \(c > 0\). If the Pontryagin manifold of \(f\) at \(y\) with basis \(b\) equals that of \(g\) at \(y\) with basis \(c\,b\), then \(f \simeq g\) Chapter7/SamePontsmoothHomotopic_of_pontryagin_eq.

Proof. Let \((N, v)\) be the common framed submanifold. If \(N = \emptyset\), both maps avoid \(y\) and the stereographic homotopy with \(U = \emptyset\) joins them. Otherwise take product-neighbourhood data for \((N, v)\) Chapter7/TubeDataexists_tubeData. The Pontryagin framing satisfies \(A_x v_i(x) = b_i\) for \(f\) and \(A_x v_i(x) = c\,b_i\) for \(g\) Chapter7/PontryaginAt_pontV, so the deformation lemma, with constants \(1\) and \(c\), gives \(f \simeq f_1\) and \(g \simeq g_1\). With \(\delta\) the smaller radius, \(f_1\) and \(g_1\) both equal \(\varphi_y^{-1}(\varphi_y(y) + Bs)\) on the open neighbourhood \(U = G(N \times B_\delta)\) of \(N\), and neither takes the value \(y\) off \(N\). The straight-line homotopy gives \(f_1 \simeq g_1\), and symmetry and transitivity finish.

(c) The map of a cobordism

Theorem. Let \((S, u)\) be a framed cobordism between framed submanifolds \(F_0 = (N_0, v^0)\) and \(F_1 = (N_1, v^1)\) of \(M\), and \(b\) linearly independent. There are a smooth \(H : M \times \mathbb R \to S^p\) and \(c > 0\) such that north is a regular value of \(H(\cdot, 0)\) and of \(H(\cdot, 1)\), and their Pontryagin manifolds at north with basis \(c\,b\) are \(F_0\) and \(F_1\) Chapter7/CobMapexists_cobMap.

The idea. Run the proof of Theorem C for \(S \subseteq M \times \mathbb R\). As \(dG_S\) is known to be bijective only over \(S \cap (M \times [-3, 4])\), \(S\) is cut to an open piece; the resulting map is smooth on a strip of times, and time is clamped into the strip.

The proof as formalized.

  1. Shared data. A bound \(C\) for \(u\) bounds \(v^0\) and \(v^1\) too Chapter7/CobMapbound_v0_of_bound_u. One clamp, with \(a_0 = \varepsilon_M/(8(pC + 1))\), serves \(S\), \(N_0\) and \(N_1\). It yields product-neighbourhood data for the ends and then the radius \(\varepsilon\) for \(S\). As \(\varepsilon_S < \tfrac12\), the time shift over the \(\varepsilon\)-tube is below \(\tfrac18\).
  2. The open piece. \(S^\circ = S \cap (M \times (-3, 4))\) is open in \(S\), hence a manifold, and the restriction \(G^\circ\) of \(G_S\) to \(S^\circ \times \mathbb R^p\) has the same derivative Chapter7/CobMapmfd_restrict_prod. So \(G^\circ\) is injective with bijective derivative on \(S^\circ \times B_\varepsilon\), its image \(V^\circ\) is open, and \((G^\circ)^{-1}\) is smooth on \(V^\circ\). If \(S^\circ = \emptyset\) then \(N_0 = N_1 = \emptyset\), as \(N_0 \times \{0\}\) and \(N_1 \times \{1\}\) lie in \(S^\circ\), and \(H \equiv \mathrm{south}\) works.
  3. The map on a strip. With \(c\) from the collapse map for the radius \(\varepsilon\), let \(H_0 = \pi_c \circ \mathrm{pr}_2 \circ (G^\circ)^{-1}\) on \(V^\circ\) and \(H_0 = \mathrm{south}\) elsewhere. It is smooth on the strip \(M \times (-2, 3)\): a point of \(V^\circ\) with time in \((-2, 3)\) and \(|s| < \varepsilon/2\) comes from a point of \(S\) with time within \(\tfrac18\), so within the strip \(H_0\) is south off the compact set \(G^\circ\bigl((S \cap (M \times [-\tfrac52, \tfrac72])) \times \bar B_{\varepsilon/2}\bigr)\).
  4. Clamping time. Let \(\lambda_1\) be the clamp on \(\mathbb R\) with \(a = \tfrac34\), \(b = \tfrac32\), and \(\rho(t) = \tfrac12 + \lambda_1(t - \tfrac12)\). Then \(\rho(t) = t\) on \([-\tfrac14, \tfrac54]\) and \(\rho(\mathbb R) \subseteq [-1, 2]\), so \(H(z, t) = H_0(z, \rho(t))\) is smooth on \(M \times \mathbb R\) and agrees with \(H_0\) at \(t = 0, 1\).
  5. The ends. \(H_0(z, t)\) is north exactly when \((z, t) \in S^\circ\), so \(H(z, 0)\) is north exactly for \(z \in N_0\) and \(H(z, 1)\) exactly for \(z \in N_1\). For \(x \in N_0\) and \(|s| < \varepsilon\), the product form of the end and the clamp give \(G_S((x, 0), s e_i) = (r(x + s\,v^0_i(x)), 0)\) Chapter7/TubeDataGx_line, so \(H(r(x + s\,v^0_i(x)), 0) = \pi_c(s e_i)\), and likewise at \(t = 1\). The corollary of V7.8 at both ends, with the same \(c\), finishes Chapter7/Identifypontryagin_eq_of_collapse Chapter7/CobMapexists_cobMap.

What the book leaves implicit. Milnor calls this construction analogous to his proof of Theorem C. Formally it is not a copy: the cobordism is not compact, injectivity far out comes from the ends’ product neighbourhoods, built with the same clamp, and cutting and clamping replace bijectivity on the whole tube.

V7.11 Theorem B, second half: framed cobordant maps are homotopic

Theorem. Let \(n + p = m\) and \(p \ge 1\). Let \(f, g : M \to S^p\) be smooth, \(y\) a regular value of \(f\) and \(y'\) one of \(g\), and \(e\), \(e'\) bases of \(\mathbb R^p\) positive at \(y\) and at \(y'\). If \((f^{-1}(y), f^*e)\) and \((g^{-1}(y'), g^*e')\) are framed cobordant, then \(f \simeq g\) Chapter7/ThmAconvsmoothHomotopic_of_framedCobordant.

The idea. Milnor’s proof, after moving both regular values to the north pole: equalise the bases by Lemma 1, realise the cobordism by a map, and apply Lemma 4 at both ends.

The proof as formalized.

  1. Rotate to north. A rotation \(R\) of \(S^p\) in a plane through \(y\) carries \(y\) to north; when \(y = \pm\,\mathrm{north}\), finding the plane needs a unit vector orthogonal to \(y\), the only use of \(p \ge 1\) Chapter7/Rotationexists_rotation_path. Rotating through a smoothly varying angle gives \(f \simeq f' = R \circ f\) Chapter7/RotHomotopyexists_rotHomotopy, and north is a regular value of \(f'\). The basis \(e_1 = dR_y\,e\) is positive at north, as \(dR\) has sign \(+1\) Chapter7/RotationsignAt_rotS, and \((R \circ f)^*e_1 = f^*(dR_y^{-1}e_1) = f^*e\), so the Pontryagin manifolds agree Chapter7/ComposepontV_comp Chapter7/ThmAconvexists_rotate_to_north. Likewise \(g\) gives \(g'\) and \(e_2\).
  2. Equal bases. \(e_1\) and \(e_2\) are both positive at north, so by Lemma 1 the Pontryagin manifolds of \(g'\) for \(e_1\) and \(e_2\) are framed cobordant Chapter7/Lemma1framedCobordant_of_orientation_eq. Symmetry and transitivity of framed cobordism Chapter7/EquivFramedCobordant.symm Chapter7/EquivFramedCobordant.trans give a framed cobordism between the Pontryagin manifolds of \(f'\) and \(g'\) at north, both with basis \(e_1\).
  3. The map of the cobordism. V7.10(c) gives \(H\) and \(c > 0\) such that the Pontryagin manifolds of \(H(\cdot, 0)\) and \(H(\cdot, 1)\) for \(c\,e_1\) are those of \(f'\) and \(g'\) for \(e_1\).
  4. Chain. Lemma 4 with the proportional bases \(e_1\) and \(c\,e_1\) gives \(f' \simeq H(\cdot, 0)\) and \(g' \simeq H(\cdot, 1)\), and \(H\) joins \(H(\cdot, 0)\) to \(H(\cdot, 1)\). So \(f \simeq f' \simeq H(\cdot, 0) \simeq H(\cdot, 1) \simeq g' \simeq g\) Chapter7/SamePontsmoothHomotopic_of_pontryagin_eq Chapter7/ThmAconvsmoothHomotopic_of_framedCobordant.

Positivity is carried through step 1 and used in step 2; \(p \ge 1\) is used only in step 1.

What the formalization taught us

  • Topological hypotheses. The uniform injectivity radius uses sequential compactness (first countable \(N\)), unique limits (Hausdorff target) and the inverse function theorem in charts (target model without boundary) Chapter7/ProdNbhdexists_injOn.
  • A compact set, not a compact manifold. Injectivity known outside a compact \(K\) lets the abstract theorem serve the non-compact cobordism \(S\) Chapter7/CobMapexists_injRadius_S.
  • Glued maps. Theorem C, the deformation and the cobordism map are smooth by a closed-core argument: off a compact subset of the open set where the formula holds, the map is constant or unchanged Chapter7/ThmBexists_map_of_framedSub Chapter7/Deformexists_deform.
  • Empty submanifolds. The inverse of the tube map is a choice function, so the empty case is treated separately three times Chapter7/ProdNbhd2Ginv Chapter7/SamePontsmoothHomotopic_of_pontryagin_eq.
  • The scalar \(c\). A fixed collapse map realises the framing for \(c\,b\), \(c > 0\), not for \(b\), so Lemma 4 is proved for proportional bases Chapter7/Collapseexists_scale Chapter7/SamePontsmoothHomotopic_of_pontryagin_eq.
  • The framing by a dimension count. Milnor’s unique normal vector with prescribed image is recognised through \(\ker d\tilde F_x = T_xN + (T_xM)^\perp\) Chapter7/PontFrameker_At_eq.
  • Lemma 4 by another route. Each map is deformed separately to a standard form in the chart at \(y\), with a first-order estimate instead of a second-order one Chapter7/Taylorexists_uniform_taylor Chapter7/Deformexists_deform.
  • Cutting and clamping. For a cobordism, \(dG_S\) is shown bijective only over a compact piece, so \(S\) is cut to times in \((-3, 4)\) and time is clamped into \((-2, 3)\) Chapter7/CobMapexists_cobMap.
  • The hypotheses of the second half of Theorem B. \(p \ge 1\) serves only to rotate a regular value to north, and positivity of the bases only to apply Lemma 1 Chapter7/ThmAconvexists_rotate_to_north Chapter7/ThmAconvsmoothHomotopic_of_framedCobordant.
← Part V. Framed cobordism, Theorem A and the first half of Theorem B (Milnor §7)Part VII. The Hopf theorem (Milnor §7, end) →

Part VII. The Hopf theorem (Milnor §7, end)

This part proves Hopf’s theorem. Let \(M \subseteq \mathbb R^{K+1}\) be a compact, connected, oriented \(m\)-dimensional submanifold with \(m \ge 1\). Two smooth maps \(M \to S^m\) are smoothly homotopic exactly when they have the same degree, and every integer is a degree. After Parts V and VI the first statement reduces, as in Milnor, to one about framed \(0\)-manifolds: two finite sets of framed points with the same signed count are framed cobordant. Milnor calls this “not difficult to see” and sketches it: move points along paths, and cancel pairs of opposite sign along an arc. The formal proof takes another route, governed by one design principle.

No cobordism is built by hand. Each elementary operation (moving a framed point, changing its frame, cancelling a pair) is a homotopy of maps \(M \to S^m\). It agrees with a fixed map outside a chart ball and is an explicit formula in chart coordinates inside it. The north pole is a regular value of the homotopy, so the construction V7.2 of Part V turns it into a framed cobordism between the Pontryagin manifolds of its two ends Chapter7/CobordismframedCobordant_of_homotopy. The characterization of Pontryagin framings (V7.8) then identifies the ends. Two tools carry the cost: a form of Milnor’s Theorem C whose map is the south pole outside a prescribed open set, and a lemma that glues a family on a chart ball into a global homotopy. Milnor’s “since \(M\) is connected” becomes a precise neighbour lemma. Matching points needs chains of neighbours, because on a circle points cannot pass one another.

Milnor closes §7 with one clause about the non-orientable case: for connected non-orientable \(M\) the maps to \(S^m\) are classified by the degree modulo 2, because a framed point carried round an orientation-reversing loop comes back with its frame reversed, so that only the parity of the number of points survives. Sections V7.18 to V7.28 prove it, and until the Appendix was finished they were the longest single addition to this book. The reason the clause hides is that it presupposes what an orientable manifold is and that a non-orientable one carries a reversing loop; neither notion existed in Mathlib, in this project, or in the book. It hides one thing more, which the last two sections settle: Milnor states his theorem with no condition on the dimension, and the proof wants \(2 \le m\) at one point, so the dimension has to be derived from non-orientability, which is a fact about one-manifolds and therefore about the Appendix. What did not have to be redone is almost everything else: a survey of the chapter found that framed submanifolds, framed cobordism, the Pontryagin construction, Theorem C and the converse of Theorem B take no orientation of \(M\) at all, and that the orientation enters in exactly one definition, the sign of a frame, and in the endgame that cancels a plus against a minus.

Map of the part.

  • Chapter7/Hopf0: finiteness; the sign of a framed point; the signed count is the degree.
  • Chapter7/ThmBsupp: Theorem C with support in a prescribed open set and scale bounded below.
  • Chapter7/Scale: large collapse scales; the derivative of the collapse map at \(0\).
  • Chapter7/Glue: chart balls; gluing a chart-local family; framings depend only on germs.
  • Chapter7/Neighbour: the neighbour lemma.
  • Chapter7/Segment: the segment property of chart balls; the neighbour lemma in \(M\).
  • Chapter7/Chain: chains of neighbours.
  • Chapter7/TuplePath: smooth paths of bases, bounded below.
  • Chapter7/MoveMap: the moving collapse map.
  • Chapter7/CancelMap: the cancelling family \(s_1^2 - a^2\rho(t)\) and its regularity.
  • Chapter7/MoveAux: frames in the chart of a ball; dual tuples.
  • Chapter7/MoveH: the glued moving homotopy.
  • Chapter7/Move: moving a framed point (V7.13).
  • Chapter7/CancelH: the glued cancelling homotopy.
  • Chapter7/Cancel: cancelling a pair (V7.14).
  • Chapter7/Reach: reflexivity, frames of both signs, good balls, reaching a component.
  • Chapter7/Gather: matching frames; gathering along shortest chains.
  • Chapter7/CancelStep: cancelling a neighbouring pair of opposite signs.
  • Chapter7/Main: equal signed counts give framed cobordant \(0\)-manifolds (V7.16).
  • Chapter7/AddPoint: adding a framed point.
  • Chapter7/Hopf: the Hopf theorem and maps of every degree (V7.17).

For the mod 2 theorem of V7.18 to V7.28:

  • Chapter7/OrientTransport: transport of an orientation through a chart; hops and chains (V7.18).
  • Chapter7/Orientable: orientability, reversing loops, the chart-level dichotomy (V7.18).
  • Chapter7/OrientBall: chart balls, ball chains, the exact dichotomy (V7.19).
  • Chapter7/ChartSign: the chart sign, the self sign, the Jacobian sign, and the bridge (V7.20).
  • Chapter7/BallChainSign: the sign of a chain, the transition cocycle, chains avoiding a set (V7.21).
  • Chapter7/Puncture: punctured balls, and the reversing loop away from a finite set (V7.22).
  • Chapter7/Slide: the slide and the flip, Milnor’s clause (V7.23).
  • Chapter7/CancelFree: cancellation with no condition on the frames (V7.24).
  • Chapter7/CountMod2: the count modulo 2 and the parity classification (V7.25).
  • Chapter7/HopfMod2: Milnor’s theorem of p. 50 (V7.26).
  • Chapter7/OneManifoldOrientable: orientations pulled back, the four models of the Appendix oriented, and the orientability of every connected one-manifold (V7.27, V7.28).

Standing notation. \(M \subseteq \mathbb R^{K+1}\) is a compact, nonempty submanifold of dimension \(m\), given by slice charts, with the manifold structure they induce. It is automatically Hausdorff and second countable. \(o\) is an orientation of \(M\) (V5.0), used wherever signs occur. Connectedness and \(m \ge 1\) are assumed only where stated. \(S^m \subseteq \mathbb R^{m+1}\) is the unit sphere with the orientation of Chapter 5 (Part 0, §0.7); all degrees and positive bases of this part refer to it. This part numbers standard basis vectors from \(1\), so the north and south poles are \(\pm e_{m+1}\); a basis of \(\mathbb R^m\) is positive at \(y\) if its orientation is that of \(S^m\) at \(y\) (Part VI) Chapter5/HairyBallsphOr Chapter7/StdMapnorth. \(\varphi_x\) is the preferred chart at \(x \in M\), with values in \(\mathbb R^m\). For a tuple \(b\) in \(\mathbb R^p\), \(B_b\) is the linear map \(e_i \mapsto b_i\) Chapter7/CollapsebasisCLM. A frame at \(x\) is an \(m\)-tuple of independent vectors of \(T_xM \subseteq \mathbb R^{K+1}\). A framed \(0\)-manifold is a framed submanifold of dimension \(0\) and codimension \(m\), and \(\sim\) denotes framed cobordism (V7.0). V7.2 is the construction of Part V: if a smooth \(H : M \times \mathbb R \to S^p\) satisfies \(H(x, t) = H(x, 0)\) for \(t \le \varepsilon\) and \(H(x, t) = H(x, 1)\) for \(t \ge 1 - \varepsilon\), for some \(0 < \varepsilon < \tfrac12\), and \(z\) is a regular value of \(H\) and of both ends, then \(H^{-1}(z)\) with its pulled-back framing is a framed cobordism between the Pontryagin manifolds of the two ends at \(z\), for any common basis Chapter7/CobordismframedCobordant_of_homotopy. The project’s docstrings call it Lemma 3; it is the construction inside Milnor’s Lemmas 2 and 3. Theorem letters are Milnor’s. In §7, Theorem B says that two maps are smoothly homotopic exactly when their Pontryagin manifolds are framed cobordant, and Theorem C that every compact framed submanifold is a Pontryagin manifold; the product neighbourhood theorem has no letter. The file names ThmB.lean and ThmBsupp.lean follow an older lettering of the project, in which Theorem C was called Theorem B.

V7.12 Framed points, their signs, and the signed count

A compact \(0\)-dimensional slice submanifold of any smooth manifold is finite. Around each of its points a slice chart sends it into \(\mathbb R^0 \times 0\), a single point, so the chart domain meets it only there, and finitely many such domains cover it. No Hausdorff hypothesis is needed Chapter7/Hopf0IsSliceSubmanifold.finite_of_dim_zero Chapter7/Hopf0FramedSub.finite_N. The tangent space of such a submanifold is zero Chapter7/Hopf0tangentN_eq_bot_of_dim_zero, so the orthogonality condition on a framing is empty. A framed \(0\)-manifold is thus a finite set \(N\) with a frame \(v(x)\) at each point.

Definition (the sign of a frame). Let \(v = (v_1, \dots, v_m)\) be tangent to \(M\) at \(x\). The chart coordinates of \(v_i\) form the vector \(w_i \in \mathbb R^m\) with \(d\iota_x(w_i) = v_i\), where \(\iota\) is the inclusion of \(M\) and \(d\iota_x\) is read in the chart at \(x\) Chapter7/Hopf0chartCoord. The sign of \(v\) at \(x\) is the sign of \(B_w\) from the standard orientation of \(\mathbb R^m\) to \(o_x\) Chapter7/Hopf0frameSign. For a frame it is nonzero, hence \(\pm 1\) Chapter7/Hopf0frameSign_ne_zero Chapter7/GatherframeSign_mem. The signed count of \((N, v)\) is \(\sum_{x \in N} \operatorname{sign} v(x)\) Chapter7/Hopf0count.

Theorem (V7.12). Let \(m \ge 1\), let \(f : M \to S^m\) be smooth, let \(y\) be a regular value of \(f\), and let \(e\) be a basis of \(\mathbb R^m\) that is positive for the orientation of \(S^m\) at \(y\). Then the signed count of the Pontryagin manifold \((f^{-1}(y), f^*e)\) is \(\deg f\). Chapter7/Hopf0count_pontryagin

The idea. \(df_x\) carries the Pontryagin frame to the positive basis \(e\), so the two signs multiply to \(+1\).

The proof as formalized. The Pontryagin frame satisfies \(d\tilde F_x(v_i) = e_i\), where \(\tilde F = \varphi_y \circ f \circ r\), with \(r\) the nearest-point retraction onto \(M\), extends \(f\) read in the chart \(\varphi_y\) of \(S^m\) at \(y\) to a neighbourhood of \(M\) (V7.1) Chapter7/PontryaginAt_pontV. Since \(d\tilde F_x \circ d\iota_x = df_x\) in the charts at \(x\) and \(y\) Chapter7/PontryaginAt_comp_mfd_val, we get \(df_x \circ B_w = B_e\). The sign of \(B_e\) from the standard orientation to the orientation of \(e\) is \(1\) Chapter7/Hopf0orSign_stdOr_basisCLM. Signs multiply Chapter5/OrSignorSign_comp, so \(1 = \operatorname{sign} df_x \cdot \operatorname{sign} v(x)\), and two integers with product \(1\) are equal Chapter7/Hopf0frameSign_pontryagin. Summing gives \(\deg(f; y)\). This is \(\deg f\), because \(S^m\) is connected for \(m \ge 1\) and the degree can be computed at any regular value, by Milnor’s Theorem A of §5 Chapter5/Degreedeg_eq. This is Milnor’s argument.

Theorem C with control of the support

A move changes a map inside a chart ball and keeps it outside. The map kept outside must be the south pole near the frontier of the ball, so that the pieces glue. It must also use the same collapse map as the local modification, so that all framings refer to one basis. A sharpened Theorem C provides both.

Proposition. Let \((N, v)\) be a framed submanifold of \(M\) of dimension \(n\) and codimension \(p\), with \(n + p = m\). Let \(b\) be a basis of \(\mathbb R^p\), \(W \subseteq M\) an open set containing \(N\), and \(\underline c \in \mathbb R\). There are a smooth \(f : M \to S^p\) with the north pole as a regular value, a number \(c > 0\) with \(c \ge \underline c\), and a compact \(K \subseteq W\) with \(f = \mathrm{south}\) outside \(K\), such that the Pontryagin manifold of \(f\) at the north pole for the basis \(cb\) is \((N, v)\). Chapter7/ThmBsuppexists_map_of_framedSub_subset

The idea. Run the construction of Theorem C (V7.9) with a tube thin enough to lie in \(W\) and a collapse scale at least \(\underline c\).

The proof as formalized. If \(N\) is empty, the constant map south works, with \(c = \max(\underline c, 1)\) and \(K = \emptyset\). Otherwise take the tube map \(G(x, s) = r\bigl(x + \sum_i \lambda(s)_i v_i(x)\bigr)\) of the product neighbourhood theorem (V7.7), where \(r\) is the retraction onto \(M\) and \(\lambda\) a smooth clamp equal to the identity near \(0\) Chapter7/Clampexists_clamp. The radius \(\varepsilon\) of the tube is so small that \(\lambda\) is the identity on it, and \(dG\) is bijective and \(G\) injective on it (V7.7). New here, it also makes \(G(N \times B_\varepsilon) \subseteq W\), which the tube lemma allows because \(N\) is compact and \(G(x, 0) = x\) Chapter7/Deformexists_tube_subset. Then \(V = G(N \times B_\varepsilon)\) is open.

The collapse map is \(\pi_{b,c}(t) = \pi(cAt)\) Chapter7/Collapsecollapse. Here \(\pi\) is the standard map of V7.9, with \(\pi^{-1}(\mathrm{north}) = \{0\}\) and \(\pi = \mathrm{south}\) for \(|t| \ge 1/2\), and \(A = (d\pi_0)^{-1}B_b\). It is south for \(|t| \ge \varepsilon/2\) once \(c \ge 2(\|A^{-1}\| + 1)/\varepsilon\), so a suitable \(c \ge \underline c\) exists Chapter7/Scaleexists_scale_ge. Put \(f = \pi_{b,c} \circ \mathrm{pr}_2 \circ G^{-1}\) on \(V\) and \(f = \mathrm{south}\) elsewhere. Then \(f\) is south outside the compact core \(K = G(N \times \bar B_{\varepsilon/2}) \subseteq V \subseteq W\). This gives the support statement, and smoothness at points outside \(V\). Also \(f^{-1}(\mathrm{north}) = N\). Along a framing line \(f(r(x + sv_i(x))) = \pi_{b,c}(se_i)\) for small \(s\), and in the chart at the north pole this has derivative \(cb_i\) at \(s = 0\) Chapter7/CollapsehasDerivAt_chart_collapse. So the extension of \(f\) sends \(v_i(x)\) to \(cb_i\). The north pole is regular, and by V7.8 the frame \(v\) is the Pontryagin frame for \(cb\) Chapter7/PontFramepontV_eq_of.

The moves use a uniform scale. There is a threshold \(c_1\) such that every \(c \ge c_1\) makes \(\pi_{b,c}\) south outside \(B_{\varepsilon/2}\) Chapter7/Scaleexists_scale_all.
