A move fixes \(c_1\) for its local family, then calls the proposition with \(\underline c = c_1\). The local family and the Theorem-C map then share \(\pi_{b,c}\), and hence the basis \(cb\). The chart derivative of \(\pi_{b,c}\) at \(0\) is \(cB_b\) Chapter7/ScalehasMFDerivAt_collapse_zero.

Gluing a chart-local homotopy into a global map

For \(x_c \in M\), \(\varphi = \varphi_{x_c}\) and \(R > 0\), the chart ball \(U_R = \{x \in \operatorname{dom}\varphi : |\varphi(x) - \varphi(x_c)| < R\}\) is open Chapter7/GlueballU Chapter7/GlueisOpen_ballU. Suppose \(\bar B(\varphi(x_c), R)\) lies in the image of \(\varphi\). Its image under \(\varphi^{-1}\) is compact, hence closed, so it contains \(\overline{U_R}\) Chapter7/Glueclosure_ballU_subset. So a frontier point of \(U_R\) lies in the chart, at distance at least \(R\) from the centre Chapter7/Gluefrontier_ballU. Without this hypothesis the frontier could leave the chart.

Proposition (gluing). Let \(M \subseteq \mathbb R^{K+1}\) be an \(m\)-dimensional submanifold (compactness is not needed). Let \(x_c \in M\), \(\varphi = \varphi_{x_c}\), and \(R > 0\) with \(\bar B(\varphi(x_c), R)\) in the image of \(\varphi\). Let \(\Phi : \mathbb R^m \times \mathbb R \to S^m\) be smooth with \(\Phi(s, t) = \mathrm{south}\) whenever \(|s - \varphi(x_c)| \ge R/2\). Let \(k : M \to S^m\) be smooth and equal to south on an open set \(O \supseteq \overline{U_R} \setminus U_R\). Then \[H(x, t) = \begin{cases} \Phi(\varphi(x), t), & x \in U_R, \\ k(x), & x \notin U_R, \end{cases}\] is smooth on \(M \times \mathbb R\). Chapter7/GlueglueH Chapter7/GluecontMDiff_glueH

The idea. Near a point outside \(U_R\), the nearby part of \(U_R\) lies where both \(\Phi\) and \(k\) are south.

The proof as formalized. On \(U_R \times \mathbb R\) the map is \(\Phi \circ (\varphi \times \mathrm{id})\). Let \(z \notin U_R\), and let \(A = \{x \in \operatorname{dom}\varphi : |\varphi(x) - \varphi(x_c)| > R/2\}\), an open annulus Chapter7/GlueisOpen_annulus. The open set \(N_0 = (O \cap A) \cup (M \setminus \overline{U_R})\) contains \(z\): either \(z \notin \overline{U_R}\), or \(z\) is a frontier point, in \(O\) and at chart distance \(\ge R\). A point of \(N_0\) inside \(U_R\) lies in \(O \cap A\), where \(\Phi\) and \(k\) are both south. So \(H = k \circ \mathrm{pr}_1\) on \(N_0 \times \mathbb R\) Chapter7/GlueglueH_eventually_eq_of_notMem, and this map is smooth.

Two facts complete the toolkit. First, the Pontryagin framing at a point depends only on the germ of the map, because it is computed from \(\varphi_y \circ f \circ r\) and \(r\) is continuous with \(r(x) = x\) on \(M\) Chapter7/GlueAt_congr Chapter7/GluepontV_congr. A time slice of \(H\) agrees with \(k\) near each point outside \(U_R\), so it has the framing of \(k\) there Chapter7/GlueglueH_slice_eventually_eq_of_notMem. Second, on \(U_R\) the derivative of a time slice is \(d(\Phi(\cdot, t))_{\varphi(x)} \circ d\varphi_x\) Chapter7/GluehasMFDerivAt_glueH_slice_of_mem.

V7.15 The neighbour lemma and chains

Milnor moves points “since \(M\) is connected”. In dimension \(1\) this is not enough, because a point on a circle cannot move past another. The formal proof uses only what connectedness gives. Let \(N\) be a finite subset of a space \(X\). For \(x \in N\), \(C(x)\) is the connected component of \(x\) in \(X \setminus (N \setminus \{x\})\), the region where \(x\) can travel without meeting the other points Chapter7/Neighbourcompl'. A point \(z \in N\) is a neighbour of \(x \in N\) if \(z \in \overline{C(x)}\) Chapter7/ChainadjN.

Theorem (V7.15, the neighbour lemma). Let \(X\) be a connected, locally connected \(T_1\) space and \(N \subseteq X\) finite. Suppose every \(x \in N\) has an open neighbourhood \(J\) with \(J \cap N \subseteq \{x\}\) and \(J \setminus \{x\} \subseteq C(x)\). If \(B \subseteq N\) and \(N \setminus B\) are both nonempty, some \(x \in B\) has a neighbour in \(N \setminus B\). Chapter7/Neighbourexists_neighbour

The idea. Otherwise \(B\) together with its regions \(C(x)\) would be a nonempty, proper, clopen set.

The proof as formalized. Each \(C(x)\) is open, as a component of an open set in a locally connected space; \(N \setminus \{x\}\) is closed because it is finite and points are closed Chapter7/NeighbourisOpen_compl'. Moreover \(\overline{C(x)} \subseteq C(x) \cup (N \setminus \{x\})\): a limit point outside \(N \setminus \{x\}\) has a connected open neighbourhood avoiding \(N \setminus \{x\}\), which meets \(C(x)\) and so joins it Chapter7/Neighbourclosure_compl'_subset. Now suppose no point of \(B\) has a neighbour in \(N \setminus B\), and put \(A = B \cup \bigcup_{x \in B} C(x)\). \(A\) is open: it contains the given \(J\) around each \(x \in B\), and each open \(C(x)\). \(A\) is closed: its closure is the finite union \(B \cup \bigcup_{x \in B} \overline{C(x)}\), whose extra points lie in \(N\), but not in \(N \setminus B\) by assumption, hence in \(B\). \(A\) is nonempty and misses \(N \setminus B\). This contradicts connectedness.

In \(M\) the hypothesis on \(J\) is a segment property of chart balls. Small chart balls lie in any neighbourhood of their centre, with the closed ball inside the chart image Chapter7/Segmentexists_ballU_subset. Let such a ball \(U_r\) around \(x \in N\) meet \(N\) only in \(x\), and let \(y \ne x\) lie in it. The chart segment \(s \mapsto \varphi^{-1}\bigl(\varphi(x) + s(\varphi(y) - \varphi(x))\bigr)\), \(0 < s \le 1\), stays in \(U_r \setminus \{x\}\), is connected, and has \(x\) in its closure. With \(x\) added it is a connected subset of \(M \setminus (N \setminus \{x\})\), so \(y \in C(x)\) Chapter7/SegmentballU_diff_subset_compl' Chapter7/Segmentexists_segment_ball. \(M\) is locally connected Chapter7/SegmentlocallyConnectedSpace_M and \(T_1\), so the neighbour lemma holds for finite subsets of a connected \(M\), compact or not Chapter7/Segmentexists_neighbour_M.

The same argument gives chains. A chain of length \(k\) from \(x\) to \(z\) with interior in \(A\) is a sequence \(x = u_0, \dots, u_k = z\) in \(N\) with each \(u_{j+1}\) a neighbour of \(u_j\) and \(u_0, \dots, u_{k-1} \in A\) Chapter7/ChainchainRel. Under the hypotheses of the neighbour lemma, let \(x_0 \in B \subseteq N\) with \(N \setminus B\) nonempty. Then a chain with interior in \(B\) leads from \(x_0\) to \(N \setminus B\). Otherwise the set \(Q\) of points so reachable lies in \(B\), and the neighbour lemma for \(Q\) and \(N \setminus Q\) extends some chain out of \(Q\) Chapter7/Chainexists_chainRel. A combinatorial lemma adds: if no chain shorter than \(k\) reaches \(w\), a chain of length \(k\) ending at \(w\) does not visit \(w\) earlier Chapter7/ChainchainRel_diff'. This lets a point step out of the way without breaking the chain behind it.

V7.13 Moving a framed point

The first operation moves one framed point inside a chart ball and gives it any frame of the same sign. Milnor slides the point along a path and carries the frame along. Here a homotopy of maps does it.

Theorem (V7.13, moving a point). Let \(m \ge 1\) and let \((N, v)\) be a framed \(0\)-manifold. Let \(x_c \in M\), \(\varphi = \varphi_{x_c}\), and \(R > 0\). Assume \(\bar B(\varphi(x_c), R)\) lies in the image of \(\varphi\), and \(\varphi\) preserves orientation (is positive) on \(U_R\): for \(z \in U_R\), \(d\varphi_z\) has sign \(1\) from \(o_z\) to \(o_{x_c}\). Let \(x_0 \in N \cap U_{R/4}\) be the only point of \(N\) in \(\overline{U_R}\). Let \(x_1 \in U_{R/4}\), and let \(v_1\) be a frame at \(x_1\) with \(\operatorname{sign} v_1 = \operatorname{sign} v(x_0)\). Then \((N, v)\) is framed cobordant to the framed \(0\)-manifold with points \((N \setminus \{x_0\}) \cup \{x_1\}\), frame \(v_1\) at \(x_1\), and frame \(v\) elsewhere. Chapter7/Moveexists_move

The idea. On \(U_R\), replace the Theorem-C map of \((N, v)\) by a collapse map. Its centre moves from \(\varphi(x_0)\) to \(\varphi(x_1)\), and its linear part moves from the inverse chart matrix of \(v(x_0)\) to that of \(v_1\). The north pole stays regular, and V7.2 does the rest.

The proof as formalized.

  1. Frames in the chart. For a frame \(\xi\) at \(x \in U_R\) with chart coordinates \(w\), let \(B_\xi = d\varphi_x \circ B_w\), the matrix of \(\xi\) in the chart \(\varphi\) Chapter7/MoveAuxchartFrameCLM. As \(\varphi\) is positive at \(x\), \(B_\xi\) is invertible, and its sign from the standard orientation to \(o_{x_c}\) is the sign of \(\xi\) Chapter7/MoveAuxorSign_chartFrameCLM. The dual tuple \(\tau\) is the tuple of columns of \(B_\xi^{-1}\): a basis with \(B_\tau = B_\xi^{-1}\) and the same sign Chapter7/MoveAuxexists_dualTuple. The dual tuples \(\tau_0\) of \(v(x_0)\) and \(\tau_1\) of \(v_1\) thus have the same orientation Chapter7/MoveAuxorientation_eq_of_orSign_basisCLM_eq.

  2. Paths. A smooth path of bases \(\tau(t)\), equal to \(\tau_0\) for \(t \le 1/4\) and to \(\tau_1\) for \(t \ge 3/4\), comes from a path in \(GL^+(m)\) (V7.3) acting on \(\tau_1\) Chapter7/BasisPathexists_basisPath. By compactness of \([0,1] \times S^{m-1}\), \(|B_{\tau(t)}z| \ge \mu|z|\) for some \(\mu > 0\) Chapter7/TuplePathexists_tuplePath. The centre moves along \(\gamma(t) = \varphi(x_0) + \sigma(t)(\varphi(x_1) - \varphi(x_0))\), with \(\sigma\) the transition function (\(0\) for \(t \le 1/4\), \(1\) for \(t \ge 3/4\)) Chapter7/Transitionexists_timeTransition. By convexity \(|\gamma(t) - \varphi(x_c)| < R/4\).

  3. The local family. With \(b\) the standard basis (\(B_b = \mathrm{id}\)), put \(\Phi(s, t) = \pi_{b,c}\bigl(B_{\tau(t)}(s - \gamma(t))\bigr)\) Chapter7/MoveMapmoveΦ. It is smooth Chapter7/MoveMapcontMDiff_moveΦ. It equals north exactly at \(s = \gamma(t)\) Chapter7/MoveMapmoveΦ_eq_north_iff, with \(s\)-derivative \(cB_{\tau(t)}\) there Chapter7/MoveMaphasMFDerivAt_moveΦ_slice. Let \(c_1\) be the threshold beyond which \(\pi_{b,c}\) is south outside the ball of radius \(\mu R/4\). For \(c \ge c_1\) and \(|s - \varphi(x_c)| \ge R/2\) we have \(|s - \gamma(t)| \ge R/4\), so \(|B_{\tau(t)}(s - \gamma(t))| \ge \mu R/4\) and \(\Phi(s, t) = \mathrm{south}\) Chapter7/MoveHmoveΦ_south_of_le.

  4. The map outside. The open set \(W = (M \setminus \overline{U_R}) \cup U_{R/2}\) contains \(N\). Theorem C with control of the support, with \(\underline c = c_1\), gives \(c \ge c_1\) and a smooth \(k\) with Pontryagin manifold \((N, v)\) at the north pole for \(cb\), south outside a compact \(K \subseteq W\). The frontier of \(U_R\) misses \(W\), so \(O = M \setminus K\) contains it Chapter7/ThmBsuppexists_map_of_framedSub_subset Chapter7/Moveexists_move.

  5. The homotopy. By the gluing lemma, \(H\) (\(\Phi \circ (\varphi \times \mathrm{id})\) on \(U_R \times \mathbb R\), \(k \circ \mathrm{pr}_1\) elsewhere) is smooth Chapter7/MoveHcontMDiff_moveH. Every time slice has the north pole as a regular value: at the moving point its derivative is the bijection \(cB_{\tau(t)} \circ d\varphi_x\) Chapter7/MoveHmfd_moveH_slice_of_mem Chapter7/MoveHisRegularValue_moveH_slice, and elsewhere it agrees with \(k\) locally. The north pole is also a regular value of \(H\), since the derivative of \(\Phi\) is already onto on \(\mathbb R^m \times 0\) Chapter7/MoveMapsurjective_mfderiv_moveΦ Chapter7/MoveHisRegularValue_moveH. \(H\) is independent of \(t\) for \(t \le 1/4\) and for \(t \ge 3/4\).

  6. The cobordism and its ends. By V7.2, the Pontryagin manifolds of \(H(\cdot, 0)\) and \(H(\cdot, 1)\) at the north pole, for \(cb\), are framed cobordant Chapter7/CobordismframedCobordant_of_homotopy. The preimage of north under \(H(\cdot, t)\) is \((N \setminus U_R) \cup \{\varphi^{-1}(\gamma(t))\}\) Chapter7/MovemoveH_slice_preimage: \(N\) at \(t = 0\), \((N \setminus \{x_0\}) \cup \{x_1\}\) at \(t = 1\). Off \(U_R\) the framing is that of \(k\), namely \(v\) Chapter7/MovepontV_moveH_slice_of_notMem. At the moving point, V7.8 identifies the frame as \(v(x_0)\) at \(t = 0\) and \(v_1\) at \(t = 1\). For \(\xi = v(x_0)\) at \(t = 0\) and \(\xi = v_1\) at \(t = 1\), the slice derivative sends the chart coordinates of the \(i\)-th vector of \(\xi\) to \(cB_{\tau(t)}B_\xi e_i = ce_i\), because \(B_{\tau(t)} = B_\xi^{-1}\) there, and orthogonality is empty in dimension \(0\) Chapter7/MovepontV_moveH_slice_of_mem.

Where the formal proof departs from Milnor. No path in \(M\) is followed and no frame is transported. A pure change of frame is the case \(x_1 = x_0\), where only the linear part moves Chapter7/Moveexists_move.

Reaching the whole component

Moves in chart balls are chained by an open–closed argument instead of a path.

Theorem (V7.13, reach). Let \(m \ge 1\), let \((N, v)\) be a framed \(0\)-manifold, and let \(x_0 \in N\). Let \(y \in C(x_0)\), the component of \(x_0\) in \(M \setminus (N \setminus \{x_0\})\), and let \(v_y\) be a frame at \(y\) with \(\operatorname{sign} v_y = \operatorname{sign} v(x_0)\). Then \((N, v)\) is framed cobordant to the framed \(0\)-manifold with points \((N \setminus \{x_0\}) \cup \{y\}\), frame \(v_y\) at \(y\), and frame \(v\) elsewhere. Chapter7/Reachexists_reach

The idea. The set of points \(x_0\) can reach is open and closed in \(C(x_0)\).

The proof as formalized. Three preparations come first. Framed cobordism of framed \(0\)-manifolds is reflexive: the constant homotopy \(k \circ \mathrm{pr}_1\) of a Theorem-C map \(k\) has the north pole as a regular value Chapter7/Lemma1isRegularValue_comp_fst, and V7.2 applies Chapter7/ReachFramedCobordant.refl'. Even this product cobordism is never written down. Every point carries frames of both signs. If \(\varepsilon_x\) is the sign of the identity from the standard orientation to \(o_x\), the frame \(d\iota_x(e_i)\) has sign \(\varepsilon_x\). The frame \(d\iota_x(Te_i)\) has sign \(-\varepsilon_x\), where \(T = I - 2e_1e_1^{\top}\) is a reflection, the matrix \(T_{-1/2}\) of the cancellation below Chapter7/Reachexists_frame_of_sign.

Finally, there are good balls. Let \(P\) be finite, \(C\) open, and \(y \in C \setminus P\). A good ball around \(y\) is a chart ball \(U_R\) centred at \(y\), with closed ball in the chart image and \(\varphi_y\) preserving orientation on it, such that \(\overline{U_R} \cap P = \emptyset\) and \(U_R \subseteq C\). Chart-continuity of orientations (V5.0) makes the set where \(\varphi_y\) is positive a neighbourhood of \(y\). A chart ball of half the radius inside it, inside \(C\) and away from \(P\), is good Chapter7/Reachexists_goodBall. In a good ball for \(P = N \setminus \{x_0\}\), V7.13 moves a point of \(U_{R/4}\) to any other point of \(U_{R/4}\), with any frame of the same sign Chapter7/Reachmove_in_ball.

Let \(s\) be the sign of \(v(x_0)\). Let \(\mathcal R\) be the set of \(z\) such that \((N, v)\) is framed cobordant to a framed \(0\)-manifold with points \((N \setminus \{x_0\}) \cup \{z\}\), a frame of sign \(s\) at \(z\), and \(v\) elsewhere. Reflexivity gives \(x_0 \in \mathcal R\). \(C(x_0) \cap \mathcal R\) is open: from a reachable \(z\), a good ball around \(z\) inside \(C(x_0)\) reaches its quarter ball, and transitivity (V7.4) composes the cobordisms Chapter7/EquivFramedCobordant.trans. \(C(x_0) \setminus \overline{\mathcal R}\) is open. A point of \(C(x_0) \cap \overline{\mathcal R}\) is reached from a reachable point in the quarter ball of a good ball around it. So the connected \(C(x_0)\) lies in \(\mathcal R\). A last move at \(y\), from \(y\) to itself, installs \(v_y\). Connectedness of \(M\) is not used.

V7.14 Cancelling a pair of opposite signs

In Milnor’s picture two points of opposite sign are joined by an arc in \(M \times [0, 1]\) that turns back in time. In the formal proof that arc is the preimage of the north pole under a homotopy, and nobody ever looks at it.

The family \(s_1^2 - a^2\rho(t)\)

Fix a unit vector \(w \in \mathbb R^m\), a centre \(c_0 \in \mathbb R^m\) and \(a > 0\). Let \(\rho : \mathbb R \to [-1, 1]\) be smooth, with \(\rho = 1\) for \(t \le 1/4\), \(\rho = -1\) for \(t \ge 3/4\), and \(\rho'(t) \ne 0\) wherever \(\rho(t) = 0\). The formal proof takes \(\rho = 1 - 2\sigma\), with \(\sigma\) the transition function, whose derivative is positive on \((1/4, 3/4)\) Chapter7/CancelMapexists_rho. Write \(s_1 = \langle w, z\rangle\) and \(z' = z - s_1w\), and put \[G_t(z) = \bigl(s_1^2 - a^2\rho(t)\bigr)w + z', \qquad \Psi(s, t) = \pi_{b,c}\bigl(G_t(s - c_0)\bigr)\] Chapter7/CancelMapcancelG Chapter7/CancelMapcancelΦ. In coordinates adapted to \(w\), \(G_t(s_1, z') = (s_1^2 - a^2\rho(t), z')\).

  • Zeros. \(G_t(z) = 0\) exactly when \(z = lw\) with \(l^2 = a^2\rho(t)\) Chapter7/CancelMapcancelG_eq_zero_iff. So \(\Psi(\cdot, t)\) equals north at \(c_0 \pm aw\) for \(t \le 1/4\) and nowhere for \(t \ge 3/4\) Chapter7/CancelMapcancelΦ_eq_north_iff.
  • Far field. If \(2a \le r \le |z|\), then \(|G_t(z)| \ge \min(r/2, r^2/4)\): either \(|z'|^2 \ge r^2/2\), or \(s_1^2 - a^2\rho(t) \ge r^2/2 - r^2/4\) Chapter7/CancelMapnorm_cancelG_ge. So \(\Psi\) is south far from \(c_0\) when the collapse scale is large Chapter7/CancelMapcancelΦ_eq_south.
  • Slices. At \(lw\) the derivative of \(G_t\) is \(T_l = 2l\,P_w + (I - P_w)\), with \(P_w\) the orthogonal projection onto \(\mathbb Rw\) Chapter7/CancelMapTcan Chapter7/CancelMaphasFDerivAt_cancelG_slice. It is diagonal in an orthonormal basis extending \(w\), so \(\det T_l = 2l\) Chapter7/CancelMapdet_Tcan, and \(T_l\) is invertible for \(l \ne 0\) Chapter7/CancelMapTcan_bijective.
  • The merging moment. When \(\rho(t^*) = 0\) the zeros merge at \(l = 0\), and \(T_0 = I - P_w\) kills \(w\). The slice \(\Psi(\cdot, t^*)\) does not have north as a regular value, but \(\Psi\) does. At a zero \((c_0 + lw, t)\) the full derivative of \((s, t) \mapsto G_t(s - c_0)\) is \((h, \theta) \mapsto T_lh - \theta a^2\rho'(t)w\) Chapter7/CancelMapDcan Chapter7/CancelMaphasFDerivAt_cancelG_full, and that of \(\Psi\) is \(cB_b\) composed with it. For \(l = 0\), a vector \(q\) is the image of \(h = q - \langle w, q\rangle w\) and \(\theta = -\langle w, q\rangle/(a^2\rho'(t^*))\) Chapter7/CancelMapsurjective_Dcan Chapter7/CancelMapsurjective_mfderiv_cancelΦ. This is exactly where \(\rho' \ne 0\) at the zeros of \(\rho\) is used.

Now let \(x_c\), \(\varphi\) and \(R\) be as in V7.13, with \(|c_0 - \varphi(x_c)| < R/8\) and \(8a \le R\). With \(r = 3R/8\), \(\Psi\) is south where \(|s - \varphi(x_c)| \ge R/2\), provided the collapse is south outside the ball of radius \(\min(3R/16, 9R^2/256)\) Chapter7/CancelHcancelΦ_south_of_le. The glued homotopy is then smooth Chapter7/CancelHcontMDiff_cancelH. A slice with \(\rho(t) \ne 0\) has north as a regular value, since its zeros have \(l \ne 0\) and invertible derivative \(cB_bT_l \circ d\varphi\) Chapter7/CancelHmfd_cancelH_slice_of_mem Chapter7/CancelHisRegularValue_cancelH_slice. The homotopy has north as a regular value at all times Chapter7/CancelHisRegularValue_cancelH.

The cancellation

Theorem (V7.14). Let \(m \ge 1\) and let \((N, v)\) be a framed \(0\)-manifold. Let \(x_c\), \(\varphi\) and \(R > 0\) be as in V7.13: \(\bar B(\varphi(x_c), R)\) lies in the image of \(\varphi\), and \(\varphi\) preserves orientation on \(U_R\). Let \(w \in \mathbb R^m\) be a unit vector, \(a > 0\) with \(8a \le R\), and \(c_0 \in \mathbb R^m\) with \(|c_0 - \varphi(x_c)| < R/8\). Let \(x_1, x_2 \in N\) lie in the domain of \(\varphi\), with \(\varphi(x_1) = c_0 + aw\) and \(\varphi(x_2) = c_0 - aw\), and let no other point of \(N\) lie in \(\overline{U_R}\). Let \(\varepsilon\) be the sign of the identity of \(\mathbb R^m\) from \(o_{x_c}\) to the standard orientation. Then there are framed \(0\)-manifolds \((N, v^0)\) and \((N \setminus \{x_1, x_2\}, v')\), both with frame \(v\) at the points other than \(x_1, x_2\), such that \(\operatorname{sign} v^0(x_1) = \varepsilon\), \(\operatorname{sign} v^0(x_2) = -\varepsilon\), and \((N, v^0) \sim (N \setminus \{x_1, x_2\}, v')\). Chapter7/Cancelexists_cancel

The idea. Run the cancelling family inside \(U_R\) on top of a Theorem-C map of \((N, v)\), and let V7.2 produce the cobordism. At \(x_1\) and \(x_2\) the family produces “standard” frames, whose signs can be computed, rather than \(v\).

The proof as formalized. Both points lie in \(U_{R/4}\). Take \(b\) the standard basis, \(\rho\) as above, the threshold \(c_1\) for the radius \(\min(3R/16, 9R^2/256)\), and a Theorem-C map \(k\) of \((N, v)\) with \(c \ge c_1\), south outside a compact subset of \(W = (M \setminus \overline{U_R}) \cup U_{R/2}\). Glue and apply V7.2. At \(t = 0\) (\(\rho = 1\)) the preimage of north is \((N \setminus U_R) \cup \{x_1, x_2\} = N\) Chapter7/CancelcancelH_slice_preimage_zero. At \(t = 1\) (\(\rho = -1\)) the equation \(l^2 = -a^2\) has no solution, and the preimage is \(N \setminus \{x_1, x_2\}\) Chapter7/CancelcancelH_slice_preimage_one. Off \(U_R\) the frames are those of \(k\), that is, \(v\) Chapter7/CancelpontV_cancelH_slice_of_notMem.

At a zero \(x_t = \varphi^{-1}(c_0 + lw)\) of a regular slice, let \(D\) be the slice derivative and \(B\) the matrix of chart coordinates of the Pontryagin frame. Then \(D \circ B = c\,\mathrm{id}\) and \(D = cT_l \circ d\varphi_{x_t}\). Now \(\operatorname{sign}(cT_l) = \operatorname{sgn}(c^m \cdot 2l) = \operatorname{sgn} l\), so the frame read in the chart of the ball has determinant of sign \(\operatorname{sgn} l\), with no orientation anywhere in the statement Chapter7/CancelchartSign_cancelH_slice. Since \(\varphi\) is positive on \(U_R\), the bridge of V7.20 multiplies that chart sign by one factor \(\varepsilon\), the same for the whole ball, to give the frame sign Chapter7/ChartSignFramed.frameSign_eq_orEps_hub_mul_chartSign; \(l = \pm a\) gives the signs \(\pm\varepsilon\).

What the book leaves implicit. The pair must carry the standard frames, whose signs depend on the chart through \(\varepsilon\). So cancelling two given points needs two changes of frame first, and the direction of \(w\) must match the signs Chapter7/CancelStepcancel_step.

Proposition (cancelling neighbours). Let \(m \ge 1\) and let \((N, v)\) be a framed \(0\)-manifold. Let \(x_0 \ne z\) in \(N\) satisfy \(\operatorname{sign} v(z) = -\operatorname{sign} v(x_0)\), with \(z\) a neighbour of \(x_0\), that is, \(z \in \overline{C(x_0)}\). Then \((N, v)\) is framed cobordant to \(N \setminus \{x_0, z\}\) with the frames \(v\). Chapter7/CancelStepcancel_step

The idea. Bring \(x_0\) close to \(z\), then cancel the pair in a chart ball around \(z\).

The proof as formalized.

  1. Take a good ball \(U_R\) around \(z\) whose closure avoids \(N \setminus \{z\}\). As \(z \in \overline{C(x_0)}\), some \(u \in U_{R/4}\) lies in \(C(x_0)\), and \(u \notin N\) Chapter7/Reachexists_goodBall. By reach, move \(x_0\) to \(u\) with a frame of the sign \(s\) of \(v(x_0)\) Chapter7/Reachexists_reach.
  2. In the chart at \(z\), \(\varphi(u)\) and \(\varphi(z)\) are \(c_0 \pm aw_0\), with \(c_0\) their midpoint, \(a = |\varphi(u) - \varphi(z)|/2\), and \(w_0\) the unit vector from \(\varphi(z)\) to \(\varphi(u)\). As \(|\varphi(u) - \varphi(z)| < R/4\), we get \(|c_0 - \varphi(z)| = a < R/8\) and \(8a \le R\).
  3. Let \(\varepsilon\) be the sign of V7.14 for the chart at \(z\), that of the identity of \(\mathbb R^m\) from \(o_z\) to the standard orientation. If \(s = \varepsilon\), cancel with \(w = w_0\), \(x_1 = u\), \(x_2 = z\). If \(s = -\varepsilon\), cancel with \(w = -w_0\), \(x_1 = z\), \(x_2 = u\). Either way the standard frames have the signs of the current frames, so two changes of frame, each a reach from a point to itself, install them Chapter7/CancelStepframedCobordant_of_frames. The cancellation is V7.14 Chapter7/Cancelexists_cancel, and transitivity chains the move, the two frame changes, and the cancellation Chapter7/EquivFramedCobordant.trans.

Removing a pair of opposite signs leaves the signed count unchanged Chapter7/CancelStepcount_of_remove_two.

V7.16 Framed 0-manifolds with the same signed count

Theorem (V7.16). Let \(m \ge 1\) and let \(M\) be connected. Two framed \(0\)-manifolds of \(M\) with the same signed count are framed cobordant. Chapter7/MainframedCobordant_of_count_eq

The idea. Cancel neighbouring pairs of opposite sign until each side has one sign. Equal counts then force the same sign and the same number of points. Match the frames at common points, then gather the remaining points of one side onto the other.

The proof as formalized. The proof is an induction on the total number of points \(|F| + |G|\) Chapter7/MainframedCobordant_of_count_eq.

  1. Both signs occur in \(F\). Apply the neighbour lemma in \(M\) to the set \(B\) of points with the sign of a given point. It yields \(x_0 \in B\) with a neighbour \(z \notin B\), necessarily of the opposite sign Chapter7/Mainexists_opposite_neighbour. The cancel step removes both. The count is unchanged and the number of points drops by two Chapter7/Maincard_of_remove_two. The same is done for \(G\), using symmetry (V7.4) Chapter7/EquivFramedCobordant.symm.

  2. One sign on each side. If \(F\) is empty, so is \(G\), as a nonempty \(G\) has count \(|G|s_G \ne 0\); then \(F = G\) Chapter7/Maincount_of_empty. Likewise with \(F\) and \(G\) exchanged. Otherwise the counts are \(|F|s_F\) and \(|G|s_G\) Chapter7/Gathercount_of_const_sign, and equality forces \(s_F = s_G =: s\) and \(|F| = |G|\).

  3. Matching frames. At a common point where the frames differ, a reach from the point to itself installs the frame of \(G\). Induction on the number of such points gives \(F' \sim F\) with all signs \(s\), \(|F'| = |G|\), and the frames of \(G\) at common points Chapter7/GatherGInv Chapter7/Gatherexists_matched.

  4. Gathering. Then \(F' \sim G\) Chapter7/Gathergather, by induction on the number of unmatched points of \(F'\), those not in \(G\). If there are none, the sets coincide (same cardinality), so do the frames, and reflexivity applies. Otherwise, within one gathering step, neighbours are taken relative to the fixed set \(N = F' \cup G\). The chain lemma with \(B = F'\) gives a chain with interior in \(F'\) from an unmatched point \(x\) of \(F'\) to an unmatched point \(z\) of \(G\) Chapter7/Chainexists_chainRel. Take a shortest one, ending in \(\dots, w, z\).

    One step is always possible. If \(u \in F'\) has a neighbour \(z \in G \setminus F'\) relative to \(N\), then \(z\) lies in the component of \(u\) relative to \(F'\), since removing fewer points only enlarges components. So reach moves \(u\) onto \(z\) with the frame of \(G\) Chapter7/Gathergather_move. If \(w\) is unmatched, moving \(w\) onto \(z\) leaves one unmatched point fewer. If \(w \in G\), move \(w\) onto \(z\) anyway. The unmatched points do not change, but the old place of \(w\) is now a vacant point of \(G\). By minimality the chain from \(x\) to \(w\) did not visit \(w\) earlier Chapter7/ChainchainRel_diff', so it is a strictly shorter chain in the new configuration. An inner induction on the length of the shortest chain concludes Chapter7/Gathergather_step.

Why chains are needed, and when. For \(m \ge 2\) the complement of a finite set in a connected manifold is connected, every point of \(N\) is a neighbour of every other, and shortest chains have length one. On a circle, \(C(x)\) is the open arc between the two points of \(N\) adjacent to \(x\). Let \(F = \{x, p, q\}\) and \(G = \{p, q, z\}\) lie in the cyclic order \(p, x, q, z\). The unmatched \(x\) has only matched neighbours and cannot reach \(z\). The chain \(x, q, z\) first moves \(q\) onto \(z\), then \(x\) onto the old place of \(q\). The formal proof is uniform in the dimension: it neither knows nor needs that chains are short when \(m \ge 2\) Chapter7/Gathergather_step.

V7.17 The Hopf theorem

Theorem (V7.17). Degrees are taken with respect to \(o\) and the orientation of Chapter 5 on \(S^m\).

  1. Let \(m \ge 1\) and let \(M\) be connected. If \(f, g : M \to S^m\) are smooth and \(\deg f = \deg g\), then \(f\) and \(g\) are smoothly homotopic. Chapter7/Hopfhopf_homotopic

  2. Let \(m \ge 1\). For every \(d \in \mathbb Z\) there is a smooth \(f : M \to S^m\) with \(\deg f = d\). Chapter7/Hopfexists_map_of_deg

Nonemptiness of \(M\) is a standing hypothesis; in (a) connectedness implies it. Part (b) does not assume connectedness Chapter7/Hopfexists_map_of_deg.

The idea. For (a), degrees are signed counts, equal counts give framed cobordant Pontryagin manifolds, and these come from homotopic maps. For (b), build a framed \(0\)-manifold with the right count and realize it by Theorem C.

Proof of (a). By Brown’s theorem \(f\) and \(g\) have regular values \(y\) and \(y'\) Chapter2/Browndense_regularValues, and since \(m \ge 1\) there are positive bases \(e\) at \(y\) and \(e'\) at \(y'\) Chapter7/Lemma2exists_posBasis. By V7.12 the two Pontryagin manifolds have signed counts \(\deg f = \deg g\). By V7.16 they are framed cobordant, and the “if” half of Milnor’s Theorem B (V7.11) gives a smooth homotopy Chapter7/ThmAconvsmoothHomotopic_of_framedCobordant. The converse, that smoothly homotopic maps have equal degrees, is Milnor’s Theorem B of §5 (V5.7) Chapter5/Degreedeg_eq_of_homotopy.

Adding a point. Let \(m \ge 1\), let \((N, v)\) be a framed \(0\)-manifold, let \(x \notin N\), and let \(v_x\) be a frame at \(x\). There is a framed \(0\)-manifold with points \(N \cup \{x\}\), frame \(v\) on \(N\), and frame \(v_x\) at \(x\) Chapter7/AddPointexists_add_point. Take a good ball around \(x\) avoiding \(N\), the dual tuple \(\tau_0\) of \(v_x\), and a lower bound for \(B_{\tau_0}\) Chapter7/AddPointexists_lower_bound_basisCLM. Glue the moving family with constant tuple \(\tau_0\) and constant centre \(\varphi_x(x)\) onto a Theorem-C map of \((N, v)\) that is south outside a compact subset of \(M \setminus \overline{U_R}\). At time \(0\) the glued map has north as a regular value with preimage \(N \cup \{x\}\), frames \(v\) on \(N\) (germs), and \(v_x\) at \(x\) (V7.8). Only a map is involved here, no cobordism.

Proof of (b). A finite set always misses a point of \(M\). \(M\) is nonempty, and for \(m \ge 1\) the chart segment \(t \mapsto \varphi^{-1}(\varphi(y_0) + te_1)\), \(0 < t < r\), is injective, so \(M\) is infinite Chapter7/Hopfexists_notMem_finite. Let \(s = 1\) if \(d \ge 0\) and \(s = -1\) otherwise. Starting from the empty framed \(0\)-manifold Chapter7/HopfemptyFramed, add \(|d|\) points with frames of sign \(s\) Chapter7/Hopfexists_framedSub_of_card. Theorem C with \(W = M\) realizes the result \(F\) as the Pontryagin manifold of a map \(k\) at the north pole for the basis \(ce'\), with \(e'\) positive there. V7.12 is stated for \(e'\) itself. The Pontryagin frames for \(ce'\) are \(c\) times those for \(e'\), and positive rescaling keeps signs, since \(\det(cI) = c^m > 0\) Chapter7/HopfframeSign_smul Chapter7/Hopfcount_pontryagin_smul. So \(\deg k\) is the signed count of \(F\), namely \(|d|s = d\).

V7.18 and V7.19 Orientability, transport, and the reversing loop of balls

Milnor’s clause at the end of §7 needs a vocabulary his book does not build. An orientation of a manifold is V5.0, his own notion; what is missing is orientability as a property, and its characterization by loops. For this section and the four that follow, \(M\) is a manifold modelled on a finite-dimensional \(E\) with \(\dim E = m\) — for the theorem at the end, the submanifold of the standing notation, but the machinery asks for nothing of the kind. Call \(M\) orientable if it carries an orientation in the sense of V5.0 Chapter7/OrientableIsOrientable.

Transport. The derivative at \(y\) of the extended chart centred at \(x\) is a linear isomorphism, so exactly one orientation of the model space at \(y\) is carried by it to a given orientation at \(x\): the transport \(\operatorname{tr}_{x \to y}\) through that chart, an involution which anticommutes with reversal Chapter7/OrientTransportorTransport. An orientation of \(M\) is exactly a family of orientations of \(E\), one at each point, which near every point is the transport of its value at that point — the continuity condition of V5.0 read backwards Chapter7/OrientTransportOrient.isTransportSection Chapter7/OrientTransportOrient.ofTransportSection.

Hops and chains. A hop from \(x\) to \(y\) is a chart whose source contains both, together with a record of which chart it is Chapter7/OrientTransportChartHop; a chain is a finite sequence of hops Chapter7/OrientTransportChartChain. Chains compose and reverse, transport along a composite is the composite of the transports, and transport along the reverse undoes the chain. In a connected manifold any two points are joined by a chain, the reachable set being open and closed. A chain-loop reverses if its transport carries some orientation at the base point to the opposite one; which of the two is tested is immaterial Chapter7/OrientableChartChain.Reverses. A step the design did not foresee: a hop must record which chart it travels through. The naive relation “some chart contains both points” induces no well-defined transport, and the obvious symmetric repair is wrong, precisely because two charts can disagree on a disconnected overlap.

Theorem (V7.18). Let \(M\) be connected. If no chain-loop at a point of \(M\) reverses, then \(M\) is orientable: transport a fixed orientation from the base point, the answer being unambiguous because two chains to the same point differ by a loop Chapter7/OrientableisOrientable_of_forall_not_reverses. Contrapositively, a connected non-orientable manifold carries at every point a chain-loop that reverses every orientation there Chapter7/Orientableexists_reverses_of_not_isOrientable. A connected orientable manifold has exactly two orientations, a given one and its pointwise reverse Chapter7/OrientableOrient.or_eq_or_eq_neg.

A warning, and it is a genuine one. The other direction — that an orientable \(M\) admits no reversing chain-loop — is false for an orientation in the sense of V5.0, whose compatibility is a condition only near each point. On \(\mathbb R\) take the atlas consisting of the identity together with the chart that is \(x\) on \((-1, 0)\) and \(3 - x\) on \((1, 2)\). This is a smooth structure on \(\mathbb R\), which is orientable; yet the orientation that is standard except reversed on \((1, 2)\) satisfies the condition of V5.0, while the loop out through the second chart and back through the identity reverses. The culprit is that a chart source may be disconnected. The converse does hold for the stronger notion of an orientation coherent with every chart on the whole of that chart’s source, and for connected \(M\) the absence of reversing chain-loops is equivalent to the existence of such an orientation Chapter7/OrientableIsChartCoherent Chapter7/Orientableexists_isChartCoherent_iff_forall_not_reverses.

The repair. A chart ball about \(c\) is the preimage under the extended chart at \(c\) of a round ball about the chart image of \(c\); when that ball lies in the chart’s target, the chart ball is connected, which is the one property a chart source lacks Chapter7/OrientBallchartBall Chapter7/OrientBallisPreconnected_chartBall. A ball hop is a hop through such a ball containing both its endpoints, a ball chain a chain all of whose hops are of that kind Chapter7/OrientBallBallHop Chapter7/OrientBallChartChain.IsBall. The whole transport algebra applies verbatim; only the predicate has to be shown closed under the constructions.

The key lemma. Every orientation of \(M\) is ball-coherent: transport along a ball hop carries the orientation at one end to the orientation at the other Chapter7/OrientBallBallHop.transport_or. On a chart ball about \(c\) the sign of the orientation at \(z\) against the orientation at \(c\), read through the derivative of the chart at \(c\), takes only the values \(\pm 1\), is locally constant by the continuity condition of V5.0, and equals \(1\) at \(c\); and a locally constant function on a connected set is constant. For a chart source the conclusion fails, and the counterexample above is exactly why.

Theorem (V7.19), the exact dichotomy. For connected \(M\) and any base point, \(M\) is orientable if and only if no loop of chart balls at that point reverses Chapter7/OrientBallisOrientable_iff_forall_not_reverses_isBall Chapter7/OrientBallballReachable_of_preconnectedSpace, and a connected non-orientable \(M\) carries at every point a ball loop reversing every orientation there Chapter7/OrientBallexists_isBall_reverses_of_not_isOrientable.

Two things are gained. Unlike V7.18 the equivalence now holds with no auxiliary notion, so a reversing ball loop is a genuine obstruction to orientability and not a symptom of a badly chosen atlas; and the loops run through round balls, which is what the moving machinery of V7.13 can follow.

Hidden hypotheses. V7.18 needs none at all: no boundarylessness, no Hausdorffness, no second countability, and \(M\) may be empty. V7.19 needs the model boundaryless, on 24 of its 61 declarations and for two independent reasons, both of which are that a chart target must be open: a ball inside the target has to exist at all, and the sign of a chart derivative has to be locally constant. Everything about a chart ball that is given needs it not.

V7.20 and V7.21 The chart sign of a frame, and the sign of a chain

The sign of a frame (V7.12) is measured against an orientation of \(M\), which a non-orientable \(M\) does not have. So the local lemmas must be restated with a sign that mentions none, and the chains of V7.19 must be given an arithmetic.

Three signs, no orientation. The chart sign of a frame \(v\) at \(x\) relative to a centre \(x_c\) is the sign of the determinant of \(v\) read in the chart at \(x_c\) Chapter7/ChartSignFramed.chartSign; the self sign is the case \(x_c = x\) Chapter7/ChartSignFramed.selfSign; the Jacobian sign is the sign of the determinant of the derivative at \(x\) of the chart at \(x_c\) Chapter7/ChartSignFramed.jacSign. All three are \(\pm 1\) for a tangent independent frame at a point of the chart’s source, none mentions an orientation, and \[\text{chart sign} = \text{Jacobian sign} \cdot \text{self sign},\] with Jacobian sign \(1\) at the centre Chapter7/ChartSignFramed.chartSign_eq_jacSign_mul_selfSign.

The bridge (V7.20). For any orientation \(o\) of \(M\), \[\operatorname{sign} v(x) = \varepsilon(x)\cdot\text{self sign}(v, x),\] where \(\varepsilon(x)\) is the sign of the identity of \(\mathbb R^m\) read from the standard orientation to \(o_x\), and so depends on the point and not on the frame Chapter7/ChartSignFramed.orEps Chapter7/ChartSignFramed.frameSign_eq_orEps_mul_selfSign. The sign of a frame against an orientation of the manifold is the determinant sign of the frame read in one chart, times a factor depending only on the point. That is what lets the local machinery run without an orientation, since every local proof compares a product of two such signs and the factor cancels. On a chart ball the same holds with the hub’s factor Chapter7/ChartSignFramed.frameSign_eq_orEps_hub_mul_chartSign, so equality of frame signs at two points of a ball is equality of their chart signs relative to the hub.

Two consequences remove case splits from the sections above. Frames of both chart signs exist at every point, with no reference to a global sign Chapter7/ChartSignFramed.exists_frame_of_selfSign — the proof of “frames of both signs at a point” collapses from sixty-five lines to one — and a frame at \(x\) may be carried to any other point of the same chart’s source as the same frame read in that chart, hence with the same chart sign Chapter7/ChartSignFramed.exists_frame_transport.

What this does to V7.13, V7.14 and V7.15. They are restated in these terms. The glued moving and cancelling homotopies no longer mention an orientation at all: six theorems lose two hypotheses each, and a lemma asserting that a chart derivative is bijective, whose hypothesis “the chart preserves orientation” was spurious, is deleted in favour of the general one. The sign of the frame at a zero of the cancelling map becomes flatly the sign of the signed distance, where before it carried a factor depending on the orientation. Four declarations cannot be restated in place, because the cancel step and the Hopf theorem call them in their oriented form; the sign-free statement then carries the proof and the oriented one is a short corollary beside it, so that no proof is duplicated. The bookkeeping costs 131 lines and buys everything below. A better primitive than expected: the self sign needs no chart-membership hypothesis, which is what makes it usable in the open-and-closed arguments of V7.23.

The sign dictionary (V7.21). Transport across a chart is multiplication by the Jacobian sign Chapter7/BallChainSignjacSign; the sign of a hop is the product of the two Jacobian signs of its chart at the two endpoints Chapter7/BallChainSignhopSign; the sign of a chain is the product of the signs of its hops Chapter7/BallChainSignchainSign. The sign of a composite is the product, a chain and its reverse have the same sign, transport along a chain is multiplication by its sign, and a loop reverses exactly when its sign is \(-1\) Chapter7/BallChainSignchainSign_comp Chapter7/BallChainSignchainSign_reverse Chapter7/BallChainSignChartChain.transport_eq_signAct Chapter7/BallChainSignChartChain.reverses_iff_chainSign. The dichotomy of V7.19 thereby becomes arithmetic. All of it holds for arbitrary chart chains, not only ball ones, at no extra cost.

The transition cocycle. For two chart centres \(p\), \(q\) and a point \(y\) in both their sources, the product of the two Jacobian signs at \(z\) is locally constant in \(z\) near \(y\) Chapter7/BallChainSigneventually_jacSign_mul_jacSign_eq. Neither factor is: each reads a fixed chart through the moving chart at \(z\). But in the product the moving chart cancels, and what is left is the determinant sign of the fixed smooth transition \(\varphi_p \circ \varphi_q^{-1}\), continuous and invertible, hence of locally constant sign. This is the technical key of the two sections that follow.

Chains that avoid a set. A hop runs inside a set \(C\) if the closed chart ball of its radius lies in \(C\) Chapter7/BallChainSignChartChain.IsBallIn. For \(C\) open and preconnected any two of its points are joined by a chain of hops running inside \(C\) Chapter7/BallChainSignexists_isBallIn, and such a chain automatically avoids every set disjoint from \(C\) — indeed each of its closed balls does Chapter7/BallChainSignexists_isBallIn_avoiding. Two hypotheses are weaker than the design asked: the avoided set need not be closed, only disjoint from the region, and the region need only be preconnected. One had to be added: avoidance is phrased through the closed chart ball and not through the topological closure of the ball, because on a non-Hausdorff manifold the closure of a chart ball need not lie in its chart — on the line with two origins, the closure of an interval about one origin contains the other. The closure form is given separately under Hausdorffness, which is free in this chapter.

V7.22 The reversing loop away from a finite set

A framed \(0\)-manifold is a finite set of points, and the loop that is to flip the frame at one of them must not disturb the others. So the dichotomy has to be run on the complement of a finite set.

Theorem (V7.22). Let \(2 \le m\). A punctured chart ball is connected Chapter7/PunctureisConnected_chartBall_diff_singleton; the complement of a finite set in a connected \(M\) is connected Chapter7/PunctureisConnected_compl_finite, and nonempty as soon as \(0 < m\), a nonempty open subset of a manifold of positive dimension being infinite Chapter7/Punctureinfinite_of_isOpen; and a family of orientations that is ball-coherent on the complement of a finite set \(P\) agrees off \(P\) with an orientation of the whole of \(M\) Chapter7/PunctureIsBallCoherentOn Chapter7/Punctureextend_ballCoherent. Hence the punctured dichotomy: a connected non-orientable manifold of dimension at least two has, at every point outside a given finite set, a loop of chart balls at that point missing the set and of chain sign \(-1\). Chapter7/PunctureHasReversingBallLoop Chapter7/PuncturehasReversingBallLoop_of_not_isOrientable

The idea. Everything rests on the extension lemma, and that is where the cocycle of V7.21 earns its keep. The value of the extended orientation at a puncture \(p\) is the value at a nearby point, transported back to \(p\). It is well defined because that assignment is locally constant on a punctured ball about \(p\) — the two Jacobian signs being separately discontinuous and jointly locally constant — and because a punctured ball is connected.

Two things came out cleaner than expected. Well-definedness holds at every point, not only at the punctures, so the extension is one total function with no case split, and the transport condition is then checked at every point at once. And no separation hypothesis is needed anywhere: charts give \(T_1\) for free.

The dimension hypothesis is sharp, not a convenience. For \(m = 1\) a punctured ball is an interval minus an interior point, and \(\mathbb R \setminus \{0\}\) is a disconnected complement of a finite set in a connected \(1\)-manifold; for \(m = 0\) a punctured ball is empty. This section therefore keeps \(2 \le m\), and keeps it sharply. It is the only place in the whole of the mod 2 theory that wants it, which is why V7.28 can delete it from everything above: the theorems that appeal to this one derive the hypothesis from non-orientability instead of assuming it.

Two small facts had to be proved: that no point of a manifold of positive dimension is isolated, and that a locally constant function on a connected set is constant — Mathlib’s version of the latter wants a discrete target, and the two orientations of a vector space carry no topology.

V7.23 to V7.25 The slide, the flip, and the count modulo 2

Now Milnor’s clause itself, and then the endgame without signs. Throughout, \(m \ge 1\) and \((N, v)\) is a framed \(0\)-manifold of \(M\).

The slide (V7.23). Given a chain of chart balls from a point \(x_0\) of \(N\) to \(y\), none of whose balls meets any other point of \(N\), \((N, v)\) is framed cobordant to a framed \(0\)-manifold with point set \((N \setminus \{x_0\}) \cup \{y\}\), the same frames elsewhere, and self sign at \(y\) equal to the chain sign of V7.21 times the self sign at \(x_0\). Chapter7/SlideFramed.exists_slide

The flip. If the chain is a loop at \(x_0\) of chain sign \(-1\), the point set and all the other frames are literally unchanged and the self sign at \(x_0\) is reversed. Chapter7/SlideFramed.exists_flip This is Milnor’s clause.

With a reversing loop in hand, the frame at a point may then be replaced by any tangent independent frame, and the point may be moved anywhere in its component of \(M \setminus (N \setminus \{x_0\})\) with any frame: this is V7.13 with the orientation and its sign hypothesis simply deleted Chapter7/SlideFramed.exists_reach_any Chapter7/SlideFramed.exists_frame_free Chapter7/SlideFramed.exists_reach_free. No orientation, no connectedness, no \(2 \le m\) and no Hausdorffness occur in the file; the only dimension hypothesis is \(0 < m\), and the reversing loop is a hypothesis, in exactly the form V7.22 produces it, so the two halves join with no glue.

Where one ball hop is not one move. A move of V7.13 needs its two points inside a quarter-radius ball whose closed ball fits in the chart, while the endpoints of a hop can be almost a full diameter apart, and the chart target need not contain a ball four times as large. So each hop is subdivided, and the sign must be shown not to notice the subdivision. That needs an open-set form of the cocycle lemma and a change-of-hub lemma, and it is where the invariant carried across a hop turns out to be the chart sign at the hop’s own hub. An improvement on the design: the sign-free reach lemma needs the reversing loop only at the starting point, not at the target.

Cancellation with no condition on the frames (V7.24). Two framed \(0\)-manifolds with the same point set and the same frames away from two distinct points are framed cobordant, with no condition relating the frames at those two points Chapter7/CancelFreeFramed.framedCobordant_of_frames_free. Hence any two distinct points of \(N\), one in the closure of the component of the other, can be cancelled — V7.14 with its opposite-sign hypothesis deleted outright Chapter7/CancelFreeFramed.cancel_step_free — and if \(N\) has two distinct points and \(M\) is connected, some two of them are neighbours in that sense, which is V7.15 with the partition \(\{x\} \sqcup (N \setminus \{x\})\) in place of a partition by sign Chapter7/CancelFreeFramed.exists_neighbour_pair.

This is where the design was most wrong, and the error is instructive. It prescribed choosing an arriving frame of the opposite sign and replacing the old case split by a new one. Neither is needed. The cancelling homotopy supplies its own two frames, of chart signs \(+1\) and \(-1\) — that is the computation of V7.14 read through V7.20 — and “frames are free at two points” connects any configuration to that one. So the arriving frame may be arbitrary, and the case split disappears rather than being replaced. The sign-free cancel step is therefore shorter than the signed one.

The count modulo 2 (V7.25). The count modulo 2 of a framed \(0\)-manifold is the cardinality of its point set read in \(\mathbb Z/2\); no orientation occurs in the definition, in contrast with V7.12 Chapter7/CountMod2Framed.countMod2. Two framed \(0\)-manifolds of a connected \(M\) with the same count modulo 2 are framed cobordant, given reversing ball loops off every finite set Chapter7/CountMod2Framed.framedCobordant_of_countMod2_eq; and the count modulo 2 of the Pontryagin manifold of \(f : M \to S^m\) at a regular value is \(\deg_2 f\), both being the parity of \(\#f^{-1}(y)\) Chapter7/CountMod2Framed.countMod2_pontryagin. Unlike V7.12 this bridge needs nothing of the framing, so the frame may be any independent tuple and not a positive basis. Together these are Milnor’s statement that the framed cobordism class is determined by the number of points modulo 2, and they are V7.16 with the signed count replaced by the parity.

The induction is simpler than the signed one. V7.16 can cancel only while both signs occur, and needs a separate gathering argument when they do not. Here the induction runs on the cruder condition “two or more points”, there is no gathering step at all, and it stops when each side has at most one point, which is then carried onto the other by the reach lemma. That is exactly where the improvement noted above is used: the loop is needed only at the point that moves.

V7.26 Milnor’s theorem for a non-orientable manifold

Theorem (V7.26). Let \(M \subseteq \mathbb R^{K+1}\) be a compact, nonempty, connected, non-orientable submanifold of dimension \(m\). Two smooth maps \(f, g : M \to S^m\) are smoothly homotopic if and only if they have the same degree modulo 2. Chapter7/HopfMod2Framed.hopf_homotopic_mod2

This is the counterpart, at the end of Milnor’s §7, of the Hopf theorem V7.17.

Proof of the easy half. It is the homotopy invariance of the mod 2 degree, the second assertion of the Theorem of §4 (V4.8), transcribed into the homotopy relation of this chapter Chapter7/HopfMod2degMod2_eq_of_smoothHomotopic Chapter7/HopfMod2Framed.degMod2_eq_of_smoothHomotopic_sph. It needs no orientation of any kind, no connectedness, and nothing of the dimension beyond \(0 < m\), which is only what the mod 2 degree asks of its target.

Proof of the substantial half, which is Milnor’s remark. By Brown’s theorem \(f\) and \(g\) have regular values \(y\) and \(y'\) Chapter2/Browndense_regularValues, and since \(m \ge 1\) there are positive bases \(e\) at \(y\) and \(e'\) at \(y'\) Chapter7/Lemma2exists_posBasis. Form the two Pontryagin manifolds (V7.1). By the parity bridge of V7.25 their counts modulo 2 are \(\deg_2 f\) and \(\deg_2 g\), hence equal; with the loops supplied by V7.22, the parity classification makes them framed cobordant Chapter7/HopfMod2Framed.framedCobordant_of_card_parity; and the converse half of Theorem B (V7.11), which is itself orientation-free, turns that into a smooth homotopy Chapter7/HopfMod2Framed.smoothHomotopic_of_degMod2_eq.

Where the orientations are. The only orientations in the whole argument are orientations of the target sphere, which the Pontryagin construction and the converse of Theorem B require. The source carries none, and is assumed not to have one. That is the point of V7.20, and it is what makes every earlier local lemma of this part usable here.

No hypothesis on the dimension, and how it went. The statement above has none, as Milnor’s has none. Each half wants \(0 < m\), which is all the mod 2 degree asks of its target, and each half now gets it from non-orientability along with everything else. Earlier editions of this section carried \(2 \le m\) and called it vacuous but unavoidable: vacuous because a connected \(1\)-manifold is diffeomorphic to the circle or to an interval and all of those are orientable, so that a connected non-orientable manifold has dimension at least two of its own accord; unavoidable because that sentence quotes the classification of one-manifolds, which was not formalized. It now is (Part XII), the deduction is V7.28 below, and because the hypothesis enters at exactly one point — the appeal to V7.22 — each of the three statements of this section that mentions non-orientability derives the bound there in one line instead of assuming it Chapter7/OneManifoldOrientabletwo_le_of_not_isOrientable_slice. V7.22 itself keeps \(2 \le m\), sharply, as a statement about punctured balls.

V7.27 and V7.28 One-manifolds are orientable, and the hypothesis goes

Five statements, whose only purpose is the sentence a connected non-orientable manifold has dimension at least two. They are the one place where the rest of the book depends on the Appendix for anything but the boundary count and its arcs, and they are what makes the theorem above match Milnor’s, which carries no condition on the dimension. Orientation and orientability are as before: an orientation of \(M\) is V5.0’s, a choice \(o(x)\) of orientation of each tangent space which near every point is carried to the value at that point by the derivative of the chart centred there, and \(M\) is orientable when it has one Chapter7/OrientableIsOrientable.

Pulling an orientation back. For an invertible continuous linear map \(T : E \to F\) between spaces of dimension \(n\) and an orientation \(b\) of \(F\), exactly one orientation of \(E\) is carried by \(T\) to \(b\) Chapter7/OneManifoldOrientableorPull Chapter7/OneManifoldOrientableorSign_orPull Chapter7/OneManifoldOrientableeq_orPull. Uniqueness holds because a space of dimension \(n\) has exactly two orientations, and an isomorphism cannot carry both of them to the same one.

Two orientations that cost nothing. If all the charts of \(M\) are literally the same partial homeomorphism, every transition is the identity, every sign is \(+1\), and a constant family is an orientation Chapter7/OneManifoldOrientableOrient.ofConst. And a manifold of dimension \(0\) is orientable whatever its charts, because in dimension \(0\) every linear map preserves every orientation: the only tuple to test is the empty one Chapter7/OneManifoldOrientableorSign_self_eq_one_of_zero Chapter7/OneManifoldOrientableOrient.ofZero.

Theorem (V7.27), transport. Let \(\Phi : M \to N\) be smooth between manifolds of the same dimension \(n\), let \(N\) carry an orientation \(o_N\), and let \(d\Phi_x\) be invertible at every \(x\). Then \(x \mapsto \operatorname{orPull}(o_N(\Phi x),\, d\Phi_x)\) is an orientation of \(M\) Chapter7/OneManifoldOrientableOrient.comap Chapter7/OneManifoldOrientableIsOrientable.comap. Nothing else is asked of \(\Phi\): it need be neither injective nor surjective nor a local diffeomorphism. In particular orientability travels backwards along a diffeomorphism, whose derivative is invertible Chapter7/OneManifoldOrientablebijective_mfd_diffeomorph Chapter7/OneManifoldOrientableIsOrientable.of_diffeomorph, and that is the direction the classification hands out.

The proof is V5.1 read backwards Chapter7/OneManifoldOrientableeventually_orSign_eq_one_of_pullback. Write \(\Phi\) in the charts at \(x_0\) and at \(\Phi x_0\) as a map \(g\) of open subsets of the model space. For \(x\) near \(x_0\) the transition of \(N\) at \(\Phi x\) composed with \(d\Phi_x\) equals \(dg\) composed with the transition of \(M\) at \(x\). The left-hand side has sign \(1\), by the definition of the pulled-back family and the compatibility of \(o_N\); the right-hand side splits as the sign of \(dg\) — locally constant, and \(1\) at \(x_0\), where \(dg = d\Phi_{x_0}\) — times the sign of the transition of \(M\). So that last sign is \(1\), which is the condition of V5.0.

The four models of Part XII are oriented. The line and the closed half-line by constant families, since each carries a single chart Chapter7/OneManifoldOrientableorientReal Chapter7/OneManifoldOrientableorientIci. The unit interval not by a constant family: Mathlib’s manifold structure on \([0,1]\) has two charts, \(z \mapsto z\) on \([0,1)\) and \(z \mapsto 1 - z\) on \((0,1]\), and their transition reverses orientation, so the family has to flip at the right-hand endpoint and that one transition derivative has to be computed — which is done by factoring the chart at \(1\) through the chart at an interior point and the reflection of the model space, an affine map Chapter7/OneManifoldOrientablemfd_extChartAt_Icc_top Chapter7/OneManifoldOrientableorientIcc. And the circle not through its own charts at all, but through the unit circle \(S^1 \subseteq \mathbb R^2\), which Chapter 8 orients as the boundary of the disk Chapter8/OrientFramesphOrStd: \(S^1\) is a nonempty compact Hausdorff connected boundaryless smooth one-manifold, so V.H hands over a diffeomorphism of it with Mathlib’s circle and transport carries the orientation across Chapter7/OneManifoldOrientableisOrientable_circle Chapter7/OneManifoldOrientableisOrientable_models. That is shorter than either direct route — the transition of the two stereographic charts, or a descent along the periodic parametrization of V.H — because the sphere is oriented already.

Theorem (V7.27), the consequence. Every connected Hausdorff σ-compact smooth one-manifold over a boundaryless model is orientable Chapter7/OneManifoldOrientableisOrientable_of_finrank_eq_one. The classification (V.J) makes such an \(M\) diffeomorphic to the circle if it is compact and to \(\mathbb R\) if it is not — the two interval models are excluded because the boundary of \(M\) is empty — and orientability travels back along that diffeomorphism Appendix/Smooth/Mainnonempty_diffeomorph_cases.

Theorem (V7.28). With the same hypotheses on \(M\) and with \(\dim E = m\): if \(M\) is not orientable then \(2 \le m\) Chapter7/OneManifoldOrientabletwo_le_of_not_isOrientable. Dimension \(0\) is excluded by the cheap orientation above and dimension \(1\) by the theorem just stated; there is nothing else to say.

In the vocabulary of this part, with every side hypothesis free: let \(M\) be a compact connected slice submanifold of a Euclidean space, charted on \(\mathbb R^m\). It is Hausdorff as a subspace of a metric space, σ-compact because it is compact, and its model is boundaryless, so its boundary is empty; if it is non-orientable then \(2 \le m\) Chapter7/OneManifoldOrientabletwo_le_of_not_isOrientable_slice. That is the form V7.26 calls, once in each of its three statements.

The one restriction, and why it costs nothing. Every transport statement assumes the model of the source boundaryless, and it is used in exactly one way: a chart target of the source has to be open in the model space, so that the map read in charts is defined on an open set, has a genuine derivative there, and that derivative is continuous in the point. For a model with boundary the argument would have to be rerun with the derivative within the model’s range, and it is not. So the orientability of one-manifolds is available for boundaryless models only — even though all four models of Part XII, the two with boundary included, are oriented above. Nothing in the book needs more: the manifolds of Chapters 7 and 8 are compact slice submanifolds of a Euclidean space, whose model is boundaryless.

What the formalization taught us

  • No cobordism is built by hand. Every move, frame change and cancellation is V7.2 applied to a homotopy glued into a chart ball, and even reflexivity is V7.2 applied to a constant homotopy. Milnor’s U-shaped arc exists only as a preimage of the north pole Chapter7/Cancelexists_cancel Chapter7/ReachFramedCobordant.refl'.
  • Theorem C needs two more parameters. The map must be south outside a prescribed open set, so that it glues near the frontier of a ball. Its scale must be bounded below, so that the local family and the Theorem-C map share the basis \(cb\) Chapter7/ThmBsuppexists_map_of_framedSub_subset Chapter7/Scaleexists_scale_all.
  • “Since \(M\) is connected” is the neighbour lemma. It uses local connectedness, closed points, and a segment property of chart balls Chapter7/Neighbourexists_neighbour Chapter7/SegmentballU_diff_subset_compl'.
  • Dimension one forces chains. Points of a circle cannot pass one another, so gathering moves the last point of a shortest chain first Chapter7/Gathergather_step.
  • Paths become an open–closed argument on the reachable points of a component. Moves happen only in chart balls where the chart preserves orientation, which exist by chart-continuity of orientations Chapter7/Reachexists_reach Chapter7/Reachexists_goodBall.
  • When the two points merge, regularity comes from time. The slice is singular there, so the time profile must satisfy \(\rho' \ne 0\) where \(\rho = 0\) Chapter7/CancelMapsurjective_Dcan Chapter7/CancelMapexists_rho.
  • Standard frames have chart-dependent signs \(\pm\varepsilon\), so a cancellation needs two frame changes first Chapter7/CancelchartSign_cancelH_slice Chapter7/CancelStepframedCobordant_of_frames. The factor \(\varepsilon\) is where the orientation enters, and V7.20 shows that it is the only place.
  • The scalar \(c\) of Theorem C reaches the degree computation. It is harmless, because positive rescaling keeps signs Chapter7/Hopfcount_pontryagin_smul.
  • Every degree is realized without connectedness. Adding points one at a time needs a point outside every finite set, that is, \(M\) infinite, and this is one place where \(m \ge 1\) and nonemptiness enter Chapter7/Hopfexists_map_of_deg Chapter7/Hopfexists_notMem_finite.
  • Finiteness of framed \(0\)-manifolds needs no Hausdorff hypothesis. Compact and discrete suffice Chapter7/Hopf0IsSliceSubmanifold.finite_of_dim_zero.
  • Orientability had to be invented before Milnor’s clause could be read. Neither Mathlib nor this project had it, and the notion of V5.0 is too weak for the converse: an orientation may be compatible near every point and still be reversed by a loop, because a chart source can be disconnected. Chart balls repair it exactly Chapter7/Orientableexists_isChartCoherent_iff_forall_not_reverses Chapter7/OrientBallisOrientable_iff_forall_not_reverses_isBall.
  • One sign is only locally constant in company. Each Jacobian sign reads a fixed chart through the moving chart and jumps; their product reads a fixed transition and does not. Every orientation extended across a puncture rests on that Chapter7/BallChainSigneventually_jacSign_mul_jacSign_eq Chapter7/Punctureextend_ballCoherent.
  • Removing a hypothesis shortened the proof. With the signs deleted the cancel step keeps no case split at all, the cancelling homotopy supplying the two frames the argument needs, and the induction of V7.16 loses its gathering step Chapter7/CancelFreeFramed.cancel_step_free Chapter7/CountMod2Framed.framedCobordant_of_countMod2_eq.
  • A vacuous hypothesis is not a cheap one. \(2 \le m\) said nothing, and deleting it cost the whole classification of one-manifolds, because the sentence that makes it vacuous — a connected one-manifold is orientable — is a theorem of the Appendix and not a remark Chapter7/OneManifoldOrientableisOrientable_of_finrank_eq_one Chapter7/OneManifoldOrientabletwo_le_of_not_isOrientable_slice.
  • Orientability travels backwards along any map with invertible derivative, not only along a diffeomorphism, and that generality is what lets the circle be oriented through the sphere, which Chapter 8 has already oriented, instead of through its own two charts Chapter7/OneManifoldOrientableOrient.comap Chapter7/OneManifoldOrientableisOrientable_circle.
← Part VI. The product neighbourhood, Theorem C and the second half of Theorem B (Milnor §7)Part VIII. Problems 1–12: degrees, approximation and bundles (Milnor §8) →

Part VIII. Problems 1–12: degrees, approximation and bundles (Milnor §8)

Milnor’s first twelve problems fall into three groups. Problems 1, 2, 6 and 7 compute degrees. Problems 3, 4, 5 and the second half of 12 replace continuous maps and homotopies, into a sphere or a compact manifold, by smooth ones. Problems 8 to 11 build new manifolds in Euclidean space: products, graphs, tangent and normal bundles. The third group rests on one criterion, proved once: a set that is locally the zero set of a submersion is a submanifold, whose tangent space is the kernel of the derivative. The approximation theorems rest on one analytic tool, a Stone–Weierstrass theorem for restrictions of smooth functions. Problem 11 reuses the nearest-point retraction of Part IV and adds the compactness argument that makes \((x, v) \mapsto x + v\) injective on a tube of uniform thickness.

Map of the part.

  • Chapter8/DegComp: Problem 1, the degree of a composition.
  • Chapter8/PolyDeg: an orientation of the Riemann sphere, and Problem 2.
  • Chapter8/NearMaps: Problem 3, the normalized-chord homotopy.
  • Chapter8/Approx: smooth Stone–Weierstrass on compact sets; normalizing a nearby vector.
  • Chapter8/Smoothing: Problems 4 and 5.
  • Chapter8/SphereMaps: Problems 6 and 7; even maps have even degree.
  • Chapter8/LocalSlice: local zero sets of submersions are submanifolds (V8.0 (i)).
  • Chapter8/ProdGraph: Problems 8 and 9.
  • Chapter8/TangentBundle: Problem 10.
  • Chapter8/NormalBundle: Problem 11, including \(r(x + v) = x\).
  • Chapter8/Retraction: the retraction as a smooth map into \(M\); the approximation half of Problem 12.
  • Chapter8/Nearest: the nearest-point half of Problem 12.

Conventions. The sphere \(S^p\) is the level set \(\{y \in \mathbb R^{p+1} : \langle y, y \rangle = 1\}\) with its slice structure; in degree computations it carries the orientation of §5 on both sides Chapter5/HairyBallSph Chapter5/HairyBallsphOr. The normalization \(\nu(y) = y/\|y\|\) is completed by a fixed base point at \(y = 0\); composed with a smooth map that never vanishes, it gives a smooth map into \(S^p\) Chapter6/Regionnv0 Chapter6/RegioncontMDiff_nv0_comp. The smooth step is Mathlib’s \(\sigma(t) = e^{-1/t}/(e^{-1/t} + e^{-1/(1-t)})\) on \((0,1)\), with \(\sigma = 0\) for \(t \le 0\) and \(\sigma = 1\) for \(t \ge 1\). Smooth homotopies are maps on \(X \times \mathbb R\) (§0.8), so every straight-line homotopy below is reparametrized by \(\sigma\): the parameter then only takes values in \([0,1]\), where the estimates hold, and the ends are still \(t = 0\) and \(t = 1\).

V8.1 Problem 1: the degree of a composition

Theorem. Let \(M\), \(N\), \(P\) be oriented smooth manifolds without boundary, modelled on real vector spaces of the same finite dimension \(n\) that lie in a common universe. Let \(M\) and \(N\) be compact, Hausdorff and second countable, \(P\) Hausdorff, and \(N\) and \(P\) preconnected (connected or empty). For smooth \(f : M \to N\) and \(g : N \to P\), \[\deg(g \circ f) = \deg g \cdot \deg f.\] Chapter8/DegCompdeg_comp

The universe condition is a formality: the degree of Part III is defined for model spaces in one universe, as all Euclidean spaces are.

The idea. Count the preimages of a point \(z\) that is regular for both \(g\) and \(g \circ f\). They fall into groups according to their image under \(f\), and each group is a signed count for \(f\).

The proof as formalized.

  1. If \(P\) is empty, there is no regular value, and both sides are \(0\) by the definition of the degree Chapter5/Degreedeg.
  2. The regular values of \(g \circ f\) are dense by Brown’s theorem, which uses that \(M\) is second countable. Those of \(g\) form an open set, as \(N\) is compact and \(P\) Hausdorff, and this set is nonempty, being dense in \(P \ne \emptyset\) by Brown’s theorem again (\(N\) is second countable). So some \(z\) is regular for both maps Chapter2/Browndense_regularValues Chapter6/RegularOpenisOpen_regularValues.
  3. Every \(y \in g^{-1}(z)\) is a regular value of \(f\). For \(x \in f^{-1}(y)\) the map \(d(g\circ f)_x = dg_y \circ df_x\) is onto, hence one-to-one since the dimensions agree; so \(df_x\) is one-to-one, hence onto. This step does not use the regularity of \(z\) for \(g\) Chapter8/DegCompisRegularValue_of_isRegularValue_comp.
  4. The fibres \(g^{-1}(z)\) and \((g \circ f)^{-1}(z)\) are finite (regular values, compact domains), hence so is every \(f^{-1}(y) \subseteq (g \circ f)^{-1}(z)\), and \((g \circ f)^{-1}(z)\) is the disjoint union of the \(f^{-1}(y)\), \(y \in g^{-1}(z)\).
  5. Compute both degrees at \(z\), and \(\deg f\) at each \(y\) separately. Regrouping the finite sum over the disjoint union gives \[\deg(g\circ f) = \sum_{y \in g^{-1}(z)}\ \sum_{x \in f^{-1}(y)} \operatorname{sign} d(g\circ f)_x, \qquad \deg g \cdot \deg f = \sum_{y \in g^{-1}(z)} \operatorname{sign} dg_y \sum_{x \in f^{-1}(y)} \operatorname{sign} df_x,\] and the two double sums agree term by term because signs multiply, \(\operatorname{sign} d(g\circ f)_x = \operatorname{sign} dg_{f(x)} \cdot \operatorname{sign} df_x\) Chapter6/SignLemmassignAt_comp'.

What the book leaves implicit. \(N\) must be compact for \(\deg g\) to make sense, and the same compactness makes the regular values of \(g\) open, which is how the common regular value is found Chapter8/DegCompdeg_comp.

V8.2 Problem 2: polynomials on the Riemann sphere

As in Part I, the Gauss sphere is replaced by the Riemann sphere \(\hat{\mathbb C} = \mathbb C \cup \{\infty\}\) with the charts \(z\) and \(1/z\), and a polynomial \(P\) of positive degree by its extension \(\hat P\) with \(\hat P(\infty) = \infty\), which is smooth Chapter1/FTApolyMap Chapter1/FTAcontMDiff_polyMap. Positive degree is used in the proof of smoothness at \(\infty\). (For a constant polynomial the extension is not even continuous there; this remark is not formalized.)

The sphere must first be oriented: every point gets the standard orientation \((1, i)\) of \(\mathbb C = \mathbb R^2\) Chapter8/PolyDegriemannOr. Continuity asks that near each point \(x\) the derivative of the chart at \(x\), read in the chart at a nearby point, have sign \(+1\). The formal proof computes it case by case: it is the identity when both charts are of the same kind, and multiplication by \(-1/u^2\) when the chart at \(\infty\) is read near a finite point \(u \ne 0\) Chapter8/PolyDegexists_hasMFDerivAt_extChartAt. Multiplication by \(w \ne 0\) is a real-linear map of determinant \(|w|^2 > 0\), so its sign is \(+1\) Chapter8/PolyDegdet_cmul Chapter8/PolyDegorSign_complexMul. The Riemann sphere is compact, Hausdorff, connected, and second countable as a compact manifold modelled on \(\mathbb C\), so Part III applies Chapter8/PolyDeginstSecondCountableTopologyRiemannSphere.

Theorem. If \(P \in \mathbb C[z]\) has degree \(n \ge 1\), then \(\deg \hat P = n\), for the orientation above on both sides. Chapter8/PolyDegdeg_polyMap

The idea. Over a regular value \(y \in \mathbb C\) the preimages are the simple roots of \(P - y\), each counted with sign \(+1\) because complex multiplication preserves orientation.

The proof as formalized. The candidate critical values, \(\infty\) and the values of \(P\) at the zeros of \(P'\), form a finite set; as \(\mathbb C\) is infinite, some \(y \in \mathbb C\) avoids it and is a regular value Chapter1/FTAcritVals_finite Chapter1/FTAisRegularValue_of_notMem_critVals. The fibre \(\hat P^{-1}(y)\) is the set of roots of \(P - y\). At each root \(z\), \(P'(z) \ne 0\) and the derivative of \(\hat P\) is multiplication by \(P'(z)\), of sign \(+1\) Chapter8/PolyDegsignAt_polyMap_coe. So \(\deg \hat P\) is the number of distinct roots of \(P - y\). A multiple root would be a zero of \(P'\) where \(P\) takes the value \(y\), which the choice of \(y\) excludes; so the roots are simple, and their number is \(\deg(P - y) = n\) by algebraic closedness Chapter8/PolyDegdeg_polyMap.

V8.3 Problem 3: the normalized chord

Theorem. Let \(f, g : X \to S^p\) satisfy \(\|f(x) - g(x)\| < 2\) for all \(x\). If \(X\) is a topological space and \(f\), \(g\) are continuous, they are homotopic. If \(X\) is a smooth manifold, modelled on any real normed space (no Hausdorff, countability or boundary assumptions), and \(f\), \(g\) are smooth, they are smoothly homotopic. Chapter8/NearMapshomotopic_of_norm_sub_lt_two Chapter8/NearMapssmoothHomotopic_of_norm_sub_lt_two

The idea. On the unit sphere, \(\|a - b\| < 2\) means \(b \ne -a\). The chord from \(a\) to \(b\) then misses the origin and can be projected radially onto the sphere.

The proof as formalized. The one lemma: for unit vectors \(a\), \(b\) with \(\|a - b\| < 2\) and \(0 \le s \le 1\), \((1-s)a + sb \ne 0\). If it vanished, taking norms would give \(1 - s = s\), so \(s = \tfrac12\) and \(a = -b\), whence \(\|a - b\| = 2\) Chapter8/NearMapschord_ne_zero. The continuous homotopy is \((t, x) \mapsto \nu((1-t)f(x) + t\,g(x))\) on \([0,1] \times X\). The smooth one is \[H(x, t) = \nu\big((1 - \sigma(t))\,f(x) + \sigma(t)\,g(x)\big), \qquad (x,t) \in X \times \mathbb R.\] The lemma applies since \(\sigma(t) \in [0,1]\), so the chord never vanishes and \(H\) is smooth; and \(\nu\) fixes unit vectors, so \(H(\cdot, 0) = f\) and \(H(\cdot, 1) = g\) Chapter8/NearMapsnv0_sph.

V8.4 Problem 4: uniform approximation and smoothing of homotopies

Where the retelling uses Weierstrass polynomials, the formal proof proves a smooth Stone–Weierstrass theorem on an arbitrary compact set.

Theorem (smooth approximation). Let \(E\), \(F\) be finite-dimensional real normed spaces, \(S \subseteq E\) compact, \(G : E \to F\) continuous on \(S\), and \(\varepsilon > 0\). There is a smooth \(Q : E \to F\) with \(\|Q(x) - G(x)\| < \varepsilon\) for all \(x \in S\). Chapter8/Approxexists_contDiff_approx_of_isCompact

The idea. Restrictions of smooth functions form a point-separating subalgebra of \(C(S, \mathbb R)\), so Stone–Weierstrass approximates each coordinate of \(G\).

The proof as formalized. The restrictions to \(S\) of smooth functions \(E \to \mathbb R\) form a subalgebra of \(C(S, \mathbb R)\) Chapter8/ApproxsmoothSubalgebraOn. It separates points, since continuous linear functionals do (Hahn–Banach) and they are smooth Chapter8/ApproxsmoothSubalgebraOn_separatesPoints. As \(S\) is compact, Stone–Weierstrass makes it uniformly dense. Fix a basis \(b_1, \dots, b_d\) of \(F\), put \(C = \sum_i \|b_i\| + 1\), and approximate each coordinate \(G_i\) of \(G\) within \(\varepsilon / C\) by a smooth \(P_i\). Then \(Q = \sum_i P_i b_i\) satisfies, on \(S\), \[\|Q - G\| \le \sum_i |P_i - G_i|\,\|b_i\| \le \tfrac{\varepsilon}{C}\,(C - 1) < \varepsilon.\] The finite dimensionality of \(E\) plays no role in the argument.

Two small facts adapt this to spheres. For a unit vector \(a\) and \(q \ne 0\), \(\|\nu(q) - a\| \le 2\|q - a\|\), because \(\|\nu(q) - q\| = |1 - \|q\|| \le \|q - a\|\) Chapter8/Approxnorm_nv0_sub_le. And a smooth homotopy restricts to a continuous one on \([0,1] \times X\) Chapter8/ApproxSmoothHomotopic.homotopic.

Theorem (Problem 4). Let \(M \subseteq \mathbb R^{K+1}\) be a compact submanifold, given by slice charts modelled on \(\mathbb R^m\). (a) For every continuous \(G : M \to S^p\) and every \(\varepsilon > 0\) there is a smooth \(f : M \to S^p\) with \(\|f(x) - G(x)\| < \varepsilon\) for all \(x\). (b) Two smooth maps \(M \to S^p\) that are homotopic are smoothly homotopic. Chapter8/Smoothingexists_smooth_approx Chapter8/SmoothingsmoothHomotopic_of_homotopic

The idea. Approximate in the ambient space and normalize. For homotopies, approximate on \(M \times [0,1]\) and close the gaps at the ends with Problem 3.

Proof of (a). Extend \(G\) by \(0\) off \(M\); the extension is continuous on the compact set \(M\). With \(\delta = \min(\varepsilon/2, 1/2)\), take a smooth \(Q\) within \(\delta\) of \(G\) on \(M\). Since \(\|G\| = 1\), \(Q\) does not vanish on \(M\), so \(f = \nu \circ Q\) is smooth on \(M\), and \(\|f - G\| \le 2\|Q - G\| < 2\delta \le \varepsilon\) Chapter8/Smoothingexists_smooth_approx.

Proof of (b), as formalized.

  1. Regard a homotopy \(H : [0,1] \times M \to S^p\) from \(f\) to \(g\) as a function on the compact set \(M \times [0,1] \subseteq \mathbb R^{K+1} \times \mathbb R\), extended by \(0\), and take a smooth \(Q\) within \(1/4\) of it there.
  2. Put \(\tilde H(x, t) = \nu(Q(x, \sigma(t)))\) on \(M \times \mathbb R\). As \(\sigma(t) \in [0,1]\), \(Q(x, \sigma(t))\) lies within \(1/4\) of a unit vector, so it is nonzero and \(\tilde H\) is smooth.
  3. Since \(\sigma(0) = 0\) and \(H(0, \cdot) = f\), \(\|f(x) - \tilde H(x, 0)\| \le 2\|Q(x, 0) - f(x)\| < \tfrac12 < 2\), and Problem 3 joins \(f\) to \(\tilde H(\cdot, 0)\). Likewise \(g\) is joined to \(\tilde H(\cdot, 1)\).
  4. \(\tilde H\) joins \(\tilde H(\cdot, 0)\) to \(\tilde H(\cdot, 1)\); symmetry and transitivity of smooth homotopy close the chain Chapter7/HomotopySmoothHomotopic.trans Chapter8/SmoothingsmoothHomotopic_of_homotopic.

Where the formal proof departs from the retelling. The retelling uses the approximation of \(H\) directly as a homotopy. Formally a homotopy must be smooth on all of \(M \times \mathbb R\), while \(Q\) is controlled only on \(M \times [0,1]\); composing with \(\sigma\) settles both points.

V8.5 Problem 5: maps into a higher sphere miss a point

Theorem. Let \(X\) be a second countable smooth manifold without boundary, modelled on a real vector space of finite dimension \(m < p\) lying in the lowest universe. Every smooth \(f : X \to S^p\) misses some point, and is smoothly homotopic to a constant map. If \(M \subseteq \mathbb R^{K+1}\) is a compact submanifold modelled on \(\mathbb R^m\), \(m < p\), every continuous map \(M \to S^p\) is homotopic to a constant. Chapter8/Smoothingexists_notMem_range_of_lt Chapter8/Smoothingexists_smoothHomotopic_const_of_lt Chapter8/Smoothingexists_homotopic_const_of_lt

The idea. A regular value of a map from a lower-dimensional manifold cannot be attained. Once a point is missed, stereographic projection from it contracts the map.

The proof as formalized.

  1. A point is missed. Brown’s theorem gives a regular value \(y\) of \(f\). If \(y = f(x)\), then \(df_x\) would map an \(m\)-dimensional space onto \(\mathbb R^p\), impossible for \(m < p\) Chapter8/Smoothingexists_notMem_range_of_lt. Brown’s theorem is stated for model spaces in a common universe, whence the universe condition.
  2. Contraction. Let \(\pi_y\) be stereographic projection from \(y\) onto the hyperplane \(y^\perp\), and \(\pi_y^{-1}\) its inverse Chapter7/Stereostereo Chapter7/StereostereoInv.
