The homotopy is \[H(x, t) = \pi_y^{-1}\big((1 - \sigma(t))\,\pi_y(f(x))\big).\] It is smooth because \(\pi_y\) is smooth away from \(y\) and \(\pi_y^{-1}\) is smooth everywhere; it lies in \(S^p\) because its argument lies in \(y^\perp\); \(H(\cdot, 0) = f\) because \(\pi_y^{-1}\pi_y = \mathrm{id}\) off \(y\); and \(H(\cdot, 1)\) is the constant \(\pi_y^{-1}(0) = -y\) Chapter8/Smoothingexists_smoothHomotopic_const_of_lt.
  3. Continuous maps. Approximate a continuous \(f\) within \(2\) by a smooth \(f'\) (Problem 4 (a)). Problem 3 makes \(f\) homotopic to \(f'\), and step 2 gives a smooth, hence continuous, homotopy from \(f'\) to a constant Chapter8/Smoothingexists_homotopic_const_of_lt.

V8.6 and V8.7 Problems 6 and 7: fixed points and antipodal pairs

Both problems rest on two facts. Points of the sphere that are not antipodal are at distance \(< 2\), by the parallelogram law \(\|a - b\|^2 + \|a + b\|^2 = 4\) Chapter8/SphereMapsnorm_sub_lt_two_of_ne_neg. And for \(n \ge 1\) smoothly homotopic self-maps of \(S^n\) have the same degree, by the homotopy invariance of §5, since \(S^n\) is connected Chapter8/SphereMapsdeg_eq_of_smoothHomotopic. The degree theory is built for smooth maps, so both problems are stated for smooth maps.

Theorem (Problem 6). For \(n \ge 1\), a smooth map \(f : S^n \to S^n\) with \(\deg f \ne (-1)^{n+1}\) has a fixed point. Chapter8/SphereMapsexists_fixedPoint_of_deg_ne

Proof. If \(f(x) \ne x\) for all \(x\), then \(f(x)\) is never antipodal to \(-x\), so \(\|f(x) - (-x)\| < 2\). Problem 3 makes \(f\) smoothly homotopic to the antipodal map, whose degree is \((-1)^{n+1}\) Chapter5/HairyBalldeg_antip.

Lemma. For \(n \ge 1\), a smooth map \(h : S^n \to S^n\) with \(h(-x) = h(x)\) for all \(x\) has even degree. Chapter8/SphereMapseven_deg_of_even_map

Proof as formalized. Take a regular value \(y\) of \(h\). The degree is the sum of the signs over the finite set \(h^{-1}(y)\); reduce it modulo \(2\). Each term is \(\pm 1 \equiv 1\), since the sign at a regular point is nonzero. As \(h\) is even, \(x \mapsto -x\) is an involution of \(h^{-1}(y)\), and it has no fixed points Chapter8/SphereMapsantip_ne. So the terms cancel in pairs, \(1 + 1 = 0\) in \(\mathbb Z/2\).

A simpler route than the retelling’s. The retelling compares the signs at \(x\) and \(-x\) through the chain rule for \(h = h \circ (-\mathrm{id})\). Parity does not need the signs, and the formal proof never compares them.

Theorem (Problem 7). For \(n \ge 1\), a smooth map \(f : S^n \to S^n\) of odd degree satisfies \(f(-x) = -f(x)\) for some \(x\). Chapter8/SphereMapsexists_antipodal_of_odd_deg

Proof as formalized. Suppose not. Then \(w(x) = f(x) + f(-x)\) never vanishes, and \(h = \nu \circ w\) is smooth and even. It is never antipodal to \(f\): if \(f(x) = -w(x)/\|w(x)\|\), then \(\langle f(x), w(x) \rangle = -\|w(x)\| < 0\), whereas \(\langle f(x), w(x) \rangle = 1 + \langle f(x), f(-x) \rangle \ge 0\) by Cauchy–Schwarz. So \(f\) and \(h\) are smoothly homotopic by Problem 3, and \(\deg f = \deg h\) is even by the lemma, a contradiction Chapter8/SphereMapsexists_antipodal_of_odd_deg.

V8.0 (i) Local zero sets of submersions are submanifolds

Lemma 1 of §2 makes a global level set \(f^{-1}(y)\) into a manifold. In Problems 8 to 11 one knows less: near each of its points the set is cut out by a function defined only near that point.

Theorem. Let \(M\) be a smooth manifold without boundary modelled on a finite-dimensional space \(E\), and let \(F\), \(Z\) be finite-dimensional with \(\dim Z + \dim F = \dim E\). Suppose that each point \(x\) of \(S \subseteq M\) has an open neighbourhood \(U\) with a map \(g : M \to F\), smooth on \(U\), such that \(S \cap U = g^{-1}(0) \cap U\) and \(dg_y\) is onto for every \(y \in S \cap U\). Then \(S\) is a submanifold, given by slice charts modelled on \(Z\) with complement \(F\). Chapter8/LocalSliceIsSliceSubmanifold.of_locally_preimage

The idea. Apply Lemma 1 to the restriction of \(g\) to \(U\), and carry the resulting slice chart back to \(M\).

The proof as formalized. The restriction of \(g\) to the open submanifold \(U\) is smooth, and \(0\) is a regular value of it, since restriction does not change derivatives Chapter6/Opensmfd_comp_subtype_val. Lemma 1 of §2 gives a slice chart of \(S \cap U = (g|_U)^{-1}(0)\) around \(x\) inside the manifold \(U\) Chapter2/LevelSetexists_sliceChart_preimage. What remains is formal but must be done: a partial diffeomorphism of \(U\) is transported to one of \(M\), with the same target, source the image of the old source, and an arbitrary value outside \(U\) Chapter8/LocalSlicePartialDiffeomorph.ofOpens. It is a slice chart for \(S\) because \(S \cap U\) is exactly the zero set of \(g\) in \(U\).

Theorem (tangent space). Let \(S \subseteq M\) carry any slice structure modelled on \(Z\), where \(\dim Z + \dim F = \dim E\). If \(x \in S\), \(g : M \to F\) is smooth on an open set \(U \ni x\), \(g = 0\) on \(S \cap U\), and \(dg_x\) is onto, then \(TS_x = \ker dg_x\), where \(TS_x\) is the image of the derivative of the inclusion. Chapter8/LocalSliceIsSliceSubmanifold.range_mfderiv_val_eq_ker

Proof. This is Lemma 2 of §2 in local form. The composite \(g \circ \iota\) vanishes near \(x\), so \(dg_x \circ d\iota_x = 0\) and \(TS_x \subseteq \ker dg_x\). As \(d\iota_x\) is injective Chapter2/LevelSetinjective_mfderiv_val, both spaces have dimension \(\dim Z = \dim E - \dim F\). Only the vanishing on \(S\) and surjectivity at \(x\) are used; an elementwise form (\(v\) is tangent iff \(dg_x v = 0\)) is also recorded Chapter8/LocalSliceIsSliceSubmanifold.mem_range_mfderiv_val_iff_of_local.

Every slice chart \(\varphi\) of a submanifold \(M\) of a vector space \(E\) supplies such a \(g\), its normal part \(a \mapsto (\varphi a)_2\): the derivative \(\mathrm{pr}_2 \circ d\varphi_a\) is onto since \(d\varphi_a\) is an isomorphism onto \(Z \times W\) Chapter8/ProdGraphsurjective_fderiv_sliceDef. The same isomorphism gives \(\dim Z + \dim W = \dim E\) as soon as \(M\) is nonempty Chapter8/ProdGraphIsSliceSubmanifold.finrank_add, so the tangent-space theorem applies: \(TM_x = \ker(\mathrm{pr}_2 \circ d\varphi_x)\) for every slice chart \(\varphi\) at \(x\) Chapter8/ProdGraphrange_mfd_val_eq_ker_sliceChart.

V8.8 and V8.9 Problems 8 and 9: products and graphs

In Problems 8 to 10, \(M \subseteq E_1\) and \(N \subseteq E_2\) are submanifolds of finite-dimensional real normed spaces, given by slice charts modelled on \(Z_1\), \(Z_2\) with complements \(W_1\), \(W_2\), all finite-dimensional (a few lemmas need less). Tangent spaces are the images of the derivatives of the inclusions.

Theorem (Problem 8). \(M \times N \subseteq E_1 \times E_2\) is a submanifold modelled on \(Z_1 \times Z_2\) with complement \(W_1 \times W_2\), and \(T(M \times N)_{(x,y)} = TM_x \times TN_y\). Chapter8/ProdGraphisSliceSubmanifold_prod Chapter8/ProdGraphrange_mfd_val_prod

Proof as formalized. Near \((x, y)\), for slice charts \(\varphi_1\) at \(x\) and \(\varphi_2\) at \(y\), the set \(M \times N\) is the zero set of \((a, b) \mapsto ((\varphi_1 a)_2, (\varphi_2 b)_2)\) on the product of the chart domains. The derivative of this map is \(D_1 \times D_2\), with \(D_i = \mathrm{pr}_2 \circ d\varphi_i\), and it is onto Chapter8/ProdGraphprodDef_eq_zero_iff Chapter8/ProdGraphsurjective_mfderiv_prodDef. The criterion gives the manifold structure, and the tangent space is \(\ker(D_1 \times D_2) = \ker D_1 \times \ker D_2 = TM_x \times TN_y\). No parametrization of \(M \times N\) is ever built.

Theorem (Problem 9). For a smooth map \(f : M \to N\), the graph \(\Gamma = \{(x, f(x))\} \subseteq E_1 \times E_2\) is a submanifold modelled on \(Z_1\) with complement \(W_1 \times E_2\), and \(T\Gamma_{(x, f(x))}\) is the image of \(u \mapsto (d\iota_x u,\ d\iota_{f(x)}\, df_x u)\), that is, the graph of \(df_x\). Chapter8/ProdGraphisSliceSubmanifold_graph Chapter8/ProdGraphrange_mfd_val_graph

Proof as formalized.

  1. Extending \(f\). For a slice chart \(\varphi\) of \(M\) at \(x\), with induced chart \(\psi\) of \(M\), put \(\tilde f(a) = f(\psi^{-1}((\varphi a)_1))\) on the open set of those \(a \in \operatorname{dom}\varphi\) for which \((\varphi a)_1\) lies in the image of \(\psi\). It is smooth and extends \(f\) Chapter8/ProdGraphgraphExt Chapter8/ProdGraphcontDiffOn_graphExt Chapter8/ProdGraphgraphExt_val.
  2. Defining function. Near \((x, f(x))\), \(\Gamma\) is the zero set of \((a, b) \mapsto ((\varphi a)_2,\ b - \tilde f(a))\), whose derivative \((v, w) \mapsto ((d\varphi\, v)_2,\ w - d\tilde f\, v)\) is onto Chapter8/ProdGraphgraphDef_eq_zero_iff Chapter8/ProdGraphsurjective_mfderiv_graphDef.
  3. Tangent space. The kernel is \(\{(v, w) : v \in TM_x,\ w = d\tilde f_x v\}\), and differentiating \(\tilde f \circ \iota_M = \iota_N \circ f\) near \(x\) gives \(d\tilde f_x \circ d\iota_x = d\iota_{f(x)} \circ df_x\) Chapter8/ProdGraphrange_mfd_val_graph.

Where the retelling shows that \(x \mapsto (x, f(x))\) is a diffeomorphism onto \(\Gamma\), the formal proof reads structure and tangent space off one defining function.

V8.10 Problem 10: the tangent bundle and \(df\)

Let \(M \subseteq E\) be modelled on \(Z\) with complement \(W\), and \(TM = \{(x, v) \in E \times E : x \in M,\ v \in TM_x\}\) Chapter8/TangentBundletangentBundleSet.

A definitional point comes first. \(TM_x\) is a subspace of \(E\), while \(df_x\) acts on the model space \(Z\). So the formal \(df\) first writes \(v \in TM_x\) in chart coordinates, as the vector \(u\) with \(d\iota_x u = v\) (unique, since \(d\iota_x\) is injective, and chosen), and then sets \(df(x, v) = (f(x),\ d\iota_{f(x)}\, df_x u)\) Chapter8/TangentBundletangentCoord Chapter8/TangentBundletangentMap.

Theorem. (a) \(TM\) is a submanifold of \(E \times E\) modelled on \(Z \times Z\) with complement \(W \times W\), of dimension \(2 \dim M\) Chapter8/TangentBundleisSliceSubmanifold_tangentBundle. (b) For smooth \(f : M \to N\), the map \(df : TM \to TN\) is smooth Chapter8/TangentBundlecontMDiff_tangentMap. (c) \(d(\mathrm{id}) = \mathrm{id}\), a statement without hypotheses, and \(d(g \circ f) = dg \circ df\) for smooth \(f : M \to N\) and \(g : N \to P\) Chapter8/TangentBundletangentMap_id Chapter8/TangentBundletangentMap_comp.

The idea. Locally, \(TM\) is cut out by the normal parts of \(a\) and of \(d\varphi_a v\); and \(df\) is locally the restriction of the differential of a smooth extension of \(f\).

Proof of (a). For a slice chart \(\varphi\), put \(g(a, v) = ((\varphi a)_2, (d\varphi_a v)_2)\) on \(\operatorname{dom}\varphi \times E\). For \(a \in M\), \(TM_a = \ker(\mathrm{pr}_2 \circ d\varphi_a)\), so \(TM\) is the zero set of \(g\) there Chapter8/TangentBundlesliceChart_mem_tangentSpace_iff. The derivative is \[dg_{(a,v)}(u, w) = \big((d\varphi_a u)_2,\ (d\varphi_a w)_2 + (d^2\varphi_a(u, v))_2\big),\] and it is onto: choose \(u\) for the first component, then \(w\) to correct the second, since \(\mathrm{pr}_2 \circ d\varphi_a\) is onto Chapter8/TangentBundlesliceChart_surjective_snd. The criterion applies.

Proof of (b). Near \((x_0, v_0)\), use the slice chart \(\varphi\) that defines the chart \(\psi\) of \(M\) at \(x_0\), and the smooth extension \(\rho(a) = f(\psi^{-1}((\varphi a)_1))\) of \(f\) to an open subset of \(E\). For \(b \in M\) near \(x_0\) and \(w = d\iota_b u \in TM_b\), differentiating \(\rho \circ \iota_M = \iota_N \circ f\) gives \(d\rho_b w = d\iota_{f(b)}\, df_b u\). So near \((x_0, v_0)\), \(df\) is the restriction to \(TM\) of the smooth map \((a, w) \mapsto (\rho(a), d\rho_a w)\), and it is smooth as a map into the manifold \(TN\) Chapter8/TangentBundlecontMDiff_tangentMap.

Proof of (c). The identity rule is \(d\iota_x u = v\). The composition rule is the chain rule \(d(g \circ f)_x = dg_{f(x)} \circ df_x\), together with the fact that the chart coordinates of \(d\iota_{f(x)}(df_x u)\) are \(df_x u\) Chapter8/TangentBundletangentCoord_mfd_val.

V8.11 Problem 11: the normal bundle and the ε-neighbourhood

Let \(M \subseteq \mathbb R^k\) be a submanifold given by slice charts modelled on \(\mathbb R^m\) with complement \(\mathbb R^w\), and \[E = \{(x, v) \in \mathbb R^k \times \mathbb R^k : x \in M,\ v \perp TM_x\}\] Chapter8/NormalBundlenormalBundleSet. For compact nonempty \(M \subseteq \mathbb R^{K+1}\), Part IV provides a radius \(\varepsilon_0 > 0\) and a map \(r : \mathbb R^{K+1} \to M\) with \(\|y - r(y)\| = \operatorname{dist}(y, M)\) for all \(y\) and \(r = \mathrm{id}\) on \(M\); on \(N_{\varepsilon_0} = \{y : \operatorname{dist}(y, M) < \varepsilon_0\}\) the nearest point is unique, \(r\) is smooth, and \(y - r(y) \perp TM_{r(y)}\) Chapter6/Tubular4tubr_spec.

Theorem. (a) If \(m + w = k\), then \(E\) is a submanifold of \(\mathbb R^k \times \mathbb R^k\) modelled on \(\mathbb R^k\), with complement \(\mathbb R^w \times \mathbb R^m\). (b) If \(M \subseteq \mathbb R^{K+1}\) is compact and nonempty and \(m + w = K + 1\), there is \(\varepsilon > 0\) such that \((x, v) \mapsto x + v\) is a diffeomorphism from the open subset \(\{(x, v) \in E : \|v\| < \varepsilon\}\) of \(E\) onto \(N_\varepsilon = \{y : \operatorname{dist}(y, M) < \varepsilon\}\). Chapter8/NormalBundleisSliceSubmanifold_normalBundle Chapter8/NormalBundleexists_normalTube_diffeomorph

The idea. Locally, \(E\) is cut out by the normal coordinates of \(x\) and the tangential components of \(v\). The sum map has invertible derivative along the zero section, compactness makes it injective on a uniformly thin tube, and the nearest-point map inverts it.

Proof of (a). Near \(p \in M\) let \(\varphi\) be the chosen slice chart at \(p\), \(\phi(z) = \varphi^{-1}(z, 0)\) the local parametrization, and \(B(a) = (d\phi_{(\varphi a)_1})^*\) the adjoint of its derivative, a map \(\mathbb R^k \to \mathbb R^m\) Chapter8/NormalBundleB. Then \(E\) is locally the zero set of \(g(a, v) = ((\varphi a)_2,\ B(a)v)\): the first component cuts out \(M\), and since \(TM_a\) is the image of \(d\phi\), \(v \perp TM_a\) if and only if \(B(a) v = 0\) Chapter8/NormalBundleg Chapter8/NormalBundlemem_normalBundleSet_iff. The adjoint \(B(a)\) is onto: \(\langle B(a)\, d\phi\, y, y \rangle = \|d\phi\, y\|^2\) and \(d\phi\) is injective, so \(B(a) \circ d\phi\) is an injective, hence bijective, endomorphism of \(\mathbb R^m\) Chapter8/NormalBundlesurjective_B. So \(dg(u, h) = ((d\varphi_a u)_2,\ B(a)h + (dB_a u)v)\) is onto, and the criterion applies Chapter8/NormalBundlesurjective_fderiv_g.

Proof of (b), as formalized.

  1. Invertible derivative on the zero section. By the kernel theorem, \(TE_{(x,0)} = \ker dg_{(x,0)}\), the pairs \((u, h)\) with \(u \in TM_x\) and \(h \perp TM_x\) (the term \((dB_a u)v\) vanishes at \(v = 0\)). The sum map \(S(x, v) = x + v\) has derivative \((u, h) \mapsto u + h\), and \(u + h = 0\) forces \(\|u\|^2 = -\langle h, u \rangle = 0\) Chapter8/NormalBundleinjective_mfd_normalSum. So \(dS_{(x,0)}\) is invertible.
  2. Local injectivity. The inverse function theorem on the \(k\)-manifold \(E\) gives \(r_x > 0\) such that \(S\) is injective on \(\{(a, v) \in E : \|a - x\| < r_x,\ \|v\| < r_x\}\) Chapter8/NormalBundleexists_radius_normalSum_injective.
  3. Uniform injectivity. Cover \(M\) by finitely many balls \(B(x_i, r_{x_i}/2)\), a nonempty family since \(M \ne \emptyset\), and let \(\varepsilon_1 = \min_i r_{x_i}/4\). If \(a + v = b + w\) with \(\|v\|, \|w\| < \varepsilon_1\) and \(\|a - x_i\| < r_{x_i}/2\), then \(\|b - x_i\| \le \|a - x_i\| + \|v\| + \|w\| < r_{x_i}\): both points lie in the injectivity neighbourhood of \((x_i, 0)\) and coincide Chapter8/NormalBundleexists_eps_normalSum_injective.
  4. The radius is \(\varepsilon = \min(\varepsilon_1, \varepsilon_0)\) Chapter8/NormalBundlenormalε.
  5. \(r(x + v) = x\). Let \((x, v) \in E\), \(\|v\| < \varepsilon\), \(y = x + v\). Then \(\operatorname{dist}(y, M) \le \|v\| < \varepsilon_0\), so \((r(y), y - r(y)) \in E\) with \(\|y - r(y)\| = \operatorname{dist}(y, M) < \varepsilon\). This point and \((x, v)\) have the same sum, so they coincide by step 3 Chapter8/NormalBundlenormalRetraction_eq.
  6. The diffeomorphism. \(S\) maps the tube into \(N_\varepsilon\), since \(\operatorname{dist}(x + v, M) \le \|v\|\). The inverse is \(y \mapsto (r(y), y - r(y))\), a smooth map into \(E\) because \(r\) is smooth; one composite is the identity trivially, the other by step 5 Chapter8/NormalBundleexists_diffeomorph_normalε.

What the book leaves implicit. The injectivity radius must be made uniform (step 3). The formal statement also assumes \(M \ne \emptyset\), because the radius of Part IV and the minimum over the finite cover need it; for empty \(M\) the claim is trivial, but that case is not treated. Note the logical order: \(r(x + v) = x\) is not an input from Part IV, which gives it only for small multiples \(sv\), \(s\) near \(0\) Chapter6/Tubular4tubr_spec; it is a consequence of injectivity Chapter8/NormalBundlenormalRetraction_eq.

V8.12 Problem 12: the retraction, and maps into \(M\)

Let \(M \subseteq \mathbb R^{K+1}\) be compact and nonempty, with \(r\), \(\varepsilon_0\) and \(\varepsilon\) as in Problem 11.

Theorem (the nearest point). If \(m + w = K + 1\) and \((x, v) \in E\) with \(\|v\| < \varepsilon\), then \(r(x + v) = x\), and \(\|(x + v) - x\| < \|(x + v) - z\|\) for every \(z \in M\) other than \(x\). Chapter8/NearestnormalRetraction_nearest

Proof. The first half is step 5 above. For the second, put \(y = x + v \in N_{\varepsilon_0}\): a point \(z \ne r(y) = x\) of \(M\) as close to \(y\) as \(x\) would be a second nearest point, which Part IV excludes on \(N_{\varepsilon_0}\) Chapter8/Retractiontubr_dist_lt.

To use \(r\) as a map into \(M\), the formal proof checks that it is smooth into the manifold \(M\): smoothness into \(\mathbb R^{K+1}\) on the open set \(N_{\varepsilon_0}\) passes to \(M\) by corestriction Chapter8/RetractioncontMDiffAt_tubr.

Theorem (Problem 12, approximation). Let \(X \subseteq \mathbb R^{L+1}\) and \(M \subseteq \mathbb R^{K+1}\) be compact submanifolds given by slice charts, with \(M\) nonempty. Every continuous \(G : X \to M\) is a uniform limit of smooth maps, and two smooth maps \(X \to M\) that are homotopic are smoothly homotopic. Chapter8/Retractionexists_smooth_approx_mfld Chapter8/RetractionsmoothHomotopic_of_homotopic_mfld

The idea. Repeat Problem 4 with \(r\) in place of \(\nu\); the nearest-point property replaces the normalization estimate.

The proof as formalized.

  1. Approximation. With \(\delta = \min(\varepsilon/2, \varepsilon_0)\) take a smooth \(Q\) within \(\delta\) of \(G\) on \(X\). Then \(Q(X) \subseteq N_{\varepsilon_0}\), so \(f = r \circ Q\) is smooth. As \(G(x) \in M\), the nearest-point property gives \(\|r(Q) - Q\| \le \|G - Q\|\), so \(\|f - G\| \le 2\|Q - G\| < \varepsilon\) Chapter8/Retractionnorm_sub_tubr_le.
  2. Nearby maps. If smooth \(f, g : X \to M\) satisfy \(\|f - g\| < \varepsilon_0\), the path \(c(x, t) = (1 - \sigma(t)) f(x) + \sigma(t) g(x)\) stays within \(\|f(x) - g(x)\|\) of \(f(x) \in M\), hence in \(N_{\varepsilon_0}\), and \(r \circ c\) is a smooth homotopy from \(r \circ f = f\) to \(r \circ g = g\). This step does not need \(X\) compact Chapter8/RetractionsmoothHomotopic_of_dist_lt_mfld.
  3. Homotopies. Approximate a homotopy on \(X \times [0,1]\) within \(\varepsilon_0/4\) by a smooth \(Q\), and put \(\tilde H(x, t) = r(Q(x, \sigma(t)))\). Its ends are within \(\varepsilon_0/2\) of \(f\) and \(g\); step 2 and transitivity finish, as in Problem 4 Chapter8/RetractionsmoothHomotopic_of_homotopic_mfld.

What the formalization taught us

  • Hidden hypotheses. Problem 1 needs \(N\) compact, so that \(\deg g\) is defined; the formal statement also asks \(P\) to be Hausdorff Chapter8/DegCompdeg_comp. The formal statements of Problem 11 (b) and of Problem 12 assume \(M\) nonempty, as the tubular radius of Part IV requires; the trivial empty case is left out Chapter8/NormalBundleexists_eps_normalSum_injective Chapter8/Retractionexists_smooth_approx_mfld.
  • Deviations. Problems 6 and 7 are stated for smooth maps, for which the degree is built Chapter8/SphereMapsexists_fixedPoint_of_deg_ne. Problem 2 is stated for \(\deg P \ge 1\), where the extension by \(\hat P(\infty) = \infty\) is continuous Chapter8/PolyDegdeg_polyMap.
  • Universes. The degree and Brown’s theorem are stated for model spaces in a common universe, a harmless side condition in Problems 1 and 5 Chapter8/Smoothingexists_notMem_range_of_lt.
  • One criterion, four constructions. Products, graphs, tangent and normal bundles are all local zero sets of submersions. One criterion yields their manifold structures, and its companion, the kernel theorem, the tangent spaces that are needed: those of products and graphs, and that of the normal bundle along the zero section. Beyond Lemma 1 of §2, the criterion costs only the transport of charts from an open subset to the ambient manifold Chapter8/LocalSlicePartialDiffeomorph.ofOpens Chapter8/LocalSliceIsSliceSubmanifold.range_mfderiv_val_eq_ker.
  • Taming time. Homotopies are smooth maps on \(X \times \mathbb R\), so every straight-line homotopy is reparametrized by a smooth step, which keeps the approximations where they are controlled Chapter8/SmoothingsmoothHomotopic_of_homotopic.
  • Parity without signs. Even maps have even degree by a count modulo \(2\), with no comparison of signs Chapter8/SphereMapseven_deg_of_even_map.
  • A different logical order in Problem 11. Uniform injectivity of \(x + v\) on a thin tube is proved by compactness, and \(r(x + v) = x\) is derived from it Chapter8/NormalBundlenormalRetraction_eq.
  • One approximation theorem. Stone–Weierstrass for restrictions of smooth functions, on any compact subset of a finite-dimensional space, serves Problems 4, 5 and 12 alike Chapter8/Approxexists_contDiff_approx_of_isCompact.
← Part VII. The Hopf theorem (Milnor §7, end)Part IX. Orientation tools and linking numbers (Milnor §8, Problem 13) →

Part IX. Orientation tools and linking numbers (Milnor §8, Problem 13)

Problem 13 asks three things about the linking number \(l(M,N)\) of disjoint compact oriented manifolds in \(\mathbb R^{k+1}\). It asks for the symmetry law \(l(N,M) = (-1)^{(m+1)(n+1)}\,l(M,N)\), for the vanishing of \(l(M,N)\) when \(M\) bounds away from \(N\), and for a definition when the manifolds lie in the sphere \(S^{m+n+1}\). The problem leaves its conventions implicit: how \(M\times N\) is oriented (the book uses product orientations without fixing one), which orientation \(S^k\) carries (elsewhere the book orients spheres as boundaries of disks), and what “bounds” means. The last request also hides a theorem with an unstated hypothesis. The formal proof first builds four tools, V8.0 (ii)–(v) of the verified edition: product orientations, orientations given by a complementary frame, local degrees for maps whose relevant preimages are compact, and some genericity facts. Problem 13 uses the first two and the last. The third serves the Hopf invariant of Part X.

Map.

  • Chapter8/OrientProd: product orientations, block maps, the swap sign \((-1)^{mn}\), relabelling along equal dimensions.
  • Chapter8/OrientFrame: “frame first” orientations; two orientations of a connected manifold agree or are opposite; Milnor’s orientation of \(S^n\).
  • Chapter8/ProperDegree: finiteness, local constancy and homotopy invariance of the signed count when only preimages are compact.
  • Chapter8/Generic: small images are meagre; the off-diagonal of \(S^p\times S^p\) is connected; local constancy on a dense set.
  • Chapter8/Linking: the linking number, its symmetry, its vanishing when the first manifold bounds.
  • Chapter8/LinkingDefs: stereographic projection, rotations, the linking number after a rotation.
  • Chapter8/LinkingSphere: admissible rotations exist, and for positive dimensions the choice does not matter.

V8.0 (ii) Product orientations and the sign of the swap

Proposition. Let \(E, F\) be real vector spaces of dimensions \(m, n\), oriented by \(a, b\).

  1. There is an orientation \(a\times b\) of \(E\times F\) for which \((e_1,0),\dots,(e_m,0),(0,f_1),\dots,(0,f_n)\) is positive whenever \(e\) is a positive basis of \(E\) and \(f\) one of \(F\).
  2. Let \(E', F'\) have dimensions \(m, n\) and orientations \(a', b'\). If \(T(v,w) = (Av,\ Cv + Bw)\) for linear maps \(A : E\to E'\), \(B : F\to F'\), \(C: E\to F'\), then \(\operatorname{sign} T = \operatorname{sign} A\cdot\operatorname{sign} B\), relative to \(a\times b\) and \(a'\times b'\).
  3. The swap \((v,w)\mapsto(w,v)\) has sign \((-1)^{mn}\) from \(a\times b\) to \(b\times a\).

Let \(M, N\) be smooth manifolds modelled on \(E, F\) (boundary allowed), with orientations \(o_M, o_N\). Then \((x,y)\mapsto o_M(x)\times o_N(y)\) is an orientation of \(M\times N\). Let \(\varphi: M\to M'\) and \(\psi: N\to N'\) be maps into oriented smooth manifolds of dimensions \(m, n\), differentiable at \(x\) and at \(y\). Then the sign of \(\varphi\times\psi\) at \((x,y)\) is the product of their signs. The swap \(M\times N\to N\times M\) has sign \((-1)^{mn}\) everywhere.

The idea. Evaluate every form on a concatenated basis. Everything then reduces to the determinant of a block-triangular matrix, and for the swap to the sign of one permutation.

The proof as formalized. Write \((e,f)\) for the concatenated basis of \(E\times F\) Chapter8/OrientProdprodBasis, and let \(\varepsilon_e(a)\) be \(+1\) if \(e\) is \(a\)-positive and \(-1\) otherwise. The product orientation is defined as the class of \(\varepsilon_{e_0}(a)\,\varepsilon_{f_0}(b)\,\det_{(e_0,f_0)}\) for fixed reference bases \(e_0, f_0\) Chapter8/OrientProdorProdGen. Other bases \(e,f\) give the same class. A family whose first \(m\) vectors are \((\alpha_j,\gamma_j)\) and whose last \(n\) are \((0,\beta_j)\) has \(\det_{(e,f)} = \det_e\alpha\cdot\det_f\beta\). Hence \(\det_{(e_0,f_0)} = \det_{e_0}(e)\det_{f_0}(f)\det_{(e,f)}\), while \(\varepsilon_{e_0}(a)\det_{e_0}(e)\,\varepsilon_e(a) > 0\) Chapter8/OrientProdprodBasis_det_apply Chapter8/OrientProdorEpsB_mul_det_mul_pos Chapter8/OrientProdrayOfNeZero_prodBasis. For positive \(e, f\) the representative is \(\det_{(e,f)}\) itself, which is statement 1 Chapter8/OrientProdorProdGen_eq. For statement 2, \(T\) maps the concatenated reference basis to a block-triangular family, so the quantity whose sign is \(\operatorname{sign}T\) factors into those for \(A\) and \(B\) Chapter8/OrientProdorSign_prod_triangular Chapter8/OrientProdorSign_prodMap.

The swap sends \((e,f)\) to \((f,e)\) composed with the block permutation of \(m+n\) letters that moves the first \(m\) letters behind the last \(n\). The formal proof identifies this permutation with the \(n\)-th power of the cyclic shift of \(m+n\) letters, whose sign is \((-1)^{m+n-1}\). Its sign is therefore \((-1)^{n(m+n-1)} = (-1)^{mn}\), since \(n(n-1)\) is even Chapter8/OrientProdfinCongr_trans_finAddFlip Chapter8/OrientProdsign_finCongr_trans_finAddFlip Chapter8/OrientProdorSign_swap.

On manifolds, the chart of \(M\times N\) at \((x,y)\) is the product of the charts, so its derivative is a product map. By statement 2, the continuity condition for \(o_M\times o_N\) is then the product of the conditions for \(o_M\) and \(o_N\) Chapter8/OrientProdOrient.prod. The derivative of \(\varphi\times\psi\) is \(d\varphi\times d\psi\), and that of the swap is the linear swap Chapter8/OrientProdsignAt_prodMap Chapter8/OrientProdsignAt_swap.

What the formal proof has to make explicit. An orientation is indexed by its dimension. One of \(E\times F\) has index \(m+n\), one of \(F\times E\) has index \(n+m\), and these are the same number written differently. So \(b\times a\) is relabelled along \(n+m = m+n\) before the two are compared Chapter8/OrientProdOrient.cast. Relabelling both orientations never changes a sign Chapter8/OrientProdorSign_reindex_finCongr Chapter8/OrientProdsignAt_cast.

V8.0 (iii) Frame orientations and Milnor’s orientation of the sphere

Milnor orients a boundary by putting the outward normal first. The formal text makes this one construction, used here for the sphere and in Part X for preimages of regular values.

Construction. Let \(S\) be a smooth manifold without boundary modelled on a space \(Z\) of dimension \(d\). Let \(E\) be a space of dimension \(d+k\), oriented by \(o\), and let \(\Omega\) be a fixed volume form representing \(o\). Let \(\iota: S\to E\) be smooth and \(\nu = (\nu_1,\dots,\nu_k) : S\to E^k\) continuous, such that for every \(q\) the \(d\)-form \(z\mapsto\Omega(\nu_1(q),\dots,\nu_k(q),\,d\iota_q z_1,\dots,d\iota_q z_d)\) on \(Z\) is nonzero. Calling \(z\) positive when this number is positive defines an orientation of \(S\).

Sign formula. Let \((S,\iota,\nu,\Omega)\) and \((S',\kappa,\mu,\Omega')\) be two such data of dimension \(d\), and let \(f: S\to S'\). Then the sign of \(f\) at \(q\) is \(\operatorname{sgn}\bigl(\Omega'(\mu(f(q)),\,d\kappa\,df_q e)\cdot\Omega(\nu(q),\,d\iota_q e)\bigr)\) for every \(d\)-tuple \(e\) in \(Z\) with \(\Omega(\nu(q), d\iota_q e)\neq 0\). The statement also assumes \(f\) differentiable at \(q\), but does not use it.

Theorem. On a preconnected manifold, two orientations either agree at every point or are opposite at every point.

The sphere. Let \(O_n\) be the frame orientation of \(S^n\) given by the inclusion into \(\mathbb R^{n+1}\), the standard orientation of \(\mathbb R^{n+1}\) and the frame \(\nu(q) = q\). Let \(O^5_n\) be the orientation of \(S^n\) built in Chapter 5. If \(n > 0\), then \(O_n = \pm O^5_n\), and the antipodal map has degree \((-1)^{n+1}\) for \(O_n\).

The idea. Read in one chart, the frame form is a continuous, nowhere vanishing family of \(d\)-forms on the fixed space \(Z\). These forms make up a line, so the family keeps its sign. On the sphere, \(T_qS^n = q^\perp\), so \(q\) is a complementary frame.

The proof as formalized.

  1. Forms. The tuple \((\nu_1,\dots,\nu_k,w_1,\dots,w_d)\) and the form \(w\mapsto\Omega(\nu,w)\) are built by inserting one frame vector at a time Chapter8/OrientFrameframeTuple Chapter8/OrientFrameframeCurry. Along a linear map \(T: Z\to E\), the frame orientation of \(Z\) is the one represented by the pulled-back form, or an arbitrary default when that form vanishes Chapter8/OrientFrameframeForm Chapter8/OrientFrameframeOr. All positive volume forms of \(E\) give the same orientation Chapter8/OrientFrameframeOr_eq. The form is nonzero on \(z\) whenever \((\nu, Tz)\) is linearly independent Chapter8/OrientFrameframeForm_apply_ne_zero_of_linearIndependent.
  2. Continuity. Fix \(q_0\), the chart \(c_0\) at \(q_0\), and \(\psi = \iota\circ c_0^{-1}\). By the chain rule, the frame form at \(q\) is the pull-back along \((dc_0)_q\) of \(\Phi(q) = \Omega\bigl(\nu(q),\,d\psi_{c_0(q)}\,\cdot\,\bigr)\), a \(d\)-form on \(Z\). On a fixed basis \(u_0\) of \(Z\), the value \(\Phi(q)(u_0)\) is continuous in \(q\), because top-degree forms, \(\nu\) and \(d\psi\) are all continuous Chapter8/OrientFramecontinuous_alternatingMap_of_finrank. Near \(q_0\) it keeps the sign of \(\Phi(q_0)(u_0)\neq 0\), so \(\Phi(q) = c\,\Phi(q_0)\) with \(c>0\). The chart has derivative the identity at \(q_0\). So \((dc_0)_q\) carries the orientation at \(q\) to the one at \(q_0\) with sign \(\operatorname{sgn}(c^{-1}) = 1\) Chapter8/OrientFrameOrient.ofFrame_cont Chapter8/OrientFrameOrient.ofFrame. The sign formula is the definition of the sign, unwound Chapter8/OrientFramesignAt_ofFrame.
  3. Two orientations. At each point, two orientations agree or are opposite. By the continuity condition for both, each of these two sets is open, so on a preconnected space one of them is everything Chapter8/OrientFrameOrient.eq_or_eq_neg.
  4. The sphere. With one frame vector, the frame form is Chapter 5’s contraction Chapter8/OrientFrameframeForm_one. Let \(G(x) = |x|^2-1\). Then \(d\iota_q\) is injective with image in \(\ker dG_q\), and \(dG_q(q) = 2\neq 0\). So by Chapter 5’s contraction lemma the frame \((q)\) is complementary everywhere Chapter5/LevelOrientcontractForm_basis_ne_zero Chapter8/OrientFramesph_frameForm_ne_zero. This defines \(O_n\) Chapter8/OrientFramestdOrE Chapter8/OrientFramesphOrStd. For \(n>0\) the sphere is connected, and step 3 gives \(O_n = \pm O^5_n\) Chapter8/OrientFramesphOrStd_eq_or_neg. In the \(+\) case the antipodal degree is Chapter 5’s value. In the \(-\) case source and target are both reversed, and no sign changes Chapter5/HairyBalldeg_antip Chapter8/OrientFramedeg_antip_std.

Why a second orientation of the sphere. Chapter 5 oriented \(S^n\) as the level set \(\{G = 0\}\). It contracted the orientation of an unspecified reference basis \(e\) of \(\mathbb R^{n+1}\) with \(-\sum_i dG(e_i)\,e_i\), a vector on which \(dG\) is negative Chapter5/HairyBallsphOr Chapter5/LevelOrientoutward. That vector points into the ball. So \(O^5_n\) is the boundary orientation of the exterior \(\{|x|\ge 1\}\), relative to an orientation of \(\mathbb R^{n+1}\) that the formal text never identifies. The degree of a map of the sphere to itself does not notice this. Linking numbers do: reversing the orientation of \(S^k\) reverses the sign at every point Chapter6/LevelZerosignAt_neg_right, hence every linking number, and with it the Hopf invariant of Part X. So linking numbers use \(O_k\), and the two orientations are related only up to sign.

V8.0 (iv) Local degrees when only preimages are compact

Chapter 5 studied the signed count \(\deg_y f = \sum_{x\in f^{-1}(y)}\operatorname{sign} df_x\) for compact \(M\). The Hopf invariant of Part X is a signed count for a map defined only on an open subset of \(S\times S\). The old proofs used compactness of \(M\) only through certain preimages, and the results below assume only that.

Theorem. Let \(M, N\) be smooth manifolds without boundary, modelled on spaces of the same finite dimension \(n\) that lie in a common universe, Hausdorff and oriented. Let \(f: M\to N\) be smooth and \(y\) a regular value of \(f\).

  1. If \(f^{-1}(y)\) is compact, it is finite. For this, \(M\) Hausdorff and \(N\) with closed points suffice, and no orientation is needed.

  2. Suppose \(f^{-1}(V)\) is compact for some neighbourhood \(V\) of \(y\), not necessarily closed. Then every \(y'\) near \(y\) is a regular value, and \(\deg_{y'} f = \deg_y f\).

  3. Let \(M\) also be second countable and \(F: M\times\mathbb R\to N\) smooth, with \(y\) a regular value of \(f_0 = F(\cdot,0)\) and of \(f_1 = F(\cdot,1)\). Suppose \(\{(x,t): F(x,t)\in V,\ 0\le t\le 1\}\) is compact for some neighbourhood \(V\) of \(y\). Then \(\deg_y f_0 = \deg_y f_1\).

The idea. Replace \(M\) by \(f^{-1}(V)\) in the old proofs. For (c), first find a value that is regular for the homotopy itself.

The proof as formalized.

  1. Finiteness. By the inverse function theorem, \(f\) is injective near each point of the fibre. Finitely many such neighbourhoods cover the compact fibre, and each contains no point of the fibre except its centre Chapter8/ProperDegreeIsRegularValue.finite_preimage_of_isCompact.
  2. Local constancy. This is Chapter 1’s argument with one change Chapter1/RegularValueIsRegularValue.eventually_finsum_preimage_eq. Around each point \(x\) of the finite fibre, take a local inverse \(L_x\) and an open \(U_x\ni x\) in its image. The \(U_x\) are pairwise disjoint, and a given weight \(\varphi\), locally constant near the fibre, is constant on each. Chapter 1 removed the closed set \(f(M\setminus\bigcup_x U_x)\). Here \(C = f(f^{-1}(V)\setminus\bigcup_x U_x)\) is compact, hence closed, and it misses \(y\). Take \(y'\in\operatorname{int}V\cap\bigcap_x L_x^{-1}(U_x)\) outside \(C\). Then every preimage of \(y'\) lies in some \(U_x\) and is regular, and \(x\mapsto L_x(y')\) is a bijection \(f^{-1}(y)\to f^{-1}(y')\) preserving \(\varphi\) Chapter8/ProperDegreeIsRegularValue.eventually_isRegularValue_and_finsum_preimage_eq_of_isCompact. The sign of \(df\) is such a weight Chapter5/Orienteventually_signAt_eq Chapter8/ProperDegreeIsRegularValue.eventually_degAt_eq_of_isCompact.
  3. A regular value of the homotopy. If \(y\) is also a regular value of \(F\), the cylinder argument of Chapter 5 Chapter5/HomotopyInvdegAt_eq_of_homotopy_of_isRegularValue is repeated, not invoked, with the compactness hypothesis in place of compactness of \(M\). Lemma 1 of §5 is applied to the region \(\{g\ge 0\}\) for \(g(x,t) = t(1-t)\), and \(\{F = y,\ g\ge0\}\), which is \(\{F = y,\ 0 \le t \le 1\}\), is compact by hypothesis Chapter5/LemmaOnelemmaOne_ambient. Since \(dg = (1-2t)\,dt\), the boundary signs are \(\operatorname{sign}(df_0)_x\) at \(t=0\) and \(-\operatorname{sign}(df_1)_x\) at \(t=1\). The end fibres are finite by step 1, because the slices at \(t = 0, 1\) are compact Chapter8/ProperDegreeisCompact_preimage_slice_of_isCompact Chapter8/ProperDegreedegAt_eq_of_homotopy_of_isRegularValue_of_isCompact'.
  4. Regularity only over \([0,1]\). Suppose \(F\) is regular only at points of \(F^{-1}(y)\) with \(0\le t\le 1\). Reparametrize time by \(\tau(t) = (1-\cos\pi t)/2\), which takes values in \([0,1]\), with \(\tau(0) = 0\), \(\tau(1) = 1\) and \(\tau'(t) = \tfrac\pi2\sin\pi t\). Then \(y\) is a regular value of \(\Phi(x,t) = F(x,\tau(t))\) everywhere. Where \(\sin\pi t\neq 0\), \(d\Phi\) has the image of \(dF\). Where \(\sin\pi t = 0\), \(\tau(t)\in\{0,1\}\), and horizontal vectors already reach everything because the end maps are regular. Compactness for \(\Phi\) follows from that for \(F\) Chapter8/ProperDegreedegAt_eq_of_homotopy_of_isRegularValue_of_isCompact.
  5. The general case. Step 2 for \(f_0\) and \(f_1\) gives an open \(U\ni y\) inside \(V\) on which both end maps are regular with constant signed counts. Since \(M\times\mathbb R\) is second countable, Brown’s theorem gives \(y'\in U\) regular for \(F\) Chapter2/Browndense_regularValues. The set \(\{F = y',\ 0\le t\le 1\}\) is closed in the compact set of the hypothesis, and step 4 at \(y'\) finishes Chapter8/ProperDegreedegAt_eq_of_homotopy_of_isCompact.

The value \(y'\) of step 5 is regular for the whole homotopy, so step 3 would already suffice there. The reparametrization proves more than this chain uses.

V8.0 (v) Genericity: small images, the off-diagonal, local constancy

Proposition. Let \(P, N\) be manifolds modelled on real normed spaces \(E, F\), with \(E\) finite-dimensional and \(\dim P<\dim N\).

  1. For any map \(g: P\to N\), no point of \(g(P)\) is a regular value. Here boundary is allowed.

  2. Let now \(P\) and \(N\) be smooth and without boundary, \(F\) finite-dimensional, \(E\) and \(F\) in a common universe, and \(P\) second countable. If \(g\) is smooth, \(N\setminus g(P)\) is dense. If \(g\) is only smooth on an open set \(U\subseteq P\), then \(N\setminus g(U)\) is dense; if moreover \(N\) is Hausdorff, then \(g(K)\) is closed and nowhere dense for every compact \(K\subseteq U\), and \(g(U)\) is meagre.

  3. For \(p\ge 1\), the set \(\{(a,b)\in S^p\times S^p : a\neq b\}\) is connected.

  4. Let \(S\) be a preconnected subset of a topological space, and \(R\) a set with \(S\subseteq\overline{R\cap S}\). Suppose every \(x\in S\) has a neighbourhood \(V\) such that \(\varphi\) is constant on \(V\cap R\cap S\). Then \(\varphi\) is constant on \(R\cap S\).

  5. In a Baire space, every nonempty open set contains points outside any given meagre set.

The proof as formalized. For (a), \(dg_x\) maps a space of smaller dimension and cannot be onto Chapter8/Genericnot_isRegularValue_of_finrank_lt. For (b), the regular values are dense by Brown’s theorem, and by (a) they avoid the image Chapter8/Genericdense_compl_range_of_finrank_lt. For \(g\) smooth on \(U\), apply this to the open submanifold \(U\) Chapter8/GenericGeneric.dense_compl_image_of_finrank_lt. The image of a compact \(K\subseteq U\) is compact, hence closed, with empty interior Chapter8/GenericisNowhereDense_image_of_finrank_lt. Being locally compact and second countable, \(U\) is a countable union of compact sets, so \(g(U)\) is a countable union of closed nowhere dense sets Chapter8/GenericisMeagre_image_of_finrank_lt.

For (c), the antipodal pairs \((c,-c)\) form a connected set off the diagonal, the image of the connected sphere. A pair \((a,b)\) with \(a\neq b\) is joined to \((a,-a)\) by \[t\mapsto\Bigl(a,\ \frac{(1-t)\,b - t\,a}{|(1-t)\,b - t\,a|}\Bigr),\qquad 0\le t\le 1.\] The vector \((1-t)b-ta\) vanishes only if \(|1-t| = |t|\), which forces \(t = \tfrac12\) and \(b = a\). If its normalization were \(a\), comparing norms in \((1-t)\,b = (t + |(1-t)b-ta|)\,a\) would again force \(b = a\) Chapter8/GenericisConnected_offDiag_sph.

For (d), let \(\psi(x)\) be the common value of \(\varphi\) on \(V_x\cap R\cap S\), which is nonempty by density. Then \(\psi = \varphi\) on \(R\cap S\), and \(\psi\) is locally constant on \(S\): for \(x'\) near \(x\), a point of \(V_{x'}\cap\operatorname{int}V_x\cap R\cap S\) shows \(\psi(x') = \psi(x)\). The formal proof gives the set of values the discrete topology, so that local constancy becomes continuity Chapter8/Genericeq_of_locallyConst_on_dense. Part (e) is Baire’s theorem Chapter8/Genericexists_mem_open_not_mem_of_isMeagre. Parts (c) and (d) serve the Hopf invariant in Part X, and (b) and (e) are used below.

V8.13 Problem 13: the linking number

The definition

Let \(A, B\) be smooth manifolds without boundary modelled on \(\mathbb R^a\) and \(\mathbb R^b\), oriented by \(o_A, o_B\). Let \(k = a+b\) and \(\alpha: A\to\mathbb R^{k+1}\), \(\beta: B\to\mathbb R^{k+1}\). The linking map is \[\lambda_{\alpha,\beta}(x,y) = \frac{\alpha(x)-\beta(y)}{|\alpha(x)-\beta(y)|}\in S^k.\] Normalization sends \(0\) to a fixed base point, so \(\lambda_{\alpha,\beta}\) is defined everywhere Chapter6/Regionnv0 Chapter8/LinkinglinkMap Chapter8/LinkinglinkMap_val. It is smooth when \(\alpha, \beta\) are smooth with \(\alpha(x)\neq\beta(y)\) for all \(x, y\) Chapter8/LinkingcontMDiff_linkMap. The linking number \(l(\alpha,\beta)\) is the degree of \(\lambda_{\alpha,\beta}\). Here \(A\times B\) carries the product orientation, relabelled from index \(a+b\) to index \(k\), and \(S^k\) carries \(O_k\), its orientation as the boundary of the disk Chapter8/LinkinglinkingNumber. Milnor’s disjoint \(M, N\subseteq\mathbb R^{k+1}\) are the case of inclusions. Allowing maps costs nothing, and the sphere part needs it.

Symmetry

Theorem. Let \(A, B\) be as above, and in addition compact, Hausdorff and second countable. Let \(k = a+b>0\), and let \(\alpha,\beta\) be smooth with \(\alpha(x)\neq\beta(y)\) for all \(x, y\). Then \[l(\beta,\alpha) = (-1)^{(a+1)(b+1)}\,l(\alpha,\beta).\]

The idea. \(\lambda_{\beta,\alpha}\) is the swap, followed by \(\lambda_{\alpha,\beta}\), followed by the antipodal map. The swap has sign \((-1)^{ab}\), the antipodal map has sign \((-1)^{k+1}\), and \(ab + k + 1 = (a+1)(b+1)\). This is the expected proof.

The proof as formalized. The identity \(\lambda_{\beta,\alpha}(y,x) = -\lambda_{\alpha,\beta}(x,y)\) is immediate Chapter8/LinkinglinkMap_swap. The swap \(B\times A\to A\times B\) has sign \((-1)^{ab}\) for the relabelled product orientations. The relabelling \(a+b\to k\) of \(A\times B\) is split as \(a+b\to b+a\to k\); the common step \(b+a\to k\) is then removed from both sides, and what remains is the swap sign of V8.0 (ii) Chapter8/Linkingorient_cast_cast Chapter8/LinkingsignAt_swap_cast. The antipodal map has sign \((-1)^{k+1}\) at every point for \(O_k\). This is Chapter 5’s value for \(O^5_k\), carried over by \(O_k = \pm O^5_k\), which needs \(k>0\) Chapter5/HairyBallsignAt_antip Chapter8/LinkingsignAt_antip_std. Brown’s theorem gives a regular value \(z\) of \(\lambda_{\alpha,\beta}\). Then \(-z\) is a regular value of \(\lambda_{\beta,\alpha}\), since by the chain rule the sign at each of its preimages is a product of three nonzero signs. Composing on either side with a bijection of constant sign \(\sigma\) multiplies the signed count by \(\sigma\) Chapter6/ComposedegAt_comp_bij' Chapter6/ComposedegAt_comp_bij_left. Hence \(\deg\lambda_{\beta,\alpha} = (-1)^{ab}(-1)^{k+1}\deg\lambda_{\alpha,\beta}\) for any orientations of \(A\times B\) and \(B\times A\) related by a swap of sign \((-1)^{ab}\) Chapter8/Linkingdeg_linkMap_swap Chapter8/LinkinglinkingNumber_symm.

Hidden hypothesis. The condition \(k>0\) is used twice. The degree may be computed at any regular value only when the target is connected, and \(S^0\) is not. The comparison of \(O_k\) with \(O^5_k\) also runs through connectedness.

Bounding

Milnor’s hypothesis “\(M\) bounds an oriented manifold \(X\) disjoint from \(N\)” is taken in the ambient form that the formal text uses for manifolds with boundary throughout.

Theorem. Let \(B\) be a smooth manifold without boundary modelled on \(\mathbb R^b\), compact, Hausdorff, second countable and oriented. Let \(W\) be a smooth manifold without boundary modelled on \(\mathbb R^{a+1}\), Hausdorff, second countable and oriented. Let \(g: W\to\mathbb R\) be smooth, with \(0\) a regular value and \(X = \{g\ge 0\}\) compact. Let \(k = a+b>0\), and let \(\bar\alpha: W\to\mathbb R^{k+1}\) and \(\beta: B\to\mathbb R^{k+1}\) be smooth with \(\bar\alpha(w)\neq\beta(y)\) whenever \(g(w)\ge 0\). Give \(A = g^{-1}(0)\) its submanifold structure and the boundary orientation, outward vector first. Then \(l(\bar\alpha|_A,\beta) = 0\).

The idea. The linking map extends over \(X\times B\), a compact region in \(W\times B\) with boundary \(A\times B = \{G = 0\}\), where \(G(w,y) = g(w)\). A map that extends over a compact region has degree \(0\) on its boundary. What must be checked is that the boundary orientation of \(A\times B\) inside \(W\times B\) is the product orientation.

The linear algebra. Let \(E_1, F, Z_1, Z\) have dimensions \(m+1, n, m, m+n\), with orientations \(o_E\) of \(E_1\) and \(o_F\) of \(F\). Let \(l\) be a linear form on \(E_1\), let \(T : Z_1\to E_1\) be injective with image in \(\ker l\), and let \(l(\nu)<0\). Let \(S: Z\to E_1\times F\) have image \(\{v : l(v_1) = 0\}\), let \(l(\nu^P_1) <0\), and let \(S\circ D = T\times\mathrm{id}_F\). Then \(D\) carries (the contraction of \(o_E\) by \(\nu\) along \(T\)) \(\times\,o_F\) to the contraction of the relabelled \(o_E\times o_F\) by \(\nu^P\) along \(S\), with sign \(+1\). Indeed \(\nu^P = c\,(\nu,0) + St\) with \(c = l(\nu^P_1)/l(\nu)>0\), and \(St\), lying in the image of \(S\), contributes nothing Chapter6/SignLemmascontractForm_eq_smul. On the concatenated basis, the target form is evaluated on the block-triangular family \(((\nu,0), (Tu_i,0), (0,f_j))\). The two forms then differ by \(c\) times squares of signs Chapter8/Linkingmul_orEpsB_pos Chapter8/LinkingorSign_contractOr_prod.

The proof as formalized.

  1. \(A\) is compact, being closed in \(X\), and \(S^{a+b}\) is connected Chapter8/LinkinglinkingNumber_eq_zero_of_bounds.
  2. \(P = W\times B\) carries the product orientation, relabelled to index \(a+b+1\). It is also transferred to the model \(\mathbb R^{a+1}\times\mathbb R^b\). Mathlib’s product of two models equals the model of the product space without being identical to it, and the level-set results are stated for the latter Chapter8/LinkingOrient.ofEqModel. The function \(G = g\circ\mathrm{pr}_1\) has \(0\) as a regular value, and \(L = G^{-1}(0)\) gets the boundary orientation Chapter6/LevelOrientMlevelOrientM.
  3. The bijection \(\varphi: A\times B\to L\), \(\varphi(w,y) = (w,y)\), is smooth, and \(d\iota_L\circ d\varphi = d\iota_A\times\mathrm{id}\). The linear algebra with \(l = dg_w\) gives \(\operatorname{sign}\varphi = +1\) everywhere Chapter8/LinkingorSign_contractOr_prod.
  4. The map \(\lambda(w,y) = (\bar\alpha(w)-\beta(y))/|\bar\alpha(w)-\beta(y)|\) is smooth on the open set \(U = \{\bar\alpha(w)\neq\beta(y)\}\), which contains \(X\times B\). The regular values of \(\lambda|_U\) are dense by Brown’s theorem. Those of the linking map of \(A\times B\) are open and dense, since \(A\times B\) is compact. The sphere is a Baire space, so the two sets share a point \(e\) Chapter6/RegularOpendense_isOpen_regularValues Chapter6/RegularOpenexists_mem_of_dense_of_isOpen.
  5. At \(x\in L\) with \(\lambda(x) = e\), both \(\lambda\) and \(\lambda|_L\) are regular: the former because \(x\in U\), the latter by the chain rule through \(\varphi\). So the kernel line of \(d\lambda_x\) is transverse to \(L\) Chapter6/LevelZeroexists_mfd_eq_zero_of_isRegularPoint_level. The set \(\{\lambda = e\}\cap(X\times B)\) is compact.
  6. Lemma 1 of §5, in its boundary form for a map smooth on an open set containing the level set, gives \(\deg_e(\lambda|_L) = 0\) Chapter6/LevelZerodegAt_level_eq_zero_of_opens. Transported along \(\varphi\), which has sign \(+1\), this is \(\deg_e\) of the linking map of \(A\times B\), that is, \(l(\bar\alpha|_A,\beta)\) Chapter6/LevelMapdegAt_comp_bij Chapter8/Linkingorient_cast_self.

V8.13′ Problem 13: linking numbers in the sphere

Milnor’s last sentence, “Define the linking number for disjoint manifolds in the sphere \(S^{m+n+1}\)”, asks for a definition. The natural one projects stereographically from a point off both manifolds. This defines something only if the result does not depend on the point, and that is a theorem.

The definition

Stereographic projection from the north pole \(N = e_{k+1}\) of \(S^{k+1}\subseteq\mathbb R^{k+2}\) is \[\operatorname{st}(x) = \frac{(x_0,\dots,x_k)}{1-x_{k+1}}\in\mathbb R^{k+1},\] Chapter 7’s projection onto the equatorial hyperplane, read in coordinates Chapter8/LinkingDefsstN Chapter8/LinkingDefsι_stN. It is injective on \(S^{k+1}\setminus\{N\}\) and smooth where \(x_{k+1}\neq 1\) Chapter8/LinkingDefsstN_injOn Chapter8/LinkingDefscontDiffAt_stN. A rotation is a linear isometry of \(\mathbb R^{k+2}\) with positive determinant Chapter8/LinkingDefsIsRotation. For \(\alpha: A\to S^{k+1}\), \(\beta: B\to S^{k+1}\) and a linear isometry \(R\), set \(l_R(\alpha,\beta) = l(\operatorname{st}\circ R\circ\alpha,\ \operatorname{st}\circ R\circ\beta)\) Chapter8/LinkingDefslinkingNumberRot. Whenever \(R\alpha\) and \(R\beta\) avoid \(N\), the projected maps are smooth, and disjoint when \(\alpha,\beta\) are Chapter8/LinkingDefscontMDiff_stN_comp Chapter8/LinkingDefsstN_comp_disjoint. Call a rotation \(R\) admissible if \(R\alpha\) and \(R\beta\) avoid \(N\). Finally, \(l_{\mathrm{sph}}(\alpha,\beta)\) is \(l_R\) for a chosen rotation \(R\) with \(R\alpha(x)\neq N\) and \(R\beta(y)\neq N\) for all pairs \((x,y)\), and \(0\) if there is none Chapter8/LinkingSpherelinkingNumberSph.

Theorem. Let \(A, B\) be smooth manifolds without boundary modelled on \(\mathbb R^a\) and \(\mathbb R^b\), second countable, with \(a,b\ge 1\) and \(k = a+b\). Let \(\alpha: A\to S^{k+1}\) and \(\beta: B\to S^{k+1}\) be smooth.

  1. There is a rotation \(R\) with \(R\alpha(x)\neq N\) and \(R\beta(y)\neq N\) for every pair \((x,y)\in A\times B\).

  2. Suppose moreover that \(A, B\) are compact, Hausdorff and oriented, and that \(\alpha(x)\neq\beta(y)\) for all \(x, y\). Then \(l_{\mathrm{sph}}(\alpha,\beta) = l_R(\alpha,\beta)\) for every rotation \(R\) with \(R\alpha(x)\neq N\) and \(R\beta(y)\neq N\) for every pair \((x,y)\in A\times B\).

When \(A\) and \(B\) are nonempty, the condition on \(R\) in (a) and (b) says that \(R\) is admissible.

The idea. An admissible rotation carries a point \(q\) off both images to the north pole. Which rotation does so is irrelevant, by linear algebra. Moving \(q\) continuously while keeping it off both images changes \(l_R\) only by a homotopy. Two admissible points can be joined through a common point \(w\) by two great-circle arcs that avoid both images, provided the bad choices of \(w\) form a meagre set. This is where \(a,b\ge 1\) enters.

The proof as formalized.

  1. Existence. By V8.0 (v), \(\alpha(A)\cup\beta(B)\) is meagre, since \(a, b<k+1\). So some \(q\) avoids it, and a planar rotation carries \(q\) to \(N\) Chapter7/Rotationexists_rotation_path Chapter8/LinkingSphereexists_admissible_rotation. The hypotheses \(a, b\ge 1\) appear in this statement but are not needed: \(a, b<k+1\) already follows from \(a+b = k\).
  2. Linear maps of positive determinant. Let \(\det T>0\). Then \(\lambda_{T\alpha,T\beta} = h\circ\lambda_{\alpha,\beta}\) with \(h(u) = Tu/|Tu|\), a bijection of \(S^k\) Chapter8/LinkingSpherebijective_nv0_linear. Its sign is \(\operatorname{sgn}\det T = +1\) at every point. Chapter 6 proved this for \(O^5_k\), and it carries over to \(O_k\) Chapter6/RadialsignAt_nv0_linear Chapter8/LinkingSpheresignAt_nv0_linear_std. Hence \(l(T\alpha,T\beta) = l(\alpha,\beta)\) for maps \(\alpha,\beta\) into \(\mathbb R^{k+1}\) as in V8.13, when \(k>0\) Chapter8/LinkingSpherelinkingNumber_comp_linear.
  3. Rotations fixing the north pole. Let \(Q\) be a rotation with \(QN = N\). It preserves the last coordinate, since \(\langle Qx,N\rangle = \langle Qx,QN\rangle = \langle x,N\rangle\). So \(\operatorname{st}(Qx) = T_Q(\operatorname{st}x)\), where \(T_Q\) is the block of \(Q\) on the first \(k+1\) coordinates Chapter8/LinkingSpherestN_map_of_fix. The last column of \(Q\) is \(e_{k+1}\), and Laplace expansion along it gives \(\det T_Q = \det Q>0\) Chapter8/LinkingSpheredet_restrictN. By step 2, \(l_{Q\circ R} = l_R\) for every linear isometry \(R\), rotation or not, with \(R\alpha\) and \(R\beta\) avoiding \(N\) Chapter8/LinkingSpherelinkingNumberRot_trans_of_fix.
  4. Families of rotations. Let \(S_t\) be linear isometries depending smoothly on \(t\), with \(S_t\alpha\) and \(S_t\beta\) avoiding \(N\) for \(0\le t\le 1\). A formal homotopy is defined for all \(t\in\mathbb R\), so time is reparametrized by a smooth transition function \(\rho\) with values in \([0,1]\), \(\rho(0) = 0\) and \(\rho(1) = 1\). The linking maps of \(\operatorname{st}\circ S_{\rho(t)}\circ\alpha\) and \(\operatorname{st}\circ S_{\rho(t)}\circ\beta\) then form a smooth homotopy on \(A\times B\times\mathbb R\). Homotopy invariance of the degree (Milnor’s Theorem B of §5) gives \(l_{S_0} = l_{S_1}\) Chapter5/Degreedeg_eq_of_homotopy Chapter8/LinkingSpherelinkingNumberRot_eq_of_family.
  5. Arcs and bad midpoints. For unit vectors \(q\) and \(w\neq -q\), one has \(w = \cos\theta\,q + \sin\theta\,v\) with \(v\) a unit vector orthogonal to \(q\) and \(0\le\theta<\pi\) Chapter8/LinkingSphereexists_arc. Suppose a point \(c\neq q\) lies on the arc \(s\mapsto\cos s\,q+\sin s\,v\), \(0\le s\le\theta\). Then \(c - rq = \mu w\) for \(\mu = \sin s/\sin\theta>0\) and \(r = \cos s-\mu\cos\theta\), so \(w = (c-rq)/|c-rq|\) Chapter8/LinkingSpherearc_avoid. Geometrically, and this picture is not formalized, a point \(c\neq\pm q\) thus spoils only the open half great circle from \(q\) through \(c\) to \(-q\). For a smooth \(\gamma: X\to S^{k+1}\), the spoiled points form the “cone”, the image of the open set \(\{\gamma(x)\neq rq\}\subseteq X\times\mathbb R\) under \((x,r)\mapsto(\gamma(x)-rq)/|\gamma(x)-rq|\). If \(\dim X+1<k+1\), the cone is meagre Chapter8/LinkingSphereisMeagre_cone. For \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) this condition reads \(a<k\) and \(b<k\), that is, \(b\ge 1\) and \(a\ge 1\). Given \(q, q'\) on the sphere, Baire’s theorem gives \(w\neq -q, -q'\) outside the four cones of \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) seen from \(q\) and from \(q'\) Chapter8/LinkingSphereisMeagre_singleton_sph Chapter8/LinkingSphereexists_good_point.
  6. One leg. Let \(R\) be admissible and \(q = R^{-1}N\), and choose \(w\) as in step 5. Put \(S_t = R\circ\operatorname{rot}_{q,v}(-t\theta)\), where \(\operatorname{rot}_{q,v}\) rotates the plane of \(q\) and \(v\) Chapter7/RotationrotCLM Chapter8/LinkingSphererotLIE. Then \(S_t(c) = N\) exactly when \(c = \cos(t\theta)\,q+\sin(t\theta)\,v\), a point of the arc. No point of \(\alpha(A)\cup\beta(B)\) lies there: such a point differs from \(q\) because \(R\) is admissible, and step 5 excludes the rest of the arc. So step 4 applies. The rotation \(S_1\) is admissible, sends \(w\) to \(N\), and has \(l_{S_1} = l_R\) Chapter8/LinkingSphereisRotation_rotLIE Chapter8/LinkingSphereexists_leg.
  7. Independence. Let \(R, R'\) be admissible, and take \(w\) good for \(q = R^{-1}N\) and \(q' = R'^{-1}N\). The two legs give admissible rotations \(S, S'\) with \(Sw = S'w = N\), \(l_R = l_S\) and \(l_{R'} = l_{S'}\). Then \(Q = S\circ S'^{-1}\) is a rotation fixing \(N\) with \(S = Q\circ S'\), so step 3 gives \(l_S = l_{S'}\) Chapter8/LinkingSphereisRotation_trans Chapter8/LinkingSphereisRotation_symm Chapter8/LinkingSpherelinkingNumberRot_eq_of_admissible.
  8. The chosen rotation. The condition in the definition of \(l_{\mathrm{sph}}\) quantifies over pairs \((x,y)\), so it says nothing when \(A\) or \(B\) is empty. That case is treated separately: both sides are degrees of a map from the empty manifold, hence \(0\). Otherwise the chosen rotation is admissible, and step 7 applies Chapter8/LinkingSpherelinkingNumber_of_isEmpty Chapter8/LinkingSpherelinkingNumberSph_eq.

Why both dimensions must be positive

The formal text states the following example as a remark and does not formalize it. Let \(a = 0\) and \(b = k\ge 1\). Let \(A\) be a point mapped to \(p\), and let \(\beta\) be the inclusion of a great \(k\)-sphere \(\Sigma\subseteq S^{k+1}\) not through \(p\). Projection from \(q\notin\Sigma\cup\{p\}\) carries \(\Sigma\) to a round sphere \(\Sigma'\subseteq\mathbb R^{k+1}\). It sends the hemisphere containing \(q\) to the unbounded side of \(\Sigma'\) and the other hemisphere to the ball. A point inside \(\Sigma'\) has linking number \(\pm1\) with it, and a point outside has linking number \(0\). So \(l_R = 0\) when \(R^{-1}N\) lies on the same side of \(\Sigma\) as \(p\), and \(l_R = \pm1\) otherwise. In the proof, the cone of \(\Sigma\) has dimension \(b+1 = k+1\) and is not meagre: a projection point cannot pass from one side of \(\Sigma\) to the other without crossing it.

What the formalization taught us

  • Dimensions are indices. Orientations carry their dimension as an index, so \(m+n\), \(n+m\) and \(k\) are matched by explicit relabelling, as are the product of two models and the model of a product. No sign changes, but every statement about products has to say so Chapter8/OrientProdsignAt_cast Chapter8/LinkingOrient.ofEqModel.
  • Milnor’s orientation of the sphere had to be built. Chapter 5’s orientation is the boundary orientation of the exterior of the ball, relative to an unspecified basis. Degrees of maps of the sphere to itself cannot see this, but linking numbers can. They use the frame orientation, related to the old one only up to sign Chapter8/OrientFramesphOrStd Chapter8/OrientFramesphOrStd_eq_or_neg.
  • Compact preimages suffice. Local constancy and homotopy invariance of the signed count need compactness only of \(f^{-1}(V)\), or of the part of \(F^{-1}(V)\) over \([0,1]\) Chapter8/ProperDegreeIsRegularValue.eventually_degAt_eq_of_isCompact Chapter8/ProperDegreedegAt_eq_of_homotopy_of_isCompact.
  • \(k>0\) for linking numbers. For \(k = 0\) the target \(S^0\) of the linking map is disconnected Chapter8/Linkingdeg_linkMap_swap.
  • The boundary orientation of a product is the product orientation, when the normal and the bounding factor both come first. No sign appears, but the check is a genuine computation Chapter8/LinkingorSign_contractOr_prod.
  • Positive dimensions in the sphere. Independence of the rotation fails for a point and a great sphere, by an example that is not formalized. The proof uses \(a,b\ge 1\) exactly to make the cones meagre, and existence of admissible rotations does not need it Chapter8/LinkingSphereisMeagre_cone Chapter8/LinkingSphereexists_admissible_rotation.
  • Conventions of the formal definitions. Homotopies are maps on \(X\times\mathbb R\), so a family that is admissible only for \(t\in[0,1]\) must be reparametrized. The linking number in the sphere is \(0\) when no rotation satisfies its admissibility clause, and that clause is vacuous when one manifold is empty Chapter8/LinkingSpherelinkingNumberRot_eq_of_family Chapter8/LinkingSpherelinkingNumberSph_eq.
← Part VIII. Problems 1–12: degrees, approximation and bundles (Milnor §8)Part X. The Hopf invariant (Milnor §8, Problems 14–15) →

Part X. The Hopf invariant (Milnor §8, Problems 14–15)

Problem 14 asks for three properties of the linking number of two fibres of a map \(f : S^{2p-1} \to S^p\); Problem 15 asks for three consequences. The formal proof organizes all six around one observation. For maps \(g, f\) into \(S^p\), the linking number of \(g^{-1}(y)\) and \(f^{-1}(z)\) is a local degree: the local degree at \(((y,z),e)\) of the map \(\Phi(x,x') = ((g(x), f(x')), \lambda(x,x'))\), defined on pairs of distinct points of \(S^{2p-1}\) away from a projection point, where \(\lambda\) is the direction between the stereographic images of \(x\) and \(x'\) Chapter8/LinkDegreedegAt_phiR_eq_linkingNumberRot. Local degrees survive homotopies whose preimages stay in a compact region, and they behave well under composition. Everything else is a matter of choosing the right homotopies. On the way the formalization has to fix how a fibre is oriented, compare two signs through a block determinant, supply a compactness argument the book leaves unsaid, and add a hypothesis to the natural two-map version of a). And when everything is computed with the book’s conventions, the Hopf fibration turns out to have Hopf invariant \(-1\), not \(+1\).

Conventions. Throughout, \(p = d+1\) with \(d \ge 1\) (so \(p \ge 2\)), and \(S\) denotes \(S^{2d+1} = S^{2p-1}\). Spheres \(S^n \subset \mathbb R^{n+1}\) carry Milnor’s orientation as boundaries of disks, outward normal first: a basis \(\zeta\) of \(T_qS^n\) is positive iff \(\det(q, \zeta_1, \dots, \zeta_n) > 0\) Chapter8/OrientFramesphOrStd Chapter8/HopfSignorientation_eq_sphOrStd_iff. For compact oriented \(A^a\), \(B^b\) and maps \(\alpha, \beta\) into \(\mathbb R^{k+1}\) with disjoint images, \(k = a+b\), the linking number is the degree of \(\lambda(x,y) = (\alpha(x)-\beta(y))/\|\alpha(x)-\beta(y)\|\) on \(A \times B\) with the product orientation Chapter8/LinkinglinkMap Chapter8/LinkinglinkingNumber. In a sphere \(S^{k+1}\) one first applies a rotation \(R\) (a linear isometry of positive determinant) that keeps the north pole \(\mathbf n = e_{k+1}\) off both images, then projects by \(\mathrm{st}(x) = (x_0, \dots, x_k)/(1-x_{k+1})\); call the result \(l_R\) Chapter8/LinkingDefsstN Chapter8/LinkingDefslinkingNumberRot. The linking number in the sphere is \(l_R\) for a chosen admissible \(R\), and \(0\) if none exists; by V8.13′ the choice does not matter when \(a, b \ge 1\) and the images are disjoint Chapter8/LinkingSpherelinkingNumberSph Chapter8/LinkingSpherelinkingNumberSph_eq. For a map \(\Phi\) between oriented manifolds of equal dimension, \(\operatorname{sign}_x\Phi\) is the sign of \(d\Phi_x\) (\(0\) if singular) and \(\deg_w\Phi = \sum_{x \in \Phi^{-1}(w)} \operatorname{sign}_x\Phi\).

Map of the part.

  1. PreimOrient: the orientation of the fibre \(f^{-1}(y)\) of a map between spheres, frame first, with its chart-level description.
  2. LinkAlg: the block-determinant lemma comparing the sign of \((x,x') \mapsto ((Dx, D'x'), L(x,x'))\) with the sign of \(L\) on the kernels.
  3. LinkDegree: the domain \(D_R\) and the map \(\Phi\); linking number \(=\) local degree; homotopy invariance (the engine).
  4. HopfInvariant: the linking number of two fibres, transport, moves, Problem 14 a), b), c), and the definition of \(H\).
  5. HopfMap: the Hopf fibration as a quadratic map, Milnor’s formula, regularity, two fibres and the pair realizing a direction.
  6. HopfSign: the fibres over \((\pm1,0,0)\) have linking number \(-1\).
  7. HopfComp: the local composition formula and its consequence for fibres of \(g \circ f\).
  8. HopfProps: Problem 15 (odd \(p\), compositions, \(H(\pi) = -1\)).

V8.0 (iii) Orienting the fibre of a regular value

Milnor says the fibres “can be oriented as in §5”. In §5 the fibre \(A = F^{-1}(y)\) was a curve. A tangent vector \(v_1\) of \(A\) is positive when, completed by \(v_2, \dots\) to a positive basis of the ambient tangent space, the vectors \(v_2, \dots\) are carried by \(dF\) to a positive basis of the target. So the tangent vector comes first and lifts of a positive basis come after. For a \(d\)-dimensional fibre of a map with \(p\)-dimensional target, the natural generalization lists the \(d\) tangent vectors first. The formalization lists them last.

Definition (fibre orientation). Let \(f : S^{d+p} \to S^p\) be smooth, \(y\) a regular value, and \(e = (e_1, \dots, e_p)\) a positive basis of \(T_yS^p\), read in the chart \(c_y\) of \(S^p\) at \(y\). The fibre \(N = f^{-1}(y)\) is a \(d\)-dimensional submanifold given by slice charts Chapter8/PreimOrientisSliceSubmanifold_preim. Let \(\tilde F(z) = c_y(f(z/|z|))\) be the radial extension of the chart expression of \(f\), let \(A = d\tilde F_x\), and let \(v_i(x) = A^*(AA^*)^{-1}e_i\). A basis \(w\) of \(T_xN\) is positive iff \((x, v_1(x), \dots, v_p(x), w_1, \dots, w_d)\), with the \(w_j\) read in \(\mathbb R^{d+p+1}\), is a positive basis of \(\mathbb R^{d+p+1}\) Chapter8/PreimOrientsphExt Chapter8/PreimOrientsphPullFrame Chapter8/PreimOrientpreimOr.

Proposition. (i) For any vectors \(u_1, \dots, u_p\) tangent to \(S^{d+p}\) at \(x\) with \(df_x(u_i) = e_i\): \(w\) is positive iff \((u_1, \dots, u_p, w_1, \dots, w_d)\) is positive for the orientation of \(S^{d+p}\) Chapter8/PreimOrientpreimOr_or_eq. (ii) Two positive bases \(e, e'\) of \(T_yS^p\) give the same orientation Chapter8/PreimOrientpreimOr_eq_of_orientation_eq.

So the formal convention is “lifts first, tangent vectors last” Chapter8/PreimOrientpreimOr_or_eq. The comparison with §5 is not a formal lemma but a count: the §5-style convention differs by moving \(p\) vectors past \(d\) vectors, a factor \((-1)^{dp}\). In the Hopf setting \(d = p-1\), so \(dp = (p-1)p\) is even and the two conventions agree; there the fibres are oriented “as in §5” literally.

The idea: an ambient frame. An orientation of a manifold in the formal library is an orientation of each chart space, varying continuously. The general device that produces one takes a smooth map \(\iota\) into a vector space \(E\) and a continuous family of frames \(\nu(q)\) such that the form \(z \mapsto \Omega(\nu(q), d\iota\,z)\) never vanishes (so \(\iota\) is an immersion and the frames are complementary), and declares \(z\) positive iff \(\Omega(\nu(q), d\iota\,z) > 0\) for a positive volume form \(\Omega\) of \(E\). Continuity is proved once, by a chart argument Chapter8/OrientFrameOrient.ofFrame. The sphere itself is oriented this way, with the one-vector frame \((q)\); the fibre uses the frame \((x, v_1(x), \dots, v_p(x))\) Chapter8/PreimOrientpreimFrame. Chapter 7’s Pontryagin framing would have been the obvious candidate, but it is set up for ambient manifolds presented with a different normal model than the formal sphere, a mismatch of presentation rather than of mathematics. The explicit extension \(\tilde F\) takes the place of its tubular retraction.

The proof as formalized.

  1. The extension. \(\tilde F\) is smooth near every point of \(N\). By the chain rule, \(A \circ d\iota_x = df_x\), where \(\iota\) is the inclusion of the sphere Chapter8/PreimOrientsphExtDer_comp_mfd_val. Since \(\tilde F\) is constant along rays, \(Ax = 0\) Chapter8/PreimOrientsphExtDer_self, and \(A\) is onto because \(df_x\) is Chapter8/PreimOrientsurjective_sphExtDer.
  2. The frame. The vector \(v_i = A^*(AA^*)^{-1}e_i\) satisfies \(Av_i = e_i\) and lies in \(\operatorname{im}A^* = (\ker A)^\perp\), so it is orthogonal to \(x\), hence tangent to the sphere Chapter8/PreimOrientsphExtDer_sphPullFrame Chapter8/PreimOrientinner_sphPullFrame. It is continuous along \(N\) (indeed smooth near it), since inversion is smooth on invertible operators Chapter8/PreimOrientcontinuous_sphPullFrame.
  3. Reduction to the sphere. Write \(v_i = d\iota(c_i)\). For any lifts \(u\) we have \(df_x(c_i - u_i) = 0\), so \(c_i - u_i\) is tangent to \(N\). An alternating form in \(d+p\) arguments vanishes when \(d+1\) of them lie in the \(d\)-dimensional space \(T_xN\). Hence the \(d\)-form \(w \mapsto \Omega(x, c, w)\) on \(T_xN\) does not change when \(c\) is replaced by \(u\). This is (i) Chapter8/PreimOrientapply_vecCons_frameTuple_eq_zero Chapter8/PreimOrientframeForm_congr_frame Chapter8/PreimOrientframeForm_preimFrame.
  4. Nondegeneracy. The family \((u, w)\) is linearly independent when \(df_x u\) is independent and \(w\) is a basis of \(\ker df_x\). So the form never vanishes, which is what the frame device needs Chapter8/PreimOrientlinearIndependent_frameTuple Chapter8/PreimOrientframeForm_lift_ne_zero.
  5. Independence of \(e\). Two bases with the same orientation are joined by a path of bases (Chapter 7’s path-connectedness of the positive-determinant group). Along the lifted path, the form evaluated on a fixed basis of \(T_xN\) is continuous and never zero, so by the intermediate value theorem it keeps its sign. The two forms are therefore positive multiples of each other Chapter8/PreimOrientexists_pos_frameForm_lift.

Linear algebra for V8.14: the block determinant

The sign of \(\Phi\) at a pair of fibre points must be compared with the sign of the linking map there. This is pure linear algebra.

Lemma (two fibres). Let \(V\) have dimension \(d+p\) with orientations \(o_V, o_V'\), let \(F\) have dimension \(p\) with orientations \(o_F, o_F'\), let \(G\) be oriented of dimension \(k = 2d\), and let \(Z, Z'\) have dimension \(d\). Let \(D, D' : V \to F\) be linear, let \(\iota : Z \to V\) and \(\iota' : Z' \to V\) be injective with \(\operatorname{im}\iota = \ker D\) and \(\operatorname{im}\iota' = \ker D'\), and let \(u, u' \in V^p\) be such that \(Du\) is a positive basis for \(o_F\) and \(D'u'\) one for \(o_F'\). Orient \(Z\) frame first (\(z\) positive iff \((u, \iota z)\) is positive for \(o_V\)), and \(Z'\) likewise with \(u'\) and \(o'_V\). Then for every linear \(L : V \times V \to G\), \[\operatorname{sign}\bigl[(x,x') \mapsto ((Dx, D'x'), L(x,x'))\bigr] = (-1)^{dp}\,\operatorname{sign}\bigl[L \circ (\iota \times \iota')\bigr],\] the left side relative to \(o_V \times o_V'\) and \((o_F \times o_F') \times o_G\), the right side relative to the product of the two frame orientations and \(o_G\) Chapter8/LinkDegreeorSign_pair_preimage₂. The special case \(o_V = o_V'\), \(o_F = o_F'\) is also proved on its own Chapter8/LinkAlgorSign_pair_preimage.

The idea. In the bases \((u, \iota z)\) and \((u', \iota' z')\) the matrix is block triangular with identity blocks on the frames. The only sign comes from reordering \((u, \iota z, u', \iota' z')\) into \((u, u', \iota z, \iota' z')\), which moves \(p\) vectors past \(d\). So the number \((-1)^{dp}\) turns up again, for a different reason than in the fibre convention, and again it is \(+1\) when \(p = d+1\).

The proof as formalized.

  1. Frame orientation and positive bases. \((u, \iota z)\) is a basis, and it is positive for \(o_V\) iff \(z\) is positive for the frame orientation Chapter8/LinkAlglinearIndependent_frameTuple Chapter8/LinkAlgframeOr_basis_iff. Signs are computed in arbitrary bases as the sign of (orientation sign of source basis) \(\times\) (orientation sign of target basis) \(\times\) (determinant) Chapter8/LinkAlgorSign_eq_sgn_det.
  2. One fibre, no sign. Let \(W\) be oriented of dimension \(b\) with \(d+b = k\), and let \(L : V \times W \to G\). Then \((x,w) \mapsto (Dx, L(x,w))\) has the sign of \(L \circ (\iota \times \mathrm{id})\). In the bases \((u, \iota z, w)\) and \((Du, g)\), the vector \(u_j\) goes to \((Du_j, \ast)\), while \(\iota z_i\) and \(w_l\) go to \((0, L(\cdot))\). The matrix is block lower triangular with identity upper block, and the orientation signs of the chosen bases match Chapter8/LinkAlgorSign_single_preimage.
  3. The mirror case. With the fibre in the second factor, \((w,x) \mapsto (Dx, L(w,x))\) has \((-1)^{bp}\) times the sign of \(L \circ (\mathrm{id} \times \iota)\). Compose with the swaps \(W \times V \to V \times W\) (sign \((-1)^{b(d+p)}\)) and \(Z \times W \to W \times Z\) (sign \((-1)^{db}\)) Chapter8/LinkAlgorSign_single_preimage_right Chapter8/OrientProdorSign_swap.
  4. Two fibres. Rebracket \((F \times F) \times G \to F \times (F \times G)\), which has sign \(+1\) Chapter8/LinkAlgorSign_prodAssoc. Then apply step 2 to the first factor with \(W = V\), and step 3 to the second factor with \(W = Z\) and \(b = d\).

V8.14, the engine: linking numbers of fibres are local degrees

For a linear isometry \(R\) of \(\mathbb R^{2d+2}\), let \[D_R = \{(x,x') \in S \times S : Rx \ne \mathbf n,\ Rx' \ne \mathbf n,\ x \ne x'\},\] an open set Chapter8/LinkDegreedomR. For smooth \(g, f : S \to S^{d+1}\) define on \(D_R\) \[\Phi(x,x') = \bigl((g(x), f(x')),\ \lambda_R(x,x')\bigr), \qquad \lambda_R(x,x') = \frac{\mathrm{st}(Rx)-\mathrm{st}(Rx')}{\|\mathrm{st}(Rx)-\mathrm{st}(Rx')\|} \in S^{2d}.\] It is smooth on \(D_R\): \(\mathrm{st}\) is smooth off \(\mathbf n\) and injective there, so the difference never vanishes Chapter8/LinkDegreephiR Chapter8/LinkDegreelamR Chapter8/LinkDegreecontMDiffAt_phiR. Source and target both have dimension \(4d+2\). \(D_R\) carries the product orientation of \(S \times S\), and the target \((S^{d+1} \times S^{d+1}) \times S^{2d}\) carries the product of the sphere orientations Chapter8/LinkDegreeorDomR Chapter8/LinkDegreeorTarget.

Theorem (linking number \(=\) local degree). Let \(d \ge 1\) and let \(f, g : S \to S^{d+1}\) be smooth. Let \(y\) be a regular value of \(g\) and \(z\) one of \(f\), with positive bases \(e_y, e_z\) orienting \(g^{-1}(y)\) and \(f^{-1}(z)\), and suppose the two fibres are disjoint. Let \(R\) be a rotation with \(Rx \ne \mathbf n\) for all \(x \in g^{-1}(y) \cup f^{-1}(z)\), and let \(e \in S^{2d}\) be a regular value of the linking map of \(\mathrm{st}\circ R\) on \(g^{-1}(y) \times f^{-1}(z)\). Then \(((y,z),e)\) is a regular value of \(\Phi\) on \(D_R\), and \[\deg_{((y,z),e)}\Phi = l_R\bigl(g^{-1}(y), f^{-1}(z)\bigr)\] Chapter8/LinkDegreeisRegularValue_phiR Chapter8/LinkDegreedegAt_phiR_eq_linkingNumberRot.

The hypothesis that \(R\) has positive determinant is carried along but not used. It matters only for independence of \(R\) (V8.13′).

The idea. The fibre of \(\Phi\) over \(((y,z),e)\) is the fibre of the linking map over \(e\). At corresponding points the two signs agree, by the lemma above with \(p = d+1\), where \((-1)^{d(d+1)} = 1\).

The proof as formalized.

  1. Signs at corresponding points. At \((x,x')\) with \(g(x) = y\) and \(f(x') = z\), the derivative is \(d\Phi = ((dg_x, df_{x'}), d\lambda_R)\), and the derivative of the linking map is \(d\lambda_R \circ (d\iota \times d\iota')\). The tangent spaces of the fibres are the kernels Chapter8/LinkDegreerange_mfd_val_eq_ker. By the chart description, the fibre orientations are frame orientations for lifts of \(e_y\) and \(e_z\). The block lemma applies with \(V = \mathbb R^{2d+1}\) (the chart spaces at \(x\) and \(x'\), carrying the sphere’s orientation at each point), \(F = \mathbb R^{d+1}\) and \(G = \mathbb R^{2d}\) Chapter8/LinkDegreesignAt_phiR_eq.
  2. Regularity. At a fibre point, the sign of the linking map is nonzero because \(e\) is regular. So the sign of \(\Phi\) is nonzero, and \(d\Phi\) is invertible Chapter8/LinkDegreeisRegularValue_phiR.
  3. Fibres. The map \((x,x') \mapsto (x,x')\) carries the fibre of the linking map bijectively onto the fibre of \(\Phi\). It lands in \(D_R\) by disjointness and avoidance of \(\mathbf n\), and it is onto because \(\Phi(q) = ((y,z),e)\) forces \(g(q_1) = y\) and \(f(q_2) = z\). The linking number is the degree of the linking map, computed at the regular value \(e\); here \(d \ge 1\) makes \(S^{2d}\) connected. Corresponding terms of the two sums are equal Chapter8/LinkDegreedegAt_phiR_eq_linkingNumberRot.

Theorem (homotopy invariance, the engine). Let \(d \ge 1\) and let \(G, F : S \times \mathbb R \to S^{d+1}\) be smooth, with \(G_t = G(\cdot,t)\) and \(F_t = F(\cdot,t)\). (The smoothness of the four end maps is listed separately, though it follows.) Let \(y\) be a regular value of \(G_0\) and of \(G_1\), \(z\) one of \(F_0\) and of \(F_1\), and \(e_y, e_z\) positive bases. Let \(R\) be a rotation. Suppose that for every \(t \in [0,1]\) the sets \(G_t^{-1}(y)\) and \(F_t^{-1}(z)\) are disjoint and do not meet \(R^{-1}(\mathbf n)\). Then \[l_R\bigl(G_0^{-1}(y), F_0^{-1}(z)\bigr) = l_R\bigl(G_1^{-1}(y), F_1^{-1}(z)\bigr)\] Chapter8/LinkDegreelinkingNumberRot_eq_of_homotopy.

No regularity is assumed at intermediate times: \(G_t^{-1}(y)\) need not be a manifold for \(0 < t < 1\), and only disjointness and avoidance of \(R^{-1}(\mathbf n)\) are required there. This is what makes the engine flexible, and everything below uses it.

The proof as formalized.

  1. A common direction. The regular values of each end’s linking map form an open dense set, since its domain is compact. So there is a common regular value \(e\), and \(((y,z),e)\) is regular for \(\Phi_0\) and \(\Phi_1\) Chapter6/RegularOpendense_isOpen_regularValues Chapter8/LinkDegreecontMDiff_linkMap_preim.
  2. The homotopy. \(\Psi(q,t) = ((G_t(q_1), F_t(q_2)), \lambda_R(q))\) is smooth on \(D_R \times \mathbb R\), with ends \(\Phi_0\) and \(\Phi_1\) Chapter8/LinkDegreelinkingNumberRot_eq_of_homotopy.
  3. Compactness. There are closed neighbourhoods \(V_1 \ni y\) and \(V_2 \ni z\) such that, for \(t \in [0,1]\), \(G_t(x) \in V_1\) and \(F_t(x') \in V_2\) imply \((x,x') \in D_R\) Chapter8/LinkDegreeexists_isClosed_nhds_domR. To see this, let \(K = R^{-1}(\mathbf n) \times [0,1]\). The compact sets \(G(K)\) and \(F(K)\) miss \(y\) and \(z\). The compact set \(\{(G(w), F(w)) : w \in S \times [0,1]\}\) misses \((y,z)\), by disjointness. One shrinks a product neighbourhood accordingly. The part of \(\Psi^{-1}(V_1 \times V_2 \times S^{2d})\) over \([0,1]\) is then closed in the compact space \(S \times S \times [0,1]\) and contained in \(D_R \times [0,1]\), hence compact, although \(D_R\) is not.
  4. Proper homotopy invariance. A local degree does not change along a homotopy on a non-compact manifold, provided the value is regular for both end maps and the part over \([0,1]\) of the preimage of some neighbourhood of the value is compact Chapter8/ProperDegreedegAt_eq_of_homotopy_of_isCompact. That result passes to a nearby value that is regular for the whole homotopy (Sard) and has the same local degrees at the ends, and then argues as in §5, with time reparametrized by \((1-\cos\pi t)/2\) so that regularity at the ends suffices. By the previous theorem, the local degrees at the two ends are the two linking numbers.

What the book leaves implicit. Milnor’s arguments move fibres around. The formal statement says exactly what must not happen along the way. The moving fibres must not meet, or \(\lambda\) is undefined. They must not cross the point from which one projects. And the relevant preimages must stay in a compact part of the non-compact domain \(D_R\) Chapter8/LinkDegreeexists_isClosed_nhds_domR.

V8.14 Problem 14: the Hopf invariant

The linking number of two fibres

For smooth \(g, f : S \to S^{d+1}\), a regular value \(y\) of \(g\) and a regular value \(z\) of \(f\), the symbol \(l(g^{-1}(y), f^{-1}(z))\) denotes the linking number in the sphere \(S^{2d+1}\) of the two fibres, oriented by chosen positive bases of \(T_yS^{d+1}\) and \(T_zS^{d+1}\) Chapter8/HopfInvariantposB Chapter8/HopfInvariantlinkPre. By V8.0 (iii) the chosen bases do not matter. If the fibres are disjoint and a rotation \(R\) keeps \(\mathbf n\) off both, then \(l = l_R\) Chapter8/HopfInvariantlinkPre_eq_linkingNumberRot.
