This is V8.13′ with \(a = b = d\), which asks for \(d \ge 1\); it is one place where the hypothesis \(p \ge 2\) enters (for \(p = 1\) the fibres would be finite sets in \(S^1\)).

Every point \(q\) is carried to \(\mathbf n\) by a rotation \(R_q\) Chapter8/HopfInvariantexists_rotation_to_north. Avoiding \(R_q^{-1}(\mathbf n)\) then simply means avoiding \(q\). Fibres of regular values are meagre, so a point outside any two of them exists Chapter8/HopfInvariantisMeagre_preim Chapter8/HopfInvariantexists_ne_ne. In this form the engine reads:

Proposition (engine with a base point). Let \(d \ge 1\), let \(G, F : S \times \mathbb R \to S^{d+1}\) be smooth (the smoothness of the four end maps is again listed separately), let \(y\) be a regular value of \(G_0\) and of \(G_1\), and let \(z\) be one of \(F_0\) and of \(F_1\). Suppose that for \(t \in [0,1]\), \(G_t(x) = y\) implies \(F_t(x) \ne z\), and that some \(q \in S\) satisfies \(G_t(q) \ne y\) and \(F_t(q) \ne z\) for all \(t \in [0,1]\). Then \(l(G_0^{-1}(y), F_0^{-1}(z)) = l(G_1^{-1}(y), F_1^{-1}(z))\) Chapter8/HopfInvariantlinkPre_eq_of_homotopy.

Transport and moves

Proposition (transport). Let \(d \ge 1\), let \(g, f\) be smooth, let \(y\) be regular for \(g\) and \(z\) for \(f\), and suppose \(g^{-1}(y) \cap f^{-1}(z) = \emptyset\). Let \(\rho_1, \rho_2\) be orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms of \(S^{d+1}\) (smooth bijections of sign \(+1\) everywhere). Suppose also that \(\rho_1 \circ g\) and \(\rho_2 \circ f\) are smooth and that \(\rho_1(y)\), \(\rho_2(z)\) are regular values of them; these hypotheses are listed although they follow from the others. Then \[l\bigl((\rho_1 g)^{-1}(\rho_1 y), (\rho_2 f)^{-1}(\rho_2 z)\bigr) = l\bigl(g^{-1}(y), f^{-1}(z)\bigr)\] Chapter8/HopfInvariantIsPosDiffeo Chapter8/HopfInvariantlinkPre_comp_posDiffeo.

The two sides concern the same sets, but their orientations are built from different positive bases and different maps. The formal proof never compares these orientations. It chooses \(q\) outside both fibres, the rotation \(R_q\), and a common regular value \(e\) of the two linking maps. Then both sides are local degrees, of \(\Phi\) at \(((y,z),e)\) and of \(\Phi' = ((\rho_1 \times \rho_2) \times \mathrm{id}) \circ \Phi\) at \(((\rho_1 y, \rho_2 z), e)\). Composing with a bijection of constant sign \(+1\) does not change local degrees Chapter6/ComposedegAt_comp_bij_left. Planar rotations of the sphere are such diffeomorphisms Chapter8/HopfInvariantisPosDiffeo_rotS.

Proposition (moves). Let \(\rho_i(\theta)\) be the rotation by \(\theta\) in the plane of an orthonormal pair \(u_i, v_i\) Chapter7/RotationrotCLM. Let \(d \ge 1\), let \(g, f\) be smooth, and let \(y\) be regular for \(g\) and \(z\) for \(f\). Let \(y' = \rho_1(\theta_1)y\) be regular for \(g\) and \(z' = \rho_2(\theta_2)z\) regular for \(f\). Suppose that for \(t \in [0,1]\) the equalities \(g(x) = \rho_1(t\theta_1)y\) and \(f(x) = \rho_2(t\theta_2)z\) never hold together, and that a fixed \(q\) has \(g(q) \ne \rho_1(t\theta_1)y\) and \(f(q) \ne \rho_2(t\theta_2)z\). Then \(l(g^{-1}(y), f^{-1}(z)) = l(g^{-1}(y'), f^{-1}(z'))\) Chapter8/HopfInvariantlinkPre_move.

Proof. Apply the engine to \(G_t = \rho_1(-t\theta_1) \circ g\) and \(F_t = \rho_2(-t\theta_2) \circ f\) with the fixed values \(y, z\). Then \(G_t^{-1}(y) = g^{-1}(\rho_1(t\theta_1)y)\), and \(y\) is regular for \(G_1\) because \(y'\) is regular for \(g\) Chapter8/HopfInvariantrotHom Chapter8/HopfInvariantisRegularValue_rotS_comp. Transport by \(\rho_1(\theta_1) \times \rho_2(\theta_2)\) then turns \(G_1\) back into \(g\) and \(y\) into \(y'\). The values passed on the way need not be regular.

a) Local constancy

Theorem (V8.14 a). Let \(d \ge 1\), let \(f : S \to S^{d+1}\) be smooth, and let \(y \ne z\) be regular values of \(f\). There is a neighbourhood \(U\) of \(y\) such that every regular value \(y' \in U\) of \(f\) satisfies \(l(f^{-1}(y'), f^{-1}(z)) = l(f^{-1}(y), f^{-1}(z))\). The same holds in \(z\) Chapter8/HopfInvariantlinkPre_self_eventually_eq Chapter8/HopfInvariantlinkPre_self_eventually_eq_right.

Both are the case \(g = f\) of a two-map statement: for smooth \(g, f\), a regular value \(y\) of \(g\) and \(z\) of \(f\) with \(g^{-1}(y) \cap f^{-1}(z) = \emptyset\), the same conclusion holds for regular values \(y'\) of \(g\) near \(y\) Chapter8/HopfInvariantlinkPre_eventually_eq. When \(g = f\), disjointness is just \(y \ne z\).

Proof. Take \(q\) outside both fibres. The set \(K = g(f^{-1}(z))\) is compact and does not contain \(y\); choose \(\varepsilon\) with \(B(y,\varepsilon) \cap K = \emptyset\). For \(y'\) within \(\min(\varepsilon, |g(q)-y|)\) of \(y\), the great-circle arc from \(y\) to \(y'\) stays within \(|y'-y|\) of \(y\) Chapter7/Rotationexists_rotation_path. So the arc misses \(g(q)\) and every \(g(x)\) with \(f(x) = z\), and the move with \(z\) fixed applies Chapter8/HopfInvariantlinkPre_move_left.

A correction to a natural generalization. For two maps, the formal statement does not settle for \(y \ne z\): it assumes that the fibres are disjoint at \(y\), and this is exactly the form b) needs Chapter8/HopfInvariantlinkPre_eventually_eq. The reason is geometric, and it is not formalized (no counterexample is checked by machine). At values \(y\) where \(g^{-1}(y)\) meets \(f^{-1}(z)\) the symbol \(l(g^{-1}(y), f^{-1}(z))\) is still defined but no longer a linking number of disjoint manifolds, and moving \(y\) past such a value pushes one fibre through the other, as when two circles in \(\mathbb R^3\) pass through each other; the linking number can jump there.

b) Nearby maps

Theorem (V8.14 b). Let \(d \ge 1\) and let \(f, g : S \to S^{d+1}\) be smooth. Let \(y \ne z\) be regular values of both \(f\) and \(g\), and suppose \(\|f(x)-g(x)\| < \|y-z\|\) for all \(x\). Then \[l\bigl(f^{-1}(y), f^{-1}(z)\bigr) = l\bigl(g^{-1}(y), f^{-1}(z)\bigr) = l\bigl(g^{-1}(y), g^{-1}(z)\bigr)\] Chapter8/HopfInvariantlinkPre_eq_of_norm_lt.

The idea. Deform \(f\) into \(g\) in one slot along the normalized chord and keep the other slot fixed. A chord point is never farther from \(f(x)\) than \(g(x)\) is, so the moving fibre of \(y\) never meets \(f^{-1}(z)\).

The proof as formalized (first equality; the second is symmetric).

  1. The chord. Let \(m = \max_x\|f(x)-g(x)\|\), attained by compactness; then \(m < \|y-z\| \le 2\). Let \(C_t = (1-\sigma(t))f + \sigma(t)g\), normalized, where \(\sigma\) is a smooth transition function equal to \(0\) for \(t \le 0\) and \(1\) for \(t \ge 1\). It is a smooth homotopy from \(f\) to \(g\) Chapter8/HopfInvariantchord. For unit vectors \(a, b\) with \(|a-b| < 2\) and \(s \in [0,1]\), the point \(w = (1-s)a + sb\) has \(|w| \le 1\), and normalizing moves it by \(1-|w| \le |w-b|\). Hence \(|w/|w| - a| \le (1-s)|a-b| + s|a-b| = |a-b|\), and likewise for \(b\) Chapter8/HopfInvariantnorm_nv0_chord_sub.
  2. Disjointness at the start. \(g^{-1}(y) \cap f^{-1}(z) = \emptyset\), since otherwise \(\|f(x)-g(x)\| = \|z-y\|\).
  3. A good value. Take \(q\) with \(f(q) \ne z\). Choose \(y'\) near \(y\) with the following properties: it is regular for \(f\) and for \(g\); it lies in the neighbourhoods given by a) for \(f\) and by the two-map form of a) for \((g,f)\), the latter available by step 2; it satisfies \(m < \|y'-z\|\); and it avoids the curve \(t \mapsto C_t(q)\), \(t \in [0,1]\) Chapter8/HopfInvariantexists_regular_off. Such a \(y'\) exists because regular values are open (proved here for compact domains in arbitrary dimensions; Chapter 6 had only equal dimensions) and dense, and a smooth curve in a sphere of dimension \(\ge 2\) is nowhere dense Chapter8/HopfInvariantisOpen_setOf_isRegularValue Chapter8/GenericisNowhereDense_image_of_finrank_lt.
  4. The engine with \(G = C\) and \(F_t = f\). If \(C_t(x) = y'\) and \(f(x) = z\), then \(\|y'-z\| \le \|f(x)-g(x)\| \le m < \|y'-z\|\), which is impossible Chapter8/HopfInvariantnorm_chord_sub_left Chapter8/HopfInvariantlinkPre_eq_of_homotopy. The base point stays off both fibres: \(f(q) \ne z\) by the choice of \(q\), and \(C_t(q) \ne y'\) by the choice of \(y'\).
  5. The chain. \(l(f^{-1}y, f^{-1}z) = l(f^{-1}y', f^{-1}z)\) by a); \(= l(g^{-1}y', f^{-1}z)\) by the engine, since \(C_0 = f\) and \(C_1 = g\); \(= l(g^{-1}y, f^{-1}z)\) by the two-map form of a).

The detour through \(y'\) is forced by the base point: \(y\) itself may lie on the trajectory of \(q\).

c) Independence and homotopy invariance

Definition. If \(f\) is smooth and has two distinct regular values, \(H(f) = l(f^{-1}(y_0), f^{-1}(z_0))\) for a chosen pair \(y_0 \ne z_0\) of regular values; otherwise \(H(f) = 0\) Chapter8/HopfInvarianthopfInvariant. For \(d \ge 1\) every smooth \(f\) has such a pair Chapter8/HopfInvariantexists_regular_pair, so only non-smooth maps get the value \(0\) by default.

Theorem (V8.14 c). Let \(d \ge 1\). (i) If \(f : S \to S^{d+1}\) is smooth, then \(l(f^{-1}(y), f^{-1}(z)) = H(f)\) for all regular values \(y \ne z\) of \(f\) Chapter8/HopfInvariantlinkPre_eq_hopfInvariant. (ii) If \(f, g\) are smooth and smoothly homotopic, then \(H(f) = H(g)\) Chapter8/HopfInvarianthopfInvariant_eq_of_smoothHomotopic.

Proof of (i). Let \(X = \{(y,z) \in S^{d+1} \times S^{d+1} : y \ne z\}\). It is connected, and pairs of regular values are dense in it. If every point of \(X\) has a neighbourhood on which the linking number is constant over the regular pairs, then it is constant over all regular pairs in \(X\) Chapter8/GenericisConnected_offDiag_sph Chapter8/Genericeq_of_locallyConst_on_dense. Local constancy near \((p_1,p_2) \in X\) is proved directly with simultaneous moves Chapter8/HopfInvariantlinkPre_eq_linkPre_of_ne:

  1. If \(f\) is constant, a constant map has no regular value in its image, so every fibre of a regular value is empty and every linking number is \(0\) Chapter8/HopfInvariantnot_isRegularValue_const Chapter8/HopfInvariantlinkPre_eq_zero_of_forall_ne.
  2. Otherwise some \(q\) has \(f(q) \notin \{p_1, p_2\}\). If not, \(f^{-1}(p_1)\) would be both open and closed in the connected \(S\). Let \(r = \min(|p_1-p_2|, |f(q)-p_1|, |f(q)-p_2|)/8\).
  3. Two regular pairs \((a_1,a_2)\) and \((b_1,b_2)\) in \(B(p_1,r) \times B(p_2,r)\) are joined by great-circle arcs \(a_i \to b_i\), each staying within \(3r\) of \(p_i\). The arcs miss \(f(q)\), which is at distance \(\ge 8r\). They cannot pass through a common value \(f(x)\) at the same time, since that would give \(|p_1-p_2| < 6r\). The move lemma applies Chapter7/Rotationexists_rotation_path Chapter8/HopfInvariantlinkPre_move.

Proof of (ii). A smooth homotopy is a smooth \(H : S \times \mathbb R \to S^{d+1}\) with \(H(\cdot,0) = f\) and \(H(\cdot,1) = g\). Fix any \(q\). Choose \(y\), a common regular value of \(f\) and \(g\) off the curve \(t \mapsto H(q,t)\), \(t \in [0,1]\), and then \(z \ne y\) with the same properties. Such values exist by the genericity argument of b) Chapter8/HopfInvariantexists_regular_off. The engine with \(G = F = H\) applies: disjointness is automatic because \(y \ne z\), and \(q\) avoids both fibres by choice Chapter8/HopfInvariantlinkPre_eq_of_homotopy. It gives \(l(f^{-1}y, f^{-1}z) = l(g^{-1}y, g^{-1}z)\), and both sides are Hopf invariants by (i).

Where the formal proof departs from Milnor. The book’s order suggests deducing c) from b) by cutting a homotopy into steps shorter than \(\|y-z\|\). The formal proof does not use b) for c). It applies the engine to the homotopy itself, once the two values avoid the trajectory of a single base point, and b) stands as a separate result Chapter8/HopfInvarianthopfInvariant_eq_of_smoothHomotopic. The dependence on \(y\) and \(z\) is settled by connectedness of \(X\) and simultaneous moves of both values; a) itself is not used Chapter8/HopfInvariantlinkPre_eq_linkPre_of_ne. Deviation: homotopies are smooth.

V8.15 Problem 15: odd \(p\) and compositions

Theorem (odd \(p\)). Let \(d \ge 1\) with \(d+1\) odd, and let \(f : S \to S^{d+1}\) be smooth. Then \(H(f) = 0\) Chapter8/HopfPropshopfInvariant_eq_zero_of_odd.

Proof. Take distinct regular values \(y, z\), a point \(q\) outside \(f^{-1}\{y,z\}\), and \(R\) with \(Rq = \mathbf n\). Both \(l(f^{-1}y, f^{-1}z)\) and \(l(f^{-1}z, f^{-1}y)\) are Euclidean linking numbers after \(R\) Chapter8/HopfInvariantlinkPre_eq_linkingNumberRot. The symmetry of Problem 13 relates them by the factor \((-1)^{(d+1)(d+1)} = -1\) Chapter8/LinkinglinkingNumber_symm. Both are \(H(f)\) by c), so \(H(f) = -H(f)\).

Theorem (compositions). Let \(d \ge 1\), and let \(f : S \to S^{d+1}\) and \(g : S^{d+1} \to S^{d+1}\) be smooth. Then \(H(g\circ f) = (\deg g)^2 H(f)\), with the degree taken for Milnor’s orientation on both sides Chapter8/HopfPropshopfInvariant_comp.

The idea. Write \(\Phi_h\) for the map \(\Phi\) built from \(g = f = h\). Then \(\Phi_{g\circ f} = ((g \times g) \times \mathrm{id}) \circ \Phi_f\), and the local degree of a composition is a sum over the fibre of the outer map.

The proof as formalized.

  1. Local composition formula. Let \(\Phi : M \to N\) and \(\Gamma : N \to P\) be smooth, where \(M\) and \(N\) are oriented manifolds of dimension \(n\) and \(P\) carries an orientation in degree \(n\) (the statement does not fix the dimension of \(P\); in the application all three have dimension \(4d+2\)). Let \(w \in P\) be such that \(\Gamma^{-1}(w)\) and \((\Gamma\circ\Phi)^{-1}(w)\) are finite. Then \(\deg_w(\Gamma \circ \Phi) = \sum_{w' \in \Gamma^{-1}(w)} \operatorname{sign}_{w'}\Gamma \cdot \deg_{w'}\Phi\). No regularity is needed, since signs multiply at every point Chapter8/HopfCompdegAt_comp_eq_finsum Chapter6/SignLemmassignAt_comp'.
  2. Fibres downstairs. If \(y\) is a regular value of \(g \circ f\) and \(g(y_i) = y\), then \(y_i\) is a regular value of \(f\): \(dg \circ df\) is onto, so \(dg\) is onto, hence injective in equal dimensions, so \(df\) is onto Chapter8/HopfCompisRegularValue_of_comp.
  3. Linking numbers under composition. Let \(y \ne z\) be regular for \(g\) and \(g \circ f\), let \(R\) be admissible for \((g \circ f)^{-1}\{y,z\}\), and let \(e\) be a regular value of all the linking maps involved. Then \[l_R\bigl((g f)^{-1}y, (g f)^{-1}z\bigr) = \sum_{y_i \in g^{-1}(y)}\ \sum_{z_j \in g^{-1}(z)} \operatorname{sign}_{y_i}g\,\operatorname{sign}_{z_j}g\ l_R\bigl(f^{-1}y_i, f^{-1}z_j\bigr).\] The fibre of \(\Gamma = (g\times g)\times\mathrm{id}\) over \(((y,z),e)\) is \((g^{-1}y \times g^{-1}z) \times \{e\}\), and the sign of \(\Gamma\) there is \(\operatorname{sign}_{y_i}g\,\operatorname{sign}_{z_j}g\). The fibre of \(\Phi_{gf}\) is finite, being the image of a fibre of a linking map Chapter8/OrientProdsignAt_prodMap Chapter8/HopfCompfinite_preimage_phiR Chapter8/HopfComplinkingNumberRot_comp_eq_finsum. A common \(e\) exists: a dense set meets finitely many open dense sets Chapter6/RegularOpenexists_mem_of_dense_of_isOpen Chapter8/HopfComplinkingNumberRot_comp_eq_finsum'.
  4. Assembly. Distinct common regular values of \(g\) and \(g \circ f\) exist Chapter8/HopfPropsexists_regular_pair_comp. Each \(l_R(f^{-1}y_i, f^{-1}z_j)\) equals \(H(f)\) by c), since \(y_i \ne z_j\). Each sum of signs is \(\deg g\) Chapter8/HopfCompfinsum_signAt_eq_deg.

Where the formal proof departs from Milnor. The usual argument decomposes \((g\circ f)^{-1}(y)\) as \(\bigsqcup f^{-1}(y_i)\), with orientations changed by \(\operatorname{sign} dg_{y_i}\), and uses bilinearity of linking numbers. The formal proof proves neither the orientation comparison nor bilinearity over disjoint unions. Both are absorbed in the local composition formula Chapter8/HopfCompdegAt_comp_eq_finsum.

V8.15 The Hopf fibration

Definition. With \(z_1 = x_0 + ix_1\) and \(z_2 = x_2 + ix_3\) (Milnor’s \(x_1, \dots, x_4\) shifted to start at \(0\)), \[\pi(x) = \bigl(2(x_0x_2 + x_1x_3),\ 2(x_1x_2 - x_0x_3),\ x_0^2 + x_1^2 - x_2^2 - x_3^2\bigr) = \bigl(2z_1\bar z_2,\ |z_1|^2 - |z_2|^2\bigr).\] One has \(\|\pi(x)\| = \|x\|^2\), so \(\pi\) maps \(S^3\) smoothly to \(S^2\) Chapter8/HopfMaphopfPoly Chapter8/HopfMapnorm_hopfPoly Chapter8/HopfMapcontMDiff_hopfMap.

Proposition.

  1. Milnor’s formula. If \(z_2 \ne 0\) then \(\pi(x) = h^{-1}(z_1/z_2)\), where \(h^{-1}(w) = (2\operatorname{Re}w, 2\operatorname{Im}w, |w|^2-1)/(|w|^2+1)\) is the inverse of stereographic projection from \((0,0,1)\). If \(z_2 = 0\) then \(\pi(x) = (0,0,1)\) Chapter8/HopfMapinvStereoC Chapter8/HopfMaphopfMap_eq_milnor Chapter8/HopfMaphopfMap_eq_top.

  2. Every point of \(S^2\) is a regular value. Let \(D\) be the derivative of the polynomial map at \(x\). Then \(DD^{\mathsf T} = 4\|x\|^2\) and \(\langle x, D^{\mathsf T}u\rangle = 2\langle\pi(x), u\rangle\) Chapter8/HopfMaphopfPoly_fderiv_apply Chapter8/HopfMapinner_hopfAdj Chapter8/HopfMapfderiv_hopfAdj. So for \(u\) tangent at \(\pi(x)\), the vector \(v = \tfrac14 D^{\mathsf T}u\) is tangent at \(x\) and \(Dv = u\) Chapter8/HopfMapisRegularValue_hopfMap.

  3. Two fibres. \(\pi(x) = (1,0,0)\) iff \(z_1 = z_2\), and \(\pi(x) = (-1,0,0)\) iff \(z_1 = -z_2\). These are great circles, the intersections of \(S^3\) with two planes. For the first, \(2(x_0x_2 + x_1x_3) = 1\) and \(|x| = 1\) give \((x_0-x_2)^2 + (x_1-x_3)^2 = 0\) Chapter8/HopfMaphopfMap_eq_e0_iff Chapter8/HopfMaphopfMap_eq_neg_e0_iff.

  4. The pair realizing a direction. Let \(\mathrm{st}(x) = (x_0,x_1,x_2)/(1-x_3)\) Chapter8/HopfMapstereoTop Chapter8/HopfSignstN_eq_stereoTop. For \(x\) in the fibre over \((1,0,0)\) and \(x'\) in the fibre over \((-1,0,0)\), the vector \(\mathrm{st}(x) - \mathrm{st}(x')\) is a positive multiple of \((0,-1,0)\) iff \[x = a = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(0,-1,0,-1), \qquad x' = a' = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(0,1,0,-1)\] Chapter8/HopfMaphopf_link_pair_iff. The first and third coordinates of the difference give \(x_0 = x'_0 = 0\). Then \(x_1^2 = x_1'^2 = \tfrac12\). After clearing positive denominators, the sign condition on the second coordinate reads \(x_1 - x'_1 + 2x_1x'_1 < 0\), and of the four sign choices only \(x_1 = -\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\), \(x'_1 = \tfrac1{\sqrt2}\) satisfies it.

V8.15 The sign: \(H(\pi) = -1\)

Theorem. \(H(\pi) = -1\) Chapter8/HopfPropshopfInvariant_hopfMap. More precisely, with \(y = (1,0,0)\), \(z = (-1,0,0)\), fibres oriented as above, and the identity rotation, \(l_{\mathrm{id}}(\pi^{-1}(y), \pi^{-1}(z)) = -1\) Chapter8/HopfSignlinkingNumberRot_hopfMap.

The idea. By the theorem “linking number \(=\) local degree”, this linking number is the local degree of \(\Phi(x,x') = ((\pi x, \pi x'), \lambda(x,x'))\) at \(((y,z),e)\), with \(e = (0,-1,0)\). The fibre is the single point \((a,a')\), so everything reduces to one sign. That sign is a product of three explicit determinants.

The proof as formalized.

  1. Admissibility. The fibres are disjoint. Neither contains \(\mathbf n = (0,0,0,1)\): on them \(x_3 = \pm x_1\), which would give \(1 = 0\). So the identity rotation is admissible Chapter8/HopfSignhopf_disj Chapter8/HopfSignhopf_north_y Chapter8/HopfSignhopf_north_z.
  2. The fibre of \(\Phi\). \(\lambda(x,x') = e\) means \(\mathrm{st}(x)-\mathrm{st}(x')\) is a positive multiple of \(e\). By (iv), the fibre of \(\Phi\) over \(((y,z),e)\) is \(\{(a,a')\}\) Chapter8/HopfSigneq_q₀_of_phiR Chapter8/HopfSignpreimage_phiR.
  3. Reduction. The block lemma with \(d = 1\), \(p = 2\) (factor \((-1)^2 = 1\)) reduces the sign of \(\Phi\) at \((a,a')\) to the sign of \(d\lambda \circ (\iota \times \iota') : \mathbb R \times \mathbb R \to T_eS^2\). Here \(\iota, \iota'\) are the inclusions of the lines spanned by the fibre directions \(t = \tfrac1{\sqrt2}(1,0,1,0)\) at \(a\) and \(t' = \tfrac1{\sqrt2}(-1,0,1,0)\) at \(a'\); these lines are the kernels of \(d\pi\) Chapter8/HopfSignD_vt Chapter8/HopfSignrange_toSpanSingleton_eq_ker. (As one checks by hand, outside the formal proof, they are the velocities of the circle action \((z_1,z_2) \mapsto (e^{i\phi}z_1, e^{i\phi}z_2)\).)
  4. Lifts. At \(a\) take \(u_1 = (1,0,-1,0)\) and \(u_2 = (0,-1,0,1)\), with \(d\pi\,u_1 = 2\sqrt2\,(0,1,0)\) and \(d\pi\,u_2 = 2\sqrt2\,(0,0,1)\). They lift a positive basis at \(y\), because \(\det(y, d\pi u_1, d\pi u_2) = 8\). At \(a'\) take \(w_1 = (0,1,0,1)\) and \(w_2 = (1,0,1,0)\), with \(d\pi\,w_1 = 2\sqrt2\,(0,0,1)\) and \(d\pi\,w_2 = 2\sqrt2\,(0,1,0)\), and \(\det(z, d\pi w_1, d\pi w_2) = 8\) Chapter8/HopfSigndet_D_uA Chapter8/HopfSigndet_D_uA'.
  5. The fibres are oriented against \(t\) and \(t'\). \(\det(a, u_1, u_2, t) = \det(a', w_1, w_2, t') = -2\) Chapter8/HopfSigndet_eVA Chapter8/HopfSigndet_eVA'. By the chart description of the fibre orientation and the determinant test for the sphere, \(t\) and \(t'\) are negative Chapter8/HopfSignorEpsB_frameOr_A Chapter8/HopfSignorEpsB_frameOr_A'.
  6. The direction map. \(w_0 := \mathrm{st}(a) - \mathrm{st}(a') = 2(\sqrt2-1)(0,-1,0)\). The derivative of \(v \mapsto v/|v|\) at \(w_0\) is \(|w_0|^{-1}\) times the identity on \(w_0^\perp\) Chapter8/HopfSignexists_hasFDerivAt_normalize Chapter8/HopfSignexists_mfd_lamR. Also \(d\,\mathrm{st}_a(t) = (\sqrt2-1)(1,0,1)\) and \(d\,\mathrm{st}_{a'}(t') = (\sqrt2-1)(-1,0,1)\). Hence \(d\lambda(t,0) = c(1,0,1)\) and \(d\lambda(0,t') = c(1,0,-1)\) with \(c = (\sqrt2-1)/|w_0|\) Chapter8/HopfSignmfd_lamR_t Chapter8/HopfSignmfd_lamR_t'. By the formula for \(w_0\), \(c = \tfrac12\); the formal proof only uses \(c > 0\) Chapter8/HopfSigncl_pos. Since \(\det(e, c(1,0,1), c(1,0,-1)) = -2c^2 < 0\), these two vectors form a negative basis of \(T_eS^2\) Chapter8/HopfSigndet_βl Chapter8/HopfSignorEpsB_ξe.
  7. The sign. \(\operatorname{sign}\bigl((-1)(-1)\cdot(-1)\bigr) = -1\) Chapter8/HopfSignorSign_lam Chapter8/HopfSignsignAt_q₀. So the local degree is \(-1\) Chapter8/HopfSigndegAt_hopf. Because the only fibre point has nonzero sign, \(e\) is a regular value of the linking map Chapter8/HopfSignisRegularValue_linkMap_hopfE, and the linking number is \(-1\). Since \(y \ne z\) are regular values, this linking number is \(H(\pi)\).

Which conventions give \(+1\). This analysis is not formalized; it combines the formal lemmas cited in it with the multiplicativity of signs. Among the natural variations of the conventions, only changes to the linking number itself move the value. Three changes flip it. (a) The direction \((x'-x)/\|x'-x\|\) instead of \((x-x')/\|x-x'\|\) composes \(\lambda\) with the antipodal map of \(S^2\), of degree \((-1)^3\) Chapter8/OrientFramedeg_antip_std. (b) Orienting the domain as \(\pi^{-1}(z) \times \pi^{-1}(y)\) while keeping the direction composes with the swap of two circles, of sign \((-1)^{1\cdot1}\) Chapter8/OrientProdsignAt_swap. (c) The opposite orientation on the target \(S^2\) of \(\lambda\). Several changes leave \(-1\) unchanged:

  • Listing tangent vectors first in the fibre convention: \((-1)^{dp} = +1\).
  • Exchanging the two fibres, which does (a) and (b) together: \((-1)^{(1+1)(1+1)} = +1\) Chapter8/LinkinglinkingNumber_symm.
  • Reversing the orientation of the source \(S^3\) or of the target of \(\pi\): this reverses both fibres, and the product orientation survives.
  • Another pole or a complex conjugation in Milnor’s \(h\): this replaces \(\pi\) by \(\rho\circ\pi\) for an isometry \(\rho\) of \(S^2\), and \(H(\rho\circ\pi) = (\deg\rho)^2H(\pi)\) by the composition theorem Chapter8/HopfPropshopfInvariant_comp.

So a value \(+1\) comes from redefining the linking number itself, by an odd number of the changes (a)–(c). The choices listed that concern only the fibres or the map leave \(-1\), and the book’s conventions, taken literally, give \(-1\); the last statement is the formal theorem. Either way the invariant is nonzero. A constant map has \(H = 0\), since it has no regular value in its image and so its fibres over regular values are empty Chapter8/HopfInvariantnot_isRegularValue_const Chapter8/HopfInvariantlinkPre_eq_zero_of_forall_ne. With c), the Hopf fibration is therefore not smoothly null-homotopic, a one-line consequence that the formal text does not state separately.

What the formalization taught us

  • \(p \ge 2\) is a hypothesis. Linking numbers of fibres go through V8.13′ with \(a = b = p-1\), which needs \(a, b \ge 1\) Chapter8/HopfInvariantlinkPre_eq_linkingNumberRot.
  • The fibre convention is a choice. The formal fibre orientation puts the frame first; by an informal count it differs from the §5-style convention by \((-1)^{dp}\), which is \(+1\) for \(d = p-1\) Chapter8/PreimOrientpreimOr.
  • The two-map form of a) assumes disjoint fibres. Without disjointness the linking number can jump (a geometric observation, not machine-checked); Milnor’s one-map statement is safe because \(y \ne z\) Chapter8/HopfInvariantlinkPre_eventually_eq.
  • Values regular only at the ends. The engine asks for regularity of \(y\) and \(z\) at \(t = 0, 1\) only. In return it requires the moving fibres to stay disjoint and away from the projection point, and it needs a compactness argument on the non-compact domain \(D_R\) Chapter8/LinkDegreelinkingNumberRot_eq_of_homotopy Chapter8/LinkDegreeexists_isClosed_nhds_domR.
  • A base point replaces “a point outside”. Projecting from a point \(q\), and keeping \(q\) off every moving fibre, is what the choice of values in b) and c) is arranged around Chapter8/HopfInvariantlinkPre_eq_of_homotopy Chapter8/HopfInvariantexists_regular_off.
  • Regular values of maps between different dimensions form an open set when the domain is compact. This had to be proved afresh; Chapter 6’s version was for equal dimensions Chapter8/HopfInvariantisOpen_setOf_isRegularValue.
  • Orientations are compared through local degrees. Transport and the composition formula never compare two fibre orientations directly Chapter8/HopfInvariantlinkPre_comp_posDiffeo Chapter8/HopfComplinkingNumberRot_comp_eq_finsum.
  • c) does not go through b). Homotopy invariance applies the engine to the homotopy itself; independence of the values uses connectedness of the off-diagonal and treats constant maps separately Chapter8/HopfInvarianthopfInvariant_eq_of_smoothHomotopic Chapter8/HopfInvariantlinkPre_eq_linkPre_of_ne.
  • \(H(\pi) = -1\). With outward-normal-first spheres, the fibre orientation of V8.0 (iii) (which is §5’s in this dimension) and \(\lambda = (x-x')/\|x-x'\|\) on the product, the Hopf fibration has Hopf invariant \(-1\), not the book’s \(1\) Chapter8/HopfPropshopfInvariant_hopfMap.
← Part IX. Orientation tools and linking numbers (Milnor §8, Problem 13)Part XI. Transversality and the cohomotopy group (Milnor §8, Problems 16–17) →

Part XI. Transversality and the cohomotopy group (Milnor §8, Problems 16–17)

Milnor’s last two problems ask for three things. A framed submanifold can be moved slightly to meet a given submanifold transversally, and the transverse intersection is a manifold (Problem 16). Transverse intersection induces a product \(\Pi^p(M) \times \Pi^q(M) \to \Pi^{p+q}(M)\) of framed cobordism classes, and for \(p \ge \frac12 m + 1\) disjoint union makes \(\Pi^p(M)\) an abelian group (Problem 17). The formal solution, about 4,800 lines, is assembled from the machinery of §7 but has to open it up. “Keep the cobordism away from the other piece” is a statement about the underlying set of a cobordism, which the existence theorems of §7 hide, so several are re-proved with the set recorded. Two ideas carry the part. A framed submanifold is moved within its class not by deforming it but by changing the regular value of a map that realizes it. And the product and the inverse are both computed as Pontryagin manifolds of explicit maps, then identified exactly, framings included, with the intersection and with a pair of parallel copies.

Map. - Chapter8/Transversality: transversality, the intersection of transverse submanifolds, the transverse translate inside a product neighbourhood. - Chapter8/FramedOps: reflexivity, the set of classes, disjoint unions of framed submanifolds and of cobordisms, Lemma 1 and the homotopy construction with the underlying set exposed. - Chapter8/CohomotopyProduct: dual forms, the framed intersection, a map \(\mu : S^p \times S^q \to S^{p+q}\), transverse representatives, the intersection product. - Chapter8/CohomotopyGroup: disjoint representatives, independence of the sum, the monoid laws, the cancelling pair, the group.

Conventions

\(M \subseteq \mathbb R^{K+1}\) is a submanifold of dimension \(m\) given by slice charts (normal model \(\mathbb R^w\)), with the structure they induce; as a subspace of Euclidean space it is Hausdorff and second countable. Wherever Pontryagin manifolds or classes appear, \(M\) is also compact and nonempty. Tangent spaces \(T_xM\), \(T_xN\) are subspaces of \(\mathbb R^{K+1}\), images of the derivatives of the inclusions Chapter7/FramedtangentM Chapter7/FramedtangentN.

A framed submanifold \(F = (N, v)\) of dimension \(n\) and codimension \(p\) is a compact \(N \subseteq M\) given by slice charts (model \(\mathbb R^n\), normal model \(\mathbb R^p\), \(n + p = m\)) with smooth \(v_1, \dots, v_p : N \to \mathbb R^{K+1}\), tangent to \(M\), orthogonal to \(T_xN\) and linearly independent Chapter7/FramedFramedSub. A framed cobordism from \(F_0\) to \(F_1\) is an \((n+1)\)-dimensional submanifold \(S \subseteq M \times \mathbb R\) given by slice charts, equal to \(N_0 \times \mathbb R\) over \(t < \varepsilon\) and to \(N_1 \times \mathbb R\) over \(t > 1 - \varepsilon\) (some \(0 < \varepsilon < \frac12\)), compact over \([0,1]\), framed in \(M \times \mathbb R\) by vectors equal to \((v^0_i, 0)\) and \((v^1_i, 0)\) at the ends; \(F_0 \sim F_1\) means one exists Chapter7/FramedFramedCob Chapter7/FramedFramedCobordant.

For \(f : M \to S^p\) smooth with regular value \(y\), a basis \(b\) of the model space \(\mathbb R^p\) at \(y\), and \(n + p = m\), \(\mathrm{Pont}(f, y, b)\) is \(f^{-1}(y)\) with the framing \[(f^*b)_i(x) = A^*(AA^*)^{-1}b_i, \qquad A = A_f(x) = d\tilde f_x : \mathbb R^{K+1} \to \mathbb R^p,\] where \(\tilde f\) is \(f\) precomposed with the nearest-point retraction onto \(M\) and read in the chart at \(y\) Chapter7/PontryaginAt Chapter7/PontryaginpontV Chapter7/Pontryaginpontryagin. As \(\ker A = T_xf^{-1}(y) \oplus (T_xM)^\perp\), \((f^*b)_i(x)\) is the unique vector tangent to \(M\), normal to \(f^{-1}(y)\), with \(A\)-image \(b_i\) Chapter7/PontFrameker_At_eq Chapter7/PontFramepontV_eq_of. Positive bases are positive for the orientation of \(S^p\) fixed in Chapter 5 and used throughout §7 Chapter7/Lemma2exists_posBasis; it need not be the outward-normal-first orientation of Part X, and the statements of this part do not involve it. \(e_k\) is a standard basis vector.

Results of §7 carry Milnor’s names: Lemma 1 (the positive basis does not matter), Theorem A (nor does the regular value), Theorem B (homotopic if and only if framed cobordant), Theorem C (every framed submanifold is a Pontryagin manifold), and the homotopy construction in the proofs of Lemmas 2 and 3 (the preimage of a regular value of a homotopy constant near the ends). Theorem C is used in the form: for every framed \(F\) and basis \(b\) there are \(f\) with regular value north and \(c > 0\) with \(\mathrm{Pont}(f, \mathrm{north}, cb) = F\) Chapter7/ThmBexists_map_of_framedSub. The scalar \(c\) recurs as a nuisance, removed by Lemma 1 for a positive diagonal matrix.

V8.16 Problem 16: transverse intersections and the transverse translate

Submanifolds \(N\) (model \(\mathbb R^n\), normal model \(\mathbb R^p\)) and \(N'\) (model \(\mathbb R^{n'}\), normal model \(\mathbb R^{p'}\)) of \(M\), given by slice charts, meet transversally if \(T_xN + T_xN' = T_xM\) for all \(x \in N \cap N'\) Chapter8/TransversalityTransverse. Since the derivative of \(M \hookrightarrow \mathbb R^{K+1}\) is injective, this is equivalent to the images of the derivatives of \(N \hookrightarrow M\) and \(N' \hookrightarrow M\) spanning \(\mathbb R^m\), and all proofs work at this chart level Chapter8/TransversalityTransversality.transverse_iff.

Milnor’s parenthesis. If \(n + p = m\), \(n' + p' = m\), \(N\) and \(N'\) meet transversally and \(n + n' < m\), then \(N \cap N' = \varnothing\): at a common point, \(m = \dim(T_xN + T_xN') \le n + n'\) Chapter8/Transversalityinter_eq_empty_of_transverse. The two equations are hypotheses, but this dimension count does not need them.

The intersection

Theorem. Let \(N, N' \subseteq M\) be given by slice charts, with models \(\mathbb R^n, \mathbb R^{n'}\) and normal models \(\mathbb R^p, \mathbb R^{p'}\), where \(n + p = m\) and \(n' + p' = m\); suppose they meet transversally, and let \(r + (p + p') = m\). Then \(N \cap N'\) is a submanifold of \(M\) given by slice charts, with model \(\mathbb R^r\) and normal model \(\mathbb R^{p+p'}\), and \(T_x(N \cap N') = T_xN \cap T_xN'\) for every \(x \in N \cap N'\). Chapter8/TransversalityisSliceSubmanifold_inter Chapter8/TransversalitytangentN_inter

No compactness is needed. Since \(r\) must be supplied, the case covered is \(p + p' \le m\); otherwise the parenthesis applies.

The idea. Near a common point, \(N\) and \(N'\) are the zero sets of the normal coordinates of slice charts. The pair of normal coordinates cuts out \(N \cap N'\), and transversality is exactly what makes it a submersion.

The proof as formalized. 1. For a slice chart \(\varphi\) of \(N\), the normal coordinate \(\mathrm{pr}_2 \circ \varphi\) is smooth with surjective derivative \(D\), and at points of \(N\), \(\ker D\) is the chart-level tangent space of \(N\) Chapter8/Transversalitysurjective_sliceSnd Chapter8/Transversalityker_sliceSnd_eq_range. The last fact is an instance of a principle proved for Chapter 8: the tangent space of a local zero set of a map with surjective derivative is the kernel of that derivative Chapter8/LocalSliceIsSliceSubmanifold.range_mfderiv_val_eq_ker. 2. Near \(x \in N \cap N'\), with slice charts \(\varphi, \varphi'\) on \(U, U'\), the map \(g = (\mathrm{pr}_2\varphi, \mathrm{pr}_2\varphi')\), read in \(\mathbb R^{p+p'}\), is smooth on \(U \cap U'\), vanishes there exactly on \(N \cap N'\), and has derivative \((D, D')\) Chapter8/Transversalityexists_local_inter. 3. If \(D, D'\) are onto and \(\ker D + \ker D'\) is everything, then \((D, D')\) is onto: given \((a, a')\), pick \(Du = a\), \(D'u' = a'\) and split \(u - u' = k + k'\) along the kernels; then \(u - k = u' + k'\) solves both. Transversality says the kernels span, so \(g\) has surjective derivative along \(N \cap N'\), with kernel \(\ker D \cap \ker D'\) Chapter8/Transversalitysurjective_prod_of_ker_sup. 4. Local zero sets of such maps are submanifolds given by slice charts Chapter8/LocalSliceIsSliceSubmanifold.of_locally_preimage. By step 1’s principle their chart-level tangent space is \(\ker D \cap \ker D'\), and the injective map \(d(M \hookrightarrow \mathbb R^{K+1})\) preserves intersections Chapter8/TransversalityTransversality.tangentN_inter_of.

The transverse translate

Product-neighbourhood data for \(F = (N, v)\) (the Product Neighborhood Theorem) consist of \(G(x, u) = r\big(x + \sum_i \lambda(u)_i v_i(x)\big)\), with \(r\) the nearest-point retraction and \(\lambda\) a smooth clamp equal to the identity for \(|u| \le a_0\), and a radius \(\varepsilon \le a_0\) such that \(G\) is injective with bijective derivative on \(N \times B_\varepsilon\) Chapter7/TubeDataTubeData; such data exist for every \(F\) Chapter7/TubeDataexists_tubeData. The image \(V = G(N \times B_\varepsilon)\) is open, \(G\) has a smooth inverse on it, and \(\pi = \mathrm{pr}_2 \circ G^{-1} : V \to \mathbb R^p\) is the fibre coordinate.

Theorem. Let \(M\) be compact and nonempty, \(F = (N, v)\) a framed submanifold of dimension \(n\) and codimension \(p\), \((G, \varepsilon)\) product-neighbourhood data for \(F\), \(N' \subseteq M\) a submanifold given by slice charts (model \(\mathbb R^{n'}\), normal model \(\mathbb R^{p'}\)), and \(\delta > 0\). Then there is \(u \in \mathbb R^p\) with \(|u| < \delta\) and \(|u| < \varepsilon\) such that \(N_u = G(N \times \{u\})\) is a submanifold of \(M\) given by slice charts (model \(\mathbb R^n\), normal model \(\mathbb R^p\)) meeting \(N'\) transversally, \(x \mapsto G(x, u)\) is injective on \(N\), and \(|G(x,u) - x| < \delta\) for all \(x \in N\). Chapter8/Transversalityexists_transverse_deformation

The idea. \(N_u = \pi^{-1}(u)\) has tangent space \(\ker d\pi\), so it is transverse to \(N'\) at \(z\) exactly when \(d\pi_z(T_zN') = \mathbb R^p\), that is, when \(z\) is a regular point of \(\pi|_{N'}\). Sard’s theorem in Brown’s form supplies such regular values \(u\) arbitrarily near \(0\).

The proof as formalized. 1. For \(|u| < \varepsilon\), \(z \in N_u\) if and only if \(z \in V\) and \(\pi(z) = u\) Chapter8/Transversalitymem_range_tube_iff. From \(\pi \circ G = \mathrm{pr}_2\) near the tube, \(d\pi \circ dG = \mathrm{pr}_2\), so \(\pi\) is a submersion on \(V\) Chapter8/Transversalitymfd_fib_comp_G Chapter8/Transversalitysurjective_mfd_fib. Hence \(N_u\), the zero set of \(\pi - u\) on \(V\), is a submanifold with chart-level tangent space \(\ker d\pi_z\) Chapter8/TransversalityisSliceSubmanifold_range Chapter8/Transversalityrange_mfd_val_range_eq_ker. 2. As \(G(x, 0) = x\) and \(N\) is compact, some \(\rho_1 > 0\) gives \(|G(x,t) - x| < \delta\) for all \(x \in N\), \(|t| < \rho_1\). 3. Brown’s theorem for \(\pi\) on the open subset \(N' \cap V\) of \(N'\) gives a regular value \(u\) with \(|u| < \min(\delta, \varepsilon, \rho_1)\) Chapter2/Browndense_regularValues. 4. At \(z \in N_u \cap N'\), \(d\pi_z \circ d(N' \hookrightarrow M)_z\) is onto, and a second small lemma (if \(A \circ B\) is onto, then \(\ker A + \operatorname{range} B\) is everything) gives \(\ker d\pi_z + T_zN' = \mathbb R^m\) at chart level Chapter8/Transversalityker_sup_range_eq_top_of_surjective_comp. 5. Injectivity is that of \(G\) on the tube; if \(N = \varnothing\), \(u = 0\) will do.

What the book leaves implicit. “Deformed slightly” becomes a translate in the product neighbourhood with three quantitative properties. No framing of \(N_u\) is produced, and Problem 17 does not use this theorem.

Framed cobordism classes and disjoint unions

Reflexivity and the set of classes. Chapter 7 proved symmetry and transitivity, but reflexivity only for framed points Chapter7/ReachFramedCobordant.refl'. Rather than build \(N \times \mathbb R\) as a cobordism by hand, the formal proof writes \(F = \mathrm{Pont}(k, \mathrm{north}, ce)\) by Theorem C and applies the homotopy construction to the constant homotopy \((x, t) \mapsto k(x)\), in every dimension and codimension Chapter8/FramedOpsframedCobordant_refl. For \(M\) compact and nonempty, \(\Pi_{n,p}(M)\) is the quotient of the framed submanifolds of dimension \(n\) and codimension \(p\) by framed cobordism Chapter8/FramedOpsframedSetoid Chapter8/FramedOpsFramedClass. It is Milnor’s \(\Pi^p(M)\) when \(n + p = m\), and empty otherwise.

Proposition. If \(F = (N, v)\) and \(G = (N', v')\) are framed submanifolds of dimension \(n\) and codimension \(p\) with \(N \cap N' = \varnothing\), then \(F \sqcup G = (N \cup N', v \cup v')\) is a framed submanifold of dimension \(n\) and codimension \(p\). Chapter8/FramedOpsFramedSub.union

Near a point of \(N\) the union agrees with \(N\) on the open set \(M \setminus N'\) (\(N'\) is compact), where slice charts of \(N\) serve for the union Chapter8/FramedOpsisSliceSubmanifold_of_locally_eq Chapter8/FramedOpsisSliceSubmanifold_union_of_isClosed. There the two inclusions factor through each other, so the union has tangent space \(T_xN\); smoothness of \(v \cup v'\) is checked piecewise Chapter8/FramedOpstangentN_eq_of_inter_eq Chapter8/FramedOpscontMDiff_unionFun.

Proposition. Let \(X\) be a framed cobordism from \(F_0\) to \(F_1\) and \(Y\) one from \(G_0\) to \(G_1\), all of dimension \(n\) and codimension \(p\), with disjoint underlying sets, \(F_0 \cap G_0 = \varnothing\) and \(F_1 \cap G_1 = \varnothing\). Then \(X \cup Y\), with collar width \(\min(\varepsilon_X, \varepsilon_Y)\), is a framed cobordism from \(F_0 \sqcup G_0\) to \(F_1 \sqcup G_1\) with underlying set \(S_X \cup S_Y\). Chapter8/FramedOpsFramedCob.union Chapter8/FramedOpsframedCobordant_union

The argument is the same once underlying sets are known to be closed. They are not compact, but \(S = \{(x,t) \in S : 0 \le t \le 1\} \cup N_0 \times (-\infty, 0] \cup N_1 \times [1, \infty)\) is a union of three closed sets Chapter8/FramedOpsFramedCob.isClosed_S.

The set exposed. Chapter 7 asserts only that Pontryagin manifolds are cobordant; the following versions record the cobordism.

Homotopy construction, with its set. Let \(M\) be compact and nonempty, \(n + p = m\), \(0 < \varepsilon < \frac12\), and \(H : M \times \mathbb R \to S^p\) smooth with regular value \(z\), with \(H(x,t) = f(x)\) for \(t \le \varepsilon\) and \(H(x,t) = g(x)\) for \(t \ge 1 - \varepsilon\), where \(f, g\) are smooth with regular value \(z\); let \(b\) be linearly independent. Then there is a framed cobordism from \(\mathrm{Pont}(f, z, b)\) to \(\mathrm{Pont}(g, z, b)\) with underlying set exactly \(H^{-1}(z)\). Chapter8/FramedOpsexists_framedCob_of_homotopy

Lemma 1, with its set. The dual forms and the framed intersection

For a framing \(v(x) = (v_1, \dots, v_p)\) let \(Uc = \sum_j c_jv_j\). Then \(F \cap G = (N \cap N', w)\) is a framed submanifold of dimension \(r\) and codimension \(p + q\), and its framing vectors satisfy \[\big(\alpha_F(x)w_k(x),\ \alpha_G(x)w_k(x)\big) = k\text{-th standard basis vector of } \mathbb R^p \times \mathbb R^q.\] Chapter8/CohomotopyProductFramedSub.inter Chapter8/CohomotopyProductdual_inter_v

Transverse representatives

Theorem. Let \(M\) be compact and nonempty and \(p \ge 1\). For all \(c \in \Pi_{n,p}(M)\) and \(c' \in \Pi_{n',q}(M)\) there are \(F \in c\) and \(G \in c'\) meeting transversally. Chapter8/CohomotopyProductexists_transverse_rep

The idea. Keep \(G\), and replace \(F\) by the Pontryagin manifold of its Theorem-C map \(f\) at a value \(z\) regular both for \(f\) and for \(f|_{N'}\). The regular values of \(f\) form an open set containing north (\(M\) is compact) and those of \(f|_{N'}\) a dense set (Brown), so such \(z\) exist Chapter7/RegOpenisOpen_regularValues_sph.

The proof as formalized. With a positive basis \(b\) at north, \(F_0 = \mathrm{Pont}(f, \mathrm{north}, cb)\); take \(z\) as above, a positive basis \(e'\) at \(z\), and \(F = \mathrm{Pont}(f, z, e')\). Theorem A gives \(F \sim \mathrm{Pont}(f, \mathrm{north}, b)\), and Lemma 1 for \(cI\) gives \(F_0 \sim \mathrm{Pont}(f, \mathrm{north}, b)\) Chapter7/Lemma2framedCobordant_of_regularValues Chapter8/CohomotopyProductframedCobordant_diag. Where the formal proof departs from Milnor. The translate of V8.16 is not used: it carries no framing, and relating it to \(F\) would need a cobordism of its own. Moving the regular value gets the cobordism free from Theorem A.

A smooth map \(\mu : S^p \times S^q \to S^{p+q}\)

Informally, \(\mu\) plays the role of the collapse \(S^p \times S^q \to S^p \wedge S^q \cong S^{p+q}\); the formal proofs use only the three properties in the proposition below. Let \(\sigma(a) = (1 + a_{p+1})^{-1}(a_1, \dots, a_p)\) be stereographic projection from the south pole, \(\pi_{\rm std} : \mathbb R^k \to S^k\) the standard collapse map of §7 (north only at \(0\), south outside the ball of radius \(\frac12\)), and \(\Gamma : \mathbb R^p \times \mathbb R^q \to \mathbb R^{p+q}\) a linear isomorphism. Define \[\mu_\Gamma(a, b) = \pi_{\rm std}\big(E_\Gamma(\sigma(a), \sigma(b))\big) \ \text{ if } a, b \ne \text{south}, \qquad \mu_\Gamma(a,b) = \text{south otherwise},\] with \(E_\Gamma = (d\pi_{\rm std,0})^{-1} \circ \Gamma \circ (d\sigma_{\rm north} \times d\sigma_{\rm north})^{-1}\) Chapter8/CohomotopyProductsig Chapter8/CohomotopyProductmuE Chapter8/CohomotopyProductmu; \(d\sigma_{\rm north}\) is invertible because inverse stereographic projection is a right inverse of \(\sigma\) Chapter8/CohomotopyProductmfd_sig_comp_mfd_tau.

Proposition. \(\mu_\Gamma\) is smooth, \(\mu_\Gamma^{-1}(\text{north}) = \{(\text{north}, \text{north})\}\), and its derivative at \((\text{north}, \text{north})\), read in the charts at the north poles, is \(\Gamma\). The delicate point is smoothness where a coordinate is the south pole, and the formal proof makes it quantitative. If \(C\) is an antilipschitz constant of \(E_\Gamma\) and the last coordinate of \(a\) is below \(-1 + 1/(C^2+1)\), then \(|\sigma(a)| > C\), so \(|E_\Gamma(\sigma(a), \sigma(b))| \ge \frac12\) and \(\pi_{\rm std}\) already returns the south pole: \(\mu_\Gamma\) is locally constant there Chapter8/CohomotopyProductlt_norm_sig Chapter8/CohomotopyProducteventually_mu_eq_south.

The Pontryagin manifold of \(\mu \circ (f, g)\) is the framed intersection

Theorem. Let \(M\) be compact and nonempty; \(f : M \to S^p\) and \(g : M \to S^q\) smooth with north a regular value of both; \(b, b'\) linearly independent families in \(\mathbb R^p, \mathbb R^q\); \(n + p = m\), \(n' + q = m\), \(r + (p+q) = m\); and suppose \(\mathrm{Pont}(f, \mathrm{north}, b)\) and \(\mathrm{Pont}(g, \mathrm{north}, b')\) meet transversally. Then for every linear isomorphism \(\Gamma\), \(h = \mu_\Gamma \circ (f, g)\) is smooth, north is a regular value of \(h\), and \[\mathrm{Pont}(h, \mathrm{north}, \beta) = \mathrm{Pont}(f, \mathrm{north}, b) \cap \mathrm{Pont}(g, \mathrm{north}, b'), \qquad \beta = \big(\Gamma(b_1, 0), \dots, \Gamma(b_p, 0), \Gamma(0, b'_1), \dots, \Gamma(0, b'_q)\big).\] Chapter8/CohomotopyProductpontryagin_mu_eq Chapter8/CohomotopyProductmuBasis

The equality is of framed submanifolds: same set, same vector fields.

The idea. The ambient derivative of \(h\) is \(\Gamma\) applied to those of \(f\) and \(g\), and the ambient derivative of a Pontryagin map factors through the dual forms of its own framing. So \(A_h\) is an invertible matrix times \((\alpha_F, \alpha_G)\), and uniqueness of Pontryagin framing vectors does the rest.

The proof as formalized. 1. \(h^{-1}(\text{north}) = f^{-1}(\text{north}) \cap g^{-1}(\text{north})\), since \(\mu_\Gamma^{-1}(\text{north}) = \{(\text{north}, \text{north})\}\). 2. Along \(F = \mathrm{Pont}(f, \mathrm{north}, b)\), \(A_f(x) = B_b \circ \alpha_F(x)\) with \(B_bc = \sum_i c_ib_i\) Chapter8/CohomotopyProductAt_eq_basisCLM_dual: \(A_f\) kills vectors orthogonal to all \((f^*b)_i\), which span the range of \(A_f^*\) Chapter8/CohomotopyProductAt_eq_zero_of_forall_inner, and \(A_f(f^*b)_i = b_i\). 3. Near \(h^{-1}(\text{north})\), \(\tilde h\) is \(\mu_\Gamma\) in the product chart composed with \((\tilde f, \tilde g)\), so \(A_h(x) = \Gamma \circ (A_f(x), A_g(x)) = B \circ A(x)\) with \(B = \Gamma \circ (B_b \times B_{b'})\) invertible Chapter8/CohomotopyProductAt_mu Chapter8/CohomotopyProductAt_mu_eq. 4. \(A(x)\) is onto by transversality, so north is a regular value of \(h\). 5. \(w_k(x)\) is tangent to \(M\), normal to \(h^{-1}(\text{north})\), and \(A_h(x)w_k = Be_k = \beta_k\); the Pontryagin vector \((h^*\beta)_k(x)\) is the unique such vector Chapter7/PontFramepontV_eq_of.

Invariance and the product

Theorem. Let \(M\) be compact and nonempty, \(p, q \ge 1\), \(r + (p+q) = m\). If \(F \sim F_1\) (dimension \(n\), codimension \(p\)) and \(G \sim G_1\) (dimension \(n'\), codimension \(q\)), with \(F\) meeting \(G\) and \(F_1\) meeting \(G_1\) transversally, then \(F \cap G \sim F_1 \cap G_1\). Chapter8/CohomotopyProductframedCobordant_inter

The idea. Turn the cobordisms into homotopies (Theorem B, “if”), compose with \(\mu\), and turn back (Theorem B, “only if”). The friction is in the bases: Theorem B wants positive bases, while \(\beta\) is built from Theorem C’s rescaled bases. The formal proof chooses \(\Gamma\) to make \(\beta\) a positive diagonal rescaling of a positive basis.

The proof as formalized. 1. Take positive bases \(b, b', \gamma\) at the north poles of \(S^p, S^q, S^{p+q}\) Chapter7/Lemma2exists_posBasis. Theorem C gives \(F = \mathrm{Pont}(f, \mathrm{north}, cb)\), \(F_1 = \mathrm{Pont}(f_1, \mathrm{north}, c_1b)\), \(G = \mathrm{Pont}(g, \mathrm{north}, db')\), \(G_1 = \mathrm{Pont}(g_1, \mathrm{north}, d_1b')\), with \(c, c_1, d, d_1 > 0\). 2. \(\mathrm{Pont}(f, \mathrm{north}, b) \sim F \sim F_1 \sim \mathrm{Pont}(f_1, \mathrm{north}, b)\) by Lemma 1 at the ends, so \(f \simeq f_1\); likewise \(g \simeq g_1\) Chapter7/ThmAconvsmoothHomotopic_of_framedCobordant. 3. Let \(\Gamma(b_i, 0) = \gamma_i\) and \(\Gamma(0, b'_j) = \gamma_{p+j}\) Chapter8/CohomotopyProductgammaOf. Composing the homotopies with \(\mu_\Gamma\) joins \(h = \mu_\Gamma \circ (f, g)\) to \(h_1 = \mu_\Gamma \circ (f_1, g_1)\). 4. By the previous theorem, \(F \cap G = \mathrm{Pont}(h, \mathrm{north}, \beta)\) with \(\beta = (c\gamma_1, \dots, c\gamma_p, d\gamma_{p+1}, \dots, d\gamma_{p+q})\), and likewise \(F_1 \cap G_1\) with \(c_1, d_1\) Chapter8/CohomotopyProductmuBasis_gammaOf. 5. Lemma 1 for positive diagonal matrices replaces \(\beta\) by \(\gamma\) at both ends, and Theorem B with basis \(\gamma\) joins them Chapter7/ThmAframedCobordant_of_homotopic: \(F \cap G \sim \mathrm{Pont}(h, \mathrm{north}, \gamma) \sim \mathrm{Pont}(h_1, \mathrm{north}, \gamma) \sim F_1 \cap G_1\).

Theorem (V8.17). Let \(M\) be compact and nonempty, \(r + (p+q) = m\), \(p \ge 1\) and \(q \ge 1\). There is a map \(\Pi_{n,p}(M) \times \Pi_{n',q}(M) \to \Pi_{r,p+q}(M)\) sending \(([F], [G])\) to \([F \cap G]\) whenever \(F\) and \(G\) meet transversally. Any two maps with this property coincide (for this, \(p \ge 1\) suffices). Chapter8/CohomotopyProductexists_intersection_product Chapter8/CohomotopyProductintersection_product_unique

The map is defined by choosing transverse representatives of each pair of classes; invariance makes the value independent of the choice, and uniqueness holds because such representatives always exist. Neither \(\Gamma\) nor \(\mu\) enters the product, only its proof; the ordering, with the \(p\) vectors from \(F\) first, is built into \(w\).

Hidden hypotheses. \(p, q \ge 1\) (positive bases, Theorems A and B), and \(p + q \le m\) through \(r\). The case \(p + q > m\) is not stated, since no natural number \(r\) has \(r + p + q = m\). Informally it is trivial: then \(n + n' < m\), the parenthesis of V8.16 makes transverse representatives disjoint, and Milnor’s product is the class of \(\varnothing\).

V8.17′ Problem 17: the group \(\Pi^p(M)\) for \(2p \ge m + 2\)

Assume \(m + 2 \le 2p\). With \(n + p = m\) this gives \(p \ge 1\) and \(n + 1 < p\), so even an \((n+1)\)-manifold has image of dense complement in \(S^p\). That is the only way Milnor’s hypothesis \(p \ge \frac12 m + 1\) enters.

Room in the sphere

Lemma. If \(G\) is framed of dimension \(n\) and codimension \(p\) with \(n + 1 < p\), and \(H : M \times \mathbb R \to S^p\) is smooth, then \(S^p \setminus H(N_G \times \mathbb R)\) is dense. Chapter8/CohomotopyGroupdense_compl_range

By Brown’s theorem, the regular values of \(H\) on the \((n+1)\)-manifold \(N_G \times \mathbb R\) are dense, and none lies in the image, since no linear map out of \(\mathbb R^{n+1}\) is onto \(\mathbb R^p\). For a single image \(f(N_G)\) the lemma is applied to \(H = f \circ \mathrm{pr}_1\) Chapter8/CohomotopyGroupdense_compl_image, so that case too carries \(n + 1 < p\), though \(n < p\) would do.

Lemma. Let \(p \ge 1\), \(U \subseteq S^p\) open with \(\text{north} \in U\), and \(D \subseteq S^p\) dense. There are an orthonormal pair, with rotations \(r_\tau\) by angle \(\tau\) in its plane, and \(\theta_0 \ge 0\) with \(r_{\theta_0}(\text{north}) \in D\) and \(r_\tau(\text{north}) \in U\) for all \(\tau \in [0, \theta_0]\). Chapter8/CohomotopyGroupexists_arc

Take \(z \in D\) in a ball about north inside \(U\); the rotation path from north to \(z\) never gets farther from north than \(z\).

Lemma (rotation arc). Let \(M\) be compact and nonempty, \(n + p = m\), \(f\) smooth with regular value north, \(r_\tau\) as above with \(\theta_0 \ge 0\) and every \(r_\tau(\text{north})\), \(\tau \in [0, \theta_0]\), a regular value of \(f\), and \(b\) linearly independent. Then \(r_{\theta_0}(\text{north})\) is a regular value, \(dr_{\theta_0}b\) is independent, and there is a framed cobordism from \(\mathrm{Pont}(f, r_{\theta_0}(\text{north}), dr_{\theta_0}b)\) to \(\mathrm{Pont}(f, \text{north}, b)\) all of whose points \((x, t)\) have \(f(x) = r_\tau(\text{north})\) for some \(\tau \in [0, \theta_0]\). Chapter8/CohomotopyGroupexists_rotCob

The homotopy \((x,t) \mapsto r_{\theta_0\rho(t)}(f(x))\), with \(\rho\) a smooth transition from \(0\) (\(t \le \frac14\)) to \(1\) (\(t \ge \frac34\)), hits \(r_{\theta_0}(\text{north})\) exactly when \(f(x) = r_{\theta_0(1-\rho(t))}(\text{north})\), a point of the arc. There \(f\) is regular and the rotation is a diffeomorphism, so the \(x\)-derivative alone is onto Chapter8/CohomotopyGroupisRegularValue_rotHom, and the homotopy construction gives a cobordism with that preimage as its set. Its far end, \(\mathrm{Pont}(r_{\theta_0} \circ f, r_{\theta_0}(\text{north}), dr_{\theta_0}b)\), equals \(\mathrm{Pont}(f, \text{north}, b)\), the framing pulling back through \(dr_{\theta_0}^{-1}\) Chapter7/ComposepontV_comp. This is Milnor’s rotation proof of Lemma 2, with the set recorded and no orientation bookkeeping: the rotated basis is used as it is.

Disjoint representatives

Theorem. Let \(M\) be compact and nonempty and \(m + 2 \le 2p\). For framed \(F, G_1, G_2\) of dimension \(n\) and codimension \(p\) there is \(F'\) with \(F \sim F'\) and \(F'\) disjoint from \(G_1\) and \(G_2\). Hence any two classes in \(\Pi_{n,p}(M)\) have disjoint representatives. Chapter8/CohomotopyGroupexists_cobordant_disjoint Chapter8/CohomotopyGroupexists_disjoint_rep

Write \(F = \mathrm{Pont}(f, \mathrm{north}, ce)\). The complement of the compact set \(f(N_{G_1}) \cup f(N_{G_2})\) is dense, so an arc of regular values of \(f\) runs from north to some \(z\) outside it, and the rotation arc gives \(F \sim \mathrm{Pont}(f, z, dr(ce))\), whose set \(f^{-1}(z)\) misses both. Two submanifolds are avoided at once because associativity and independence each need it.

Independence of the sum

Theorem (V8.17′). Let \(M\) be compact and nonempty and \(m + 2 \le 2p\). If \(F \sim F_1\) and \(G \sim G_1\), all of dimension \(n\) and codimension \(p\), with \(F \cap G = \varnothing\) and \(F_1 \cap G_1 = \varnothing\), then \(F \sqcup G \sim F_1 \sqcup G_1\). The idea. Never move both pieces at once. Choose \(G' \sim G\) disjoint from \(F\) and \(F_1\); move \(G\) to \(G'\) with \(F\) fixed, \(F\) to \(F_1\) with \(G'\) fixed, and \(G'\) to \(G_1\) with \(F_1\) fixed Chapter8/CohomotopyGroupframedCobordant_union_of_framedCobordant'. Each move is an instance of the following lemma.

Lemma (one component). Let \(M\) be compact and nonempty, \(m + 2 \le 2p\), \(F \sim F_1\), and \(G\) disjoint from \(F\) and from \(F_1\), all of dimension \(n\) and codimension \(p\). Then \(F \sqcup G \sim F_1 \sqcup G\). Chapter8/CohomotopyGroupunion_left_of_framedCobordant

The proof as formalized. 1. With a positive basis \(b\) at north, Theorem C gives \(F = \mathrm{Pont}(f, \mathrm{north}, cb)\) and \(F_1 = \mathrm{Pont}(f_1, \mathrm{north}, c_1b)\). Lemma 1 and Theorem B give \(f \simeq f_1\), via a homotopy \(H\) constant for \(t \le \frac14\) and \(t \ge \frac34\) Chapter7/HomotopySmoothHomotopic.exists_const_near_ends. 2. The common regular values of \(f\) and \(f_1\) outside \(f(N_G) \cup f_1(N_G)\) form an open set \(U\) containing north, since \(f^{-1}(\text{north}) = N_F\) and \(f_1^{-1}(\text{north}) = N_{F_1}\) miss \(N_G\). The regular values of \(H\) outside \(H(N_G \times \mathbb R)\) form a dense set \(D\), as \(H(N_G \times \mathbb R) = H(N_G \times [0,1])\) is compact with dense complement. Take an arc from north to \(z \in D\) inside \(U\). 3. Four cobordisms follow, each with set disjoint from \(N_G \times \mathbb R\). \(X_1\), from \(\mathrm{Pont}(f, z, dr(cb))\) to \(F\), is the rotation arc for \(f\), lying over \(f^{-1}(\text{arc})\), which misses \(N_G\). \(X_2\), to \(\mathrm{Pont}(f_1, z, dr(cb))\), is the homotopy construction for \(H\), with set \(H^{-1}(z)\). \(X_3\), to \(\mathrm{Pont}(f_1, z, dr(c_1b))\), is Lemma 1 for \((c/c_1)I\), with set \(f_1^{-1}(z) \times \mathbb R\). \(X_4\), to \(F_1\), is the rotation arc for \(f_1\). 4. The product cobordism \(Y\) from \(G\) to itself has set exactly \(N_G \times \mathbb R\), by Theorem C and the homotopy construction for a constant homotopy Chapter8/CohomotopyGroupexists_framedCob_prod. Uniting each \(X_i\) with \(Y\) and chaining gives \(F \sqcup G \sim F_1 \sqcup G\) Chapter8/FramedOpsframedCobordant_union.

What the book leaves implicit. The hint “use the disjoint union operation” hides that a cobordism from \(F\) to \(F_1\) may run through \(G\). The formal proof rules this out by rebuilding the cobordism from a homotopy and a well-chosen regular value, recording where each piece lies; the dimension hypothesis pays for the sweep \(H(N_G \times \mathbb R)\).

The model maps, all south for \(|s| \ge r_0\), are: - the cancelling map \(\kappa(s) = \mathrm{col}_c\big((s_1^2 - a^2)e_1 + (s - s_1e_1)\big)\), with zeros \(\pm ae_1\) and derivative \(c\,T_{\sigma a}\) at \(\sigma ae_1\), \(\sigma = \pm 1\) Chapter8/CohomotopyGroupcan0 Chapter8/CohomotopyGroupcan0_eq_north_iff Chapter8/CohomotopyGrouphasMFDerivAt_can0; - the folded maps \(\phi_\sigma(s) = \mathrm{col}_c\big(T_{\sigma a}(s - \sigma ae_1)\big)\), with the single zero \(\sigma ae_1\) and the same derivative \(c\,T_{\sigma a}\) there Chapter8/CohomotopyGroupfoldΦ_eq_north_iff Chapter8/CohomotopyGrouphasMFDerivAt_foldΦ.

The proof as formalized. 1. \(P, Q\) are the Pontryagin manifolds, at north with basis \(ce\), of the tube maps of \(\phi_+, \phi_-\): the parallel copies \(G(N \times \{\pm ae_1\})\), disjoint as \(ae_1 \ne -ae_1\). 2. \(P \sqcup Q\) equals the Pontryagin manifold of the tube map of \(\kappa\) Chapter8/CohomotopyGrouppontryagin_can0_eq_union. The sets agree. Where \(\pi(z) = \sigma ae_1\), the tube maps of \(\kappa\) and \(\phi_\sigma\) have the same derivative, since a tube map composed with \(G\) is \(\Phi \circ \mathrm{pr}_2\) and \(dG\) is invertible Chapter8/CohomotopyGroupmfd_tubeMap_eq. And a Pontryagin framing depends only on the value and derivative at the point, for \(A_f(x)\) kills \((T_xM)^\perp\) and agrees with \(df_x\) on \(T_xM\) Chapter8/CohomotopyGroupAt_eq_of_mfd_eq Chapter8/CohomotopyGrouppontryagin_v_eq_of_mfd_eq. 3. \(P \sqcup Q \sim \varnothing\). §7’s cancellation family \(\mathrm{col}_c\big((s_1^2 - a^2\rho(t))e_1 + (s - s_1e_1)\big)\), with \(\rho = 1\) for \(t \le \frac14\), \(\rho = -1\) for \(t \ge \frac34\), \(|\rho| \le 1\) and \(\rho' \ne 0\) at zeros of \(\rho\) Chapter7/CancelMapexists_rho, gives a tube family with north regular: where \(\rho(t) = 0\) the zero is \(s = 0\), \(T_0\) kills \(e_1\), and the \(t\)-derivative supplies that direction. At \(t = 1\) north is not attained (\(s_1^2 = -a^2\)), and the homotopy construction gives the cobordism to \(\varnothing\) Chapter8/CohomotopyGroupframedCobordant_can0. 4. \(F \sim P\) and \(F^- \sim Q\) via the moving family \(\Phi_t(s) = \mathrm{col}_c\big(T_{l(t)}(s - \gamma(t))\big)\), with \(l(t) = \sigma\big(\frac12 + (a - \frac12)\rho_0(t)\big)\), \(\gamma(t) = \rho_0(t)\,\sigma ae_1\) and \(\rho_0\) a transition from \(0\) to \(1\) Chapter8/CohomotopyGrouplPath Chapter8/CohomotopyGroupγPath. At \(t = 1\) this is \(\phi_\sigma\); at \(t = 0\) it is \(\mathrm{col}_c(T_{\sigma/2}s)\), the plain collapse for \(\sigma = 1\) and the collapse after reversing \(s_1\) for \(\sigma = -1\). As \(G(x, se_i) = r(x + sv_i(x))\), the time-\(0\) tube map equals \(\mathrm{col}_c(se_i)\) along \(s \mapsto r(x + s\sigma_iv_i(x))\), where \(\sigma_1 = \sigma\) and \(\sigma_i = 1\) otherwise Chapter8/CohomotopyGroupTcan_half_line. §7’s identification lemma then makes its Pontryagin manifold \((N, (\sigma v_1, v_2, \dots, v_p))\), which is \(F\) or \(F^-\) Chapter8/CohomotopyGrouppontryagin_tubeMap_eq Chapter7/Identifypontryagin_eq_of_collapse. Since \(|T_{l(t)}z| \ge 2a|z|\) and \(|\gamma(t)| \le a\), the family is south for \(|s| \ge r_0\) Chapter8/CohomotopyGroupnorm_Tcan_ge Chapter8/CohomotopyGroupmoveΦ_south; each slice has derivative \(c\,T_{l(t)}\) at its only zero \(\gamma(t)\), so the homotopy construction applies Chapter8/CohomotopyGroupframedCobordant_fold.

The moving family translates the zero from \(0\) to \(\sigma ae_1\) while rescaling the \(e_1\)-direction from \(\sigma\) to \(2\sigma a\), exactly the derivative of \(\kappa\) there. That match makes step 2 an equality rather than one more cobordism.

The group as stated

Negation is defined through a chosen representative, \(-[F] = [F_c^-]\) for some \(F_c \sim F\) Chapter8/CohomotopyGroupcohomotopyNeg. That \([F^-]\) depends only on \([F]\) is never proved by a cobordism. It follows from uniqueness of inverses: if \([F_0] = [F]\), then \([F_0^-] = [F_0^-] + [F] + [F^-] = [F_0^-] + [F_0] + [F^-] = [F^-]\) Chapter8/CohomotopyGroupcohomotopyNeg_mk.

Theorem (V8.17′, the group). Let \(M \subseteq \mathbb R^{K+1}\) be a compact, nonempty submanifold of dimension \(m\) given by slice charts, and let \(n + p = m\), \(m + 2 \le 2p\) and \(p \ge 1\). Then \(\Pi_{n,p}(M)\) is an abelian group in which \([F] + [G] = [F \sqcup G]\) for disjoint representatives, the zero is \([\varnothing_{n,p}]\), and \(-[F] = [F^-]\). Chapter8/CohomotopyGroupcohomotopyGroup Chapter8/CohomotopyGroupcohomotopyGroup_add Chapter8/CohomotopyGroupcohomotopyGroup_neg

The structure is a definition depending on the three hypotheses, not a global instance; three lemmas identify its addition, zero and negation Chapter8/CohomotopyGroupcohomotopyGroup_zero. The hypothesis \(p \ge 1\) follows from \(m + 2 \le 2p\) and only names the first framing vector. The hypothesis \(n + p = m\) is genuine: without it there is no empty framed submanifold, indeed no class at all.

What the formalization taught us

  • Reflexivity is not free. Chapter 7 had it only for framed points; in every codimension the formal proof obtains it from Theorem C and the homotopy construction Chapter8/FramedOpsframedCobordant_refl.
  • Cobordisms are closed, not compact. They extend over all of \(M \times \mathbb R\), so disjoint unions need a proof that underlying sets are closed Chapter8/FramedOpsFramedCob.isClosed_S.
  • The hints hide sets. Disjointness of cobordisms concerns sets, so Lemma 1, the homotopy construction and the rotation argument of Lemma 2 were re-proved with the set recorded Chapter8/FramedOpsexists_framedCob_of_homotopy Chapter8/CohomotopyGroupexists_rotCob.
  • Move the regular value, not the submanifold. Transverse and disjoint representatives both come from a new regular value of a Theorem-C map; the translate of Problem 16 goes unused Chapter8/CohomotopyProductexists_transverse_cobordant.
  • Identifications are exact. The Pontryagin manifolds of \(\mu \circ (f, g)\) and of the cancelling map are the framed intersection and the union of the folded copies on the nose, because Pontryagin framings are determined by the derivative Chapter8/CohomotopyProductpontryagin_mu_eq Chapter8/CohomotopyGroupAt_eq_of_mfd_eq.
  • A choice of \(\Gamma\) absorbs orientations, reducing them to positive diagonal rescalings Chapter8/CohomotopyProductmuBasis_gammaOf.
  • Hidden hypotheses and scope. The product assumes \(p, q \ge 1\) (transverse representatives and uniqueness only \(p \ge 1\)) and is stated only for \(p + q \le m\) Chapter8/CohomotopyProductexists_intersection_product. The group needs \(n + p = m\); its \(p \ge 1\) is redundant Chapter8/CohomotopyGroupcohomotopyGroup. Milnor’s parenthesis carries two equations that its proof does not need Chapter8/Transversalityinter_eq_empty_of_transverse.
  • Where \(2p \ge m + 2\) is spent. Only on disjoint representatives and independence of the sum; the cancelling pair works for every \(p \ge 1\) Chapter8/CohomotopyGroupunion_left_of_framedCobordant Chapter8/CohomotopyGroupexists_cancel_pair.
  • Negation comes free. That reversing the first framing vector respects framed cobordism follows from uniqueness of inverses Chapter8/CohomotopyGroupcohomotopyNeg_mk.
