Part XII. The Appendix: one-manifolds (Milnor pp. 54–56)

Milnor’s Appendix proves one theorem, that every smooth connected one-manifold is diffeomorphic to the circle or to an interval, and draws from it the one corollary the book uses: the boundary points of a compact 1-manifold come in pairs, the two ends of an arc (§§2, 4, 5). This part has two halves, written in that order and set out in that order.

The first half (V.A, V.A′) is the corollary alone, proved without the classification and for a merely topological 1-manifold with boundary, which is stronger than the book in the hypothesis and weaker in the conclusion. It keeps Milnor’s idea, to parametrize as far as possible, and changes the three tools that carry it: arc-length parametrizations become arbitrary homeomorphisms onto intervals; Milnor’s lemma on overlapping parametrizations becomes a lemma about arcs starting at a boundary point, the only kind ever extended, so no circle appears; and the maximal parametrization is reached by a finite induction over a cover by chart arcs. A short second file connects the result to the manifolds with boundary produced by Lemma 4 of §2. This is the half that Parts I to III depend on, and nothing else in the book does.

The second half (V.B to V.J) is Milnor’s theorem itself, in nine stages, this time with his arc-length parametrizations and in a sharper form than he states: a connected Hausdorff σ-compact smooth one-manifold is diffeomorphic to exactly one of the circle, \([0,1]\), \([0,\infty)\) and \(\mathbb R\), the case being read off from whether it is compact and whether its boundary is empty. It ends by proving the corollary a second time, as Milnor does, from the classification, with the two boundary points of a component identified as the two ends of one parametrization rather than counted modulo two. The first half is left in place untouched, because Chapters 2 and 4 cite it; the second is used by nothing in the book, and is here because the book states it — and by one thing outside the book, the dimension of a non-orientable manifold in Part VII.

Map. - Appendix/OneManifold: V.A; arcs, the end lemma for two arcs, the overlap of an arc from a boundary point with any arc, gluing, the finite induction to a closed arc, the pairing of boundary points. - Appendix/HalfSpace: V.A′; the half-space over a zero space is a half-line, and the half-slice submanifolds of Chapter 2 satisfy the hypotheses of V.A. - Appendix/TwoComponents: V.B; Milnor’s Appendix Lemma 1, the topological half, with the circle case counted. - Appendix/Smooth/Setup, Appendix/Smooth/SmoothArc: V.C, V.D; the one-dimensional model and smooth arcs. - Appendix/Smooth/LengthElement, Appendix/Smooth/ArcLength: V.E; a Riemannian metric in dimension one, and unit-speed arcs. - Appendix/Smooth/Affine: V.F; Lemma 1 in full, and the extension theorem that preserves the coordinate. - Appendix/Smooth/Compact, Appendix/Smooth/Circle, Appendix/Smooth/NonCompact: V.G, V.H, V.I; Milnor’s four cases. - Appendix/Smooth/Main: V.J; the theorem, its six exclusions, and the boundary count drawn from it.

V.A The boundary count for compact topological 1-manifolds

Theorem (V.A). Let \(H\) be a topological space and \(\varphi : H \to [0,\infty)\) a homeomorphism. Let \(M\) be a compact Hausdorff space with a charted-space structure modelled on \(H\): an atlas of homeomorphisms from open subsets of \(M\) onto open subsets of \(H\), and for each point a chosen chart of the atlas whose domain contains it. Let \(B \subseteq M\) be such that, for every chart \(e\) of the atlas and every \(x\) in the domain of \(e\), \[x \in B \iff \varphi(e(x)) = 0 .\] Then \(B\) is finite and has an even number of points. Appendix/OneManifoldeven_ncard_boundary

The condition on \(B\) is called boundary compatibility, and \(\varphi(e(x))\) is the coordinate of \(x\) in the chart \(e\) Appendix/OneManifoldBoundaryCompatible Appendix/OneManifoldcoord.

Stronger than the book. Milnor’s manifolds are smooth subsets of \(\mathbb R^k\). Here \(M\) is abstract, and a Mathlib charted space imposes no compatibility between its charts, so \(M\) is any compact Hausdorff topological 1-manifold with boundary: no smooth structure, no embedding, no second countability, and no derivative anywhere in the proof. The model is any space homeomorphic to \([0,\infty)\), so that the half-space models of Chapter 2 fit without re-charting Appendix/HalfSpacehalfSpaceHomeomorph.

Weaker than the book. This theorem does not state the classification. On the way, its proof shows that the component of a boundary point is the homeomorphic image of a closed interval whose two ends are its only boundary points Appendix/OneManifoldexists_closed_arc Appendix/OneManifoldIsFrom.source_eq_of_mem. Components without boundary points are never examined, since they contribute nothing to the count, and the circle case therefore never arises. The classification itself is V.J, in the second half of this part, and V.J draws the boundary count from it a second time; but that is a statement about smooth one-manifolds, so it neither subsumes V.A nor is subsumed by it.

What the book leaves implicit. Milnor’s boundary, the points that charts send to \(\partial H^m\), is tacitly independent of the chart. The formal statement takes a set \(B\) and assumes that every chart sends exactly \(B\) to \(0\); the proof uses this only for the chosen chart at each point Appendix/OneManifoldexists_arc_of_mem_boundary Appendix/OneManifoldexists_arc_of_notMem_boundary. Hausdorffness, automatic in \(\mathbb R^k\), is a genuine hypothesis, as an example outside the formal text shows: two copies of \([0,1]\) glued along \([0,1)\) form a compact space, locally homeomorphic to open subsets of \([0,\infty)\), whose evident charts send exactly \(0\) and the two copies of \(1\) to \(0\). It has three boundary points.

The idea. Start at a boundary point \(p\) with a chart arc \([0,\varepsilon) \to M\) and extend it. While its interval is half-open, its domain is not the whole component of \(p\), so some chart arc contains a frontier point of the domain, and the two glue to an arc from \(p\) containing both. Finitely many chart arcs cover \(M\) and each gluing swallows a new one, so eventually the interval is closed, \([0,c]\); the domain is then the component, and its far end is the only other boundary point there. So “the other end of my component” is a fixed-point-free involution of \(B\). The one hard lemma: the overlap of an arc from a boundary point with any arc is connected Appendix/OneManifoldoverlap_ordConnected.

The proof as formalized.

1. Arcs, and the finiteness of \(B\)

An arc of \((M,B)\) is a homeomorphism \(A\) from an open set \(U_A \subseteq M\) onto a bounded interval \(T_A \subseteq \mathbb R\) with more than one point, such that for \(x \in U_A\) \[x \in B \iff A(x) \notin \operatorname{int} T_A\] Appendix/OneManifoldArc. As \(\operatorname{int} T_A = (\inf T_A, \sup T_A)\) Appendix/OneManifoldinterior_target, the points of \(B\) in \(U_A\) are those whose coordinate is an endpoint of \(T_A\) lying in \(T_A\). Boundedness makes \(\inf T_A\) and \(\sup T_A\) real numbers, and every limit argument below is about them. An arc can be reversed, \(x \mapsto -A(x)\) onto \(-T_A\) Appendix/OneManifoldneg. An arc from \(p\) has \(p \in U_A\), \(A(p) = 0\) and \(0 \in T_A \subseteq [0,\infty)\) Appendix/OneManifoldIsFrom; its interval is \([0,c)\) or \([0,c]\), with \(c = \sup T_A > 0\) Appendix/OneManifoldIsFrom.target_eq.

Arcs come from charts. Restrict a chart to the points whose coordinate lies in a bounded interval \(J \subseteq [0,\infty)\) with more than one point. If the model points with coordinate in \(J\) form an open subset of \(H\) inside the chart’s image, and no point of \(J\) other than \(0\) is an endpoint of \(J\), the result is an arc with interval \(J\), by boundary compatibility of the chart Appendix/OneManifoldarcOfChart. The chart at \(y\) contains all model points whose coordinate is within some \(\varepsilon > 0\) of that of \(y\) Appendix/OneManifoldexists_radius. At \(p \in B\) the coordinate is \(0\), and \(J = [0,\varepsilon)\) gives an arc from \(p\); at \(y \notin B\) the coordinate \(t_0\) is positive, and \(J = (t_0 - \delta, t_0 + \delta)\) with \(\delta = \min(\varepsilon, t_0)\) gives an arc around \(y\) with open interval, whose domain misses \(B\) Appendix/OneManifoldexists_arc_of_mem_boundary Appendix/OneManifoldexists_arc_of_notMem_boundary.

So \(B\) is closed Appendix/OneManifoldisClosed_boundary, and an arc from \(p\) with interval \([0,\varepsilon)\) meets \(B\) only in \(p\) Appendix/OneManifoldboundary_inter_source_eq. As \(B\) is compact, finitely many such arcs cover it, and \(B\) is finite Appendix/OneManifoldfinite_boundary. This half of the conclusion uses neither Hausdorffness nor gluing.

2. Two arcs: monotone transitions and the end lemma

Fix arcs \(A\) and \(A'\). The overlap in \(A\)’s coordinate, \(S = A(U_A \cap U_{A'})\), is relatively open in \(T_A\), and the transition \(\tau = A' \circ A^{-1} : S \to T_{A'}\) is continuous and injective Appendix/OneManifoldoverlap Appendix/OneManifoldtrans Appendix/OneManifoldoverlap_relOpen. Where the formal proof departs from Milnor. Milnor differentiates: arc length forces \(\tau' = \pm 1\), so the graph of \(\tau\) consists of segments of slope \(\pm 1\). The formal proof uses only that a continuous injection on an interval is strictly monotone Appendix/OneManifoldstrictMonoOn_or_strictAntiOn_of_ordConnected, and it names the components of \(S\) without topology, through the hull \[\operatorname{hull}_S(t_0) = \{\, t : [t, t_0] \subseteq S \,\},\] the largest interval in \(S\) through \(t_0\), with \([t,t_0]\) the segment between the two points in either order Appendix/OneManifoldhull. Two hulls are equal or disjoint, and the hulls of a relatively open subset of an interval are relatively open Appendix/OneManifoldhull_eq_or_disjoint Appendix/OneManifoldhull_relOpen. Call an endpoint of a hull free (our term) if it lies in \(T_A\) but not in \(S\).

The end lemma. Let \(\beta = \sup K\) be a free endpoint of a hull \(K\). As \(s \uparrow \beta\) in \(K\), \(\tau(s)\) converges monotonically to \(L = \sup \tau(K)\) or \(L = \inf \tau(K)\), as \(\tau\) increases or decreases on \(K\) Appendix/OneManifoldtendsto_sSup_of_monotoneOn Appendix/OneManifoldtendsto_sInf_of_antitoneOn, and \(L \notin T_{A'}\) Appendix/OneManifoldend_lemma. Indeed \(y = A^{-1}(\beta)\) lies in \(U_A \setminus U_{A'}\). If \(L \in T_{A'}\), then \(A^{-1}(s) \to y\) by continuity of \(A^{-1}\) at \(\beta\), while \(A^{-1}(s) = A'^{-1}(\tau(s)) \to A'^{-1}(L)\) by continuity of \(A'^{-1}\) at \(L\); limits in \(M\) are unique, so \(y = A'^{-1}(L) \in U_{A'}\), a contradiction. The interval \(T_{A'}\) contains the values \(\tau(s)\), all on one side of \(L\), but not \(L\), so it lies entirely on that side Appendix/OneManifoldlt_of_end_lemma_upper. Say the free end reaches the upper edge of \(T_{A'}\) if \(L\) is a strict upper bound of \(T_{A'}\) (so \(L = \sup T_{A'} \notin T_{A'}\)), and the lower edge likewise; every free end, left or right, reaches an edge Appendix/OneManifoldend_right Appendix/OneManifoldend_left. This is Milnor’s remark that the segments of the graph cannot end inside the rectangle \(I \times J\), and it is the first use of Hausdorffness.

Clash. Free ends of two distinct hulls cannot reach the same edge Appendix/OneManifoldclash_upper Appendix/OneManifoldclash_lower: the images of the hulls would be intervals with the same unattained supremum (or infimum), such intervals meet Appendix/OneManifoldinter_nonempty_of_sSup_eq, and injectivity of \(\tau\) turns a common value into a common point. Nor can a free end reach an edge that belongs to \(T_{A'}\) Appendix/OneManifoldnot_upper_of_sSup_mem Appendix/OneManifoldnot_lower_of_sInf_mem. Together these give Milnor’s count of at most one segment ending on each edge of the rectangle.

3. The overlap with an arc from a boundary point is an interval

Lemma. Let \(M\) be Hausdorff, \(A\) an arc with \(p \in U_A\), \(A(p) = 0\) and \(T_A = [0,c)\) for some \(c > 0\), and \(A'\) any arc. Then \(A(U_A \cap U_{A'})\) is an interval. Appendix/OneManifoldoverlap_ordConnected

First, each hull of \(S\) has at least two points, and an endpoint of a hull other than \(0\) and \(c\) is free: if it lay in \(S\) it would lie in the hull, which, being relatively open, would extend past it Appendix/OneManifoldhull_nontrivial Appendix/OneManifoldsSup_hull_notMem Appendix/OneManifoldsInf_hull_notMem. Second, \(p \in B\) Appendix/OneManifoldp_mem_boundary, so if \(0 \in S\) then \(\tau(0) = A'(p)\) is an endpoint of \(T_{A'}\) belonging to \(T_{A'}\): \(p\) occupies an edge, which no free end can reach Appendix/OneManifoldtrans_zero_eq_sInf_or_sSup.

Now suppose \(t_1 < u < t_2\) with \(t_1, t_2 \in S\) and \(u \notin S\), and let \(K_1, K_2\) be the hulls of \(t_1, t_2\), so that \(K_1 < u < K_2\). The right end of \(K_1\) is at most \(u < c\) and the left end of \(K_2\) at least \(u > 0\), so both are free. The left end of \(K_1\) is free, or else it is \(0\) and \(0 \in S\). In the first case \(K_1\) has two free ends, which reach opposite edges since \(\tau\) is monotone on \(K_1\), and the free left end of \(K_2\) must share an edge with one of them: a clash. In the second case \(p\) occupies one edge, so the free right end of \(K_1\) and the free left end of \(K_2\) both reach the other: again a clash Appendix/OneManifoldoverlap_ordConnected. In Milnor’s picture the graph of \(\tau\) lies in the rectangle \(T_A \times T_{A'}\), with four edges. The formal count needs only the two edges of \(T_{A'}\): the right edge of \(T_A\) is never examined, and the left one enters only through the corner \((0, \tau(0))\), which the boundary point \(p\) pins to an edge of \(T_{A'}\). Milnor’s two-component case, the circle, cannot occur.

4. Gluing two arcs

Lemma. Let \(M\) be Hausdorff, \(A\) an arc from \(p\) with \(T_A = [0,c)\), \(c > 0\), \(A'\) an arc, and \(x \in U_{A'} \setminus U_A\) a point of the closure of \(U_A\). Then there is an arc \(\tilde A\) from \(p\) with \(U_A \cup U_{A'} \subseteq U_{\tilde A}\). Appendix/OneManifoldexists_extension

Normalization. Put \(d = A'(x)\) and \(S' = A'(U_A \cap U_{A'}) = \tau(S)\), an interval. By injectivity \(d \notin S'\), and \(d \in \overline{S'}\) because \(x\) is a limit of points of \(U_A \cap U_{A'}\) and \(A'\) is continuous at \(x\). So \(S'\) lies on one side of \(d\); after reversing \(A'\) if necessary Appendix/OneManifoldoverlap_neg_left, \(S' < d = \sup S'\). The normalized case Appendix/OneManifoldexists_extension_aux runs as follows, with \(\sigma = A \circ A'^{-1} : S' \to S\) the inverse of \(\tau\).

  1. The overlap sits at the far end of \(T_A\). The end \(d\) of \(S'\) is free for the pair \((A', A)\), so \(\sigma(t)\) reaches an edge of \(T_A = [0,c)\) as \(t \uparrow d\). The lower edge is excluded because \(0 \in T_A\); hence \(\sigma\) is increasing, \(\sup S = c\), and \(\tau\) is increasing Appendix/OneManifoldend_right.
  2. Below \(d\), everything is overlap. If \(\inf S \notin S\), it is a free end, and \(\inf S'\) is a strict lower bound of \(T_{A'}\) Appendix/OneManifoldend_left. If \(\inf S \in S\), then \(\inf S = 0\) (a positive one would be free), and \(\tau(0)\) is an endpoint of \(T_{A'}\) lying in \(T_{A'}\), the lower one since \(\tau(0) < \tau(s) < d\) for \(s > 0\) in \(S\) Appendix/OneManifoldtrans_zero_eq_sInf_or_sSup. Either way every \(t \in T_{A'}\) below \(d\) lies in \(S'\), so a point \(y \in U_{A'}\) lies in \(U_A\) exactly when \(A'(y) < d\).
  3. The new arc. With \(c'' = c + \sup T_{A'} - d\), define on \(U_A \cup U_{A'}\) and on \(T = \{\, t \ge 0 : t < c \text{ or } d + t - c \in T_{A'} \,\}\) \[\tilde A(y) = \begin{cases} A(y), & y \in U_A,\\ c + A'(y) - d, & y \notin U_A,\end{cases} \qquad \tilde A^{-1}(t) = \begin{cases} A^{-1}(t), & t < c,\\ A'^{-1}(d + t - c), & t \ge c;\end{cases}\] \(T\) is an interval with \((0,c'') \subseteq T \subseteq [0,c'']\) Appendix/OneManifoldexists_extension_aux. Milnor extends \(\tau\) to an affine map \(L\) and pieces \(f\) together with \(g \circ L\). Here \(\tau\) is only monotone, so beyond \(c\) the formal proof uses \(A'^{-1}\) composed with the translation \(t \mapsto d + t - c\), which agrees with \(\tau\) only in the limit at the seam.
  4. Continuity at the seam. On \(U_{A'}\), \(\tilde A = G \circ A'\) with \(G = \sigma\) below \(d\) and \(G(t) = c + t - d\) from \(d\) on. \(G\) is continuous on \(T_{A'}\): below \(d\) it is \(\sigma\) on the neighbourhood \(S'\) (step 2), \(\sigma(t) \to c = G(d)\) as \(t \uparrow d\) (step 1), and above \(d\) it is affine Appendix/OneManifoldtendsto_sSup_of_monotoneOn. As \(U_A\) and \(U_{A'}\) are open, \(\tilde A\) is continuous on their union. Dually, at \(c\): \(S\) contains \((\inf S, c)\), and there \(\tilde A^{-1}(s) = A'^{-1}(\tau(s)) \to A'^{-1}(d) = x = \tilde A^{-1}(c)\) Appendix/OneManifoldexists_extension_aux.
  5. The rest. Step 2 decides the branches, and the inverse identities follow. A point of \(U_A\) is in \(B\) iff \(A(y) = 0\) iff \(\tilde A(y) \notin (0,c'')\); a point of \(U_{A'} \setminus U_A\) has \(A'(y) \ge d > \inf T_{A'}\), so it is in \(B\) iff \(A'(y) = \sup T_{A'}\) iff \(\tilde A(y) = c''\) Appendix/OneManifoldexists_extension_aux.

At some 370 lines this is the longest proof of the part: the formal cost of Milnor’s “\(f\) and \(g \circ L\) piece together to yield the required extension” once the pieces are merely monotone.

5. The closed arc

Proposition. Under the hypotheses of V.A, for every \(p \in B\) there is an arc from \(p\) whose interval contains its supremum, that is, equals \([0,c]\). Appendix/OneManifoldexists_closed_arc

Choose for each \(y \in M\) a chart arc containing \(y\); by compactness finitely many of them, indexed by a finite set \(s\), cover \(M\). Start from the arc from \(p\) with interval \([0,\varepsilon)\) and induct on the number of \(z \in s\) whose arc’s domain is not contained in the current domain \(U_A\). If \(\sup T_A \in T_A\) we are done. Otherwise \(T_A = [0,c)\), and \(U_A\) is not the whole component of \(p\): the component is closed, hence compact, so if it were \(U_A\) then \(T_A = A(U_A)\) would be compact and contain \(c\). As \(U_A\) is an open proper subset of this connected component and contains \(p\), some \(x \notin U_A\) lies in its closure Appendix/OneManifoldexists_mem_closure_of_ne. This \(x\) lies in the domain of the cover arc of some \(y \in s\), and gluing gives an arc from \(p\) whose domain contains both domains. The count drops: \(y\) was not absorbed before (its domain contains \(x\)) and is now. Milnor extends to a maximal parametrization instead; no maximality principle is needed here.

A closed arc fills its component Appendix/OneManifoldIsFrom.source_eq_of_mem: its domain \(A^{-1}([0,c])\) is compact, hence closed because \(M\) is Hausdorff (the second use), and it is open, connected and contains \(p\) Appendix/OneManifoldisPreconnected_source. By the boundary condition, \[B \cap \operatorname{comp}(p) = \{\, p,\ A^{-1}(c) \,\}\] Appendix/OneManifoldIsFrom.boundary_inter_component.

6. Pairing and parity

Each \(p \in B\) thus has a partner \(q = A^{-1}(c) \in B\), distinct from \(p\) as \(A(q) = c > 0 = A(p)\), with \(B \cap \operatorname{comp}(p) = \{p, q\}\) Appendix/OneManifoldexists_partner. Choosing a partner \(\iota(p)\) for each \(p\) gives an involution: \(\iota(p)\) lies in the component of \(p\), so \(\iota(\iota(p)) \in \{p, \iota(p)\}\), and it is not \(\iota(p)\). The count is a line of algebra Appendix/OneManifoldeven_ncard_of_involution: over a finite set with a fixed-point-free involution, \(\prod(-1) = 1\) because the factors cancel in pairs, so \((-1)^{\#B} = 1\) and \(\#B\) is even. With step 1 this is V.A Appendix/OneManifoldeven_ncard_boundary.

V.A′ The count for the manifolds with boundary of Lemma 4

Theorem (V.A′). Let \(M\) be a Hausdorff smooth manifold modelled, through a model with corners, on a real normed space \(E\) (finite dimension and empty boundary are not required), and let \(Z\) be a real normed space with at most one point, that is, \(Z = 0\). Let \(B \subseteq X \subseteq M\), and suppose that \(X\) is a half-slice submanifold of \(M\) with boundary \(B\) over \(Z\): every point of \(X\) lies in the domain of a half-slice chart, a diffeomorphism \(\Phi\) from an open subset of \(M\) onto an open subset of \(\mathbb R \times Z\) such that, for \(q\) in its domain, \(q \in X \iff \Phi(q)_1 \ge 0\) and \(q \in B \iff \Phi(q)_1 = 0\) (the chart also carries a base point of \(X\) in its domain). If \(X\) is compact, then \(B\) is finite and has an even number of points. Appendix/HalfSpaceIsHalfSliceSubmanifold.even_ncard_boundary

Half-slice charts and the half-space model \(\{(t,z) \in \mathbb R \times Z : t \ge 0\}\) are those of V2.4 Chapter2/BoundaryHalfSliceChart Chapter2/BoundaryIsHalfSliceSubmanifold. The atlas of \(X\) consists of the restrictions to \(X\) of all half-slice charts, with a chosen one at each point Chapter2/BoundarytoChart Chapter2/BoundarychartedSpace. For this structure the boundary of \(X\) in Mathlib’s sense consists exactly of the points of \(X\) that lie in \(B\), which under the hypothesis \(B \subseteq X\) is all of \(B\) Chapter2/Boundaryboundary_eq: V.A′ counts the genuine boundary.

The idea. For \(Z = 0\) the half-space is a half-line, the boundary hypothesis of V.A is built into the definition of a half-slice chart, and V.A applies to \(X\) itself.

The proof as formalized. For \(Z = 0\), \((t,z) \mapsto t\) is a homeomorphism of the half-space onto \([0,\infty)\), with inverse \(t \mapsto (t,0)\) Appendix/HalfSpacehalfSpaceHomeomorph. Each chart of \(X\) is induced by a half-slice chart \(\Phi\), its coordinate at \(q\) is the first component of \(\Phi(q)\), and by definition this vanishes exactly on \(B\); so \(X\) is boundary compatible for \(\{q \in X : q \in B\}\), for every chart of the atlas Appendix/HalfSpaceIsHalfSliceSubmanifold.boundaryCompatible. Finally \(X\) is a compact space, Hausdorff as a subspace of \(M\); V.A applies, and the inclusion \(X \to M\), injective and carrying \(\{q \in X : q \in B\}\) onto \(B\) because \(B \subseteq X\), transports finiteness and the count Appendix/HalfSpaceIsHalfSliceSubmanifold.even_ncard_boundary. Only the continuity of \(\Phi\) and \(\Phi^{-1}\) is used. A lemma that a zero-dimensional space has at most one point is included Appendix/HalfSpacesubsingleton_of_finrank_eq_zero, though the applications take \(Z\) to be a zero subspace and check this directly.

From Lemma 4 to V.A′. Lemma 4 (V2.6) makes these manifolds Chapter2/WithBoundaryisHalfSliceSubmanifold_levelSet. For \(f : M \to N\) smooth between boundaryless manifolds modelled on finite-dimensional spaces, \(y\) a regular value, and \(g : M \to \mathbb R\) smooth such that at each point of \(f^{-1}(y) \cap g^{-1}(0)\) some tangent vector is killed by \(df\) but not by \(dg\), it makes \(\{g \ge 0\}\) a half-slice submanifold of the level set \(f^{-1}(y)\) with boundary \(\{g = 0\}\), over a space \(Z'\) of dimension \(\dim M - \dim N - 1\). When \(\dim M = \dim N + 1\), \(Z' = 0\): the ambient manifold of V.A′ is the level set, a 1-manifold, and \(X = f^{-1}(y) \cap \{g \ge 0\}\). The two applications of V.A′ supply Hausdorffness from the ambient space and compactness by exhibiting \(X\) as closed in a compact set.

  • Brouwer (V2.10). With \(g(x) = 1 - \|x\|^2\) and \(f\) the retraction onto the sphere, extended by a cutoff, \(X\) is compact inside the unit ball, and V.A′ makes \(\#B\) even although \(B = \{y\}\) Chapter2/Brouwerexists_fixedPoint_of_contDiff.
  • The homotopy lemma, case 1 (V4.3). Lemma 4 with the two functions \(t\) and \(1 - t\) (V4.1) Chapter4/CylinderisHalfSliceSubmanifold_levelSet_two makes \(F^{-1}(y) \cap (M \times [0,1])\) a half-slice submanifold, compact because \(M\) is; V.A′ gives the parity of \(\#f^{-1}(y) + \#g^{-1}(y)\) Chapter4/Homotopyhomotopy_lemma_of_isRegularValue.
  • Lemma 1 of §5 (V5.3) needs the arcs themselves. Through the same identification it applies the closed-arc proposition of step 5 to \(f^{-1}(y) \cap \{g \ge 0\}\), whose compactness is a hypothesis there, pairs each boundary point with the far end of its arc, and shows that the two ends carry opposite signs Chapter5/LemmaOnelemmaOne_ambient'.

The classification: what it says, and why arc length

Theorem (V.J). Let \(M\) be a connected, Hausdorff, σ-compact, nonempty smooth one-manifold. Then \(M\) is diffeomorphic to exactly one of four models, and which one is settled by two questions. If \(M\) is compact, it is the circle when its boundary is empty (V.H) and \([0,1]\) when it is not (V.G). If \(M\) is not compact, it is \(\mathbb R\) when its boundary is empty and \([0,\infty)\) when it is not (V.I). Appendix/Smooth/Mainnonempty_diffeomorph_or Appendix/Smooth/Mainmodels_pairwise_not_diffeomorph

That is Milnor’s Appendix theorem, with the four models named instead of “some interval of real numbers” and with the mutual exclusions proved. This section says what the setting is, why the proof has to use arc length, and where the hypotheses go; the seven that follow set out its nine stages, V.B to V.J, in the order in which they are used rather than the order in which they were written.

The setting. \(M\) is charted, through a model with corners \(I\), on a real normed space \(E\) of dimension one, and “boundary” means Mathlib’s boundary of \(M\) relative to \(I\) — which V.C shows to be the set of points whose coordinate in any chart lies on the frontier of the model’s range, so that it is the boundary in the naive sense and needs no compatibility hypothesis of the kind V.A has to assume. The model itself is not assumed boundaryless: V.C sorts its range into three shapes, the line, a closed half-line and a nondegenerate compact interval, and all three stay alive to the end, the third making \(M\) a one-manifold with corners. Smooth means \(C^\infty\) except where \(C^1\) is noted. Where the boundary is assumed empty, that is a statement about \(M\) and not about the model.

Why arc length, and not arbitrary charts. Milnor parametrizes by arc length and observes that the transition between two such parametrizations has derivative \(\pm 1\), hence is \(s \mapsto \pm s + k\). It is tempting to read this as a convenience, since a transition between one-dimensional charts is in any case a monotone diffeomorphism, and monotonicity is all that V.A needs. It is not a convenience, and V.F says exactly why. The engine of the whole proof is an extension step: an arc that does not yet fill its component is glued to a chart arc reaching past its end. With merely monotone transitions the glued arc contains a reparametrization of the old one, and the strongest conclusion one can state is an existential that forgets the witness’s coordinate — from the statement alone the transition from the old parameter to the new could be \(s \mapsto s^2\). With arc length the transition is \(s \mapsto s\), the sign and the constant both being pinned by the normalization, so the old parameter is the new parameter on the old domain. That is what makes a chain of extensions mean anything, and it is what fixes the period in the circle case. Milnor states his lemma for arc-length parametrizations because it has to be stated for them.

What arc length presupposes. A Riemannian metric. Milnor’s manifolds sit in \(\mathbb R^k\) and he restricts the Euclidean metric without comment. In dimension one a Riemannian metric is a length element: a positive smooth density transforming by the absolute value of the derivative of a transition. It is the one piece of general theory the classification needs and Mathlib does not have, so it is built here (V.E), and it is the single place where σ-compactness enters the whole nine stages. There the hypothesis is not a technicality but a necessity: a manifold carrying a Riemannian metric is metrizable, the long line carries none, and the long line is a connected smooth one-manifold which is neither the circle nor an interval. Everything after the length element — the arcs, the curves, the propagation lemma, all four cases — uses only Hausdorffness, connectedness, and whether or not \(M\) is compact.

The shape of the proof. Milnor’s Lemma 1 and its two-component picture come first (V.B, V.F), then unit-speed arcs (V.C to V.E), then the four cases in two pairs. With a boundary point there is an honest exhaustion, because an arc issuing from a boundary point has a half-open interval and can therefore be extended: finitely many chart arcs cover a compact manifold, each gluing swallows one more, and the arc that results is the diffeomorphism (V.G). Without a boundary point there is no such exhaustion, because every arc then has an open interval and the extension theorem needs a half-open one; so injectivity is dropped, arcs are replaced by curves — maps of the line agreeing near each time with an arc-length parametrization — a propagation lemma makes them unique, and compactness makes them close up into Milnor’s periodic parametrization (V.H). The two non-compact cases run the same curve machinery without the closing up (V.I). The assembly (V.J) needs two invariants to tell the four models apart: compactness, and the number of boundary points.

V.B and V.C Lemma 1’s topological half, and the one-dimensional model

Lemma (V.B). Let \(A\) and \(A'\) be arcs of a Hausdorff \((M, B)\) in the sense of V.A, and let \(S = A(U_A \cap U_{A'})\) be the overlap read in \(A\)’s coordinate, whose components are its hulls. Call a hull inner when both of its ends are interior to \(T_A\). Then an inner hull is carried by the transition onto the whole of \(T_{A'}\) and is the only hull, so that \(S\) is a single interval; every hull that is not inner reaches an end of \(T_A\); hence \(S\) has at most two components; and two distinct components reach opposite ends of \(T_A\). Appendix/TwoComponentsIsInnerHull Appendix/TwoComponentsimage_trans_hull_eq_of_isInnerHull Appendix/TwoComponentsordConnected_overlap_of_isInnerHull Appendix/TwoComponentsencard_hulls_le_two Appendix/TwoComponentssInf_eq_and_sSup_eq_of_hull_ne

This is Milnor’s Appendix Lemma 1 with its affine clause removed, and it is his picture: the graph of the transition lies in the rectangle \(T_A \times T_{A'}\) in at most two segments, neither of which can end inside it, and when there are two they end on opposite edges of \(T_A\) — which is the circle case, the one V.A excludes by fiat by always starting an arc at a boundary point. Here it is counted rather than excluded.

The idea the earlier file lacked is to single out the inner hull. Both of its ends are free, so by the end lemma of V.A the transition runs off both ends of \(T_{A'}\) at once; being monotone, its image is all of \(T_{A'}\); and injectivity then leaves no room for a second hull Appendix/TwoComponentshull_eq_of_isInnerHull. The two clash lemmas of V.A are therefore not needed here at all, and V.A’s normalization turns out to have been doing nothing essential Appendix/TwoComponentssInf_eq_or_sSup_eq_of_not_isInnerHull. Two byproducts: an inner hull occurs exactly when \(A'\) sits inside \(A\) Appendix/TwoComponentssource_subset_of_isInnerHull, and an inner hull forces \(A'\) to contain no boundary point at all Appendix/TwoComponentsnot_isInnerHull_of_mem_boundary — which is why V.A, extending only arcs from boundary points, never met one. Hypotheses: \(M\) Hausdorff, where V.A’s end lemma already needs it, and the two arcs’ own data. No charts, no smoothness, no compactness, no dimension.

The one-dimensional model (V.C). A closed convex subset of the line with nonempty interior is the line, a closed half-line, or a nondegenerate compact interval Appendix/Smooth/Setupclosed_convex_cases, so the model range, read through a linear identification of \(E\) with \(\mathbb R\) normalized once and for all Appendix/Smooth/SetupmodelCoord, is \(\mathbb R\), a half-line \([a,\infty)\), or a nondegenerate \([a,b]\) — never \((-\infty, a]\) Appendix/Smooth/SetupmodelRange_cases. Every chart then carries a real coordinate, whose image is an open set cut by the model range Appendix/Smooth/SetupchartCoord; derivatives along the model range are unique, so the derivative within it is unambiguous even at an endpoint Appendix/Smooth/SetupuniqueDiffOn_modelRange; and the boundary is chart-independent, a point in the source of any chart being a boundary point exactly when its real coordinate lies on the frontier of the model range, by Mathlib’s \(C^1\) theorem Appendix/Smooth/Setupmem_boundary_iff_chartCoord_mem_frontier. What this does to V.A: the boundary compatibility that the topological theorem has to assume is a theorem for a \(C^1\) one-manifold with a half-line model, with no side condition at all Appendix/Smooth/SetupboundaryCompatible, so the count of the first half applies to smooth one-manifolds unconditionally. Two normalized local models close the stage: every boundary point has a chart-derived coordinate onto \([0,\varepsilon)\), every interior point one onto \((-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)\) Appendix/Smooth/Setupexists_boundaryModel Appendix/Smooth/Setupexists_interiorModel.

Three things that looked dangerous were handled rather than avoided. The compact-interval case stays live, and no statement of this half excludes it; charts at interior points are shrunk away from the model’s own endpoints before \(\varepsilon\) is chosen; and the sign of the identification with \(\mathbb R\) is normalized twice, globally and again at an endpoint, the local sign mattering because it is what keeps the far endpoint out of a normalized chart. \(C^1\) suffices throughout, and neither Hausdorffness nor compactness nor boundarylessness occurs.

V.D and V.E Smooth arcs, the length element, and unit speed

Smooth arcs (V.D). A smooth arc is an arc of V.A whose coordinate is smooth as a map of manifolds into \(\mathbb R\) and whose parametrization is smooth as a map of \(\mathbb R\) into \(M\), so that the whole apparatus of V.A is inherited Appendix/Smooth/SmoothArcSmoothArc. The interval of an arc is convex with nonempty interior, so derivatives within it are unambiguous at its endpoints Appendix/Smooth/SmoothArcuniqueDiffOn_target; the transition between two smooth arcs is smooth on the relatively open piece of the interval where it is defined, which is V.A’s overlap Appendix/Smooth/SmoothArcSmoothArc.contDiffOn_trans Appendix/Smooth/SmoothArctransSource; the two transition derivatives multiply to \(1\), so neither vanishes Appendix/Smooth/SmoothArcSmoothArc.derivWithin_trans_mul_derivWithin_trans Appendix/Smooth/SmoothArcSmoothArc.derivWithin_trans_ne_zero — this is where Milnor’s “the derivative is \(\pm 1\)” first appears, in a form that does not yet presuppose arc length; a smooth arc is an immersion, endpoints included Appendix/Smooth/SmoothArcSmoothArc.derivWithin_ne_zero; and every point lies on a smooth arc, with interval \([0,\varepsilon)\) at a boundary point and \((-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)\) elsewhere Appendix/Smooth/SmoothArcexists_smoothArc_of_mem_boundary Appendix/Smooth/SmoothArcexists_smoothArc_of_notMem_boundary. The one-sided smoothness that looked like the technical heart of the stage cost nothing: smoothness on a set is already relative to that set, so at an endpoint it is the one-sided condition. The one real wrinkle was that a transition is defined only on a relatively open piece of the interval, so a derivative is computed there and then transported to the whole of it.

The length element (V.E). A density in dimension one, indexed not by charts but by local real parameters — a partial homeomorphism of an open subset of \(M\) onto a subset of \(\mathbb R\) with unique derivatives, smooth both ways Appendix/Smooth/LengthElementRealChart — of which both a chart read in V.C’s coordinate and a smooth arc are instances Appendix/Smooth/LengthElementSmoothArc.toRealChart, which is what lets a length element be evaluated along an arc with no intermediate layer. A length element assigns to each local parameter \(c\) a positive smooth \(\rho_c\) with \[\rho_c(u) = \rho_\kappa(\tau(u))\,|\tau'(u)|\] for the transition \(\tau\) from \(c\) to \(\kappa\) Appendix/Smooth/LengthElementLengthElement. Its engine is the transition-derivative calculus on possibly half-open sets: the chain rule at an endpoint, the cocycle rule, non-vanishing, and smoothness one degree down Appendix/Smooth/LengthElementtransDeriv Appendix/Smooth/LengthElementtransDeriv_comp Appendix/Smooth/LengthElementtransDeriv_ne_zero Appendix/Smooth/LengthElementcontDiffOn_transDeriv. Existence is a partition of unity, \(\rho_c(u) = \sum_i \lambda_i(c^{-1}u)\,|\tau'_{c \to \kappa_i}(u)|\) with \(\lambda\) subordinate to the chart sources and \(\kappa_i\) the real coordinate of the chart at \(i\) Appendix/Smooth/LengthElementnonempty_lengthElement, and it needs exactly four things: dimension one, smoothness of class \(C^\infty\) (partitions of unity are built from smooth bumps, and a transition derivative loses a degree, so a \(C^n\) manifold would give only a \(C^{n-1}\) element), \(M\) Hausdorff, and \(M\) σ-compact, these last two being the hypotheses of Mathlib’s subordinate partition of unity. Those two are used nowhere else in the whole classification, and all three shapes of V.C stay alive.

Unit-speed arcs, Milnor’s “by a straightforward change of variables”. Call an arc unit-speed when the length element read in its own parameter is identically \(1\) Appendix/Smooth/ArcLengthUnitSpeed. Then every point lies on a unit-speed arc sending it to \(0\), with interval \([0,\varepsilon)\) at a boundary point and \((-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)\) elsewhere Appendix/Smooth/ArcLengthexists_reparam Appendix/Smooth/ArcLengthexists_unitSpeed. The new parameter of the point at old parameter \(u\) is \(\sigma(u) = \int_0^u \rho\) Appendix/Smooth/ArcLengtharcLength Appendix/Smooth/ArcLengtharcParam, and all the work is at the endpoint of a half-open interval, where Mathlib’s two-sided inverse function rule says nothing at all. So the one-sided rule is proved rather than dodged: if \(g\) inverts \(f\) on a set, is continuous there, and \(f\) has nonzero derivative within its own set at \(g(v)\), then \(g\) has derivative \(1/f'\) within that set at \(v\), both derivatives allowed to be one-sided Appendix/Smooth/ArcLengthhasDerivWithinAt_of_leftInvOn; smoothness of the inverse then follows by bootstrapping on the order Appendix/Smooth/ArcLengthcontDiffOn_arcParamInv. Two devices made the endpoints painless: all the analysis happens on a compact interval inside the arc’s interval, where the fundamental theorem of calculus holds at the endpoints and compactness gives continuity of the inverse for nothing Appendix/Smooth/ArcLengthcontinuousOn_leftInvOn_of_isCompact; and the window is chosen in the new parameter, since arc length need not be symmetric about the base point.

V.F Milnor’s Appendix Lemma 1 in full, and the extension theorem

Lemma (V.F, Milnor’s Appendix Lemma 1, p. 54). Let \(A\) and \(A'\) be unit-speed smooth arcs for a common length element. Then on each component of the overlap the transition is \(s \mapsto \pm s + k\), with a sign and a constant belonging to that component; the overlap has at most two components; and if it has two they reach opposite ends of \(T_A\). Appendix/Smooth/Affinemilnor_appendix_lemma_one

The affine half is one line from the cocycle rule. In a unit-speed parameter the density is \(1\), so the rule reads \(1 = 1 \cdot |\tau'(u)|\) and \(|\tau'| = 1\) at every parameter of the overlap, endpoints of a half-open interval included Appendix/Smooth/Affineabs_transDeriv_eq_one. Being continuous and omitting \(0\), \(\tau'\) is constantly \(+1\) or constantly \(-1\) on each component Appendix/Smooth/Affineexists_sign_transDeriv — if it took both values the intermediate value theorem would produce a parameter at which it vanished — and a function with constant derivative within an order-connected set is affine there Appendix/Smooth/Affineexists_affine_trans. The other two clauses are V.B, which uses no smoothness whatever. Unit speed survives reversal of the parameter, the transition being \(s \mapsto -s\) Appendix/Smooth/AffineUnitSpeed.neg, and that is what lets the extension theorem drop a normalization by negating a coordinate.

Theorem (the extension theorem, V.F). Let \(A\) be a unit-speed arc from a boundary point \(p\) with \(A(p) = 0\) and interval \([0,c)\), let \(A'\) be any unit-speed arc, and let \(x \in U_{A'} \setminus U_A\) lie in the closure of \(U_A\). Then there is a unit-speed smooth arc \(\tilde A\) from \(p\) whose domain is the union \(U_A \cup U_{A'}\) and whose coordinate equals \(A\) at every point of \(U_A\). Appendix/Smooth/Affineexists_extension_unitSpeed Appendix/Smooth/Affineexists_extension_aux_unitSpeed

Where the expected route was wrong, and it governs everything after. V.A’s topological extension theorem cannot be reused with smoothness added. Its conclusion is an existential that forgets the witness’s coordinate, and from the statement alone one recovers only that the transition from old to new is an increasing homeomorphism fixing \(0\); it could be \(s \mapsto s^2\). So the theorem is restated for smooth arcs, reusing the apparatus beneath it verbatim and transcribing the parts of its proof that carry over. About 75 lines of the original then disappear: both one-sided limit computations at the junction, and the trichotomy proofs of continuity there. They disappear because with unit-speed arcs the two branches are the same affine function on the whole overlap and not merely near the seam, so there is no junction to be continuous at. The strong form is not a bonus but forced: the transition being \(s \mapsto \pm s + k\), and the normalization pinning down both the sign and the constant, the old parameter is the new parameter on the old domain. This is the sharp reason Milnor states his lemma for arc-length parametrizations and not for arbitrary charts.

Hypotheses. The affine half needs a length element and unit speed and nothing else: no dimension, no Hausdorffness, no compactness, no boundarylessness. Lemma 1 and the extension theorem add Hausdorffness, because V.B and V.A’s overlap apparatus are stated for Hausdorff spaces, and the extension theorem inherits V.A’s normalization, that the first arc starts at a boundary point with coordinate \(0\).

V.G Milnor’s first case: a compact one-manifold with boundary is \([0,1]\)

Theorem (V.G). Let \(M\) be a compact Hausdorff smooth one-manifold with a boundary point \(p\). Then there are a unit-speed smooth arc \(A\) and a length \(\ell > 0\) with \(A(p) = 0\), interval exactly \([0,\ell]\) and domain exactly the connected component of \(p\), and the boundary inside that component is \(\{p, A^{-1}(\ell)\}\) Appendix/Smooth/Compactexists_unitSpeedArc_component. If \(M\) is moreover connected, the domain is all of \(M\) Appendix/Smooth/Compactexists_unitSpeedArc_of_preconnected, the arc rescaled by \(1/\ell\) is a diffeomorphism \(M \to [0,1]\) Appendix/Smooth/CompactSmoothArc.diffeomorphIcc Appendix/Smooth/Compactnonempty_diffeomorphIcc, and the boundary of \(M\) is exactly the two points \(p\) and \(A^{-1}(\ell)\) Appendix/Smooth/Compactboundary_eq_pair Appendix/Smooth/Compactncard_boundary_eq_two.

The last clause is Milnor’s own corollary, and where V.A counts the boundary points modulo two it identifies them.

The proof is Milnor’s Step 2, run with unit-speed arcs Appendix/Smooth/Compactexists_closed_unitSpeedArc. Cover \(M\) by the domains of unit-speed arcs, one arc per point by V.E, and take a finite subcover. Start from a unit-speed arc at \(p\) with interval \([0,\varepsilon)\), and induct on the number of members of the subcover not yet swallowed. If the interval attains its supremum we are done. Otherwise it is \([0,c)\), and the domain is not yet the whole component of \(p\): the component is closed, hence compact, so if the domain were all of it then the interval, being its continuous image, would be compact and would contain \(c\). Being an open proper subset of that component and containing \(p\), the domain then has a point of its closure outside itself; the subcover arc containing that point extends the arc by V.F, and it does so swallowing at least one more member, since its own domain was not contained in the old one and is contained in the new. When the interval closes up to \([0,\ell]\) the domain is compact, hence closed, hence — being also open, connected and nonempty — the whole component; and the boundary condition of an arc then names its two ends. The diffeomorphism is the arc itself, rescaled by \(1/\ell\) Appendix/Smooth/CompactSmoothArc.equivIcc.

Three things worth recording. Compactness is used three times, and σ-compactness would not do for two of them: to extract a finite subcover, which is what makes the induction terminate, and to know that the component of \(p\) is compact, which is what forbids a proper open subarc from exhausting it. Only the third use, feeding the length element of V.E, is σ-compactness in disguise, which is why the compact cases need no countability hypothesis of their own. Connectedness is needed nowhere in the exhaustion: the honest conclusion is about the component of \(p\), which is the form V.J wants and which makes the disconnected case there cheap. And the conversion of the rescaled arc into a diffeomorphism, through Mathlib’s two bridges for \([0,1]\), cost about twenty lines — the cheapest part of the stage rather than the dearest.

Deviation. V.A’s finite-cover induction is restated rather than reused, for three independent reasons. Its conclusion is a topological arc, and the induction feeds its own output back in, so the object it carries must be the object the next step consumes. Its extension step is V.A’s, which does not record that the coordinate is preserved, so V.F’s is the theorem the loop calls. And its hypothesis of boundary compatibility demands a homeomorphism of the model space with a half-line, which does not exist when the model range is a compact interval — a shape V.C deliberately admits. Nothing in V.A’s file is edited.

V.H Milnor’s second case: a compact boundaryless one-manifold is the circle

Theorem (V.H). Let \(M\) be a nonempty compact Hausdorff connected smooth one-manifold with empty boundary. Then there are a length element, a period \(T > 0\) and a map \(\gamma : \mathbb R \to M\) which is an arc-length parametrization near every time, is \(T\)-periodic and onto, is injective on \([0,T)\), has \(T\) as its least period, and satisfies \(\gamma(s) = \gamma(t)\) exactly when \(s - t\) is an integer multiple of \(T\) Appendix/Smooth/Circleexists_periodic_parametrisation. In words, such an \(M\) is a closed geodesic of length \(T\), which is Milnor’s Step 5. And \(M\) is diffeomorphic to the circle Appendix/Smooth/Circlenonempty_diffeomorphCircle.

Where the whole programme had to be corrected. The exhaustion of V.G does not exist here. Every arc of a manifold with empty boundary has an open interval Appendix/Smooth/CircleArc.isOpen_target_of_boundary_eq_empty Appendix/Smooth/CircleSmoothArc.isOpen_target, whereas V.F’s extension theorem needs the first arc’s interval to be half-open, that is, to start at a boundary point. So V.G’s induction has no boundaryless analogue in the shape one expects, and the obstruction is not technical: there is nothing to start the induction with.

The replacement is to drop injectivity. A unit-speed curve on a set \(U\) of times is a map \(\gamma : \mathbb R \to M\) which near every time of \(U\) agrees with the arc-length parametrization \(s \mapsto A^{-1}(s - k)\) of a unit-speed arc Appendix/Smooth/CircleIsUnitSpeedCurveOn. Unlike an arc it is not injective — which is the whole point, since the curve that wraps round a circle is not — and unlike an arc it is a genuine function on the line, so two of them can be compared time by time. Every unit-speed arc of a boundaryless manifold is one Appendix/Smooth/CircleisUnitSpeedCurveOn_arc.

The propagation lemma. Two unit-speed curves on the same interval of times which agree near one time agree at every time. Appendix/Smooth/CircleeqOn_of_eventuallyEq

This is the engine of the stage, and it replaces the uniqueness theorem for integral curves, which Mathlib proves only for manifolds without boundary and only for genuine flows. Its proof is a connectedness argument run in the parameter of one arc rather than in the time, and the reason is exactly the two-component picture of V.B: the set of times at which the two curves agree on a neighbourhood is open but not obviously closed, because an overlap can have two components. Pushed into a single component — a hull — the transition is affine by V.F and is pinned down by two coincidences Appendix/Smooth/Circletrans_eq_add_of_two_points, so in the arc’s parameter the set of agreement is closed, and the set of parameters having a whole neighbourhood of agreement is closed there too; being open, nonempty and closed in an interval, it is everything. Hausdorffness enters here, for uniqueness of limits, and nothing else does: no compactness, no dimension, no boundarylessness, no connectedness of \(M\). With curves, continuation needs no gluing of injective arcs and no two-component bookkeeping at all.

The maximal curve. Say that \(x\) is reached at time \(t\) from a fixed unit-speed arc \(A_0\) when some unit-speed curve that agrees with \(A_0\) near time \(0\) sends \(t\) to \(x\) Appendix/Smooth/CircleReach. Propagation makes that single-valued Appendix/Smooth/CircleReach.unique Appendix/Smooth/Circlesubset_dom_and_eqOn, so a function can be extracted from it: the set \(\mathrm{Dom}\) of reached times Appendix/Smooth/CircleDom and the curve on it Appendix/Smooth/CircleglobalCurve Appendix/Smooth/CircleisUnitSpeedCurveOn_globalCurve. That set is an open interval containing \(0\) Appendix/Smooth/CircleisOpen_dom Appendix/Smooth/CircleordConnected_dom Appendix/Smooth/Circlezero_mem_dom, and none of this uses compactness. Compactness is what makes it the whole line: as the time approaches an end of the interval the curve accumulates somewhere, a unit-speed arc about the accumulation point receives it, and a five-line gluing continues it past the end Appendix/Smooth/Circlenot_bddAbove_dom Appendix/Smooth/Circledom_eq_univ.

The period, and Milnor’s matching directions. Compactness again: as the time tends to \(+\infty\) the curve accumulates at some \(q\), and the propagation lemma — not a germ argument — shows that it passes exactly through \(q\), at two distinct times, the two visits being far enough apart in the accumulation for the times they produce to differ Appendix/Smooth/Circleexists_cluster Appendix/Smooth/CircleIsUnitSpeedCurveOn.exists_shift. Two times with the same value then give a period Appendix/Smooth/Circleexists_period, and that step is the geometric heart: it is the one part of Milnor’s Step 5 with no counterpart in V.A’s file Appendix/Smooth/Circleperiodic_of_eq. Read in a unit-speed arc \(B\) centred at the common value, the curve has slope \(\sigma_1 = \pm 1\) near \(t_1\) and \(\sigma_2 = \pm 1\) near \(t_2\) Appendix/Smooth/Circleexists_unitSpeed_centred Appendix/Smooth/CircleIsUnitSpeedCurveOn.exists_sign. If the two signs agree then \(\gamma\) and \(\gamma(\cdot + (t_2 - t_1))\) agree near \(t_1\), hence everywhere by propagation, and \(t_2 - t_1\) is a period. If they disagree the curve would have to reflect: \(\gamma\) and \(\gamma(t_1 + t_2 - \cdot)\) would agree near \(t_1\), hence everywhere, so that \(\gamma(m + w) = \gamma(m - w)\) about the midpoint \(m\) — which contradicts the injectivity of a unit-speed curve near a time Appendix/Smooth/CircleIsUnitSpeedCurveOn.exists_injOn. So the two directions must match, and that is Milnor’s observation, proved by excluding the reflection.

The minimal period. The set of periods is a subgroup of the line, closed because the curve is continuous, and discrete, because a unit-speed curve is injective near every time and so no period can be smaller than the radius of an interval of injectivity. The positive periods are therefore the elements of a closed set bounded below, whose infimum belongs to it, and every period is an integer multiple of that least one Appendix/Smooth/Circleexists_minimal_period. Surjectivity finishes the geometry: the image of the curve is the image of \([0,T]\), hence compact, hence closed, and it is open because the curve is locally a parametrization, so it is a nonempty clopen subset of a preconnected \(M\) Appendix/Smooth/CircleIsUnitSpeedCurveOn.isOpen_range Appendix/Smooth/Circlesurjective_of_periodic.

The descent, and why it cannot go through a quotient. Mathlib has no quotient-manifold theory, so \(\mathbb R / T\mathbb Z\) is not available as a smooth manifold and the descent goes through local inverses of the exponential. The map \(t \mapsto \exp(2\pi i t/T)\) is smooth, is onto by an explicit section built from the principal argument, and identifies exactly the times differing by a multiple of \(T\) Appendix/Smooth/CirclecircleParam Appendix/Smooth/CirclecontMDiff_circleParam Appendix/Smooth/CirclecircleSection Appendix/Smooth/CirclecircleParam_eq_iff; and it is a local diffeomorphism, obtained without computing a chart of the circle — the two coordinate functions \(z \mapsto \operatorname{re} z\) and \(z \mapsto \operatorname{im} z\) pull back to \(\cos\) and \(\sin\), whose derivatives cannot both vanish, and rescaling whichever does not gives a smooth left inverse of the derivative Appendix/Smooth/CircleisLocalDiffeomorph_circleParam. Since \(\gamma\) and the exponential identify the same pairs of times, the descended map is a bijection, and it is a local diffeomorphism because near each point it agrees with \(\gamma\) composed with a local inverse of the exponential Appendix/Smooth/CircleIsUnitSpeedCurveOn.isLocalDiffeomorphAt. One friction is worth recording: Mathlib’s tangent spaces carry no norm, so “a nonzero linear map between one-dimensional spaces is invertible” had to be stated for topological modules with the inverse supplied as data, which that left inverse provides Appendix/Smooth/CircleisInvertible_of_finrank_one.

Hypotheses. Hausdorff three times: the length element, V.F’s apparatus, and — essentially — the propagation lemma. Compact twice, and σ-compactness would not do for either: to make the curve accumulate as its time approaches the end of its interval, which is what lets it be continued, and to make it accumulate at \(+\infty\), which is what forces it to return. Preconnected only for surjectivity, and nonempty only to choose a base point. No second countability, no orientability. And V.B turns out not to be used here: what this stage needs from V.A’s file is the relative openness of hulls and V.F’s affine half, not the counting of components. V.B remains the right statement of Milnor’s lemma; the expectation that V.H would depend on it was wrong.

V.I Milnor’s third and fourth cases: \([0,\infty)\) and \(\mathbb R\)

Theorem (V.I). Let \(M\) be a connected Hausdorff σ-compact smooth one-manifold which is not compact. If its boundary is empty, \(M\) is diffeomorphic to \(\mathbb R\) Appendix/Smooth/NonCompactnonempty_diffeomorphReal. If it has a boundary point \(p\), then \(M\) is diffeomorphic to \([0,\infty)\) and \(p\) is its only boundary point Appendix/Smooth/NonCompactnonempty_diffeomorphIci Appendix/Smooth/NonCompactboundary_eq_singleton.

One fact organises the whole stage: no value of a unit-speed curve is a boundary point Appendix/Smooth/NonCompactIsUnitSpeedCurveOn.notMem_boundary. It is why the boundary point has to be adjoined by hand, why the curve stops exactly at it, and why a repeated value is impossible.

The boundaryless case. Start from a unit-speed arc centred at an arbitrary point and take the maximal curve of V.H, whose construction uses no compactness at all. Its image is open, because the curve is locally a parametrization Appendix/Smooth/NonCompactIsUnitSpeedCurveOn.isOpen_image, and closed, because every point of the closure which is not a boundary point already lies in it — and here emptiness of the boundary makes every such point eligible Appendix/Smooth/NonCompactmem_image_dom_of_mem_closure. Being a nonempty clopen subset of a preconnected space it is everything. Injectivity is where non-compactness enters, and it enters only there: a repeated value makes the curve satisfy a shift identity Appendix/Smooth/NonCompacteqOn_add_of_eq, and then the image of one compact interval of times is both compact and open, hence all of \(M\), hence \(M\) compact Appendix/Smooth/NonCompactisCompact_isOpen_image_Icc_of_eq. What comes out is a parametrization of \(M\) by an open interval of times Appendix/Smooth/NonCompactexists_parametrisation_of_boundary_eq_empty — the honest form, since without compactness the interval need not be the whole line, as \((0,1)\) shows — and every nonempty open interval of the line is diffeomorphic to the line Appendix/Smooth/NonCompactexists_param_of_isOpen_ordConnected.

The case with a boundary point. The arc issuing from \(p\) has interval \([0,\varepsilon_0)\), so it is not a legitimate starting arc for a curve. Restricting it to \((0,\varepsilon_0)\) and recentring gives one that is Appendix/Smooth/NonCompactSmoothArc.shrink Appendix/Smooth/NonCompactSmoothArc.unitSpeed_shrink, and the maximal curve from it has \(-\varepsilon_0/2\) as the unattained left end of its interval of times, because it tends to \(p\) there Appendix/Smooth/NonCompacttendsto_left_halfline and cannot take that value Appendix/Smooth/NonCompactleft_notMem_dom. Shift the time and adjoin the single time \(0\) with value \(p\): the result is a ray, a parametrization of \(M\) by \([0,\infty)\) or by some \([0,b)\) Appendix/Smooth/NonCompactshape_of_halfline Appendix/Smooth/NonCompactexists_ray_of_mem_boundary, and each of those is diffeomorphic to \([0,\infty)\) Appendix/Smooth/NonCompactexists_param_halfline. Injectivity needs no compactness here: a repeated value would make the image everything, and the image cannot contain \(p\) Appendix/Smooth/NonCompactinjOn_dom_halfline. Surjectivity is the long step, and it is the only place non-compactness is used in this case. A second boundary point in the closure has to be excluded, and reading the curve in an arc issuing from such a point shows that the curve arrives exactly there at an end of its interval of times; if that is the far end then \(M\) is covered by three compact pieces and so is compact, which is V.G Appendix/Smooth/NonCompactinsert_image_dom_eq_univ.

No inverse function theorem is used anywhere in this stage, and in particular none at a boundary endpoint, where there would be none to use. The four shapes of open interval and the two of half-line are reparametrized by explicit elementary formulas — built from the exponential, the logistic curve and a Möbius map — with their logarithmic or rational inverses written down beside them, so both halves of every diffeomorphism are exhibited Appendix/Smooth/NonCompactexists_param_of_isOpen_ordConnected Appendix/Smooth/NonCompactexists_param_halfline. The inverse coordinate of the curve itself, the map \(M \to \mathbb R\) that reads off a point’s time, is likewise assembled from the local parametrizations rather than obtained by inverting anything Appendix/Smooth/NonCompactexists_inverse_coord Appendix/Smooth/NonCompactexists_inverse_coord'.

What had to be built. \([0,\infty)\) as a manifold with boundary. Mathlib has \([a,b]\) only, and there through two charts; here a single chart is a homeomorphism onto the whole model half-space Appendix/Smooth/NonCompacticiHomeomorph Appendix/Smooth/NonCompactinstIciChartedSpace Appendix/Smooth/NonCompactinstIciIsManifold, with the two bridges — inclusion into \(\mathbb R\), projection from it — that make a map into or out of it smooth exactly when its real expression is Appendix/Smooth/NonCompactcontMDiff_subtypeVal_Ici Appendix/Smooth/NonCompactcontMDiffOn_iciProj.

Where σ-compactness is. It is used once and only once, to build the length element of V.E. Everything after that — the arcs, the curves, the propagation lemma, the maximality of the interval of reached times, the continuation step and both classifications — uses only Hausdorffness, connectedness and the failure of compactness. And that one use is exactly where the hypothesis is necessary; see the end of V.J. Milnor gets it free by sitting in Euclidean space, and uses it silently, the metric he restricts to \(M\) being a Riemannian metric.

Two corrections to the expected route, both instructive. A repeated value gives a period only once the curve is known to run on the whole line, which here it need not, so injectivity is proved instead from the compact-and-open image above. And a unit-speed curve cannot take a boundary value at all, so it cannot run on a closed half-line of times; the boundary point has to be adjoined by hand, and showing that no second boundary point appears in the closure is the long step rather than a formality.

V.J The theorem, its six exclusions, and the count again

The four cases are assembled by splitting on compactness and on emptiness of the boundary Appendix/Smooth/Mainnonempty_diffeomorph_cases Appendix/Smooth/Mainnonempty_diffeomorph_or, each model carrying its own model with corners. Nothing is assumed about the boundary, about orientability or about second countability, and no compatibility hypothesis is assumed anywhere, V.C having proved chart-independence of the boundary.

Exclusivity is a statement about the four models alone, and all six exclusions are proved Appendix/Smooth/Mainmodels_pairwise_not_diffeomorph. Two invariants suffice. Compactness separates the circle and \([0,1]\) from \([0,\infty)\) and \(\mathbb R\), which settles four of the six, a diffeomorphism being in particular a homeomorphism Appendix/Smooth/MaincompactSpace_of_diffeomorph Appendix/Smooth/Mainnot_compactSpace_Ici. The number of boundary points settles the remaining one in each compactness class: a diffeomorphism carries boundary onto boundary — a theorem of Mathlib, here wanted for two different models with corners at once — so that number is a diffeomorphism invariant Appendix/Smooth/Mainncard_boundary_eq_of_diffeomorph, and its values on the four models are \(0\), \(2\), \(1\) and \(0\) Appendix/Smooth/Mainncard_boundary_Icc Appendix/Smooth/Mainncard_boundary_Ici Appendix/Smooth/MainisEmpty_diffeomorph_Icc_Ici.

The slice form, and Milnor’s corollary a second time. In Chapter 2’s language, let \(X\) be a compact half-slice submanifold with boundary \(B\) of a Hausdorff ambient manifold, over a one-point \(Z\) — that is, a compact one-manifold with boundary in the sense of V.A′. Then every connected component of \(X\) is diffeomorphic to the circle or to \([0,1]\) Appendix/Smooth/MainIsHalfSliceSubmanifold.component_diffeomorph; the components carrying a boundary point are exactly those of the second kind Appendix/Smooth/MainIsHalfSliceSubmanifold.nonempty_diffeomorphIcc_component_iff Appendix/Smooth/MainIsHalfSliceSubmanifold.nonempty_diffeomorphCircle_component_iff; each of those meets \(B\) in exactly two points Appendix/Smooth/MainIsHalfSliceSubmanifold.ncard_boundary_inter_component; every boundary point has exactly one partner Appendix/Smooth/MainIsHalfSliceSubmanifold.exists_boundary_partner; and \(B\) is finite of even cardinality Appendix/Smooth/MainIsHalfSliceSubmanifold.even_ncard_boundary_of_classification. That last is V.A′ again, and the point of the stage is that it now follows from the classification, as in the book: the pairing is “the other end of my own component”, and it is realised by the two ends of a single arc-length parametrization rather than by an abstract parity argument Appendix/Smooth/Mainboundary_inter_component_eq_pair Appendix/Smooth/Maineven_ncard_boundary_of_compact. V.A′ is not cited and is left untouched; what is reused from V.A’s file is only the pure combinatorics, that a fixed-point-free involution of a finite set has even cardinality Appendix/OneManifoldeven_ncard_of_involution.

Three bridges had to be built, and the project will want all three. The connected components of a one-manifold are open Appendix/Smooth/MainisOpen_connectedComponent_of_oneManifold, hence are manifolds in their own right Appendix/Smooth/MaincomponentOpens Appendix/Smooth/Mainboundary_componentOpens, which is what lets a theorem needing connectedness be applied to a disconnected manifold; it needs nothing but dimension one and smoothness, since V.D gives every point a neighbourhood which is the domain of an arc, and the domain of an arc is preconnected. The boundary of the model half-line is a single point Appendix/Smooth/Mainboundary_Ici, which Mathlib could not supply, having no half-line manifold. And the boundary count for a possibly disconnected compact one-manifold, whose finiteness is the harder half and could not reuse V.A, because V.A wants a compatibility hypothesis available only when the model range is a half-line Appendix/Smooth/Mainfinite_boundary_of_compact.

σ-compactness is necessary, and the long line says why. The classification is false without a countability hypothesis. The long line — two copies of the closed long ray \(\omega_1 \times [0,1)\) with the lexicographic order topology, glued along their least elements — is a connected Hausdorff smooth one-manifold without boundary which is neither compact nor σ-compact, and it is not even homeomorphic, let alone diffeomorphic, to any of the four models, since it is not second countable and all four are. So the two non-compact cases must assume σ-compactness, and they do. In the compact cases nothing extra is needed: compact plus Hausdorff plus a finite-dimensional model gives second countability by Mathlib’s own theorem. And the failure is located exactly: it is the length element that does not exist, since a manifold carrying a Riemannian metric is metrizable, so the long line carries none, and Milnor’s arc-length reparametrization has nothing to start from. Milnor’s manifolds sit in \(\mathbb R^k\), hence are second countable, and he uses this silently.

Size. 9,276 lines for the nine stages: 463 for V.B, and 8,813 in the nine files of the smooth Appendix — 820 for V.C, 630 for V.D, 1,315 for V.E, 929 for V.F, 421 for V.G, 1,712 for V.H, 2,202 for V.I and 784 for V.J. With V.A and V.A′ the Appendix is 11,054 lines in twelve files. Those 9,276 lines are the largest single addition the project has had, exceeding the mod 2 remark of Part VII, which held the record before; and the two largest files are the two whose route had to be invented rather than transcribed, V.H and V.I. A design pass estimated the whole at about 4,000 lines in nine stages; the nine stage boundaries held, which no previous estimate in this project managed, and the lines came to more than twice the estimate.

What the formalization taught us

  • No smoothness, for the count. It holds for compact Hausdorff topological 1-manifolds; slopes \(\pm 1\) become strict monotonicity Appendix/OneManifoldstrictMonoOn_or_strictAntiOn_of_ordConnected, and in V.A′ the smooth structure is carried but unused Appendix/HalfSpaceIsHalfSliceSubmanifold.even_ncard_boundary. The classification, by contrast, cannot do without it: a topological one-manifold has no arc length.
  • The boundary is an input. That every chart sends exactly \(B\) to \(0\) is assumed, though the proof uses it only for the chosen charts Appendix/OneManifoldBoundaryCompatible; in Chapter 2 it holds by construction Appendix/HalfSpaceIsHalfSliceSubmanifold.boundaryCompatible. The topological fact that would make it automatic (a homeomorphism between open subsets of the half-line preserves the point \(0\)) is never proved; in the smooth setting the hypothesis is now discharged instead, by the chart-independence of the boundary for a \(C^1\) manifold Appendix/Smooth/SetupboundaryCompatible.
  • Hausdorff, twice: to identify two limits in the end lemma Appendix/OneManifoldend_lemma, and to know that the compact domain of a closed arc is closed Appendix/OneManifoldIsFrom.source_eq_of_mem. In the doubled-endpoint example both fail: the arc from \(0\) to one copy of \(1\) is compact but not closed, and its points converge to both copies.
  • Compactness, three times: for the finiteness of \(B\) Appendix/OneManifoldfinite_boundary, for the finite cover by chart arcs, and to see that an arc with interval \([0,c)\) cannot fill a component Appendix/OneManifoldexists_closed_arc.
  • No circle, no maximality, in the first half. Only arcs from boundary points are extended, so overlaps are intervals Appendix/OneManifoldoverlap_ordConnected, and a finite induction replaces the maximal parametrization Appendix/OneManifoldexists_closed_arc; the price is that the count, and not the classification, is what comes out. In the second half the circle case is counted instead of excluded Appendix/TwoComponentsencard_hulls_le_two, and the normalization that excluded it turns out to have been doing nothing essential.
  • A Riemannian metric is the only general theory the classification needs, and in dimension one it is a positive smooth density on local real parameters. Mathlib has no metric-existence theorem, so it was built; smooth bumps are why it is \(C^\infty\) and not merely \(C^1\) Appendix/Smooth/LengthElementnonempty_lengthElement.
  • Arc length is not a convenience. Monotone transitions suffice for the count, but an extension theorem stated with them forgets the witness’s coordinate, and then a chain of extensions says nothing. Unit speed makes the transition \(s \mapsto s\), so the extended arc genuinely extends the old one Appendix/Smooth/Affineexists_extension_unitSpeed. That is why Milnor’s lemma is about arc-length parametrizations and not about charts.
  • The exhaustion does not exist without boundary. Every arc of a boundaryless manifold has an open interval, and the extension theorem needs a half-open one Appendix/Smooth/CircleArc.isOpen_target_of_boundary_eq_empty. Dropping injectivity repairs it: unit-speed curves, made unique by a propagation lemma proved in the parameter of an arc rather than in the time, because the overlap can have two components Appendix/Smooth/CircleeqOn_of_eventuallyEq.
  • σ-compactness enters once, to build the length element, and there it is necessary: the long line carries no Riemannian metric, so arc length has nothing to start from, and the long line is a connected smooth one-manifold which is none of the four models Appendix/Smooth/NonCompactnonempty_diffeomorphReal.
  • Two invariants separate the four models, compactness and the number of boundary points, and the second needs a diffeomorphism to carry boundary onto boundary across two different models with corners Appendix/Smooth/Mainncard_boundary_eq_of_diffeomorph Appendix/Smooth/Mainmodels_pairwise_not_diffeomorph.
  • Components of a one-manifold are open, hence manifolds, which is the whole bridge from a theorem about connected manifolds to a statement about a disconnected one Appendix/Smooth/MainisOpen_connectedComponent_of_oneManifold.
  • The seam. Gluing arcs with a merely monotone transition is the longest proof of the first half; continuity at the seam comes down to two monotone limits Appendix/OneManifoldexists_extension_aux. With unit speed there is no seam, and those seventy-five lines simply vanish Appendix/Smooth/Affineexists_extension_aux_unitSpeed.
  • Parity by involution: the product of \(-1\) over \(B\), paired off by “the other end of my component” Appendix/OneManifoldexists_partner Appendix/OneManifoldeven_ncard_of_involution. Proved twice with the same combinatorics and two different pairings: an abstract one in V.A, and in V.J the two ends of one arc-length parametrization Appendix/Smooth/MainIsHalfSliceSubmanifold.exists_boundary_partner.
  • The arcs are reused. Chapter 5 needs the pairing by arcs, not only the parity Chapter5/LemmaOnelemmaOne_ambient'. And the classification is reused too, outside the book’s own dependencies: Part VII takes from it that a connected one-manifold is orientable Chapter7/OneManifoldOrientableisOrientable_of_finrank_eq_one.

MeasureTheory.Measure.IsAddHaarMeasureline 7660.2 Spaces, derivatives and smoothness
formal statement
class IsAddHaarMeasure {G : Type*} [AddGroup G] [TopologicalSpace G] [MeasurableSpace G]
    (μ : Measure G) : Prop
    extends IsFiniteMeasureOnCompacts μ, IsAddLeftInvariant μ, IsOpenPosMeasure μ

/-- A measure on a group is a Haar measure if it is left-invariant, and gives finite mass to
compact sets and positive mass to open sets.

Textbooks generally require an additional regularity assumption to ensure nice behavior on
arbitrary locally compact groups. Use `[IsHaarMeasure μ] [Regular μ]` or
`[IsHaarMeasure μ] [InnerRegular μ]` in these situations. Note that a Haar measure in our
sense is automatically regular and inner regular on second countable locally compact groups, as
checked just below this definition. -/
@[to_additive existing]
class IsHaarMeasure {G : Type*} [Group G] [TopologicalSpace G] [MeasurableSpace G]
    (μ : Measure G) : Prop
    extends IsFiniteMeasureOnCompacts μ, IsMulLeftInvariant μ, IsOpenPosMeasure μ

variable [Group G] [TopologicalSpace G] (μ : Measure G) [IsHaarMeasure μ]

@[to_additive (attr := simp)]
